title: CFPB Ordered to Stop All Work, Nearly Defunded — Federal Judge Called It 'Hanging by a Thread'
institution: Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB)
status: Ongoing litigation (as anticipated in this entry's prior update, Vought's acting-director authority under the FVRA expired August 1, 2026; CFPB Deputy Director Mark Paoletta became Acting Director that same day); permanent-director nominee Brian Johnson's Senate Banking Committee vote had not been scheduled as of the most recent reporting reviewed, and Vought is reported to be remaining at CFPB in a senior-adviser capacity pending Johnson's confirmation
date_of_action: 2025-02-10 (stop-work order issued) through 2025-12-30 (federal judge's 'hanging by a thread' ruling)
what_changed: On February 10, 2025, newly installed Acting Director Russell Vought (who simultaneously serves as OMB Director) ordered all CFPB staff and contractors to stop working entirely and not return to agency offices. DOGE personnel were given access to CFPB's HR, payroll, and enforcement-records systems around the same time; Elon Musk posted 'CFPB RIP' on social media. A federal judge issued a temporary restraining order on February 14, 2025 blocking further firings, data destruction, or funding cuts, but by then CFPB's website had already been taken down and staff locked out of buildings and systems. Vought separately moved to cut off the agency's Federal Reserve funding entirely and canceled roughly $100 million in CFPB contracts. Court filings from CFPB leadership itself, filed in March 2025, proposed shrinking authorized staff from 1,174 to 556, sparing only the legal division (which defends the agency in the litigation over its own dismantling) from cuts. In April 2025, despite the court order, about 1,400 employees who had chosen to remain received layoff notices -- a reduction that would have left only about 200 of the agency's original ~1,700 staff. By December 2025, more than 30% of CFPB's authorized staff had departed. On December 30, 2025, the same federal judge overseeing the case rejected the administration's argument that Vought could lawfully withhold the agency's funding, ordering him to request continued Federal Reserve funding, which he did -- keeping CFPB funded through at least March 2026. A February 2026 report from Sen. Elizabeth Warren's office estimated that changes imposed after Vought took control of CFPB had cost Americans at least $19 billion in lost financial relief -- $15 billion from two rescinded rules (an overdraft-fee cap projected to save $5 billion/year, and a credit-card late-fee cap projected to save roughly $10 billion) plus nearly $4 billion from dropped enforcement actions and unfulfilled consent orders. In May 2026, CFPB removed roughly 1,700 web pages of consumer advisories, press releases, and testimony predating February 2025 from its public website (The Guardian's later, more precise count -- comparing the current site against Internet Archive Wayback Machine snapshots and a mirror site maintained by a former CFPB employee -- found at least 2,200 pages deleted as of early June 2026; the two figures describe the same underlying deletion campaign rather than separate events, with the most common deleted-page topics being enforcement, mortgages, banking, and rulemaking; CFPB also deleted its blog entirely and removed all press releases predating February 2025). Also in May 2026, acting CFPB Director Russell Vought ordered all remaining CFPB staff -- including roughly 450 workers previously based out-of-state -- to relocate to a new, smaller Washington, D.C. headquarters, ending remote work entirely; the bureau terminated leases on all four of its regional offices (San Francisco, Atlanta, Chicago, and New York). The new headquarters space, at 445 12th Street SW, has capacity for only about 550 workers -- roughly half the bureau's remaining headcount of approximately 1,100 -- a mismatch reporting characterized as designed to drive further attrition beyond the office's stated capacity limit alone. Relocation began June 1, 2026 with a hard compliance deadline of August 31 or termination. In June 2026, Trump nominated Brian Johnson -- a former CFPB deputy director under Kathy Kraninger and current Capital One executive -- to be permanent CFPB Director. Sen. Elizabeth Warren, ranking member of the Senate Banking Committee, said: 'Starting in August, Russ Vought can no longer legally serve as Donald Trump's hatchet man at the CFPB. So here comes the next hatchet man to try to finish the job.' Also in June 2026, CFPB removed all prior public reports describing its own supervisory activity. On June 22, 2026, Senate Banking Committee Democrats sent a formal letter to Acting Director Vought demanding an accounting of the deleted content and its legal basis. Senior leadership reported to the new headquarters starting July 6, 2026, with full D.C.-area staff required back five days a week by July 13. The Senate Banking Committee held Brian Johnson's confirmation hearing on July 23, 2026; Johnson declined to endorse eliminating the CFPB and said he keeps an 'open mind' about staffing levels, while deflecting questions about the agency reportedly dropping 42 enforcement cases against presidential donors. Separately, the D.C. Circuit remanded NTEU v. CFPB (the litigation over the Bureau's proposed 2026 reduction-in-force) back to the district court and held the appeal in abeyance, after CFPB and NTEU jointly asked for a stay pending Johnson's confirmation so he could decide whether to proceed with, modify, or abandon the RIF plan. Committee advancement is expected before the August recess, with a full Senate vote anticipated in September 2026 -- meaning Johnson is very unlikely to be confirmed before Vought's August 1 FVRA deadline, raising the practical likelihood that Acting Deputy Director Mark Paoletta becomes acting director in the interim (if Johnson is not confirmed by August 1, 2026, Paoletta would become acting director in Vought's place). Ahead of a Vought oversight hearing, a July 2026 follow-up report from Sen. Warren's office found an additional $7.5 billion in costs in the first half of 2026 -- ~$15 billion cumulative from abandoning the credit-card late-fee cap, ~$7.5 billion from repealing the overdraft-fee cap, and ~$4 billion from dropped enforcement actions and abandoned settlements/consent orders (including the 42 dropped enforcement cases against presidential donors) -- bringing the cumulative total Warren's office attributes to the CFPB rollbacks to up to $26.5 billion. Update 2026-08-17: as this entry's prior update anticipated, Vought's FVRA-based authority to run CFPB expired August 1, 2026, and Deputy Director Mark Paoletta -- CFPB's chief legal officer -- became Acting Director that day. Reporting indicates Vought is expected to remain involved at CFPB in a senior-adviser role even after formally leaving the acting-director post, pending Johnson's confirmation. As of the most recent reporting reviewed, the Senate Banking Committee had not yet scheduled a vote on Johnson's nomination following his July 23 hearing, meaning the 'before the August recess' committee-vote timeline this entry previously anticipated has slipped. Update 2026-08-29: the Senate Banking Committee had not scheduled a vote on Brian Johnson's nomination as of this update, following his July 23, 2026 confirmation hearing. Mark Paoletta continues serving as Acting Director since his August 1, 2026 transition, with Russell Vought reported remaining at CFPB in a senior-adviser capacity -- no material change from the prior update.

title: CFTC Lost 24% of Its Staff, Including Its Entire Chicago Enforcement Team, Following Court-Cleared Federal Purges
institution: U.S. Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC)
status: Ongoing -- staffing reductions (layoffs, buyouts, early retirements) continued into 2026, with the agency at its lowest staffing level in 15 years as of February 2026
date_of_action: 2025-07-17 (initial post-ruling layoffs begin) through 2026-02 (staffing figures confirm 24% cumulative reduction)
what_changed: On July 17, 2025, days after the Supreme Court's July 8, 2025 ruling in Trump v. AFGE cleared the way for agency-wide federal reductions in force, the CFTC -- the independent agency responsible for regulating derivatives, commodities futures, and (since 2023) significant crypto-market enforcement -- began layoffs affecting more than two dozen employees across its enforcement, market oversight, administration, and data divisions. The cuts continued via a combination of layoffs, buyouts, and early retirements through 2026: by February 2026, the agency had 535 employees, down from 636 full-time staff in fiscal 2025 -- a 24% reduction, leaving the CFTC at its lowest staffing level in 15 years. The enforcement division was hit particularly hard: requested funding supported only 108 enforcement positions for the coming year, down from 140 filled positions in 2025 (a 23% drop), and the CFTC's Chicago office -- a historically significant post given Chicago's status as a major U.S. derivatives-trading hub -- went from 20 enforcement lawyers to zero. Update 2026-08-18: the CFTC's own Inspector General, in a January 2026 report, put the reduction at 708 full-time-equivalent staff at the end of fiscal 2024 down to 556 at the end of fiscal 2025 -- a 21% one-year drop, measured on a different fiscal-year-end basis than this entry's existing 636-to-535 (24%) figures from Cryptopolitan's February 2026 reporting (see caveat below on the differing baselines). In July 2026, Sen. Elizabeth Warren asked the Government Accountability Office to investigate whether the CFTC's workforce reductions -- which she put at 25% since January 2025, a third measurement point distinct from the two fiscal-year figures above -- have contributed to the enforcement decline. Warren's GAO request specifically asks the watchdog to determine whether the cuts complied with federal law, their impact on CFTC's regulatory mandate, and whether they contributed to, detracted from, or had no impact on fraud and waste at the agency -- a fuller framing than previously captured. No GAO findings had been published as of this recheck.

title: CIA Offers Buyouts Agency-Wide and Freezes Hiring to Realign Workforce with New Priorities
institution: Central Intelligence Agency
status: Implemented -- buyout offer and hiring freeze took effect February 2025; broader multi-year workforce reduction plan reported as ongoing. Updated 2026-08-30: the pace of departures is now reported as historic/unprecedented and is overwhelming the retirement-processing system, with new retirees facing months-long waits for their first pension check.
date_of_action: 2025-02-04 (buyout offer announced, February 6 deadline) through at least 2025-05 (multi-year reduction plan reported)
what_changed: On February 4, 2025, the CIA under newly confirmed Director John Ratcliffe offered buyouts to its entire workforce, giving employees until February 6, 2025 to accept -- a two-day window -- in exchange for eight months of pay plus benefits if they chose to resign. The agency simultaneously imposed a hiring freeze and began reviewing already-extended conditional job offers to new recruits, indicating offers not aligned with the agency's new focus were likely to be rescinded. Ratcliffe framed the changes as realigning the CIA toward new priorities, including a greater focus on the Western Hemisphere (targeting drug cartels and other threats not traditionally treated as top-tier adversaries) and covert operations, rather than legacy Cold War-era regional priorities. Beginning around March 7, 2025, the CIA also began terminating some probationary employees (generally those with fewer than two years on the job) citing a review of personnel suitability, following a federal judge's ruling allowing Director Ratcliffe to dismiss employees at his discretion -- a distinct, involuntary action layered on top of the earlier voluntary buyout program. National-security reporting at the time warned that the cuts came as U.S. intelligence had confirmed Russia and China were actively attempting to recruit recently fired or at-risk federal employees with security clearances, using LinkedIn, TikTok, and job postings, raising concern that thinning the intelligence workforce during a period of active foreign recruitment efforts compounded the risk. Reporting in May 2025 indicated this was part of a broader, multi-year plan across U.S. intelligence agencies to reduce the CIA's workforce by approximately 1,200 positions, with several hundred employees already having taken early retirement or the buyout by that point. The Washington Post reported August 20, 2026 that the pace of CIA retirements and resignations by mid/late 2026 had become historic -- current and former officials described it as outstripping anything in recent memory -- and, combined with OPM's own staffing cutbacks, is overwhelming the federal retirement-processing system: new CIA retirees can wait as long as nine months for their first full pension check, receiving only interim payments (60-80% of the eventual benefit) in the meantime. Some employees have reportedly withdrawn retirement paperwork already filed because they can't sustain the income gap. Precise current departure totals remain classified, so this doesn't update the 1,200-position target itself, but it is independent evidence the pace of departures is real and significant enough to strain a downstream federal system outside the CIA's own control. This reporting was corroborated across the Washington Examiner, MSN, and multiple regional reprints of the same wire/syndicated account. Update 2026-09-01 (GSR recheck batch 52): identified the structural cause behind the pension-processing backlog this entry already documents -- OPM's own workforce, the agency responsible for processing retirement claims government-wide (including CIA retirees'), fell by roughly a third, from just over 3,000 employees in FY2024 to about 1,980 in FY2026, while average retirement-claims processing time rose from 79 days in October 2025 to 109 days by July 2026. Directly-fetched OPM data corroborates the backlog's scale independent of the cause figures: OPM's Pennsylvania retirement operations center had 34,587 pending claims as of October 2025, the highest level since a roughly 36,000-claim peak during the COVID-19 pandemic in March 2022, against a prior (Biden-era) steady-state goal of roughly 13,000 pending claims. The CIA has responded by moving additional personnel into its own Retirement Branch to help work through the backlog; retiree hardship reports describe former officials drawing down savings, taking second mortgages, or delaying planned retirements because they could not afford months without expected income.

title: CISA Lost Roughly One-Third of Its Workforce, Including Election Security and Threat-Sharing Capacity
institution: Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), Department of Homeland Security
status: Ongoing (Kristi Noem was replaced as DHS Secretary by Markwayne Mullin, confirmed March 24, 2026; Mullin says the president has met with a likely CISA director nominee; DHS plans roughly 600 new CISA hires once a director is confirmed, with an initial 329-role 'mission-critical' hiring plan already underway -- about 180 tentative offers were out by the end of June 2026)
date_of_action: 2025-01 through 2026-06 (rolling cuts across multiple rounds: buyouts, layoffs, forced reassignments)
what_changed: Since January 2025, CISA -- the nation's primary civilian cyber-defense agency, created in 2018 specifically to coordinate federal response to critical infrastructure attacks -- lost roughly 1,000 employees, about one-third of its workforce, through a combination of buyout offers, early retirements, formal layoffs (reduction-in-force notices), and Management Directed Reassignments transferring CISA staff to ICE, CBP, FEMA, and the Federal Protective Service (refusing a reassignment could be grounds for termination). DHS Secretary Kristi Noem personally halted federal funding for the Multi-State Information Sharing and Analysis Center (MS-ISAC) in March 2025, eliminating roughly $8.3 million of its remaining 2025 budget -- MS-ISAC provided threat-sharing services to state and local governments. The cuts disproportionately hit CISA's election security and disinformation-monitoring functions, which had drawn Republican criticism as politically biased 'censorship' under the prior administration. The agency has operated without a permanent, Senate-confirmed director since January 2025. The early 2025 cuts had specific, named costs: by March 4, 2025, NOTUS reported over 100 CISA cybersecurity experts had been laid off, including agents specifically assigned to track Salt Typhoon and Volt Typhoon, the Chinese state-sponsored hacking campaigns that had already infiltrated U.S. telecom networks and critical infrastructure; by March 8, 2025, CBS News reported the toll had grown to 130+, including top recruits working on CyberSentry, a program built specifically to detect cyberattacks against the U.S. power grid, pipelines, and water systems. On March 5, 2025, former NSA cybersecurity director Rob Joyce testified to Congress that the mass federal firings -- more than 100,000 workers government-wide by that point, including 130+ from CISA -- would set back U.S. cyber defenses against China. Joyce continued sounding this warning publicly: at the Black Hat security conference in August 2025, CISA spokesperson Marci McCarthy defended the staffing purges as a return to the agency's 'core mission,' while Joyce countered that the U.S. had 'backslid' and lost critical national-defense capability, with nearly a third of CISA's workforce gone by that point. Congress's own October 2025 government shutdown compounded the damage months before the separate February 2026 DHS funding lapse described below: the Washington Post reported only about 35% of CISA staff remained active during the October shutdown even as ransomware and Chinese cyberattacks intensified, and Politico reported the 2015 Cybersecurity Information Sharing Act -- the law providing legal liability protection for companies that voluntarily share cyber-threat data with the government -- lapsed during the same shutdown, prompting some companies to halt that cooperation entirely. Later that month, House Democrats formally accused DHS, under Secretary Noem, of unlawfully reassigning CISA cybersecurity staff to ICE, CBP, and the Federal Protective Service during the shutdown -- the same Management Directed Reassignment mechanism described above -- alleging the diversions violated the Antideficiency Act; a separate New York Times report the same week noted the cuts had also reached the State Department's cyber-diplomacy function. During the shutdown, on November 10, 2025, WIRED reported the Congressional Budget Office itself was hacked by a suspected foreign actor, an incident experts tied directly to the shutdown-driven halt in routine federal patching, monitoring, and device management. In December 2025, Bloomberg reported the administration eliminated CISA's retention-incentive pay program -- a tool used to keep cyber defenders from leaving for better-paying private-sector jobs -- despite the agency already having lost over a third of its staff; the change exposed many remaining employees to pay cuts of up to 25%, a further attrition risk on top of the losses already documented here. The February 2026 DHS funding lapse compounded this attrition: The New York Times reported CISA furloughed more than half of its remaining workforce during the shutdown, leaving fewer than 1,000 employees on duty at the nation's primary civilian cyber-defense agency during the funding gap; ABC News separately reported that with DHS unfunded for 45 days during that same shutdown, CISA furloughed roughly 60% of its remaining workforce, disrupting vulnerability assessments and further weakening federal cyber defenses at a time when officials were warning of rising Iran-linked cyber threats to critical infrastructure, including power, water, and federal civilian networks. Also in February 2026, acting CISA Director Madhu Gottumukkala moved to reassign two senior career officials -- CIO Bob Costello (CISA's CIO for over four years) and acting Chief Human Capital Officer Kevin Diana -- giving them seven days to accept new roles elsewhere in DHS or resign, following an earlier unsuccessful attempt to oust Costello over a contracting-decision dispute that other political appointees had previously intervened to stop. Kristi Noem was replaced as DHS Secretary by Markwayne Mullin, confirmed by the Senate 54-45 on March 24, 2026. In April 2026, Sean Plankey, Trump's first nominee to lead CISA, withdrew his own nomination, writing 'After thirteen months since my initial nomination, it has become clear the Senate will not confirm me' -- the nomination had been held up by a mix of Democratic senators (Ron Wyden, over a withheld telecom-security report) and Republican senators (Rick Scott, over an unrelated Coast Guard shipbuilding dispute), plus broader holds affecting all DHS nominees. CISA is now led by acting director Nick Andersen. Mullin has since said the president has met with a likely CISA director nominee (not yet named or formally nominated as of this update) and that DHS believes CISA needs roughly 600 new hires, though a full rebuild can't proceed in earnest until a director is confirmed. CISA has begun an initial hiring plan for 329 'mission-critical' roles, with about 180 tentative job offers extended by the end of June 2026 -- the first concrete numbers behind CISA's previously-announced, more general 2026 hiring push, which agency officials had cited the workforce reductions as having hampered preparedness for potential conflict with China. By June 2026, of CISA's authorized 3,292 positions, only 2,324 were actually filled -- a nearly 1,000-position gap. Five of the agency's ten regional directors were serving only in acting capacity, disrupting the primary points of contact state and local governments rely on for federal cybersecurity assistance. Update 2026-07-27: state election officials from both parties told USA Today that, ahead of the 2026 midterms, they no longer expect federal agencies to reliably share election-threat intelligence with them -- a direct downstream consequence of the CISA staffing cuts and reduced regional-director capacity already described above. States say they're increasingly relying on private technology companies and nonprofits to fill the gap in federal threat-sharing coordination.

title: Administration Strips 'Climate' From Federal Research Funding, Websites, and Course Materials
institution: Multiple federal science and research-funding agencies, government-wide
status: Ongoing -- through at least March 2026, per Grist's NSF grant-title analysis showing the pattern continuing and deepening
what_changed: The Guardian reported on February 21, 2025 that the administration was cutting funding for scientific research that mentioned 'climate,' stripping grants from affected projects both domestically and abroad, altering government websites and course materials to remove the term, and in some cases forcing researchers to remove or retitle studies specifically to avoid the word in order to remain eligible for funding or publication. USA Today's July 2025 reporting found this pattern continuing at NOAA specifically: scientists described being told to avoid the word 'climate' in their work, alongside operational tool cuts including Saildrone ocean-monitoring devices going undeployed and forecasting quality suffering as a result of the broader staffing and budget cuts documented elsewhere in this database. Update 2026-08-17: Grist reported (March 27, 2026) that NSF grant titles mentioning "climate change" fell from 889 in 2023 to 148 in 2025 -- a 77% drop -- with a corresponding rise in the substitute term "extreme weather," evidence the pattern this entry documents continued and deepened through 2025. The same reporting identified a March 2025 USDA Agricultural Research Service memo, obtained by the outlet More Perfect Union, banning more than 100 words and phrases from agency communications and research materials, roughly a third of them climate-related (including "climate change," "global warming," "climate science," and "carbon sequestration," alongside unrelated banned terms like "DEI"). Ethan Roberts, union president at USDA's National Center for Agricultural Utilization Research, and Trent Ford, Illinois's state climatologist, were both quoted describing having personally altered their own language in proposals and public communications to avoid the banned terms. Update 2026-08-30 (GSR recheck batch 41): a March 2026 Wyden/Investigate Midwest review of the same USDA Agricultural Research Service memo found the 110-term banned-word list extended well beyond climate-specific language -- including "clean water," "safe drinking water," "equity," and "microplastics." Sen. Ron Wyden, Reps. Andrea Salinas, Chellie Pingree, and Jill Tokuda, joined by 22 additional colleagues, sent USDA Secretary Brooke Rollins an April 11, 2025 letter -- predating this entry's own 2026-08-08 creation date by nearly four months and missed by both prior rechecks -- warning the banned-word list would harm rural communities facing wildfires, drought, and food insecurity, calling it "an intentional effort to hinder, distort, and improperly steer federal scientific work in the name of political expediency." Separately, Government Executive's own March 2026 reporting on the same NSF grant-title data found "DEI"-related terms have vanished from NSF grants entirely, with "clean energy" and "pollution" also declining, though less sharply than "climate change." A broader, separately tracked mechanism -- an OMB rule proposed June 2026 that would give political appointees final say over federal research grant awards, with an American Meteorological Society scientist specifically warning it could chill hurricane and heat-wave warnings given climate change's politicization -- would escalate this entry's self-censorship pattern into outright political control of funding decisions; that rule's own status and timeline are tracked in this database's separate white-house-200b-research-funding-overhaul-2026 entry, not duplicated here.

title: Community Health Centers Serving 32-34 Million Patients Faced a Grant Freeze, a Lapsed Federal Fund, and OBBBA Medicaid Cuts All at Once
institution: Health Resources and Services Administration (HRSA); federally qualified community health centers nationwide
status: Ongoing -- Community Health Center Fund extended only through December 2026 via the Feb. 3, 2026 Consolidated Appropriations Act, with no multi-year reauthorization secured; underlying Medicaid-revenue pressure from OBBBA continues
date_of_action: 2025-03 (Medicaid funding freeze and proposed budget cuts first threaten centers) through 2026-02 (short-term Community Health Center Fund reauthorization)
what_changed: Community health centers -- federally qualified clinics serving roughly 32-34 million patients nationally, 90% of them at or below 200% of the federal poverty level -- faced four compounding federal funding and administrative threats across 2025-2026. First, beginning around March 2025, a Trump administration freeze on already-approved federal grants left health centers in at least 10 states experiencing payment delays, on top of a broader Medicaid funding freeze and proposed budget cuts that advocates warned could force closures or service reductions; centers rely on roughly $4.4 billion in annual federal grants (versus the $5.8 billion advocates say is needed) plus Medicaid, which made up 43% of the $46.7 billion in 2023 health-center revenue nationally. Second, HRSA itself -- the $12-billion-a-year HHS agency that administers this and other grant programs to clinics, rural hospitals, and workforce initiatives -- lost about a quarter of its roughly 2,700-person workforce between February and August 2025 across two rounds of cuts (a 7% RIF on February 14, 2025, followed by a larger DOGE-driven reduction on March 27, 2025), including analysts, auditors, grant managers, and nursing consultants; DOGE reportedly cut 40% of staff specifically at HRSA's Bureau of Primary Health Care, the office that directly oversees the Health Center Program funding these clinics, a direct contributor to the payment-processing delays documented above. Third, the Community Health Center Fund -- which provides about 70% of centers' federal funding -- was extended only to September 30, 2025, and then lapsed when Congress failed to pass renewal legislation before the government shutdown began; a temporary extension to January 30, 2026 was included in the continuing resolution that ended the 43-day shutdown in November 2025, and a further extension through December 2026 (with a modest increase to $4.6 billion for FY2026) came via the February 3, 2026 Consolidated Appropriations Act -- short-term stopgaps rather than the multi-year reauthorization advocates had sought. Fourth, the One Big Beautiful Bill Act's Medicaid provisions layered a projected $32 billion five-year revenue loss onto the sector, per a Commonwealth Fund estimate, compounding the funding and staffing uncertainty. Trump's proposed FY2026 budget separately called for eliminating HRSA entirely, along with specific programs including rural hospital grants, workforce training, Ryan White HIV/AIDS programs, and emergency medical services for children. An analysis cited by health-center advocates found one in four community health centers could close or reduce services within two years absent increased funding, and concrete harm had already begun by late 2025: a rural New Hampshire community health center shuttered, and a Des Moines, Iowa hospital system laid off dozens of employees and closed a clinic explicitly citing its 'ongoing response to the One Big Beautiful Bill Act.' Light-touch update 2026-08-18 (GSR recheck batch 22): beyond the Community Health Center Fund's Dec. 2026 mandatory-funding expiration already documented above, health centers also rely on a separate, smaller stream of annual discretionary Section 330 appropriations that runs on the standard federal fiscal-year cycle and expires September 30, 2026 -- a second, nearer-term funding cliff that requires its own timely congressional action independent of the CHCF extension. No reporting reviewed indicates either deadline has been further extended or resolved since the February 2026 appropriations act.

title: Congress Rescinded $1.1B From Public Broadcasting; CPB Dissolved After 58 Years
institution: Corporation for Public Broadcasting (CPB)
status: Complete (CPB formally dissolved January 5, 2026)
date_of_action: 2025-04 (board members fired) through 2026-01-05 (CPB board votes to dissolve)
what_changed: In April 2025, Trump fired three members of CPB's board of directors; the fired directors argued in subsequent legal action that the dismissal was governmental overreach targeting an entity whose congressional charter specifically guarantees its independence from political control. In July 2025, Congress passed a $9 billion rescissions package (canceling previously appropriated funds) requested by the White House, including $1.1 billion earmarked for CPB through fiscal year 2027 -- the first time in nearly 60 years Congress had voted to not fund CPB. The House vote was 216-213, with all but two Republicans in favor; in the Senate, only Susan Collins (R-ME) and Lisa Murkowski (R-AK) broke with their party to vote against the package, alongside two House Republicans (Brian Fitzpatrick, Mike Turner). Trump signed the bill and wrote on Truth Social: 'REPUBLICANS HAVE TRIED DOING THIS FOR 40 YEARS, AND FAILED....BUT NO MORE.' CPB announced August 1, 2025 that it would begin winding down, eliminating most staff positions by the September 30 fiscal year-end and retaining a small transition team through January 2026 to handle compliance and music-rights obligations. When the Senate Appropriations Committee subsequently declined to restore any funding for the following budget year, CPB's board voted to formally dissolve the organization entirely on January 5, 2026, rather than continue to exist in a defunded, vulnerable state -- CPB President and CEO Patricia Harrison described this as protecting 'the integrity of the public media system' by closing on the organization's own terms.

primary_proponent.name: Donald Trump
primary_proponent.role: President
primary_proponent.note: Personally pushed the rescission package and has repeatedly called CPB a 'monstrosity,' arguing public broadcasting -- particularly NPR -- displays 'extreme liberal bias.' OMB Director Russell Vought, who requested the rescissions package on the administration's behalf, told reporters afterward the administration would 'likely' send additional rescissions packages, saying 'there is still a great enthusiasm for these rescissions bills, because Congress wants to be a part of voting for these cuts and making them permanent.'

estimated_impact.summary: CPB funded more than 1,500 local radio and television stations nationwide; roughly 70% of its money went directly to 330 PBS and 246 NPR member stations. NPR President and CEO Katherine Maher estimated approximately 96% of all classical music broadcast in the United States airs on public radio stations specifically. The impact fell most heavily on rural and small-market stations with fewer alternative funding sources: specific documented effects include KCTS in Seattle abandoning long-form journalism ambitions, WFAE in Charlotte closing its community engagement facility, and WPSU in State College, Pennsylvania considering shutting down its radio station entirely. Sen. Susan Collins, despite voting to preserve funding, articulated the underlying tension directly: 'I share the frustration with the biased reporting by NPR, and I would support defunding it. Nevertheless, local TV and radio stations continue to provide important coverage' -- citing Maine-specific examples like the emergency alert network and local high school sports coverage.

title: CPSC's Three Democratic Commissioners Fired, Battery-Safety Standard Withdrawn, Agency Left in Republican-Only Rump
institution: Consumer Product Safety Commission
status: Complete (firings litigated and now final following the June 29, 2026 Trump v. Slaughter ruling)
date_of_action: 2025-05-08 (firings) through 2026-06-29 (Supreme Court finalization)
what_changed: On May 8, 2025, President Trump fired three of the CPSC's five commissioners -- Alexander Hoehn-Saric, Mary Boyle, and Richard Trumka Jr., all Biden appointees -- citing 'neglect of duty or malfeasance in office' without further detail, hours after the three had voted to block DOGE representatives from entering CPSC headquarters to fire staff employees. The CPSC's founding statute allows removal only for 'neglect of duty or malfeasance in office' and requires no more than three of five commissioners share a political party, structural protections designed to preserve a bipartisan agency that regulates the safety of thousands of consumer products. The fired commissioners sued; a federal judge in Maryland ruled the firings unlawful and ordered reinstatement, and the Fourth Circuit declined to stay that order, but the Supreme Court granted an emergency stay on July 23, 2025, allowing the firings to proceed while the appeal continued. During the roughly five weeks the three commissioners were absent, the two remaining Republican-aligned commissioners -- Acting Chairman Peter Feldman and Douglas Dziak -- withdrew a previously approved (3-2 vote) e-bike and lithium-ion battery safety testing standard from public comment; lithium-ion battery fires from e-bikes and similar devices have been a rising home-fire and fatality concern nationally. The same two commissioners released a CPSC FY2026 budget request proposing to cut the agency's funding and staffing and to transfer CPSC's functions to the Department of Health and Human Services, led by Secretary Robert F. Slaughter -- which held FTC commissioners' for-cause removal protections unconstitutional -- prompted CPSC Acting Chairman Feldman to state publicly that the fired commissioners' 'claims should now fail as a matter of law,' effectively finalizing the terminations. title: Federal Disease Surveillance Cuts Coincide With Emergence of Flesh-Eating Bacteria, Screwworm, and Malaria-Reintroduction Risk
institution: HHS/CDC and USDA disease-surveillance programs
status: Ongoing -- most surveillance reductions remain in place as of mid-2026; the ocean-monitoring-instrument removal was reversed after congressional opposition
date_of_action: 2025 (surveillance program cuts begin) through 2026-07 (reporting on emerging health threats)
what_changed: The Trump administration reduced or eliminated multiple federal disease-surveillance programs beginning in 2025. As of July 1, 2025, CDC's FoodNet (the Foodborne Diseases Active Surveillance Network, a CDC/USDA/FDA/state partnership covering 10 sites) stopped requiring reporting on six of the eight pathogens it was built to track -- Campylobacter, Cyclospora, Listeria, Shigella, Vibrio, and Yersinia all became optional, leaving only Salmonella and STEC (E. coli) mandatory; Cyclospora surveillance had been mandatory since 1997. The administration also began removing hundreds of deep-sea ocean-monitoring instruments used to track ocean conditions that help predict pathogen proliferation, including Vibrio; this removal was later reversed following congressional opposition. USDA lost 18% of its workforce (more than 20,000 employees) in the first half of 2025. USAID, dismantled entirely in 2025, had provided global disease-surveillance and response funding, including stripping more than $300 million from the UN Food and Agriculture Organization and targeting roughly 80% of global malaria grants for termination, ending a U.S. malaria-prevention investment that had exceeded $9 billion since 2005. These reductions coincided with the emergence or resurgence of multiple disease threats in 2026: a 2026 Cyclospora outbreak that food-safety commentators say the weakened surveillance system was slower to detect and characterize (though some analyses argue the surveillance changes did not directly cause the outbreak itself -- see caveat); Vibrio vulnificus ('flesh-eating bacteria') cases in Florida and detections in New York coastal waters (CDC estimates roughly 80,000 Vibrio infections annually, with about 1 in 5 Vibrio vulnificus wound infections fatal, sometimes within days); the first confirmed U.S. case of New World Screwworm in June 2026, with over a dozen animals infected, threatening the cattle industry; and a CDC warning in May 2026 that 'the country remains susceptible to malaria reintroduction' despite the disease's 1951 eradication in the U.S. Update 2026-08-17: the 2026 Cyclospora outbreak referenced above has a documented scale -- as of mid-July 2026 reporting, over 700 confirmed cases in Michigan alone (the largest cluster), with additional cases in Ohio (177), Illinois (141), New York (120), North Carolina (110), and Texas (48), for a total spanning at least 18 states. Separately, CDC's Division of Parasitic Diseases and Malaria was dissolved in 2025, a specific staffing/capacity fact not previously captured in this entry that bears directly on the malaria-reintroduction-risk warning already documented above. Update 2026-08-30: the New World Screwworm outbreak referenced above has a documented trajectory since the first confirmed animal case in June 2026 -- monthly counts fell from 30 cases in June (29 in Texas, 1 in New Mexico) to 14 in July (all Texas) to 3 in August (two sheep and one goat, all in the Big Bend area near the Mexican border, with no cattle cases reported that month), a cumulative 47 cases, per trade-press reporting attributing the slowdown to a coordinated USDA/APHIS and state eradication effort. This is presented as evidence of the outbreak's trajectory and current containment status, not a resolution of the underlying surveillance-capacity concern this entry documents -- it rests on a single trade outlet (Oklahoma Farm Report) rather than the multi-outlet corroboration this entry's other figures have, and a direct fetch of USDA APHIS's own case-count page (screwworm.gov) timed out during this recheck, so this addition is flagged MODERATE pending independent primary-source confirmation.

Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins separately denied that USDA staffing cuts caused the screwworm's return.

title: DOE's nuclear waste cleanup office loses nearly half its workforce, GAO finds
institution: Department of Energy, Office of Environmental Management
status: Ongoing -- 45% vacancy rate at end of FY2025 per GAO, with site-level rates as high as 100%; DOE plans to hire 174 workers in FY2026
date_of_action: 2025-03-04 (first Carlsbad Field Office lease-termination attempt) through 2026-05 (GAO report)
what_changed: The Carlsbad Field Office's eventual collapse to 100% vacancy had an earlier warning sign than the GAO report alone shows: on March 4, 2025, DOGE included the Carlsbad Field Office's 90,000-square-foot Skeen-Whitlock Building lease on a spreadsheet of more than 7,000 federal leases marked for termination, citing roughly $810,000 in annual savings. The office, staffed by about 200 workers, directly manages the Waste Isolation Pilot Plant (WIPP) -- the only U.S. site licensed to permanently dispose of transuranic nuclear waste, including plutonium-contaminated material, stored in a deep salt formation -- and includes an emergency response center for handling nuclear-material accidents. Gabe Vasquez among others) over the national-security and public-safety risk of disrupting the only facility of its kind, GSA reinstated the lease within days, confirming by March 6, 2025 the office was no longer slated for termination. That reversal, however, did not stop the underlying workforce attrition documented below: a Government Accountability Office report found the Department of Energy's Office of Environmental Management -- responsible for cleaning up nuclear contamination from World War II- and Cold War-era weapons programs at sites across the country -- ended FY2025 with a 45% vacancy rate, roughly half its needed workforce. Of 409 staff who left in 2025, 76% (312) departed through the White House's deferred resignation program; nearly half of those departures (180) were in positions GAO classified as mission-critical, spanning engineering, contracting, physical sciences, and IT management. Vacancy rates varied sharply by site: 62% at Los Alamos National Laboratory, and 100% -- every position empty -- at the Carlsbad Field Office, the same office whose building lease had been targeted, then spared, a year earlier. GAO further warned that 35% of DOE-EM's remaining 856 employees will be eligible to retire by the end of 2030, meaning attrition is likely to continue independent of any further resignation programs. DOE has said it plans to hire 174 workers in FY2026, which GAO's analysis indicates would still leave significant workforce gaps.

title: DOE Dismantles Office of Clean Energy Demonstrations, Cancels $3.7B+ in Awarded Projects
institution: Department of Energy (Office of Clean Energy Demonstrations)
status: Complete (office wound down; zero FY2026 funding provided by Congress)
date_of_action: 2025-05-30 (first project terminations announced) through 2026 appropriations (OCED zeroed out)
what_changed: The Office of Clean Energy Demonstrations (OCED) was created in 2021 to manage roughly $27 billion in funding for large-scale clean energy demonstration projects -- hydrogen hubs, direct air capture hubs, long-duration energy storage, and industrial decarbonization -- and had committed over $18 billion to about 100 projects by November 2025. Congress's FY2026 appropriations bill, passed in early 2026, formalized the outcome by providing zero new funding to OCED and directing DOE to report quarterly on the redistribution of the office's remaining obligated and unobligated funds.

title: DOGE/GSA Targeted 793 Federal Office Leases for Termination Government-Wide -- Then Repeatedly Cut Back the List as Agencies Were Blindsided
institution: General Services Administration (GSA), coordinating with DOGE (Department of Government Efficiency) across dozens of federal agencies including IRS, Social Security Administration, and U.S. Geological Survey
status: Target list repeatedly reduced -- from 793 leases (mid-March 2025) to 485 (June 2025) to 384 (August 2025); GSA had finalized only about 30% of the roughly 900 government-wide lease terminations it had sent to landlords by February 2026
date_of_action: 2025-03-15 (793-lease list first reported) through 2026-02 (finalization rate reported at ~30%)
what_changed: CBS News reported on March 15, 2025 that DOGE/GSA had listed 793 federal office leases for termination government-wide, covering roughly nine million square feet and targeting a claimed ~$500 million in savings. Agencies including the IRS, Social Security Administration, and U.S. Geological Survey were among those affected, with reporting describing agencies as blindsided by the cancellations and left scrambling to relocate staff and operations with little notice; some cancellations were reported as made in error and later reversed. Individual agencies saw partial rollbacks under political pressure -- for example, USDA cut its own office-closure list roughly in half. By February 2026, Federal News Network reported GSA had finalized only about 30% of the approximately 900 government-wide lease terminations it had sent to landlords earlier in 2025, indicating the bulk of the originally announced list was never actually executed. This entry documents the government-wide program as a whole; individual high-profile instances within it -- including the National Park Service's 34 targeted buildings and the Alaska/Hawaii volcano observatories -- are tracked in their own separate entries (national-park-service-lease-terminations-2025, doge-volcano-observatory-lease-terminations-2025) cross-referenced here as specific examples of this broader push.

title: NLRB Deleted DOGE System-Access Records Before GAO Investigators Could Examine Them
institution: National Labor Relations Board (NLRB)
status: Complete -- GAO report published; the underlying account-access records cannot be recovered
date_of_action: 2025-04-16 (DOGE detail begins) through 2025-08 (access records deleted, after DOGE detail ended and before GAO could examine them)
what_changed: Two DOGE staffers were formally detailed to the National Labor Relations Board beginning April 16, 2025, under agreements running through July 25, 2025, and requested access to seven internal HR systems covering personnel records, payroll, and hiring databases -- a request that prompted an NLRB IT staffer to file a whistleblower disclosure with Congress and the agency's inspector general to open an investigation into a potential data breach. Access logs for sensitive systems are generally subject to a six-year retention requirement under the General Records Schedule; the deleted records were only months old.

title: DOGE's 'Fraud Review' of $8.6 Trillion in Social Security Payments Found Almost No Fraud, Slowed Claims 25%, and Led to an Unauthorized Server Holding 300M+ Americans' Data
institution: Social Security Administration (SSA); DOGE (Department of Government Efficiency)
status: Ongoing litigation, now proceeding to discovery after the government's own bid to block it failed -- the Fourth Circuit vacated the injunction limiting DOGE's SSA data access and remanded (April 10, 2026); on remand, the district court lifted its stay and granted plaintiffs' motion for discovery (April 14, 2026); the government's Motion to Rescind that discovery order was denied on June 26, 2026, in an opinion finding SSA and DOGE had made 'serious if not egregious misrepresentations' to the court; SSA reportedly considering rolling back the anti-fraud phone checks; a June 5, 2026 sworn whistleblower declaration separately alleges a DOGE official proposed marking 2.7 million living Social Security recipients as dead to pressure them into self-deporting or expose them to ICE detention, which SSA disputes as ever having been implemented
date_of_action: 2025-03-08 (review publicly reported) through 2026-04-10 (Fourth Circuit ruling); data-access disclosures continuing into 2026
what_changed: Starting in mid-February 2025, Elon Musk publicly laid the political groundwork for DOGE's Social Security fraud review with two separate, since-debunked claims: that 20 million people 'definitely dead' were still marked alive in SSA's Numident database, and, in a March 11, 2025 Fox Business interview, that $500-700 billion in Social Security 'waste' needed to be eliminated. Fact-checkers and SSA's own then-acting commissioner rejected both claims -- SSA data traces the '150-year-olds' figure to a database-structure quirk (SSA's own inspector general found improper payments of all kinds, fraud included, totaled less than 1% of the $8.6 trillion paid out from FY2015-2022), and experts told ABC News Trump and Musk were falsely implying millions of dead Americans were actively receiving benefits rather than merely still appearing as unremoved records. In March 2025, ABC News and other outlets reported that DOGE was searching through $8.6 trillion in Social Security payment records as part of the same stated anti-fraud effort, with DOGE engineer Aram Moghaddassi and Musk separately claiming that up to 40% of phone calls to SSA requesting direct-deposit changes came from fraudsters -- a narrower claim used to justify new anti-fraud identity checks on phone-based claims starting in early April 2025. Acting SSA Commissioner Leland Dudek later confirmed the review's scope in a letter to Congress. The actual results, revealed in internal SSA documents reported by Nextgov/FCW and cited by Sen. Elizabeth Warren in a May 15, 2025 release, contradicted the fraud claims: of more than 110,000 phone claims examined under the new checks, only 2 were found to have a high probability of fraud, and fewer than 1% were flagged as even potentially fraudulent at all -- consistent with SSA's own data showing fraud is a negligible share (a fraction of the already-small 0.3%) of the program's improper payments. The new checks themselves caused documented harm: an internal SSA document from May 2025 found they slowed retirement claim processing by 25% and caused a 'degradation of public service,' with over 140,000 retirement claims left unprocessed for more than 60 days, prompting SSA to consider walking the policy back. Separately, and more seriously, court filings beginning in January 2026 revealed that DOGE staff had improperly accessed and shared SSA data well beyond the stated fraud-review purpose: a January 16, 2026 DOJ court filing corrected prior sworn agency testimony and admitted a DOGE employee had copied Social Security records covering more than 300 million Americans onto an unauthorized, inadequately secured cloud server that SSA itself could not fully audit for who had accessed it. The same filing revealed a DOGE employee had signed an agreement to share SSA data with an outside political advocacy group seeking to find evidence of voter fraud and 'overturn results in certain States,' prompting a Hatch Act referral for two DOGE employees to a federal watchdog. A federal court had issued a temporary restraining order in March 2025 limiting DOGE's SSA data access -- U.S. District Judge Ellen Hollander's order barring DOGE affiliates from accessing SSA's sensitive personal data -- and Acting Commissioner Dudek initially told reporters the order applied so broadly it would force him to shut down the agency; Hollander responded in two same-day letters to counsel calling that characterization 'inaccurate' and then 'patently incorrect,' clarifying the order applied only to SSA staff working on the DOGE data-access effort specifically, and Dudek reversed himself hours later, saying the agency would remain open and continue operating under the TRO. Reporting found DOGE associates continued accessing sensitive data even after that order; a further whistleblower complaint reported in March 2026 alleged a former DOGE associate planned to take sensitive citizen data to a subsequent government-contractor job. On April 10, 2026, the Fourth Circuit Court of Appeals vacated the district court's preliminary injunction restricting DOGE's SSA data access, with the majority finding plaintiffs had not shown 'irreparable harm' -- over a dissent arguing the prior record was 'materially erroneous' given the January 2026 disclosures. Update 2026-08-29: on remand, the U.S. District Court for the District of Maryland lifted its stay of the case on April 14, 2026 and granted plaintiffs' motion for discovery -- meaning the case is now proceeding to fact-finding on the scope of DOGE's SSA data access, rather than simply sitting dormant after the Fourth Circuit's ruling. No further ruling or discovery outcome was identified as of this recheck. Update 2026-08-31 (real correction): this entry's prior text stopped at the April 14, 2026 discovery order and found no subsequent ruling. In fact, defendants moved to rescind that order (ECF 215), arguing discovery was improper and citing the DOGE Temporary Organization's then-upcoming July 4, 2026 expiration date. On June 26, 2026, Judge Ellen Lipton Hollander (D. Md.) denied the Motion to Rescind in a 39-page opinion, holding that defendants' own January 16, 2026 Notice of Corrections -- which disclosed that SSA had falsely assured the court of TRO compliance, concealed the DOGE Team's full systems access, and misrepresented that DOGE work was confined to fraud detection -- itself justified the discovery, and declined defendants' request to cap it at five requests for production, five interrogatories, five requests for admission, and zero depositions. The opinion quotes Judge King's concurring and dissenting opinion within the Fourth Circuit's en banc ruling (AFSCME VI, 172 F.4th 361) -- not the court's own holding -- in which he wrote that, given the corrected record, 'we should not accord the defendants any benefit of the doubt or readily trust in anything they say.' The same district court opinion detailed further specifics of the Voter Data Agreement beyond what was previously known: SSA says it first learned of the agreement during an unrelated November 2025 review, and documents produced in a related FOIA suit (Democracy Forward Found. v. SSA, ABA-26-1188, D. Md.) show a member of the SSA DOGE Team separately emailed a password-protected Excel workbook containing personally identifiable information on 971 beneficiaries to DOGE personnel at the Department of Homeland Security and the Department of Labor. Separately, and more seriously, plaintiffs' June 5, 2026 'Second Factual Notice' (ECF 233) attached a sworn declaration from former SSA senior executive Jeremiah Schofield, who says he was present when a DOGE official, Jon Koval, laid out a plan to mark roughly 2.7 million living Social Security recipients as dead in SSA's Death Master File -- with the stated purpose, per Schofield, of forcing those individuals to either self-deport or go to a local SSA office to prove they were alive, where ICE could then detain and deport them. Sens. Warren and Blumenthal made the declaration public and sought records and answers from SSA Commissioner Bisignano and the named DOGE-affiliated staff. SSA publicly disputes the account, saying it 'did not add a list of 2.7 million names to the Death Master File' and that the plan, as alleged, was never implemented. Plaintiffs' earlier March 10, 2026 'First Factual Notice' (ECF 208), already reflected in this entry as a March 2026 whistleblower complaint, is clarified by the June 26 opinion to have specifically alleged the departing DOGE associate took restricted SSA databases to a private-sector employer potentially on a thumb drive. As of this recheck, defendants' separate May 1, 2026 Motion to Dismiss for Lack of Jurisdiction remains pending and undecided; no ruling on it, and no outcome of the now-authorized discovery itself, has been identified.

title: DOGE Canceled 585 VA Contracts After Backlash Forced It Down From an Initial 875 -- Officials Gave Congress Inconsistent Figures
institution: Department of Veterans Affairs (VA), with DOGE (Department of Government Efficiency)
status: Implemented, with ongoing congressional oversight pressure over transparency and inconsistent figures
date_of_action: 2025-02 (initial ~875-contract cancellation list) through 2025-05-16 (Collins gives Congress a differing figure)
what_changed: DOGE, under Elon Musk, moved to cancel roughly 875 VA contracts as part of its cost-cutting campaign. Reporting and VA employees flagged that many targeted contracts covered essential services, including cancer-registry maintenance, sterility certification for medical equipment, air-quality testing, suicide-prevention support, physician recruitment and retention, and safety inspections at VA medical facilities. Frontline Veterans Health Administration employees warned the cuts would imperil safety at the VA's nearly 1,400 hospitals and clinics. Facing that backlash, the VA paused its planned cuts, then announced the termination list had fallen by about a third, to 585 contracts, with an alleged combined value of $1.8 billion; the VA said the reductions would let it redirect more than $900 million to health care, benefits, and services for VA beneficiaries. The VA declined to disclose the full list of canceled contracts despite congressional requests, drawing criticism from senators including Richard Blumenthal and Angus King over the lack of transparency and consultation. VA Secretary Doug Collins subsequently gave Congress inconsistent figures on the scope of the cuts -- telling lawmakers on May 16, 2025 that the VA had canceled more than 440 contracts worth $120 billion, a figure sharply at odds with the earlier 585-contract/$1.8 billion accounting, without a public reconciliation of the discrepancy identified in sourcing reviewed. Update 2026-08-30: identified the specific mechanism behind the cancellation list -- an AI review tool built and operated by a DOGE software engineer with no prior healthcare or government experience, which ProPublica reported was error-prone and, per Government Executive/Nextgov reporting on a June 11, 2025 forum, appeared to select contracts for termination by matching keywords rather than individualized review. House and Senate Veterans' Affairs Committee Democrats raised the AI tool's use directly at that forum. A concrete example of the tool's effect: Task Order 169, a contract held by Aptive Resources (a veteran-owned and woman-owned small business) supporting VA's Electronic Health Record Modernization program by resolving identity-record anomalies in the VA's master person index, was terminated abruptly and without a transition plan despite having resolved 13,400 such anomalies -- inaccuracies that can otherwise block veterans from receiving medical care, disability compensation, or other earned benefits. At least six contracts directly supporting the EHR-modernization rollout, all held by service-disabled or veteran-owned small businesses, were similarly terminated. Separately, DOGE's broader public accounting of its savings claims, including the VA figures described above, was reported to have quietly removed some previously touted savings figures from its own public tracking website after they were found to be inflated or erroneous, though no source reviewed specifically confirms whether the VA contract figures in this entry were among those quietly revised.

date_of_action: 2025-03-06 (leases publicly reported as targeted) through 2026-04 (new permanent Hawaii facility opened)
what_changed: In early March 2025, NOTUS and the Washington Post reported that DOGE/GSA had listed the leases for the Anchorage office housing the USGS Alaska Volcano Observatory and the Hilo, Hawaii office housing the USGS Hawaiian Volcano Observatory (which monitors Kilauea) among hundreds of federal office leases slated for termination as part of the administration's real-estate cost-cutting push, with GSA claiming roughly $2.2 million in savings from the Anchorage lease alone. Scientists and local officials warned that ending these leases -- on top of concurrent GSA staffing cuts complicating any relocation of specialized monitoring equipment and servers -- risked degrading real-time eruption-warning capability near active volcanoes in both states; a former observatory scientist specifically flagged the difficulty of moving a recently purchased $500,000 backup generator and critical monitoring servers without risking data loss or monitoring gaps. In Alaska, Rep. Nick Begich's office intervened with the Department of the Interior and GSA, and the Anchorage lease was reinstated by March 18, 2025, according to the Anchorage Daily News and Begich's own office -- though GSA itself did not confirm the reversal on the record to the Anchorage Daily News, leaving the reinstatement independently reported but not agency-confirmed. In Hawaii, the Hilo Ironworks Building lease -- always a temporary arrangement dating to 2018, when the observatory's original Kilauea-summit headquarters was damaged beyond repair by earthquakes -- was listed for termination effective September 30, 2025; that threat did not require a comparable reversal because a new, permanent, non-leased Hawaiian Volcano Observatory headquarters (funded separately through congressional disaster-recovery appropriations after the 2018 damage, shared with the Pacific Island Ecosystems Research Center) opened in Hilo in April 2026, mooting the lease question for that observatory's long-term housing.

estimated_impact.summary: Two of the nation's volcano-hazard monitoring facilities were briefly slated for lease termination with no documented relocation plan for specialized, hard-to-move monitoring equipment, at a time when both regions had active volcanic activity (Kilauea eruptions in Hawaii) -- an example of a blanket cost-cutting process moving without an apparent case-by-case safety review.

title: DOJ Civil Rights Division Lost 70% of Its Attorneys — Voting Section Down From 30 to 3
institution: Civil Rights Division, U.S. Department of Justice
status: Ongoing (departure rate now over 75%; Voting Section led in acting capacity by a former Public Interest Legal Foundation attorney; White House reportedly considering defunding a related election-observer program); a former division attorney's August 2026 whistleblower disclosure to Congress separately alleges predetermined outcomes in three high-profile antisemitism investigations (Harvard, Brown, Columbia) and bar-discipline-driven departures among current attorneys
date_of_action: 2025-01 (initial departures begin) through 2025-10 (Justice Connection's most recent departure count)
what_changed: Since President Trump's January 2025 inauguration, an estimated 250-260 attorneys -- roughly 70% of the division's approximately 365-person attorney roster -- have resigned, accepted the administration's deferred-resignation offer, or been reassigned elsewhere within DOJ. By October 2025, Justice Connection (a support network founded by former division attorneys) estimated the departure count had grown to nearly 400 people, about 75% of attorneys. The Voting Section specifically -- responsible for enforcing the Voting Rights Act -- fell from an estimated 30 attorneys in January to just 3 by May 2025. The section devoted to ensuring nondiscrimination by recipients of federal funds was left with no attorneys whatsoever, per the Leadership Conference on Civil and Human Rights. Assistant Attorney General for Civil Rights Harmeet Dhillon, confirmed in April 2025, sent new mission statements to each of the division's 11 sections shortly after taking office, redirecting the Voting Section's focus from protecting against discrimination toward pursuing voter fraud, and telling the Educational Opportunities Section that its work required 'the full dedication of this section's resources, attention and energy to the priorities of the president.' Career section-chief managers -- in some cases with decades of institutional tenure spanning multiple administrations of both parties -- were removed from leadership roles and reassigned to processing public records requests or complaint intake, which several described as a deliberate push to induce their resignation. By August 2025, DOJ was actively soliciting permanent internal transfers from other CRT sections to refill the most depleted offices (Voting, Employment Litigation, Educational Opportunities), some of which were themselves already down more than 75% of their attorneys. The Voting Section is now led in an acting capacity by Maureen Riordan, previously an attorney at the Public Interest Legal Foundation, a conservative legal group whose stated mission is to 'fight against lawlessness in American elections' -- a notable leadership choice for a section this entry documents was redirected toward pursuing voter fraud rather than voting-rights enforcement. As of March 2026, the White House was reportedly considering ending funding for a separate, longstanding DOJ election-observer program aimed at protecting minority voting rights, according to CBS News sources. Departures across the division have continued to be counted at roughly 75%, consistent with Justice Connection's October 2025 estimate already in this entry, rather than climbing further as of this update. Update 2026-07-26: a DOJ spokesperson has since gone on the record denying the reported consideration of ending the election-observer program's funding, stating the Department 'has no plans to end its monitorship program which is integral to assessing compliance with federal voting rights laws across the country.' This resolves the 'reportedly considering' item from the prior update with an explicit denial, though it does not address or retract the underlying reporting that such defunding had been discussed internally. Reuters reporting (Feb. 2026) found the division's unit prosecuting police and federal-agent misconduct lost roughly two-thirds of its attorneys, from about 40 down to as few as 13, with charges under the civil rights statute most commonly used in federal excessive-force cases falling about 36% to 54 total in 2025 -- the lowest since 2020. Section supervisors reportedly instructed staff early in the administration that law-enforcement-misconduct investigations would proceed only in egregious circumstances (e.g. a death in custody or sexual assault), with state and local authorities expected to lead most other cases. Former DOJ lawyers cited in the reporting expressed doubt the diminished section could conduct thorough investigations of recent incidents, including the fatal shootings of Renee Good and Alex Pretti by federal immigration agents in Minneapolis -- the same shootings this tracker's prosecution/cabinet-level/bondi-doj-renee-good-widow-investigation-2026.json entry documents DOJ leadership blocking a standard investigation of and instead pressuring an investigation of Good's widow. Update 2026-08-17: in July 2026, Dhillon swore in more than 100 new attorneys and staff to the Civil Rights Division, beginning to refill the roster this entry documents was hollowed out by departures. The division's new composition drew public scrutiny after DOJ published a group photo of the incoming class; commentators (Atlanta Black Star) highlighted the demographic makeup of the new hires as a marker of the division's redirected priorities. Coverage citing DOJ deputy leadership (Jeffrey Morrison, elevated to Deputy Assistant Attorney General by May 2026 and now counsel on the department's Title VI suit against the University of California; Eric Sell, who followed Dhillon from the Center for American Liberty) describes a division now oriented toward Second Amendment cases, litigation against transgender-related policies, and alleged campus antisemitism -- confirming the mission-redirection this entry already documents is now staffed with new personnel aligned to it, rather than remaining merely depleted. Update (2026-08-30 recheck): a whistleblower disclosure from former Civil Rights Division attorney Haley Van Erem, filed through the Government Accountability Project and forwarded to four congressional committees including the House Judiciary Committee (reported Aug. 18-19, 2026), alleges that DOJ and HHS officials departed from longstanding investigative practices in at least three high-profile antisemitism investigations -- Harvard, Brown, and Columbia -- conducted under the administration's Task Force to Combat Antisemitism (led by DOJ official Leo Terrell), claiming the investigations' outcomes were 'predetermined, without regard to the evidence' and that for at least some of them there was 'little to no factual predicate justifying opening them.' Van Erem, who spent nearly a decade in the Special Litigation Section before being reassigned off five active ADA cases onto Title VI investigations on March 21, 2025, left DOJ May 30, 2025, citing unwillingness to continue in what she described as politically motivated investigations. Per Above the Law's coverage, her disclosure separately provides 'the first direct acknowledgment' that some departing Civil Rights Division attorneys' exits were driven by concern that continued participation in the division's current work -- including alleged use of 'poison pill' settlement language designed to force litigation rather than resolution, and opening at least one investigation based on a single news article -- could expose them to state bar discipline.

primary_proponent.role: Assistant Attorney General for Civil Rights
primary_proponent.note: Personally authored and sent the new mission statements redirecting each section's priorities. At a Federalist Society event, she likened the division's work under Democratic administrations to a 'speeding train' and, addressing the departing attorneys directly, said 'we wish them well in their future endeavors and their passions. They need to pursue them elsewhere. That's not going to be happening at the DOJ.'

estimated_impact.summary: Stacey Young, an 18-year Civil Rights Division veteran who resigned in January 2025 and founded Justice Connection to support current and former staff, described the scale of change as unprecedented in the division's near-70-year history: 'Every presidential administration has its own policy priorities, but I don't think there's any precedent for an administration almost completely refocusing the civil rights division's enforcement priorities the way this one has.' Joseph Rich, who led the Voting Section from 1999-2005 under both a Democratic and Republican administration, raised a specific operational concern about the reduced Voting Section potentially bringing voter-fraud suits 'right in the middle of an election.'

The 250 vs. 260 vs. 400 figures reflect different snapshot dates from the same source network (Justice Connection) rather than conflicting estimates -- the count grew over the year as departures continued, not because of methodological disagreement.

Re-verified 2026-08-30 (real correction): Van Erem's whistleblower disclosure and its core claims (25-28 page disclosure, House Judiciary Committee referral, the Harvard/Brown/Columbia investigations, the predetermined-outcome allegation) are well-corroborated across CBS News, ABC News, the Jewish Telegraphic Agency, jweekly, Higher Ed Dive, and the Government Accountability Project's own press release -- HIGH confidence. The specific 'poison pill' settlement-language and single-article-triggered-investigation details are sourced to Above the Law's fuller writeup of the disclosure and were not independently cross-checked against the disclosure document itself -- MODERATE confidence on those two specific procedural details.

A former attorney's August 2026 whistleblower disclosure to Congress separately alleges the division's Harvard, Brown, and Columbia antisemitism investigations had predetermined outcomes, and that some departures were driven by attorneys' concern over exposure to state bar discipline for the division's current work.
