title: DOJ and DHS Canceled Hundreds of Millions in Public-Safety and Violence-Prevention Grants in 2025, With Most Recipients Still Unreimbursed Months Later
institution: U.S. Department of Justice (Office of Justice Programs) and U.S. Department of Homeland Security (Center for Prevention Programs and Partnerships / FEMA)
status: Ongoing -- most DOJ grant recipients remained unreimbursed as of November 2025 reporting; the lead legal challenge to the DOJ cancellations (Vera Institute v. DOJ, D.C. Cir. No. 25-5248) remains pending on appeal with no ruling identified as of this 2026-08-31 recheck; DHS's CP3 office continued operating in reduced, redirected form rather than closing outright; a stipulated injunction barring DOJ from re-obligating the terminated grant funds has been repeatedly extended and remains in effect through at least September 1, 2026, with a further extension decision pending a status report due August 28, 2026 whose outcome was not identified as of this recheck; both officials who led the original 2025 cuts, AG Bondi and DHS Secretary Noem, have since left their posts, replaced by AG Todd Blanche (confirmed by the Senate August 8, 2026) and DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin (confirmed March 23, 2026), though neither successor is reported to have altered the underlying cancellations or CP3's reduced posture; a May 2026 one-year retrospective found affected organizations still had not recovered, including at least one full nonprofit closure
date_of_action: 2025-02 (CP3 cuts and workforce reductions begin) through 2025-11 (NPR follow-up documenting unreimbursed DOJ grantees)
what_changed: Two parallel cancellation waves hit federal public-safety and violence-prevention grantmaking in 2025. At DHS, in a single week in late February/early March 2025, the department cut roughly $20 million from more than two dozen programs tied to its Center for Prevention Programs and Partnerships (CP3) -- the office responsible for terrorism and targeted-violence-prevention grants -- including counterterrorism and school-shooter-prevention initiatives; the roughly $90 million CP3 had awarded to community groups and law enforcement since 2020 was placed in jeopardy. Affected programs included a Boston Children's Hospital intervention team for violent youth behavior, the Eradicate Hate prevention umbrella group, research into far-right-extremist disengagement, a national threat-compilation database for law enforcement, and hate-crimes training programs; one recipient told ProPublica that programs based in 'sanctuary states' resisting deportation cooperation were specifically targeted. FEMA's separate Nonprofit Security Grant Program, which funds physical security upgrades at religious institutions including synagogues, was also frozen amid the same review. On March 3, 2025, CP3 dismissed roughly 20% of its workforce through probationary-employee terminations; Director William Braniff resigned the same night, calling the terminations 'wrongful.' DHS's own framing, in a July 2025 press release, characterized $18.5 million in canceled CP3 grants as eliminating 'wasteful, misdirected spending' rather than shutting the office down, and DHS materials indicate CP3 continued operating afterward in a reduced form -- a more precise characterization than some contemporaneous reporting describing the office as fully 'shut down.' A ProPublica investigation published June 4, 2025 found DHS had installed Thomas Fugate, a 22-year-old with a one-year-old undergraduate degree and no counterterrorism background, to lead CP3's remaining work. Separately at DOJ, the Office of Justice Programs (OJP) abruptly canceled roughly 350-373 grants worth more than $800 million on April 22, 2025, terminating funding mid-cycle for programs supporting crime victims, opioid-abuse and trauma recovery, rural law enforcement, disability services, and legally mandated functions including prison-rape-elimination-act audits; a Council on Criminal Justice analysis found more than 550 organizations affected, almost all nonprofits. Five organizations -- the Vera Institute of Justice, the Center for Children and Youth Justice, Chinese for Affirmative Action, FORCE Detroit, and Health Resources in Action -- sought a preliminary injunction and reversal in a lawsuit filed May 2025; in July 2025, U.S. District Judge Amit Mehta denied the injunction and dismissed the case for lack of jurisdiction and failure to state a constitutional claim, while separately calling DOJ's conduct 'shameful' and likely to harm vulnerable communities. Plaintiffs appealed to the D.C. Circuit the next day (case no. 25-5248); the appeal was argued October 14, 2025, and no ruling had been issued as of this recheck (docket last updated June 22, 2026) -- the case remains open on appeal, not finally resolved as this entry previously implied. Six months after the cancellations, NPR reported in November 2025 that most affected organizations still had not been reimbursed for money already spent under the canceled grants, forcing layoffs, draws on reserve funds, and reduced services; organizations that appealed the cancellations reported no response, and several had filed additional lawsuits. DOJ told NPR the government shutdown then underway -- which began roughly five months after the cancellations -- was hindering its ability to process appeals and reimbursements, though the cancellations themselves predated the shutdown by months. Update 2026-08-29: a May 1, 2026 Vera Institute one-year retrospective found the damage from the DOJ cancellations had not been reversed by the pending appeal -- affected organizations remained, in the piece's own framing, 'on life support,' many having rolled back programs and reduced services, and at least one 20-year-old community-violence-intervention nonprofit, Equal Justice USA, had closed entirely as a result of the funding loss. The piece noted that restoring funding, if it happens, would not undo harm already done to organizations that folded. The D.C. Circuit appeal (No. 25-5248) remained pending with no ruling identified as of this recheck. Update 2026-08-31: neither of the two officials who directed the original 2025 cuts remains in office. Attorney General Pam Bondi, under whom DOJ's Office of Justice Programs implemented the April 2025 grant cancellations, was removed by President Trump on April 2, 2026 (reporting cited frustration over her handling of the Epstein files) and replaced on an acting basis by Todd Blanche, who was then confirmed by the Senate in a narrow 50-49 vote on August 8, 2026 as permanent Attorney General. DHS Secretary Kristi Noem, under whom the parallel CP3 cuts were carried out, was separately removed effective March 31, 2026 amid criticism of her department's handling of the immigration crackdown and disaster response, and was succeeded by Sen. Markwayne Mullin, confirmed by the Senate 54-45 and sworn in March 24, 2026; Noem moved to a newly created role as special envoy for a security initiative called the Shield of the Americas. No reporting identified in this recheck indicates either successor has revisited the CP3 cuts or the DOJ grant cancellations themselves. Separately, the stipulated injunction in Vera Institute v. DOJ barring DOJ from re-obligating or further diminishing the terminated grant funds -- entered July 21, 2025 and previously described in this entry's prior recheck only via a since-superseded February 25, 2026 status report extending it to May 5, 2026 -- has in fact been extended multiple additional times since, most recently (per an April 30, 2026 joint status report) to July 10, 2026 and (per a July 8, 2026 joint status report) currently through September 1, 2026; the parties' next joint status report, due August 28, 2026, was to determine whether the injunction is extended further, but no report content or ruling was identified as of this recheck. The D.C. Circuit appeal (No. 25-5248) itself remains pending with no opinion issued, consistent with this entry's existing account.

primary_proponent.name: Pam Bondi
primary_proponent.role: Attorney General
primary_proponent.note: DOJ's Office of Justice Programs implemented the April 2025 mid-cycle grant cancellations under her leadership; Bondi was removed as Attorney General by President Trump on April 2, 2026 and succeeded, after an interim acting period, by Todd Blanche, confirmed by the Senate August 8, 2026. The parallel DHS/CP3 cuts were carried out under Secretary Kristi Noem, who was separately removed effective March 31, 2026 and succeeded by Sen. Markwayne Mullin (confirmed March 24, 2026); DHS's own July 2025 press materials framed those cuts as eliminating 'wasteful, misdirected spending' rather than a program shutdown. No reporting identified in this recheck indicates either successor has revisited the cuts.

estimated_impact.summary: The cuts hit two overlapping but distinct public-safety functions: DOJ's cancellations pulled funding mid-cycle from crime-victim services, opioid/trauma recovery, rural law enforcement, and disability and audit programs at over 550 organizations, most of which remained unreimbursed for already-spent money six months later; DHS's CP3 cuts and workforce reduction weakened the federal government's community-based terrorism and targeted-violence prevention capacity, including programs serving religious institutions and at-risk youth, at a time independent reporting elsewhere in this tracker has documented rising political violence.

No ruling on the D.C. Circuit appeal (No. 25-5248) was identified as of this update. Re-verified 2026-08-31 (real correction): confirmed via CNN, NPR, CBS News, and Time that Bondi was removed as Attorney General April 2, 2026 and, per NPR and Axios, that Todd Blanche was confirmed as her permanent successor by the Senate August 8, 2026 (50-49); confirmed via CBS News, ABC News, CNN, and DHS's own press release that Noem was removed as DHS Secretary effective March 31, 2026 and that Markwayne Mullin was confirmed by the Senate (54-45) and sworn in March 24, 2026. Also corrected, via the Civil Rights Litigation Clearinghouse's case-docket summary (drawing on the parties' own joint status reports), this entry's prior implication that the stipulated grant-preservation injunction had lapsed after its May 5, 2026 extension deadline: the injunction has instead been extended multiple further times and remains in effect through September 1, 2026, with an August 28, 2026 status report due to determine the next extension; that report's outcome was not identified in this recheck's sourcing.

Both officials who directed the original 2025 cuts have since left office -- Bondi fired as AG in April 2026 (Blanche confirmed permanent successor in August 2026), Noem removed as DHS Secretary in March 2026 (Mullin confirmed successor) -- with no indication either successor has revisited the cuts.

status: Ongoing and formalized — beyond the sustained attorney exodus documented through mid-2026, the division itself was renamed in June 2026 with an explicit mission shift away from environmental enforcement, and Trump has since used the pardon power to unwind Clean Air Act criminal cases the division's remaining attorneys had prosecuted
date_of_action: 2025-01-27 (initial reassignments) through 2025-03-25 (formal DOJ-wide reorganization memo), with effects documented into 2026
what_changed: In the days immediately following Trump's January 20, 2025 inauguration, DOJ began reassigning senior career officials across multiple divisions -- national security, civil rights, and public corruption staff were transferred into a newly created Sanctuary Cities Enforcement Working Group, often into roles outside their expertise. The Environment and Natural Resources Division (ENRD) was hit hardest: all four Environmental Enforcement Section chiefs, including section chief Tom Mariani (who had led the section since 2016), were told they were being involuntarily transferred to the working group; Mariani chose retirement instead, leaving in February 2025. The division's civil-rights-focused work was also frozen -- DOJ reportedly halted all Civil Rights Division cases pending review. Separately, career staff working on environmental-justice and diversity initiatives were placed on administrative leave, incoming Honors Program job offers to new attorneys were rescinded, and DOJ requested a list of probationary employees from the White House, raising concerns about a broader mass-firing push. On March 25, 2025, Deputy Attorney General Todd Blanche issued a formal memorandum cementing a sweeping DOJ-wide reorganization, including further ENRD reassignments to the Office of Sanctuary Cities. Follow-up reporting over a year later (Inside Climate News and E&E News, July-August 2026) found the damage was substantial and lasting: ENRD, which began 2025 with roughly 400 attorneys, had lost at least a third of its lawyers, representing more than 260 combined years of legal experience among just the 11 senior attorneys and managers interviewed; and DOJ's civil environmental lawsuits referred by EPA fell to just 16 in Trump's first year back in office, a 76% drop from the first year of the Biden administration. A separate, October 2025 Bloomberg Law report adds a concrete budget-request figure to this attrition: the administration's FY2026 budget request sought $90 million for ENRD, a 22.5% drop from FY2025, and proposed cutting division staffing from 641 to 449 positions, including 79 attorney positions. The same report quotes former Environmental Enforcement Section head Tom Mariani putting the section's own headcount at roughly 120 lawyers in February 2025, down to 65-70 by October 2025 -- a steeper, more specific decline than the single-digit-months-later 'at least a third' figure this entry already cites from the later Inside Climate News/E&E News reporting, and consistent with it. Section-level detail from the same Inside Climate News/E&E News reporting, not previously broken out in this entry: the Environmental Crimes Section fell from 42 attorneys to roughly 21 (a 50% cut), and the Environmental Enforcement Section dropped to less than half its prior size -- both steeper than the division-wide 'at least a third' figure, consistent with section chiefs and senior staff being disproportionately targeted in the initial 2025 reassignments. In June 2026, DOJ formally renamed ENRD to the Energy and Natural Resources Division, per the department's own press release, explicitly reorienting its stated mission toward 'advancing U.S. energy dominance' rather than environmental protection -- confirmed directly against justice.gov, whose ENRD landing page now carries the new name. On July 3, 2026, Trump pardoned nine people convicted of Clean Air Act violations for installing 'defeat devices' that bypass diesel-engine emissions controls (part of a larger 11-person pardon batch that included non-CAA cases), calling the recipients victims of Biden-era 'persecution' for 'fixing their car'; this followed DOJ's own earlier 2026 directive ordering federal prosecutors to drop pending defeat-device prosecutions, meaning the division's remaining attorneys are now unwinding cases their own predecessors built rather than only losing capacity to bring new ones. Separately, Law360 reported August 19, 2026, citing court filings, that a top deputy in the renamed division left the agency; the deputy's identity and reason for departure were not accessible in sourcing reviewed (Law360's full report sits behind a paywall), so this is noted as an unconfirmed-detail data point rather than asserted as fact.

title: DOJ Reassigned the Senior Attorneys Running Its 60-Year-Old Program Accrediting Non-Lawyers to Help Indigent Immigrants, Freezing Its Core Functions
institution: Department of Justice / Executive Office for Immigration Review
status: Ongoing -- as of late April 2026 reporting, the program had not approved a single new accreditation application since the March 2026 reassignments, and Illinois-based immigration advocacy organizations independently described the office as being 'quietly gutted'; applications continue to accumulate (40-60 per week) with no staff authorized to process them, and no reversal identified in sourcing reviewed
date_of_action: 2026-03 (senior attorneys reassigned)
what_changed: CBS News reported DOJ abruptly reassigned the handful of senior attorneys who operate the Recognition and Accreditation program -- a more than 60-year-old program, administered by DOJ's Executive Office for Immigration Review, that accredits non-attorneys working for largely faith-based legal-aid organizations (such as Catholic Charities and Jewish Family Services) so they are legally authorized to assist low-income immigrants with matters ranging from naturalization petitions to representation in immigration court. The reassignment orders came from Jamee Comans, Acting Assistant Director for DOJ's Office of Policy, which administers the program. Most of the reassigned attorneys were told they would now work as entry-level law clerks in immigration courts -- a role typically reserved for people fresh out of law school -- while only two support staff remained in the accreditation office, neither with legal authority to approve or renew accreditation applications. A DOJ official told CBS the program 'isn't ending or being abolished' and 'will continue,' but confirmed the office kept receiving 40-60 new applications per week even after the reassignment, with no staff able to act on them, creating a growing backlog.

title: DOJ Cuts Over 4,000 Jobs at FBI, ATF, DEA, and National Security Division While Immigration Enforcement Gets More Funding
institution: U.S. Department of Justice (FBI, ATF, DEA, National Security Division)
status: Documented via DOJ's own management-unit records, obtained by Reuters under FOIA and reported April 23, 2026; no reversal or correction identified as of this entry
date_of_action: Cuts accumulated across fiscal year 2024 through early 2026; reported 2026-04-23
what_changed: Justice Department management-unit records obtained by Reuters under the Freedom of Information Act show the Trump administration cut more than 4,000 employees from several of the DOJ's top law-enforcement components even as the administration publicly vowed to get tough on crime. The FBI's total employee count dropped more than 7% since fiscal year 2024, a loss of about 2,600 people. The Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF) lost about 14% of its staff. The Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) lost about 6% of its staff. The National Security Division, which handles intelligence and terrorism matters, lost nearly 38% of its staff -- the steepest cut of any of the components named. One notable exception to the pattern: the arm of DOJ handling immigration enforcement secured billions of dollars in additional funding over the same period, as the administration pushed to increase deportations -- making this both a staffing cut at the named components and a funding redirection toward immigration enforcement specifically.

title: DOJ's Attorney Corps Nearly Cut in Half Since January 2025, With Its Entry-Level Recruitment Pipeline Frozen and a Growing Public Archive of Resignation Letters
institution: U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ) -- department-wide attrition, distinct from this tracker's Civil Rights Division- and Environment Division-specific entries
status: Ongoing (Justice Connection's own more granular full-year count, published April 2026, has not been updated with a fresher figure since; DOJ has not published its own current attorney headcount)
date_of_action: 2025-01 (hiring freeze, Honors Program cancellation) through 2025-11 (Justice Connection's ~5,500-departure estimate, farewell-letters archive reporting)
what_changed: President Trump's January 20, 2025 government-wide federal hiring freeze immediately triggered cancellation of the Attorney General's Honors Program -- DOJ's 'premier' entry-level attorney recruitment pipeline, in place since 1953 and typically responsible for more than 100 hires per year from top law schools. Accepted job offers were revoked, with rescission emails citing the freeze directly; the program was later reopened for the 2025-26 recruiting cycle, but the initial cancellation disrupted a full incoming class and, per legal-trade reporting, left the program with diminished appeal to law students and law-school career offices. Over the following months, DOJ's overall attorney corps -- an estimated 10,000 people before January 2025 -- was, per Washington Post reporting, 'nearly cut in half' by September 2025 through resignations, retirements, reassignments, and terminations; the Appellate Section specifically lost more than 40% of its attorneys since February 2025. Replacement hiring filled only a fraction of the resulting vacancies, and reporting found new hires skewed toward candidates with more overtly political or ideological alignment with the administration, including hires drawn from Republican congressional offices and conservative advocacy groups rather than DOJ's traditional recruitment channels. The understaffing forced DOJ attorneys to repeatedly seek case-schedule delays across multiple active litigation matters, per the ABA Journal. Justice Connection, a support network for departed DOJ staff founded by former DOJ Civil Division attorney Stacey Young, separately estimated in reporting through November 2025 that roughly 5,500 people -- not exclusively attorneys -- had left the department via resignation, transfer, buyout, or termination since January 2025; by November 23, 2025, Young said the cumulative purge had 'eclipsed 5,000 employees.' Justice Connection also maintains a public 'farewell messages' page (thejusticeconnection.org/farewell-messages) that had grown, by that point, into a chronicled archive of DOJ resignation letters, including from senior officials, describing political interference, retaliation, and pressure to pursue cases some departing attorneys viewed as targeting the administration's perceived critics rather than legitimate law-enforcement priorities. This entry documents DOJ's department-wide attorney attrition and recruitment-pipeline collapse; two narrower threads already tracked in this database document specific divisions in more depth -- the Civil Rights Division's roughly 75% attorney exodus (see doj-civil-rights-division-exodus-trump2.json) and the Environment and Natural Resources Division's career-staff purge (see doj-enrd-career-staff-purge-2025.json) -- both consistent with, and contributing to, the department-wide pattern documented here. Update (2026-08-17 recheck): Justice Connection published its own detailed "By the Numbers" accounting on April 7, 2026, covering the full period from January 2025 through January 2026 -- a later, more granular count than the Washington Post/ABA Journal "nearly cut in half" figure this entry originally led with. Justice Connection's own count puts DOJ's attorney corps at 12,955 as of December 31, 2024 (a larger baseline than the ~10,000 figure the Post used) and documents 3,402 attorney departures between January 2025 and January 2026 -- "over a quarter of its legal machinery in a year," per the group's own framing, not a figure it characterizes as nearly half. The breakdown: 1,421 departures from DOJ headquarters (including 338 in leadership roles), 1,356 from U.S. Attorneys' Offices (including 260 leaders), and 370 from the Executive Office for Immigration Review. The average departing employee had 16.6 years of federal service (over 22 years among departing leaders), and 2,069 of the 3,402 resigned before becoming eligible for retirement -- consistent with departures driven by working conditions rather than planned retirements. This is a later, more precise count from the same organization already cited in this entry, not a contradiction from a new or less credible source; it should be read alongside, not as flatly replacing, the earlier Washington Post/ABA Journal reporting, since the two also cover different measurement windows (a September 2025 snapshot vs. a full January 2025-January 2026 year). Update 2026-08-30 (GSR recheck batch 34): identified a formal, dated policy response to the recruitment-pipeline collapse that this entry's existing Honors Program discussion had not captured. On March 13, 2026, DOJ headquarters sent U.S. Attorneys' offices nationwide a memo titled "Suspension of Attorney One Year Experience Requirement," waiving the department's longstanding requirement that newly hired federal prosecutors have at least one year of legal practice experience -- permitting hiring directly from law school with only a law degree and active state bar membership. The suspension, which cites an "exigent hiring need for attorneys across the department," remains in effect through February 28, 2027. Job postings reflecting the change appeared in multiple U.S. Attorneys' offices with documented attrition, including Minnesota, Southern Florida, Montana, Alaska, and Louisiana. Harvard Law School affiliates and former federal prosecutors quoted in press coverage said the policy could expand access to public-service legal careers but risks oversight and mentorship gaps for prosecutors trying cases without prior practice experience. Update 2026-09-01 (GSR recheck batch 52): DOJ leadership imposed a new caseload floor on the prosecutors it has retained -- in the weeks before a July 14, 2026 Bloomberg Law report, the deputy attorney general's office told all 93 U.S. Attorney's offices that Assistant U.S. Attorneys must maintain at least 25 open matters at all times, with DOJ leadership monitoring case-management databases to flag prosecutors falling below that line for possible transfer. DOJ spokesperson Kiersten Pels defended the floor as 'the bare minimum' -- noting hundreds of AUSAs already juggle 100+ open matters -- and framed it as a tool to push out 'low productivity AUSAs.' Former DOJ official Mark Yancey and other critics warned the quota risks pressuring prosecutors, especially those handling long-running white-collar, corruption, or national-security matters that can occupy a full docket for months, into bringing weak or premature charges to hit the number. This is a direct operational consequence of the attorney-corps attrition this entry documents -- a formal productivity mandate imposed on the shrunken remaining workforce rather than a new departure or hiring datapoint.

The experience-requirement waiver is a concrete, department-wide lowering of hiring standards in response to the same shortage.

The experience-waiver memo is independently corroborated across three separate outlets.

title: Trump Halted Labor Department Contractor Civil-Rights Enforcement on Day One, Killing a Near-Complete BAE Systems Sexual-Harassment Case
institution: Department of Labor / Office of Federal Contract Compliance Programs (OFCCP)
status: Complete -- enforcement office's core function halted; underlying investigations, including BAE Systems, not resolved
date_of_action: 2025-01-20 (executive order revoking EO 11246) through 2025-01-24 (DOL acting secretary's cease-and-desist order)
what_changed: On January 20, 2025 -- his first day back in office -- Trump signed an executive order revoking Executive Order 11246, the 1965 order requiring federal contractors to comply with anti-discrimination and affirmative-action obligations, and directed the Department of Labor office enforcing it to stop most of its work. Acting Labor Secretary Vincent Micone followed on January 24 with an order directing DOL staff to 'immediately cease and desist' enforcing contractor compliance under the revoked framework. This effectively shut down the Office of Federal Contract Compliance Programs' active enforcement docket, including a nearly-complete two-year investigation into BAE Systems -- a defense contractor holding roughly $8 billion in annual federal contracts for weapons, vehicles, and cybersecurity tools -- over findings that male managers at a Norfolk, Virginia Navy shipyard had demanded oral sex and other sexual contact from female employees in exchange for promotions and overtime pay, and that Black women had been paid and promoted at lower rates than men. Investigators had been preparing to propose a resolution requiring BAE to make seven-figure payouts to affected workers and adopt reforms, or risk losing its federal contracts; that resolution was never presented as a result of the halt.

title: Defense POW/MIA Accounting Agency Budget Cut Two Years Running, Slashing Recovery Missions for Missing Servicemembers
institution: Defense POW/MIA Accounting Agency (DPAA)
status: Ongoing -- FY2026 cuts already implemented and reducing recovery missions; FY2027 budget capped lower still; new Pentagon oversight (Anthony Tata, assigned June 2026) has pledged to seek roughly $40 million in restored funding via the FY2027 NDAA, but that bill itself remains stalled in the Senate (a July 14, 2026 cloture vote failed) with no House-Senate conference yet convened, so the restoration is not close to secured; DPAA nonetheless conducted its first China recovery mission in 13 years, July-early September 2026, alongside the ongoing budget squeeze
date_of_action: 2025-02 (Hegseth-era Pentagon-wide cost-cutting first put DPAA's budget at risk) through 2026 (FY2026 cuts implemented; FY2027 funding capped)
what_changed: As part of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth's broader Pentagon-wide cost-cutting purge that began in February 2025, the Defense POW/MIA Accounting Agency -- the agency responsible for recovering and identifying America's missing servicemembers from past conflicts -- saw its budget cut across two consecutive fiscal years. The FY2026 budget request was $171.3 million for Operation and Maintenance, an 11% reduction from the previously planned $191.4 million, including the loss of 26 civilian billets; the agency's total budget fell from $185 million in FY2025 to $167 million as enacted for FY2026, with FY2027 projected to be capped at $160 million. The funding shortfall forced DPAA to cut its recovery and investigative teams operating in Vietnam from 27 to seven and in Laos from 13 to five, and reduced planned field missions from 105 to 66 -- a 59% reduction. In June 2026, Anthony Tata was assigned Pentagon oversight of DPAA and sought to reassure affected families that he had Trump and Hegseth's full support, pledging to work toward restoring roughly $40 million of the cuts through a bill then pending before Congress. A July 26, 2026 South Texas Public Radio / American Homefront Project report ('Time is passing') adds a Cambodia-specific figure this entry did not previously capture: recovery/investigative teams there were also cut, from three to one, alongside the Vietnam and Laos cuts already documented. As of that report, no restoration funding had been secured -- Sen. Fischer's push (a bill she introduced in the Senate, distinct from the general FY2026/FY2027 NDAA cycle) remained pending, and Tata's outreach to Congress had not yet produced enacted relief. Separately, CRS's DPAA budget primer (updated 2026-03-09) shows the enacted FY2026 NDAA authorized and Congress appropriated DPAA's full agency-wide budget at $171.8 million, matching the administration's original request exactly -- indicating that a $19 million above-request add Sen. Fischer secured at the Senate Armed Services Committee markup stage in July 2025 did not survive to final enactment. (This $171.8 million CRS figure is DPAA's total appropriated budget across all accounts; it is not directly comparable to the $167 million O&M-specific figure already cited in this entry from DPAA's own O&M budget justification, and this entry does not attempt to reconcile the two beyond noting neither reflects the requested restoration.) Fischer's FY2027 NDAA push for the $40 million restoration referenced in this entry was confirmed still pending as of a June 11, 2026 press release, in which she urged 'swift passage through the Senate' -- consistent with this entry's existing framing that the restoration is sought, not secured. Update 2026-08-30 (GSR recheck batch 32): the FY2027 NDAA vehicle carrying Fischer's restoration provision remains unenacted and is now specifically stalled -- the House passed its own version (H.R. 8800) 219-206 on July 22, 2026, but the Senate's companion bill (S. 4784, reported by the Senate Armed Services Committee 18-9 on June 15, 2026) failed a cloture vote on July 14, 2026 after Senate Democrats blocked floor consideration over objections to the Iran war and the bill's overall defense-spending growth, unrelated to the DPAA provision itself. No House-Senate conference has been established as of this update, meaning the $40 million DPAA restoration remains contingent on a broader defense-policy fight that has nothing to do with POW/MIA recovery specifically. Update 2026-09-01 (GSR recheck batch 48): despite the funding squeeze, DPAA recovery teams conducted a previously undocumented mission in China from roughly July through early September 2026, with an investigative team in Hunan province and field recovery operations in Guangxi province -- DPAA's own announcement describes it as the agency's first recovery mission in China in 13 years. The mission is part of renewed U.S.-China cooperation on MIA recovery that resumed in January 2024, which has since covered Hunan, Guangxi, and Liaoning provinces and included the identification of a World War II 'Flying Tiger' pilot; roughly 678 U.S. personnel remain unaccounted for in China across conflicts from World War II through Vietnam. No source reviewed confirms an outcome (a specific identification or recovery) resulted from this China mission specifically, and the Senate's cloture-vote stalemate on the FY2027 NDAA and the $40 million restoration remained unresolved as of this update -- no further procedural movement was identified beyond the July 14, 2026 failed cloture vote and Leader Thune's subsequent motion to reconsider.

title: USAID/CDC Staff Removals Slowed Response to an Unidentified Deadly Illness Cluster in DRC's Equateur Province -- Cause Never Definitively Confirmed
institution: USAID (in dismantlement) / CDC global health security programs
status: Outbreak clusters resolved/contained by spring 2025; underlying cause never definitively confirmed
date_of_action: 2025-01 (USAID/CDC staff removed from DRC posts, CDC ordered to halt WHO collaboration) through 2025-03 (illness clusters investigated and contained)
what_changed: Beginning in January 2025, two clusters of an unidentified illness caused a wave of deaths in the Bolomba and Basankusu health zones of DRC's Equateur province, eventually totaling roughly 2,969 reported cases and 66 deaths across both clusters. Wired reported that the USAID and CDC staff who would normally work directly with DRC's health ministry to identify and contain such an outbreak had been removed from their DRC posts as part of the agency's dismantlement, and that a separate January 2025 executive order required CDC to cease collaboration with the WHO -- reducing U.S. visibility into and support for the response. USAID had also supported the physical logistics of outbreak response, including training health workers on proper viral-sample storage/shipment and funding the transport of samples from remote areas to central labs; with that support degraded, identifying the cause took longer than it otherwise would have. Laboratory testing ruled out Ebola and Marburg virus disease. WHO and CDC investigators ultimately could not definitively confirm a single cause; leading hypotheses included bacterial meningitis and chemical or food-borne poisoning, with one thread of the investigation tracing part of the Bolomba cluster to three children who died after eating a bat carcass. The clusters were brought under control by late March 2025 without ever being conclusively attributed to a single pathogen or cause.

title: Department of Education Dismantled via Interagency Transfers, Without Congressional Approval
institution: U.S. Department of Education
status: Ongoing (Supreme Court allowed dismantling to continue via McMahon v. New York, July 14, 2025, pending lower-court challenges; Congress has not abolished the department and continues funding it); as of an August 24, 2026 White House event, the administration continues to publicly frame the dismantlement as substantially accomplished while using additional devolution mechanisms -- unrestricted state waivers -- alongside the interagency-transfer strategy already documented
date_of_action: 2025-03 (executive order) through 2026-06 (special education and civil rights transfers, the last core offices remaining)
what_changed: Following a March 2025 Trump executive order directing the department's effective abolition and return of control to the states, Education Secretary Linda McMahon -- following a strategy explicitly drawn from Project 2025, written in part by her now-deputy chief of staff Lindsey Burke -- began signing what would eventually total 14 interagency agreements transferring the department's functions elsewhere, since only Congress can formally eliminate the department itself. K-12, higher education, and workforce training oversight moved to the Department of Labor. On March 21, 2025, Trump separately announced that the Small Business Administration would take over management of the department's $1.6 trillion student loan portfolio; the plan drew immediate legal challenge, and a federal judge blocked the transfer on May 27, 2025, ruling the Higher Education Act assigns that responsibility to the Education Department's Federal Student Aid office and that only Congress could reassign it -- the SBA plan was never carried out, and the portfolio instead began transferring to Treasury in March 2026 as described below. McMahon sought to lay off roughly 1,400 of the department's 4,200 employees in March 2025 (litigated but largely proceeded), halving the department's staff to roughly 2,000. The layoffs' effects were visible within a day: AP News reported more than 300 Federal Student Aid staff were cut, including two dozen from its technology division -- the entire team responsible for the FAFSA systems -- and StudentAid.gov suffered an hours-long outage on March 12, 2025 that blocked students nationwide from completing the federal financial-aid application; laid-off staff, still technically employed through March 21 but with limited system access, struggled to help diagnose the outage, with roughly 70 employees stuck on an hours-long troubleshooting call. The Guardian reported the FSA cuts also gutted the office's compliance function specifically, eliminating the team responsible for policing for-profit-college fraud and abuse in the $1.6 trillion loan program; consumer advocates drew a direct parallel to the late-1980s student-loan crisis, when weak oversight of for-profit schools helped drive a 41% default rate before Congress tightened compliance requirements. An Education Department Inspector General report found 135 of the department's divisions were left with zero employees after the layoffs, and fewer than 20 retained more than five staff. The March 2025 cuts included a reduction-in-force that laid off nearly half of the Office for Civil Rights' staff and shuttered 7 of its 12 regional offices; during the period OCR was short-staffed (March-September 2025), the office received over 9,000 discrimination complaints and dismissed roughly 90% of them without full review. The Supreme Court allowed the dismantling to proceed via McMahon v. New York, decided July 14, 2025 -- an unsigned emergency-docket order staying a Massachusetts district court's May 22, 2025 injunction that had ordered the laid-off employees reinstated, with Justice Sotomayor dissenting, joined by Kagan and Jackson (correcting this entry's prior 'August 2025' date, which was imprecise) -- while litigation continues in lower courts. During the 43-day Oct-Nov 2025 shutdown, 87% of the department's staff were furloughed -- which McMahon later cited as proof the agency was 'nonessential.' The OCR reduction-in-force was rescinded in early January 2026. In February 2026, the department moved additional programs and grants to other federal agencies, including HHS and the State Department, continuing the interagency-transfer dismantlement strategy. A February 2026 GAO report found the March 2025 OCR reduction-in-force had cost taxpayers up to $38 million, since the affected employees were kept on paid administrative leave for nine months while barred from working; GAO concluded the department 'lacks reasonable assurance that its actions achieved the stated goal of reforming the federal workforce' and 'cannot ensure that OCR improved service to the American people.' The Century Foundation found nearly 25% of student-loan borrowers with payments due were delinquent as of February 2026, up from about 9% in 2019 -- roughly 7.9 million borrowers newly entering delinquency -- a sharp rise coinciding with the department's broader administrative disruption. The $1.7 trillion student loan portfolio and federal financial aid administration began transferring to Treasury in March 2026. In June 2026, the department's last two core offices -- the Office for Civil Rights (moving to DOJ) and the Office of Special Education and Rehabilitative Services, which administers IDEA protections for students with disabilities (moving to HHS) -- were also transferred, over the objection of disability advocates who participated in months of listening sessions McMahon's own office convened. Re-verified 2026-07-26: no material change to the core dismantlement/interagency-transfer narrative -- a Ninth Circuit ruling in the related Sweet v. McMahon case (July 17, 2026, on student-loan borrower claim deadlines) concerns a distinct piece of litigation over SAVE-plan borrower claims, not the interagency-transfer dismantlement this entry primarily documents, and is not folded in here. Added 2026-08-11 (round-4 candidate discovery, clusters c0133/c0136): the March 2025 layoffs eliminated some divisions entirely, including the Office of the Chief Data Officer, the unit responsible for tracking student outcomes and program data; departing staff were given roughly 30 minutes to collect their belongings before colleagues held informal 'clap out' hallway send-offs, per ABC News. Separately, 65 probationary employees fired in the department's initial rounds were ordered reinstated on March 17, 2025 by a federal judge in Maryland presiding over a companion 18-agency case (distinct from Judge Alsup's six-agency ruling covering VA/Agriculture/Interior/Energy/Defense/Treasury); the department reinstated them on paper but placed them on paid administrative leave rather than restoring their duties, and some were laid off again as their divisions were shuttered outright. During the 43-day October-November 2025 shutdown, the department issued reduction-in-force notices to 465 additional employees on the shutdown's tenth day, concentrated in the Office of Elementary and Secondary Education, the Office of Special Education and Rehabilitative Services, and the Office of Communications and Outreach; a federal judge called the firings 'likely unlawful' and ordered them paused, and the continuing resolution that ended the shutdown in November nullified the notices outright, barred the department from issuing further RIFs through the end of January 2026, and required back pay for shutdown-affected employees. On November 18, 2025, the department signed interagency agreements outsourcing six additional programs -- including the Department of Labor's assumption of oversight for $28 billion in K-12 grants and $3.1 billion in postsecondary-education grants, effectively outsourcing the Office of Elementary and Secondary Education and Office of Postsecondary Education, two of the department's largest remaining units at the time -- with Indian-education and international-studies programs separately transferred to the Departments of the Interior and State. The Guardian's reporting on this wave described staff being locked out of department accounts without explanation and described collapsing morale as programs were scattered across agencies with little coordination. Reinstated employees also faced broader benefits chaos: CNN reported in May 2025 that department staff who had been reinstated under since-stayed court orders were left without processed health insurance, pensions, or workers'-compensation claims amid a gutted HR function, consistent with the same pattern documented government-wide. title: Education Department Rescinds Disparate-Impact Standard From Title VI Civil Rights Enforcement
institution: U.S. Department of Education, Office for Civil Rights
status: Final rule, effective July 24, 2026
date_of_action: 2026-07-24 (final rule effective)
what_changed: Citing Executive Order 14281, the Department of Education finalized a rule rescinding disparate-impact provisions from its regulations implementing Title VI of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, effective July 24, 2026. Disparate-impact provisions had allowed investigators to find a school policy violated federal civil rights law based on its disproportionate effect on students of a particular race or ethnicity -- demographic outcome data alone -- even without a facially discriminatory policy or proof of discriminatory intent. Under the rescinded standard, federal investigators could challenge practices like discipline policies, tracking/placement decisions, or resource allocation that produced racially disparate outcomes, regardless of intent. The new rule clarifies that Title VI 'prohibit[s] intentional discrimination and do[es] not prohibit conduct or activities that have an unintentional disparate impact,' meaning investigators must now prove a school district specifically intended to discriminate -- a substantially higher evidentiary bar. Roughly 60 civil rights and education organizations publicly condemned the change, warning it 'will hurt Black, Latino, Asian American, and Native American students, other students of color, and other marginalized students who face higher rates of discrimination.'

title: SAVE Student-Loan Plan Dismantled Over 18 Months, From Application Freeze to Full Termination for 7.5 Million Borrowers
institution: Department of Education
status: Finalized -- SAVE plan ended; borrowers given 90 days from the July 1, 2026 servicer-notice start date to select a new plan
date_of_action: 2025-02-24 (online IDR/consolidation applications pulled down) through 2026-07 (90-day replacement-plan selection window begins)
what_changed: On February 18, 2025, the Eighth Circuit Court of Appeals ruled that the Biden-era SAVE (Saving on a Valuable Education) income-driven repayment plan -- which had reduced payments to as little as 5% of a borrower's discretionary income and offered forgiveness after 10 years for borrowers who originally borrowed $12,000 or less -- exceeded the Education Secretary's statutory authority, and directed the lower court to broaden its injunction to block the entire SAVE rule, calling into question the legality of related income-contingent plans (PAYE, REPAYE) as well. Late on February 24, 2025, the Education Department responded by pulling down the online application for all income-driven repayment (IDR) plans and Direct loan consolidation entirely -- not just SAVE -- cutting off enrollment access for borrowers who wanted to switch plans regardless of which IDR plan they were pursuing. By mid-March 2025, the Department had closed applications across every IDR plan and restricted eligibility for Public Service Loan Forgiveness, leaving millions of borrowers unable to access repayment calculators or determine their new payment obligations; some reported being unable to determine whether to take a second job or plan for default. Roughly 7.5 million borrowers who had been placed into interest-free forbearance since July 2024 while the litigation proceeded then saw that forbearance end when interest resumed accruing on their loans August 1, 2025, with the White House characterizing the SAVE plan itself as 'illegal' and borrowers facing a roughly 1.5-million-application backlog as they tried to move onto other repayment plans. On July 18, 2025, Politico reported the Department would deny roughly 460,000 of those backlogged applicants -- about a third of the 1.5 million total -- specifically because they had requested the plan with the lowest available monthly payment, with the Department stating loan servicers could not process those requests since SAVE was no longer a legal option; a December 2025 court filing later put the confirmed denial figure at 327,955 IDR applications rejected in August 2025 alone, citing an 'unforeseen ambiguity' about which plan denied borrowers should be enrolled in instead, with 802,730 IDR applications still pending as of the end of November 2025. The underlying litigation concluded with a court ruling that SAVE was unlawful, and in late March 2026 the Education Department formally directed the same 7.5 million borrowers to prepare to exit SAVE, ending their forbearance for good. Starting July 1, 2026, loan servicers began issuing notices giving borrowers 90 days to select a new repayment plan; the Department's chosen replacement option, a new income-driven plan called the Repayment Assistance Plan, ties payments to income and household size with fixed 10-25-year terms, but results in higher monthly payments for most affected borrowers than SAVE had. Borrowers exiting forbearance without selecting a new plan in time would resume payments automatically under a plan that could be substantially costlier than what they had budgeted for during the intervening period of relief.

title: EEOC Loses Quorum for Nine Months After Trump Fires Two Democratic Commissioners
institution: Equal Employment Opportunity Commission
status: Resolved as a quorum matter (quorum restored October 7, 2025 with Senate confirmation of a third commissioner); the underlying legal challenge to the firings was voluntarily dismissed July 6, 2026 after the Supreme Court's Trump v. Slaughter ruling foreclosed it
date_of_action: 2025-01-28 (firings) through 2025-10-07 (quorum restored); related litigation resolved 2026-07-06
what_changed: On January 28, 2025, President Trump fired EEOC Commissioners Charlotte Burrows and Jocelyn Samuels, both Democratic appointees, along with General Counsel Karla Gilbride -- in the agency's 60-year history, no commissioner had ever before been removed before the end of their term. Burrows's term was not set to expire until 2028, Samuels's not until 2026. Title VII requires three commissioners for the EEOC to have a quorum; without one, the agency could continue routine case processing but could not initiate formal rulemakings or issue, modify, or revoke formal guidance. The agency operated without a quorum for over eight months. In April 2025, Samuels sued Trump, the EEOC, and Chair Andrea Lucas, arguing her termination before the end of her statutory term was unlawful. Quorum was restored October 7, 2025, when the Senate confirmed Brittany Panuccio as a third commissioner, giving the EEOC a 2-Republican (Lucas, Panuccio), 1-Democrat (Kalpana Kotagal) composition, with Lucas subsequently named permanent Chair on November 5, 2025. With quorum restored, the EEOC gained the votes needed to pursue the policy changes documented elsewhere in this dataset, including the EEO-1 data-collection rescission proposal. Samuels's lawsuit remained pending until the Supreme Court ruled 6-3 in Trump v. Slaughter on June 29, 2026, substantially expanding presidential removal power over independent-agency officials and overturning the 91-year-old Humphrey's Executor precedent that had previously insulated such agencies from at-will removal. Concluding the ruling foreclosed her claim, Samuels voluntarily dismissed her lawsuit on July 6, 2026.

title: EEOC Moves to End 60 Years of Mandatory Workplace Demographic Data Collection
institution: Equal Employment Opportunity Commission
status: Ongoing (written comment period closed August 24, 2026 as scheduled; EEOC has not yet issued a final rule and must review the full comment record first)
date_of_action: Early 2025 (removal of Democratic commissioners clears the path) through 2026-06-09 (OMB review of the rescission proposal concludes); final rule still pending as of the last-verified date
what_changed: Early in his second term, President Trump removed the EEOC's Democratic commissioners, eliminating what would have been a blocking minority against a reorientation of the agency's civil rights enforcement priorities under Chair Andrea Lucas. On May 14, 2026, the EEOC submitted a proposed rule to the White House's Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs (OIRA) titled 'Rescission of EEO-1, EEO-2, EEO-3, EEO-4, EEO-5, and Reporting Requirement Under Title VII, the ADA, GINA, and the PWFA.' The proposal would eliminate the mandatory annual and biennial workforce demographic data collections that have applied since 1966 to private employers with 100 or more employees, unions, state and local governments, and public school systems, covering employee race, ethnicity, and sex data across job categories. OIRA concluded its review on June 9, 2026, clearing the way for the proposal to be published in the Federal Register for public comment. As of the last-verified date, the EEOC had not opened its EEO-1 filing portal for 2025 data, leaving employers uncertain whether any further demographic data collection will occur before a final rule is issued. The move follows the EEOC's 2025 decision to rescind the option for employers to report non-binary employees on the form, and a separate, still-pending EEOC proposal to rescind a 1979 regulation permitting voluntary affirmative action plans. Re-verified 2026-07-19: the proposed rule had still not been published in the Federal Register as of this update. The EEOC's own regulatory agenda projects publication in July 2026 with a comment period running into September 2026, and the Commission held a Sunshine Act-noticed meeting on July 17, 2026 that included the draft rescission rule -- both signs publication remains imminent, but no notice-and-comment period had formally opened as of this writing. Update 2026-07-26: On July 21, 2026, the Commission voted 2-1 along party lines to advance the Notice of Proposed Rulemaking, authorizing publication in the Federal Register and opening a 30-day public comment period (narrower than the September 2026 window earlier projected in the EEOC's own regulatory agenda); a public hearing on the proposal is scheduled for August 11, 2026. Employers remain subject to EEO-1 filing obligations for the 2026 cycle in the meantime. At the August 11, 2026 public hearing, roughly 22 witnesses testified; per National Law Review and Ogletree Deakins coverage, most urged the Commission to retain or reform the EEO-1 framework rather than eliminate it outright, with both employer-side and employee-side speakers warning that rescinding standardized reporting would not actually reduce employers' data burden, since the same information could still be sought via investigations, subpoenas, and litigation on a case-by-case basis. The EEOC took no formal action at the hearing itself. Nearly 1,500 public comments had been submitted on the NPRM as of the hearing date; the written comment period runs through August 24, 2026, after which the Commission will review comments before any final rule. Correction 2026-08-29: this entry's prior text described the proposal as covering EEO-1 through EEO-5, based on the May 14, 2026 OIRA-submission title -- but the NPRM as formally published in the Federal Register on July 23, 2026 (91 FR 46332, 'Removal of Reporting Requirements') covers EEO-1 through EEO-6. EEO-2 and EEO-6 have not actually been collected since 1981 and 1993 respectively, so their formal rescission is largely a procedural formality rather than a change to real-world data collection -- the practical stakes remain concentrated in EEO-1 (private employers), EEO-3, EEO-4, and EEO-5 as before. Separately, written comments on the NPRM closed August 24, 2026 as scheduled, with roughly 1,500 comments already submitted as of the August 11 hearing; no final rule had been issued as of this update, and the Commission must review the full comment record first.

title: EPA Moved to Eliminate the 30-Year-Old Energy Star Program; Bipartisan Congressional and Industry Pushback Forced a Transfer to DOE Instead -- Then the Administration Proposed Killing It Again a Year Later

status: Program preserved via interagency transfer, not eliminated -- fully moved to DOE by June 2026 with a congressionally mandated funding floor, but the administration's FY2027 budget (April 2026) proposed eliminating the EPA office that had housed it for a second consecutive year

In January 2026, Congress funded Energy Star at $33 million for FY2026 -- a $1 million increase over the prior year -- and for the first time attached a mandatory minimum annual spending level to the program, an explicit legislative check against future unilateral elimination attempts. Despite that outcome, the administration's FY2027 budget request, released in April 2026, again proposed eliminating EPA's Office of Atmospheric Protection -- the second consecutive year it targeted the office, though Energy Star itself was by then housed at DOE rather than EPA.

status: Court-ordered relief, partial and contested -- a federal judge ruled the mass cancellation unlawful in June 2026 and ordered EPA to resume administering the program through its original September 2026 expiration, while a separate D.C. what_changed: A court filing revealed on April 29, 2025 that EPA was canceling 781 grants under the Biden-era Environmental and Climate Justice Block Grant Program (also referred to as the Environmental and Climate Justice Program), a roughly $2.8 billion fund created by the Inflation Reduction Act to help low-income and minority communities address pollution and climate-related risk; by mid-May 2025, EPA had canceled more than 600 grants totaling over $2.7 billion. title: EPA Issues Reduction-in-Force Notices to 22 Remaining Environmental Justice Staffers, Completing a Two-Year Wind-Down of the Function
institution: Environmental Protection Agency
status: Finalized as to this round -- RIF notices issued; no reversal identified in sourcing reviewed
date_of_action: 2025-02-06 (initial administrative leave) through 2026-02 (RIF notices to the final 22 remaining EJ staffers)
what_changed: EPA's dismantlement of its Environmental Justice function played out as a multi-stage, 'roller coaster' process (E&E News's own description) over roughly a year. On February 6, 2025, EPA placed nearly 170 employees of its Office of Environmental Justice and External Civil Rights (OEJECR) on administrative leave agency-wide. Less than a month later, around March 7, 2025, EPA reinstated dozens of those employees -- reporting suggested this followed new White House guidance and reflected that some of the office's work was legally required -- reassigning the recalled staff to other duties, chiefly managing Community Change Grants and maintaining relationships with communities, tribes, and local/state partners. That reprieve did not hold: on March 12-13, 2025, as part of the same week Administrator Lee Zeldin announced a sweeping 31-rule deregulatory package, EPA shut down all 10 of OEJECR's regional Environmental Justice Divisions and placed 168 employees back on administrative leave. On April 22, 2025, EPA issued formal Reduction in Force (RIF) notices to nearly 200 of those employees, with the agency stating that a total of 280 EJ staffers -- both in Washington and across the regional offices -- would be laid off effective July 31, 2025, while another 175 employees whose roles included statutory functions were reassigned to other EPA offices rather than terminated, undertaken to comply with executive orders eliminating environmental-justice programs across the federal government. Finally, in February 2026, EPA issued RIF notices to the 22 EJ staffers still remaining after the 2025 wave -- among the last people at the agency doing this work in any form -- completing the function's elimination. According to InsideEPA, many of the 22 employees targeted in this final round were staff with disabilities. The American Federation of Government Employees (AFGE) Council 238, which represents EPA employees, publicly condemned the final round; council president Justin Chen said the union was 'outraged by the EPA's decision to issue RIF notices to 22 environmental justice employees whose work ensures that communities disproportionately burdened by environmental hazards receive the protections they are entitled to.'

title: EPA Eliminated Its Scientific Research Office, Placing the Successor Directly Under the Administrator's Political Control
institution: Office of Research and Development (ORD), Environmental Protection Agency
status: Complete (formally eliminated; Congress notified February 2026 that closure is finalized)
date_of_action: 2025-03 (plan first reported) through 2026-02-13 (EPA formally notified Congress of ORD's elimination)
what_changed: EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin announced in May 2025 that the agency's Office of Research and Development -- described by AFGE Council 238 President Justin Chen as 'the heart and brain of the EPA' -- would be eliminated and its scientists redistributed into other EPA program offices. On July 18, 2025, EPA formally announced ORD's elimination and the creation of a replacement, the Office of Applied Science and Environmental Solutions (OASES). Unlike ORD, which operated as its own independent division, OASES was placed directly under the EPA Administrator's office -- a structural change critics say subjects scientific research directly to political oversight rather than insulating it. Notably, 'research' does not appear anywhere in the new office's name, which former ORD senior science adviser Andy Miller said reflects what the reorganization was actually designed to eliminate: 'the kind of work that points out that there are still problems.' More than 300 ORD staff, including senior scientists, had already left via deferred-resignation offers before the formal announcement. As many as 1,155 of ORD's 1,540 positions -- chemists, biologists, toxicologists, and other scientists across 10 facilities nationwide -- were identified as at risk of layoff in documents reviewed by Democratic staff on the House Science Committee. EPA notified Congress on February 13, 2026 that the office's elimination was finalized, roughly nine months after Zeldin first announced the plan; the agency has not disclosed which offices remaining former-ORD employees were transferred to, or when OASES's top leadership positions would be permanently filled. Added 2026-08-11 (round-4 candidate discovery, cluster c0128): the plan was reported on before Zeldin's formal May announcement -- the New York Times reported on March 17, 2025 that EPA planned to lay off up to 1,155 ORD scientists, chemists, and toxicologists as part of a proposed 65% cut to the agency's budget, the same at-risk-positions figure later confirmed in the documents reviewed by House Science Committee Democratic staff and cited above. Wired separately reported in May 2025 that the reorganization specifically threatened the future of IRIS (the Integrated Risk Information System), ORD's program for assessing chemical health risks and a longstanding target of the chemical industry precisely because its independent findings support environmental regulation; IRIS staff were told to reapply for fewer roles, and the program's leader stepped down around the same time.

primary_proponent.name: Lee Zeldin
primary_proponent.role: EPA Administrator
primary_proponent.note: Personally announced and defended the reorganization, framing the mass layoffs using the government euphemism 'reduction in force' and stating it would ensure the agency could 'better fulfill that mission while being responsible stewards of your hard-earned tax dollars.' An EPA spokesperson separately described the restructuring as reflecting 'an unwavering commitment to gold-standard science' through 'integration of scientific expertise directly into EPA's offices' -- the administration's stated rationale is that embedding scientists in program offices improves rather than diminishes the agency's science capacity, a claim directly disputed by the researchers and former officials quoted below. This is the same EPA Administrator whose actions are covered in several deregulation-tracker entries in this project (endangerment finding rescission, MATS mercury standards, etc.) -- this entry covers the elimination of the scientific research infrastructure underlying those separate regulatory actions, not the regulatory actions themselves.

estimated_impact.summary: Independent scientists outside EPA identified specific, concrete functions at risk: ORD maintained toxicology databases used by state and local governments, industry, and nonprofits to assess chemical risks, and its atmospheric/hydrologic models are used by researchers worldwide to study pollutants like particulate matter and ozone. Allen Burton, an environmental scientist at the University of Michigan, specifically warned the closure could delay or prevent new methods for assessing risks from chemical mixtures (which can differ meaningfully from individual-substance risk, a core ORD research function). Rep. Zoe Lofgren, ranking Democrat on the House Science Committee, called it a 'travesty' with 'generational impacts on Americans' health and safety.'

title: FAA Air Traffic Controller Shortage — Chronic Structural Crisis, Acutely Worsened by 2025 Shutdown
institution: Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), Department of Transportation
status: Ongoing, unresolved (FAA released a new workforce plan in 2026; current administrator says full staffing may never be reached under the existing structure; a congressionally funded controller pay raise remains undisbursed months after enactment)

what_changed: IMPORTANT ATTRIBUTION NOTE: unlike most entries in this tracker, this is predominantly a chronic, multi-administration structural problem, not a single action taken by the current administration. GAO's own December 2025 report traces the roots to the 2013 budget sequester (which froze hiring), the 2018-2019 shutdown (35 days, further hiring/training delays), and COVID-19 (FAA Academy training suspended 4 months in 2020, reduced-rate training through 2022). The controller workforce declined about 6% since 2015 even as flight volume rose ~10%; the FAA employed 13,164 controllers at the end of FY2025, and 19 of the 30 largest facilities are staffed below 85% of FAA's own targets. What IS specific to the current administration: the 43-day Oct-Nov 2025 shutdown further disrupted hiring and training pipelines and forced acute flight reductions (see the related, separate entry on the FAA's 10% traffic cut at 40 airports). Current FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford told Congress in December 2025 that towers would 'never' reach full staffing under the agency's existing structure, stating plainly: 'The system is designed to be chronically understaffed.' Separately, a 2025 proposal to build a second controller training academy (to relieve the bottleneck at the single Oklahoma City academy) was blocked in Congress amid cost and oversight objections, despite FAA and safety experts' warnings that one campus cannot produce enough certified controllers quickly enough. The FAA's new 2026 workforce plan, released in May 2026, resolved the staffing gap partly by lowering the goal itself: full-staffing target dropped from the 14,633 controllers the agency had forecast needing in 2024 to 12,563, a reduction of more than 2,000 positions from the prior target -- the FAA frames this as a modernization-driven reassessment of actual need, not merely redefining the shortfall away, but the effect is that a large share of the 'gap closing' reflects a lower bar rather than more controllers hired. As of June 2026, the FAA was roughly 3,000 certified controllers below even its original, higher target (about 10,800 actual against a ~13,800 historical goal). The staffing shortfall had concrete summer-2026 consequences: the FAA capped Chicago O'Hare at 2,708 scheduled daily operations from May 17 through October 24, 2026, a nearly 15% cut from airline-planned schedules, with New York and Southern California TRACONs also cited as most strained. Re-verified 2026-07-26: no material change to the core FAA civilian-controller narrative; a July 21, 2026 DoD Inspector General report on military air-traffic-controller shortages concerns a separate workforce (military, not FAA/DOT) and is not folded into this entry. Update 2026-08-30 (GSR recheck batch 34): Congress funded an additional 2.8% pay increase for controllers (enacted April 2026, intended to bring 2026 controller compensation in line with the 3.8% raise military personnel received), but as of mid-to-late August 2026 -- roughly four months later -- the raise had still not reached controllers' paychecks. FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford has tied disbursement to the union agreeing to broader schedule/staffing-utilization reforms, telling reporters 'if we can figure out how we can engage with...the union leadership on the basic watch schedule questions...there's no reason we can't unlock it this year'; the FAA's 2026-28 workforce plan argues controllers' average 'time on position' during 8-hour shifts (currently ~4 hours) could rise past 5 hours through modernized scheduling. A statute reportedly gives the FAA Administrator 'sole discretion' over whether operational improvements justify releasing the retroactive raise -- meaning Bedford is using an already-enacted, congressionally funded pay increase as leverage for a separate policy concession from NATCA, rather than a simple implementation delay. NATCA did not respond to the reporting outlet's requests for comment on the delay or on Bedford's remarks.

title: FAA Cut Flights 10% at 40 Major Airports After Unpaid Controllers Began Missing Work
institution: Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), Department of Transportation
status: Complete (implemented and later lifted after shutdown ended)
date_of_action: 2025-11-05 (announced); ramped from 4% to 10% between Nov. 7-14, 2025
what_changed: During the 43-day Oct-Nov 2025 government shutdown -- the longest in U.S. history -- air traffic controllers, deemed 'essential' employees required to work without pay, began missing shifts in increasing numbers as the shutdown dragged on, compounding the FAA's already-chronic staffing shortage (see related structural staffing entry). Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford announced a mandatory flight-capacity reduction at 40 'high-volume' airports nationwide, ramping from 4% on Nov. 7 to 10% by Nov. 14, affecting an estimated 3,500-4,000 flights daily. Both officials described the move as unprecedented -- Bedford, with 35 years in aviation, said he 'could not recall a similar situation.' Duffy publicly warned the cuts could escalate to 15-20% if the shutdown continued, and separately said he could 'shut the whole airspace down' if it dragged on further. The order also restricted private jets from high-traffic airports to preserve capacity for commercial aviation. The reduction produced immediate, measurable disruption: over 1,000 flights canceled the first day, more than 2,900 cancellations and 10,000+ delays the following Sunday, and by the second weekend nearly 2,200 cancellations in a single day.

title: FBI Told to Stop Investigating Confrontations Involving Immigration Agents, Shifting Oversight to ICE's Own Investigative Arm
institution: Federal Bureau of Investigation / DHS Homeland Security Investigations
status: Guidance reportedly distributed and in effect per internal emails reviewed by CBS News; DOJ and DHS have publicly denied any policy change

what_changed: The New York Times reported, and CBS News independently confirmed via internal emails reviewed by its reporters, that FBI agents around the country were told in mid-July 2026 that the FBI would no longer investigate confrontations involving immigration agents -- including assault-on-a-federal-officer cases that can arise from violent encounters between ICE agents and members of the public. title: FBI Scaled Back Staffing and Scrapped a Tracking Tool for Domestic Terrorism Investigations
institution: Federal Bureau of Investigation / Department of Homeland Security
status: Ongoing and escalated -- a Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee report from Ranking Member Gary Peters (D-MI), released 2026-07-30, documents a broader institutional pullback beyond the March 2025 DTOS reassignments already in this entry: roughly 15,000 positions cut across DOJ and the FBI combined, and 1,300 DHS personnel cut from roles involved in preventing, countering, and responding to terrorism. The report also found the administration has skewed its domestic-terrorism focus almost exclusively toward left-wing groups while removing from public view a DOJ study showing far-right extremist attacks have outpaced all other categories of domestic terrorism since 1990; AG Bondi's December 4, 2025 directive formalizing an 'Antifa-aligned extremists' investigative priority is the primary-source mechanism behind that finding. No final decision on formally disbanding DTOS itself has been independently confirmed in sourcing reviewed for this recheck.
date_of_action: 2025-03 (initial reassignments and tool scrapping); 2025-04 (congressional oversight letter)
what_changed: FBI leadership transferred roughly 16 agents and intelligence analysts out of the Bureau's Domestic Terrorism Operations Section (DTOS), which supports domestic-terrorism investigations run out of all 55 FBI field offices and would have hundreds of employees if fully staffed, Reuters reported (citing sources familiar with the matter) on 2025-03-21. The FBI also scrapped a tool used to track domestic terrorism cases. Senior FBI officials discussed disbanding the section entirely, though no final decision had been announced as of the reporting. Agents were being redirected instead to assist the administration's immigration enforcement crackdown, while attacks on Tesla property were newly classified and prioritized as domestic terrorism. Domestic terrorism investigations have in recent years disproportionately involved violence tied to right-wing and anti-government ideologies, and FBI Director Kash Patel has been a public critic of the Bureau's domestic-terrorism investigative effort. Sen. Dick Durbin (D-IL), Ranking Member of the Senate Judiciary Committee, sent a formal oversight letter to DHS Secretary Kristi Noem and Director Patel on 2025-04-08 documenting a broader institutional pullback beyond the FBI reassignments alone: DHS had also dismantled a national database tracking domestic extremism and hate crimes and cut funding for domestic-terrorism-prevention programs supporting community groups and local law enforcement. Durbin's letter cited FBI's own data showing a 357% increase in domestic terrorism investigations between 2013 and 2021 (from 1,981 to 9,049 cases) as the backdrop against which the cuts were occurring, and urged DHS and the FBI to reverse the resource reallocations. Update 2026-08-17: A Senate HSGAC report from Ranking Member Gary Peters, released 2026-07-30 ("Peters Report Finds Trump Administration Has Dismantled Critical Counterterrorism Infrastructure and Weaponized What Remains Against Political Opponents"), documents roughly 15,000 positions cut across DOJ and the FBI combined and 1,300 DHS personnel cut from counterterrorism-related roles, a larger institutional pullback than the ~16-agent DTOS reassignment this entry originally documented. The report also found the administration's domestic-terrorism enforcement focus has shifted almost exclusively to left-wing targets, and that a DOJ study showing far-right extremist attacks have outpaced all other domestic-terrorism categories since 1990 was quietly removed from the department's website. Several outlets covering the report describe DTOS's entire remaining staff as having been reassigned, but that specific claim could not be independently confirmed against the report's own text or another primary source in this recheck; it is not asserted as fact here. Update 2026-08-30 (correction -- a primary source for the report's 'skewed toward left-wing groups' finding, missed until now): Attorney General Pam Bondi issued a domestic-terrorism directive on December 4, 2025, predating the Peters report by nearly eight months, that explicitly prioritizes investigation of 'Antifa-aligned extremists' -- defined in the memo to include those holding 'extreme viewpoints on immigration, radical gender ideology, and anti-American sentiment' -- and directs DOJ to prioritize grant funding to state/local law enforcement for domestic-terrorism programs tied to that focus. The memo also orders Joint Terrorism Task Forces to use 'all available investigative tools' to map suspected networks, requires the FBI to compile and update every 30 days a domestic-terrorist-organization list, establishes a cash-reward tip line, and orders a retrospective five-year review of agency files for Antifa-related intelligence to be transmitted to the FBI for potential new prosecutions. This directive is the concrete administrative mechanism behind the ideological-skew finding this entry already cites from the Peters report, not merely a restatement of it.

title: FDA Suspended a 40-Lab Bird Flu Milk-Testing Exercise After Eliminating Its Food Safety Lab, Then Suspended Grade-A Milk Testing Outright
institution: Food and Drug Administration (FDA), Department of Health and Human Services

what_changed: As part of the broader 2025 HHS staffing reductions (which cut roughly 3,500 FDA employees overall), the FDA eliminated its Human Food Program's Moffett Center food-safety laboratory in Illinois, including a key quality-assurance officer.
