title: Fish and Wildlife Service Loses Over 1,500 Staff; Zero New Species Listed as Endangered
institution: U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service
status: Ongoing (staffing and budget cuts continue and a further round is proposed for FY2027; the zero-new-listings streak this entry was built around ended July 21, 2026, when FWS finalized endangered status for three Florida Keys reptiles -- the term's first new listings after roughly 18 months at zero; 400+ species remain in the backlog)
date_of_action: 2025-01 to 2026-02 (staffing reductions); ongoing effects on listing backlog through the last-verified date
what_changed: Between January 2025 and February 2026, the Fish and Wildlife Service saw a net reduction of 1,538 employees, according to Office of Personnel Management data compiled by the Congressional Research Service, with independent analyses from the Center for Biological Diversity estimating the cuts included more than 500 biologists specifically. The Interior Department separately proposed a FY2026 budget cutting the agency's Endangered Species Act listing-activity funding by 36% year-over-year, part of an overall reduction in FWS's average annual appropriations from roughly $1.94 billion (2017-2025 average) to approximately $1.6 billion for FY2026; the same budget proposed eliminating funding for the State and Tribal Wildlife Grant program entirely. The Service also discontinued its Refuge System Strategic Growth Policy and, according to conservation groups, has effectively stopped conducting the annual Florida panther population count last performed in 2015. As of reporting in April 2026, the Fish and Wildlife Service had added zero new species to the federal endangered or threatened species list during Trump's second term, compared to 22 species added during the entirety of his first term, a gap the Center for Biological Diversity described as the longest period without a new listing decision since the Endangered Species Act was implemented. A backlog of more than 400 species remains pending final agency listing decisions. Recent Federal Register activity through mid-July 2026 continues the zero-new-listings pattern with specific examples: on June 16, 2026, FWS found listing 'not warranted' for two petitioned species (Sangre de Cristo peaclam, black-backed tanager); on July 14, 2026, FWS issued 90-day findings (a preliminary step, not a listing decision) for 10 more petitioned species including the Cascade red fox and plains spotted skunk; and on the same day, FWS rejected -- for the second time -- a petition to list long-tailed macaque monkeys. None of this recent activity constitutes an actual new listing, consistent with the entry's core finding. Separately, in June 2026 FWS announced a partnership with Colossal Biosciences to collect and cryopreserve cell/tissue samples from every species on the endangered list -- a genomic-preservation initiative distinct from, and not a substitute for, the listing process itself. CORRECTION 2026-07-26: on July 21, 2026, FWS finalized endangered-species status for three Florida Keys reptiles -- the Florida Keys mole skink, Key ring-necked snake, and rim rock crowned snake -- effective August 20, 2026. These are the first new species listings of Trump's second term, ending the zero-listings streak that was this entry's central, headline finding; the listing process itself took 14 years from initial proposal to finalization, so this reflects the conclusion of a long-pending case rather than a change in the administration's overall listing pace. Separately, FWS finalized an Endangered Species Act regulatory change in July 2026 removing the 'blanket rule' option that had automatically extended full endangered-level protections to newly listed threatened species by default, a change conservation groups argue weakens protection for future threatened listings even as it doesn't affect already-endangered species like these three. The 400+ species backlog and FY2026 budget/staffing cuts already documented in this entry are unaffected by this correction and remain current. Re-verified 2026-08-17: no new species listings or budget/staffing changes identified beyond the July 21, 2026 Florida Keys listings (effective August 20, 2026) already documented above; the 400+ species backlog remains the entry's current standing figure. CORRECTION 2026-08-30: this entry's FY2026 budget/staffing figures were missing the agency's own forward-looking FY2027 budget request, submitted to Congress in April 2026 (predating this entry's original write-up but never previously incorporated). That request proposes cutting FWS's total discretionary funding a further 20% ($1.65 billion enacted FY2026 to a requested $1.33 billion for FY2027) and its total employee count a further 10% (6,513 to 5,861), on top of the 1,538-employee reduction already documented above, and would zero out discretionary funding entirely for five FWS accounts including the Cooperative Endangered Species Conservation Fund and the State and Tribal Wildlife Grant program (whose FY2026 elimination this entry already noted). Notably, in P.L. 119-74 (the enacted FY2026 Interior appropriations law), Congress directed FWS to maintain staffing levels sufficient to fulfill its statutory responsibilities -- a direct tension with the administration's own FY2027 staffing-cut proposal that CRS's analysis flags explicitly. No FY2027 appropriations had been enacted as of this recheck, and no new species listings were identified beyond the three Florida Keys reptiles already documented.

title: DOGE Shut Down GSA's 18F Tech Unit; IRS Then Killed the Free Direct File Tax Program It Built
institution: General Services Administration (GSA) / Internal Revenue Service
status: Implemented -- 18F shuttered March 2025; IRS Direct File permanently discontinued, not available for Filing Season 2026
date_of_action: 2025-03 (18F shutdown) through 2025 (Direct File discontinued for the 2026 filing season)
what_changed: In February 2025, Elon Musk announced on social media that he had 'deleted' the team behind IRS Direct File, the free government tax-filing tool. In March 2025, DOGE shut down 18F entirely -- the roughly 90-person General Services Administration digital-services unit that had built or supported Direct File and other federal websites and digital tools for two decades. IRS staff assigned to Direct File were told in mid-March 2025 to stop developing it for the 2026 filing season, even though officials initially indicated the tool would stay operational through the 2025 season. Direct File accepted 296,531 tax returns in the 2025 filing season, with 94% of surveyed users rating their experience 'excellent' or 'above average,' and had been offered in 25 states. The IRS ultimately emailed those 25 states that 'IRS Direct File is now closed for Filing Season 2025' and confirmed the program would not be available for Filing Season 2026, with no relaunch date set.

primary_proponent.role: Musk publicly announced 18F's elimination and directed DOGE's cuts across GSA; IRS leadership implemented the subsequent Direct File shutdown

title: GSA Gutted the Staff Responsible for 26,000 Federally Owned Artworks, Then Listed Buildings Holding Statutorily Protected Murals for Sale -- Prompting a Senate IG-Audit Request
institution: General Services Administration (GSA) -- Fine Arts Program / Art in Architecture Program, Public Buildings Service
status: Ongoing risk, but with a possible reprieve signaled -- a GSA official told a Public Buildings Reform Board hearing in late June 2026 the agency may cancel the Cohen Building's sale over infrastructure-separation costs, though the building remains on the accelerated-disposal list and no final decision has been announced; House Democrats introduced the PRESERVE Act in July 2026 to force GSA to identify and protect at-risk artworks agency-wide, and GSA's response to the March 2026 Senate document request was still not identified in sourcing reviewed
date_of_action: 2025-03-11 (staff cuts and regional office closures first reported) through 2026-03-11 (Senate letter requesting GSA Inspector General audit)
what_changed: In March 2025, following Trump's Executive Order 14210 directing a Department of Government Efficiency-driven Reduction in Force, GSA's Fine Arts Program -- the small division responsible for preserving and tracking the federal government's collection of roughly 26,000 artworks, more than 23,000 of them New Deal-era pieces dating to the 1930s-40s -- lost at least five of its regional offices and placed more than half of its roughly three-dozen staff on leave pending termination. GSA's broader Public Buildings Service lost 44% of its full-time employees in the same reorganization. Regional impact varied sharply: the Mid-Atlantic Region 3 office alone lost over 100 workers across fine-arts officers, project managers, and engineers, leaving only about a quarter of its staff in place. Simultaneously, GSA began listing federal properties for accelerated disposal -- 46 by February 18, 2026 -- some of which house Fine Arts Collection works including textiles, sculptures, and paintings. The clearest flashpoint is the Wilbur J. Cohen Building in Washington, D.C. (former Social Security Administration headquarters), which GSA listed for sale and which contains statutorily protected New Deal murals by Ben Shahn ('The Meaning of Social Security'), Seymour Fogel, and Philip Guston, chemically bonded to the walls and unable to be removed without major cost and risk. GSA has said it will seek preservation covenants with any buyer but has not detailed how it would enforce continued access, insurance, or maintenance once the building passes into private ownership. On March 11, 2026 -- exactly one year after the initial cuts were first reported -- Sens. Sheldon Whitehouse (ranking member, Environment and Public Works) and Chuck Schumer sent GSA Administrator Ed Forst a formal document and information request, and separately asked GSA's own Inspector General to conduct an updated audit of the Fine Arts Program (the IG's last such audit was in 1994), citing the staffing cuts, the accelerated-disposal list, and the Cohen Building murals specifically as reasons for concern. No response from GSA to either request was identified in sourcing reviewed as of this entry. Update 2026-08-30: Two developments emerged since the March 2026 Senate letter. First, at a Public Buildings Reform Board hearing on Thursday, June 25, 2026, GSA senior analyst Rich Butterworth signaled for the first time that the agency wants to potentially cancel the Cohen Building's sale -- not over the murals, but because the building shares underground utilities with the adjacent Mary E. Switzer Memorial Federal Building, making separation 'extremely expensive to replicate or sever'; he suggested the building might be 'better reinvested in' unless that infrastructure problem is solved. This is a change in direction, not a final decision -- the building remained on GSA's accelerated-disposal list as of this update, and preservation advocates (Living New Deal) described the signal as cause for only cautious optimism. Second, on Monday, July 14, 2026, Reps. Dina Titus (D-Nev.) and Lloyd Doggett (D-Texas) introduced the PRESERVE Act (Protecting Resources and Ensuring Stewardship of Enduring Records of Visual Expression), which would require GSA to determine within 30 days whether any property slated for disposal contains protected artwork, notify Congress within another 30 days, convene an expert preservation committee at least 90 days before any demolition or sale, and post a public preservation plan -- protections its sponsors say would cover all 26,000 pieces in GSA's Fine Arts Collection, not just the Cohen Building murals. The bill is a Democratic-sponsored proposal with no Republican co-sponsors identified in sourcing reviewed and had not received a committee vote as of this update; it does not itself change GSA's authority or obligations unless enacted. Separately, sourcing reviewed notes the Cohen Building's sale is compelled by a Biden-era statutory requirement (a Sen. Joni Ernst amendment enacted January 2025) mandating disposal within two years of the building's last federal tenant departing, meaning Congress -- not GSA alone -- would likely need to act to permanently halt the sale even if GSA itself no longer wants to proceed.

title: GSA Briefly Published a 443-Property Sale List That Included a Sensitive CIA Facility, Then Pulled It the Next Day
institution: General Services Administration (GSA)
status: List retracted within a day; a smaller, scaled-back 'accelerated disposition' list released later without full details on the original larger list's fate
date_of_action: 2025-03-04 (list published) through 2025-03-05 (list removed)
what_changed: On March 4, 2025, GSA published a list of 443 federally owned properties -- comprising nearly 80 million rentable square feet and representing more than $8.3 billion in deferred recapitalization needs -- that the agency identified as 'not core to government operations' and intended to dispose of, as part of DOGE's broader push to shrink the federal government's real-estate footprint. The list included the Parr-Franconia Warehouse Complex in Springfield, Virginia, a facility long rumored to house a clandestine CIA training site used for surveillance, hacking, and break-in tradecraft instruction, according to Wired. Local officials and national-security experts immediately raised alarms about the security implications of publicly listing such a facility for sale, even if inadvertently. Facing that backlash -- and broader public and congressional pushback covering other listed sites, including FBI and Red Cross headquarters buildings -- GSA pulled the entire list on March 5, one day after publication, quietly scrubbing more than 120 properties including the Springfield site. An internal GSA email said the list would be republished later 'with adjustments to make it easier for stakeholders to understand the nuances of the assets listed,' citing 'an overwhelming amount of interest.' GSA subsequently released a smaller list of properties identified for an 'accelerated disposition' process, while withholding details about its plans for the larger original list.

status: Partially reversed -- a December 18, 2025 federal court order forced GSA to pause further layoffs and rescind its April 2025 RIF notices; the preceding USDS and 18F cuts were not reversed, and TTS had already lost 67% of its workforce since January 25, 2025

what_changed: In February 2025, roughly a third of U.S. Digital Service (USDS) staff were terminated via a mass, largely anonymous email as part of Elon Musk and DOGE's restructuring, affecting civil servants who worked on tax-filing, healthcare, student-aid, disaster-relief, and veterans-services technology systems; 21 remaining USDS technologists then resigned in protest, writing to the White House that they would not 'carry out or legitimize' DOGE's actions. In March 2025, DOGE eliminated GSA's roughly 90-person 18F digital-services unit entirely -- documented separately in this tracker's [[gsa-18f-shutdown-direct-file-2025]] entry on the resulting shutdown of the IRS's free Direct File tax tool. Employee frustration over the cuts became publicly visible on March 21, 2025, when Wired reported that a GSA all-hands meeting -- attended by hundreds in person and thousands more online -- turned confrontational after Ehikian unveiled a new internal generative-AI chatbot (GSAi) rather than answering questions about the ongoing reductions in force; staff responded to an internal post with over 100 'thumbs up' reactions to the comment 'We don't want an AI demo, we want answers,' also citing lost access to critical software and the concurrent return-to-office mandate as sources of frustration. In April 2025, GSA's then-acting administrator Stephen Ehikian and Technology Transformation Services (TTS) Director Thomas Shedd announced a further reduction-in-force aiming to cut TTS's workforce roughly in half, limiting its work to statutorily required and administration-designated 'critical' functions; GSA sent approximately 130 RIF-intent notices to staff in the Office of the Integrated Award Environment (IAE, which underpins core federal contracting systems), the Office of Regulatory and Oversight Systems, and parts of the Office of Solutions, while explicitly sparing FedRAMP, Login.gov, and Cloud.gov. By the time of a later court intervention, TTS had lost 67% of its total workforce since January 25, 2025. On December 18, 2025, a federal judge ruled that several agencies -- including GSA, the Department of Education, the State Department, and the Small Business Administration -- had to pause layoffs and rescind RIF notices issued since October 1, 2025, to comply with the spending law that had ended the government shutdown; GSA's Shedd subsequently rescinded the April notices sent to the roughly 130 IAE/Regulatory-and-Oversight/Solutions employees.

title: Trump Closed the White House Gun Violence Prevention Office and Cut $150M+ From Community Violence Intervention Grants
institution: White House Office of Gun Violence Prevention; DOJ Office of Justice Programs Community Violence Intervention and Prevention Initiative
status: Ongoing -- office remains closed; DOJ reopened a restructured version of the Community Violence Intervention and Prevention Initiative (CVIPI) grant program in 2025, but community violence intervention organizations can no longer apply for funding directly and must now route through law enforcement or city/state/tribal government intermediaries, with a new DHS data-sharing condition that grantees describe as excluding immigrant-serving organizations; piecemeal funding restorations have followed agency appeals, though full terms remain unsettled as of mid-2026
date_of_action: 2025-01-21 (White House office closed) through 2026-07 (continued hospital-based program funding losses reported)
what_changed: Less than 24 hours into his second term, on January 21, 2025, Trump closed the White House Office of Gun Violence Prevention and took its website offline. The Department of Justice's Office of Justice Programs subsequently cut roughly half of its $300 million Community Violence Intervention and Prevention Initiative -- about $145 million in grants for violence-intervention programs and training/technical assistance, plus $8.6 million for evaluation and research -- and in April 2025 terminated 365 previously awarded grants affecting more than 550 organizations across 48 states. The DOJ's 2026 budget proposal further reduced funding for these programs by $850 million, a 15% year-over-year decrease. Lawmakers sent a May 2, 2025 letter urging the White House to reinstate more than $150 million in canceled DOJ grants. Separately, hospital-based violence intervention programs -- which pair trauma-informed case management with gunshot-injury patients to reduce repeat violence -- have reduced staff or shut down entirely after losing federal funding, despite a documented evidence base showing these programs reduce repeat victimization and retaliatory violence. Justice Department officials have also directed the department to challenge state-level gun restrictions. Re-verified 2026-08-17: no material change identified -- no news of the office's reopening, restored CVIPI grant funding, or a resolution to the proposed further 15% DOJ funding cut since this entry was added. Update 2026-08-30 (GSR recheck batch 41, real correction): this entry's prior recheck (2026-08-17) found "no material change" -- that was incomplete. DOJ's Office of Justice Programs subsequently released a restructured Notice of Funding Opportunity reopening CVIPI funding, but under materially different terms: community violence intervention organizations are "no longer eligible to apply directly for the funds," per Everytown Support Fund's June 5, 2026 report -- groups must now access financing through law enforcement or city/state agencies acting as intermediaries. Organizations receiving the restructured funds must also agree to share data with the Department of Homeland Security, which one grantee described to Everytown as "a poison pill" that effectively excludes immigrant-serving organizations from participation. The same report describes "piecemeal restorations" following agency appeals and references ongoing litigation, though exact amounts and timelines remain unclear; as of the report's June 2026 publication, organizations were still laying off staff and operating at reduced capacity. Sen. Chris Murphy sent Attorney General Pam Bondi a December 11, 2025 letter objecting specifically to the changed grant conditions excluding community-based organizations from direct funding eligibility.

title: Hundreds of U.S.-Trained Nurses Are Emigrating to Canada Amid Healthcare Workforce Policy Turmoil

what_changed: NPR reported that the flow of U.S.-trained nurses relocating to Canada accelerated sharply since Trump returned to office: British Columbia alone approved 1,028 American nurses for licensure since April 2025, up from just 112 approvals in all of 2023 and 127 in 2024 -- roughly an eightfold increase. Alberta's provincial government has committed roughly $7 million to recruit internationally trained nurses specifically from the United States and United Kingdom, plus an additional $1 million to support nurses relocating to the province, and nursing associations in both Ontario and Alberta report increased interest from American applicants. British Columbia's own total through January 2026 was refined slightly to 1,038 U.S. nurses and nurse practitioners registered since April 2025 (consistent with, not a change from, the 1,028 figure already in this entry).

title: Hegseth Cut Pentagon Civilian-Casualty Prevention Staff From ~200 to Fewer Than 40, Over Senior Generals' Objections, Then Replaced Assessments With AI
institution: Department of Defense (Civilian Protection Center of Excellence and related civilian-harm-mitigation offices)
status: Ongoing/finalized as to the original cuts -- a partial-restoration proposal (Under Secretary of Policy Elbridge Colby's April 2026 plan to rebuild CHMR to 70 full-time staff, 35% of original capacity, under Joint Staff rather than Army oversight) has the polled commanders' support but was not confirmed as implemented in sourcing reviewed as of this recheck; separately, a DoD Inspector General evaluation found the post-cut structure violates two federal statutes governing civilian-harm-mitigation compliance, a finding Colby has disputed rather than resolved
date_of_action: 2025-03 (Guardian first reported the office was on the chopping block) through late 2025 (further decline to 9 staff at the Civilian Protection Center of Excellence)
what_changed: The cuts documented in this entry began drawing press notice earlier than Politico's March 2026 report on the generals' objections: The Guardian reported on March 15, 2025 that the Civilian Harm Mitigation and Response office and the Civilian Protection Center of Excellence were already on the chopping block as part of Hegseth's broader reshaping of the Pentagon, and The Intercept reported on April 15, 2025 that the civilian-protection mission had been slashed by about 90% by that spring, leaving only a handful of staffers even as strike tempo accelerated across Africa and the Middle East -- corroborating, with an earlier and more granular timeline, the same ~200-to-fewer-than-40 reduction Politico and The Intercept's later 2026 reporting (cited below) attributed to 2025. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth cut Pentagon personnel working on civilian-harm mitigation from roughly 200 to fewer than 40, overriding warnings from senior military leaders -- including Gen. Erik Kurilla and then-Joint Chiefs Chairman Gen. CQ Brown -- who urged him not to reduce staffing at the Civilian Protection Center of Excellence and related initiatives. Adm. Christopher Grady, former vice chair of the Joint Chiefs, argued these teams played a critical role both in assessing risk to civilians before U.S. strikes and in investigating deadly incidents afterward. The cuts continued beyond the initial reduction: the Civilian Protection Center of Excellence's staff fell further, from 40 personnel in January 2025 to just 9 by the end of the year. Politico and The Intercept reported the Pentagon has increasingly relied on AI-based assessments in place of the human civilian-harm-mitigation staff that were cut. The cuts are drawing direct scrutiny following the February 28, 2026 U.S. strike on the Shajareh Tayyebeh girls' school in Minab, Iran, which killed more than 170 children and teachers (documented separately in this tracker's Cabinet-Level entry, hegseth-iran-school-strike-minab-2026.json) -- the same offices this entry documents being gutted were the ones institutionally responsible for the kind of pre-strike risk assessment and post-strike investigation the Minab strike is now under scrutiny for lacking. Update (2026-08-17 recheck): the Senate Armed Services Committee's version of the fiscal year 2027 National Defense Authorization Act, approved in committee in June 2026, includes a provision that would withhold 75% of Secretary Hegseth's travel budget (capping it at 25%) until the Pentagon delivers unredacted civilian-harm investigation reports to Congress for the Minab school strike and for three separate 2025 U.S. strikes in Yemen, and releases footage of the Latin America boat-strike campaign -- a direct congressional response to the same institutional gap (gutted civilian-harm review capacity, no released investigation) this entry documents. As of this update, the Pentagon's Minab investigation report -- reportedly completed the prior month -- had still not been delivered to Congress. This provision is not yet enacted: the House passed its own FY2027 NDAA on July 22, 2026 (216-212), but the Senate had not yet passed its version as of early August 2026 (blocked from a floor vote by Senate Democrats over separate objections to the Iran war and defense-spending growth), and informal House-Senate conference negotiations to reconcile the two bills were ongoing as of August 4, 2026, with no final, signed law expected before late autumn or the post-election session at the earliest. Whether the travel-funds provision survives conference negotiation into the final enacted NDAA was not confirmed in sourcing reviewed. Update (2026-08-30 recheck): ProPublica's August 25, 2026 investigation (corroborated same-day by Defense One) provides fuller detail on the original 2025 commander poll -- all nine regional combatant commands rejected outright elimination, instead choosing to preserve CHMR at reduced (roughly 65%-cut) staffing, while the commands overseeing the nuclear arsenal and cyber operations separately requested maintaining full staffing. Gen. Erik Kurilla (then-CENTCOM commander) and Gen. Alexus Grynkewich (now head of European Command, co-author of a paper calling CHMR a 'watershed' development) are named alongside Adm. Brad Cooper (commander of the Iran operation, later questioned by Congress about civilian strikes); CENTCOM's own staff fell from 16 to 1, against commanders' stated 9-person minimum. Separately, a DoD Inspector General evaluation of CHMR Action Plan implementation (completed mid-2025, released June 2026) found the post-cut structure violates 10 U.S.C. Sec. 134 (requiring the designated official to develop, coordinate, and oversee compliance with civilian-harm policy) and 10 U.S.C. Sec. 184 (mandating specific Center of Excellence tasks beyond mere staffing); Colby disputed that a compliance plan was needed, arguing DoD was already compliant, and as of a June 3, 2026 review it was unclear whether his promised January/December 2026 program reviews had ever been completed. Separately from that IG dispute, Colby proposed in April 2026 to reboot CHMR at 70 full-time personnel (35% of original capacity) and move the Civilian Protection Center of Excellence from Army to Joint Staff oversight; the same commanders Hegseth had polled endorsed this partial-restoration plan, and both outlets describe the Pentagon as having backpedaled from full elimination toward this partial rebuild, though no sourcing reviewed confirms the 70-person reboot has actually been implemented as of this recheck.

title: Hegseth Cuts Pentagon's Independent Weapons Testing Office by 76%, GAO Finds Oversight Gaps
institution: Office of the Director, Operational Test and Evaluation (DOT&E), Department of Defense
status: Ongoing -- cuts implemented 2025, staffing partially recovered to 45 by September 2025 (still far below the original 126), GAO findings on resulting oversight gaps published June 30, 2026

what_changed: In May 2025, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth ordered DOT&E -- the Pentagon's independent office responsible for testing weapons systems before they reach troops -- cut from 126 authorized civilian positions to 30, a 76% reduction. Reduction-in-force notices were issued between June and October 2025; staffing partially recovered to 45 positions by September 2025, still well below the original authorized level. Hegseth's memo projected the cuts would save $300 million annually and framed the changes as intended to 'improve the lethality, readiness, and efficiency of our Armed Forces,' later stating 'speed to delivery is now our organizing principle.' Remaining 'action officers' have been assigned more programs than before, including programs in warfare areas -- electronic warfare specifically identified -- outside their area of expertise. Re-verified 2026-08-17: no Pentagon rebuttal to the GAO findings, and no further congressional action beyond the original Senate Armed Services Committee request that led to the June 30, 2026 GAO report, identified as of this update. This is the first documented instance of the annual reports' removal, a fact not previously in this entry. As of this recheck, no reporting confirming a Pentagon response to the August 26 deadline was identified -- the deadline has passed without a located public reply.

title: Hegseth Ended the Military's 80-Year Flu Vaccine Mandate; A Recruit Outbreak Followed Within Weeks
institution: Department of Defense (Army, Navy, Air Force)
status: Reversed for basic trainees -- the Army, Navy, and Air Force reinstated the flu-shot requirement for recruits after the outbreak; the broader end of the mandate for active-duty/reserve personnel generally has not been reported as reversed

what_changed: In April 2026, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth ended the flu vaccine requirement that had applied to all active-duty and reserve U.S. military personnel since 1945, making the annual flu shot optional and citing 'medical autonomy' and religious freedom, describing the prior mandate as 'overly broad and not rational.' At Joint Base San Antonio-Lackland -- the Air Force's primary basic training base -- the flu vaccination rate among incoming recruits fell from nearly 100% under the mandate to about 40% after it became optional. In response, the Army, Navy, and Air Force reinstated mandatory flu vaccination for recruits in basic training, while the underlying policy change for the broader active-duty and reserve force was not reported as reversed.

title: CNN Investigation: Hegseth's Culture of Loyalty Tests and Suspicion Has Sidelined Military Planners During an Active War

title: DOGE Bureaucratic Review Requirements Left HHS With a $1 Billion-Plus Grant Backlog, Then Left CDC Grants Frozen Under Monthly OMB Apportionment Review -- With Only Half of Laid-Off Local Health Staff Ever Rehired
institution: HHS (Administration for Children and Families) and CDC, under DOGE/OMB review requirements
status: The 2025 delays were eventually resolved with funds released -- ACF's backlog reported ongoing as of July 2025 with no confirmed full resolution in sourcing reviewed; the CDC-specific August 2025 freeze was resolved with roughly $200 million released about a month later. date_of_action: 2025-07-11 (HHS/ACF billion-dollar backlog reported) and 2025-07-28/08-28 (CDC-specific grant freeze reported and substantially resolved)
what_changed: Two related but distinct DOGE-driven bureaucratic bottlenecks disrupted already-congressionally-appropriated HHS health funding in mid-to-late 2025. First, CBS News reported on July 11, 2025 that HHS faced a grant backlog that had swelled to more than $1 billion because of new bureaucratic hurdles imposed by DOGE, with multiple HHS officials (speaking without authorization) blaming the hoops for stalling grants that needed to be awarded by the September fiscal-year-end deadline; the usual months-long application window was at risk of being compressed to as little as two weeks to meet the deadline. The backlog was compounded by staffing losses: around half of the Administration for Children and Families' grants-management staff had been laid off or left, and laid-off staff had to be asked to return to help process the backlog. Second, and separately, starting around July 2025 the White House Office of Management and Budget, under Director Russ Vought, began apportioning CDC's appropriated funds on a month-by-month basis rather than in standard tranches, requiring DOGE review of every individual grant award before release. This froze tens of millions of dollars in CDC funding for public health emergency preparedness, chronic disease prevention and education, academic prevention research centers, gun violence research, and tobacco-use programs, leaving state and local health departments uncertain whether or when they would receive money Congress had already appropriated; activities including training hospital staff and first responders for disaster preparedness were put on hold. title: HHS Purged 5,200 Probationary Staff, Offered $25,000 Buyouts Agency-Wide, and Eliminated Its Entire HIV/AIDS and Infectious Disease Policy Office
institution: Department of Health and Human Services (HHS)
status: Completed as to the HIV/AIDS policy office elimination and February 2025 probationary terminations; buyout program concluded with hundreds of acceptances. The broader agency-wide restructuring this entry's early-2025 phase was part of continued through 2025: the Supreme Court cleared the way for HHS to finalize its mass layoffs in July 2025, cumulative departures reached roughly 20,500 (18% of the workforce) by August 2025, and CDC saw a further, separate round of shutdown-era layoffs partially reversed in October 2025.
date_of_action: 2025-02-14 (probationary terminations) through 2025-04-01 (HIV/AIDS and infectious-disease office layoffs take effect)
what_changed: On February 14, 2025 -- the day after Robert F. Kennedy Jr. was sworn in as HHS Secretary -- HHS terminated roughly 5,200 probationary employees agency-wide (including 1,300 at the CDC alone), notifying most that morning and placing them on four weeks of paid administrative leave. Mother Jones reported the purge as part of a broader climate of pressured departures inside HHS, warning it was destabilizing the agency's infectious-disease response and public-health research capacity at a moment of active bird flu and measles outbreaks. The following month, HHS under Kennedy's direction offered buyouts of up to $25,000 to most of its roughly 80,000 employees -- the workforce responsible for researching disease, inspecting food, and administering Medicare and Medicaid -- an offer hundreds of employees accepted. Separately, on March 29, 2025, Forbes and CBS News reported Kennedy planned to lay off the entire Office of Infectious Disease and HIV/AIDS Policy (OIDP), the HHS office that led the 'Let's Get Real' childhood-vaccination-hesitancy campaign and coordinated the cross-agency Ending the HIV Epidemic initiative; the office's elimination took effect around April 1, 2025 and was confirmed by the Washington Blade and multiple HIV-policy organizations, with OIDP's Executive Director of the President's Advisory Council on HIV/AIDS (PACHA) among those let go and remaining HIV functions folded into a separate HHS treatment program over the objections of HIV-policy advocates, who noted prevention, surveillance, and treatment are distinct functions. CDC's separate Division of HIV Prevention was eliminated around the same time. The office cuts came bundled inside Kennedy's broader restructuring plan, reported by NPR and BioPharma Dive as targeting roughly 10,000 direct layoffs and an eventual workforce reduction, including buyout acceptances and other departures, of up to 20,000 -- about a quarter of HHS's workforce -- restructuring HHS's internal organization from 28 divisions down to 15 -- a reduction affecting HHS's 82,000-person workforce that this entry documents in its early-2025 phase (the probationary purge, the buyout offer, and the OIDP/HIV office elimination specifically); later, sub-agency-specific HHS restructuring actions are tracked in their own dedicated entries (see samhsa-staff-cuts-regional-office-closures-trump2 for SAMHSA's portion of the same reorganization). In May 2025, HHS resumed efforts to terminate thousands of probationary employees who had been placed on paid administrative leave following a court-ordered pause earlier in February, restarting a strand of the same early-2025 purge this entry documents rather than representing a new, separate action. Additional detail on the scale of the April 2025 restructuring phase: the Guardian reported on April 2, 2025 that the cuts hit programs on black lung disease (tracked in more detail in this database's msha-silica-niosh-rollback-trump2 and niosh-workforce-safety-research-gutted-2025 entries), infertility research, tobacco control, and entire divisions handling environmental health and climate-related health response -- additional named programs cut within the same restructuring this entry already documents, alongside maternal and child health programs Politico separately reported cut around April 7, 2025. That same week, Kennedy told ABC News some cut programs, including the CDC's childhood lead-poisoning prevention program, had been wrongly eliminated and would be reinstated; Politico separately reported Kennedy's claim that 20% of purged staff would be rehired was not supported by any rehiring plan sources were aware of. The restructuring's next major phase came via litigation: after a federal judge's May 2025 preliminary injunction had blocked planned RIFs at 22 agencies including HHS, the Supreme Court stayed that injunction on July 8, 2025 in an 8-1 ruling (while explicitly declining to rule on the RIFs' underlying legality), clearing the way for HHS to finalize the separations of employees who had been on paid administrative leave -- HHS notified affected employees they were officially separated effective July 14, 2025. By late August 2025, ProPublica's cumulative analysis found more than 20,500 HHS employees, or roughly 18% of the department's workforce, had left or been pushed out since January 2025 -- an analysis ProPublica itself described as an undercount, since it excluded employees still on administrative leave awaiting separation. A further, distinct round of cuts hit CDC specifically in October 2025: amid the federal government shutdown, CDC sent roughly 1,300 layoff notices, then reversed about 740 of them within days after public backlash, attributing the overreach to a 'coding error' -- the reinstated staff included employees responding to active measles and Ebola outbreaks, global-health office personnel, and nearly all staff who compile the CDC's Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report. This October 2025 CDC episode is a separate incident from the coding-error RIF documented in this database's ninds-lab-heads-coding-error-rif-2025 entry (a different April 2025 NIH/NINDS action). Other sub-threads within this same broader 2025 restructuring -- SAMHSA's regional office closures, CDC's ACIP vaccine-panel purge -- are tracked in their own dedicated entries (samhsa-staff-cuts-regional-office-closures-trump2, cdc-acip-vaccine-panel-purge-trump2) rather than duplicated here.

title: HHS reclassifies career civil servants under revived Schedule F, stripping removal protections
institution: Department of Health and Human Services (including CDC science positions)
status: Ongoing -- OPM final rule published in the Federal Register Feb. 5-6, 2026 with an effective date of roughly March 8, 2026; HHS implementation underway as of May 2026. The underlying litigation (PEER v. OPM, D. Md., 8:25-cv-00260, before Judge Xinis, joined by AFGE, AFSCME, the AFL-CIO, and Democracy Forward) remains stalled at the pleading stage as of this 2026-08-31 recheck: CORRECTION -- this entry's prior recheck (2026-08-30) reported an Aug. 18, 2026 summary-judgment deadline and an Oct. 16, 2026 hearing date sourced from a search-engine synthesis of a CRS legal sidebar; the case's own docket, per the Civil Rights Litigation Clearinghouse, shows no summary-judgment briefing schedule at all -- the case remains stuck on the parties' still-unresolved motion to amend/motion to dismiss, with the most recent docket activity being a May-June 2026 attorney-withdrawal filing, not merits briefing. Separately, a June 3, 2026 executive order converted roughly 8,000 federal positions government-wide into Schedule Policy/Career status, the first confirmed actual conversions since the rule's finalization.
date_of_action: 2026-02 (OPM final rule) through 2026-05 (HHS supervisor memo)
what_changed: The Office of Personnel Management issued a final rule in February 2026 implementing 'Schedule Policy/Career' (the revived Schedule F framework), estimated to affect roughly 50,000 federal positions government-wide by stripping them of traditional competitive-service protections and making them removable at will, without advance notice or the right to appeal to the Merit Systems Protection Board. A May 2026 memo sent to HHS supervisors announced that over 100 HHS positions were being moved into this category, with CDC separately reclassifying a number of science-focused roles -- including research biologists, epidemiologists, and other health scientists -- into the same at-will status. Trump subsequently signed an executive order in June 2026 formally converting nearly 10,000 career federal workers government-wide into Schedule Policy/Career. Update 2026-08-17: Implementation continues incrementally rather than in one mass action -- CDC officials have said several hundred GS-15 positions (not thousands) were 'tentatively identified' for the initial reclassification tranche, with additional rounds expected to follow. Separately, the framework faces active litigation: AFGE, AFSCME, the AFL-CIO, PEER, and Democracy Forward filed a Second Amended Complaint on March 4, 2026 expanding their challenge to the entire Schedule Policy/Career framework; as of the most recent reporting reviewed, a motion for a preliminary injunction in that case remained under advisement following an April 30, 2026 hearing, with the case proceeding to summary judgment on the merits regardless of the injunction's outcome. No court has yet ruled on the framework's legality. Update (2026-08-30 recheck): identified the specific underlying litigation as PEER v. OPM, D. Md., before Judge Xinis (an Obama appointee). AFGE re-joined this case (voluntarily dismissing a separate D.D.C. suit) alongside AFSCME, the AFL-CIO, PEER, and Democracy Forward, and the coalition filed a Second Amended Complaint March 4, 2026 expanding the challenge to the entire Schedule Policy/Career framework -- the underlying executive order and OPM's final rule itself, not merely HHS's implementation of it. Judge Xinis paused the government's motion-to-dismiss response deadline March 12, 2026 pending resolution of the amendment motion. Separately, on June 3, 2026, President Trump signed an executive order converting roughly 8,000 federal positions into Schedule Policy/Career status government-wide -- the first confirmed actual conversions since the rule was finalized, corroborated by NPR and Government Executive, and not limited to HHS. CORRECTION (2026-08-31 recheck): this entry's prior update (2026-08-30) stated, at MODERATE confidence, that a summary-judgment motion was due August 18, 2026 ahead of an October 16, 2026 hearing, attributing those dates to a search-engine synthesis of CRS Legal Sidebar LSB11412 that could not be independently fetched at the time. This recheck fetched both the CRS sidebar itself (via its everycrsreport.com mirror, since congress.gov continues to block direct retrieval) and the case's own docket via the Civil Rights Litigation Clearinghouse. Neither source supports the prior claim: the CRS sidebar's text on this case goes no further than noting PEER and four other unions filed the Maryland suit, without any summary-judgment or hearing dates; and the Clearinghouse's docket summary, current through August 31, 2026, shows no summary-judgment briefing schedule ever entered. The docket's actual most recent activity is a March 12, 2026 order pausing the government's motion-to-dismiss response deadline pending resolution of plaintiffs' motion to amend (filed March 4, 2026, the same Second Amended Complaint this entry already documents), followed only by a May 21, 2026 motion to withdraw as counsel for one government attorney, granted June 18, 2026 -- procedural housekeeping, not merits progress. In other words, five months after the coalition's amended complaint, the case remains stalled at the pleading stage: the motion to amend and the paused motion to dismiss are both still unresolved, and no summary-judgment schedule exists yet for a court to have set a hearing against. This corrects the entry's own prior claim rather than reflecting a new development in the litigation.

The House returned from recess August 31, 2026, leaving a narrow window before the September 30 funding deadline for a House-Senate conference to reconcile the two versions -- meaning this House-passed WIC cut remains without a clear path to enactment, contingent on how (or whether) that conference process resolves.
date_of_action: 2026-06-04 (House floor vote)
what_changed: The House passed a fiscal year agriculture appropriations bill by a 213-210 vote, with five Republicans voting against and four Democrats (Reps. Donald Davis, Adam Gray, Vicente Gonzalez, and Marie Glusenkamp Perez) voting for it, providing the margin of passage. The bill, aiming to trim 1.5% from federal agriculture spending, underfunds WIC overall and specifically cuts the program's Cash Value Benefit for fruits and vegetables. Per the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities, the bill would cut WIC fruit-and-vegetable funding by $141 million, affecting benefits for nearly 5.4 million enrolled children and pregnant/postpartum women. The National WIC Association estimated the specific benefit reduction: from $52 to $13 per month for breastfeeding mothers, and from $26 to $10 per month for young children. The bill also fails to make WIC's pandemic-era virtual/telehealth service option permanent. As of this entry's sourcing, the bill awaits Senate action and is not yet law. Update 2026-08-17: This bill is the FY2027 agriculture appropriations process (H.R. 8646), separate from the FY2026 agriculture appropriations act Congress had already enacted on November 12, 2025 as part of the shutdown-ending minibus (P.L. 119-37) -- that earlier, FY2026 bill fully funded WIC and rejected the fruit-and-vegetable cuts House Republicans had also proposed for that fiscal year. The FY2027 fight covered in this entry is a renewed version of the same dispute for the following fiscal year. As of the most recent reporting reviewed, the Senate Appropriations Committee had twice postponed its planned markup of the FY2027 Agriculture bill (originally set for early June 2026, then rescheduled to June 25) after committee leadership failed to reach a bipartisan agreement on overall discretionary spending levels -- so the House-passed cuts described in this entry remain pending, with no Senate committee action yet as of this update.

title: Trump Administration Cuts Funding for the Nation's 50-Year Acid Rain Monitoring Program at Hubbard Brook
institution: National Science Foundation (funder of the Hubbard Brook Long-Term Ecological Research site)
status: Funding cut (already executed) as of March 2025 reporting -- not reversed. The separate, larger proposed FY2026 NSF budget cut (55-57% reduction) that this entry previously tracked as a distinct, unresolved risk to Hubbard Brook and up to 26 LTER sites nationwide was rejected by Congress: the FY2026 Commerce-Justice-Science appropriations act (P.L. 119-74, H.R. 6938, signed 2026-01-23) provided NSF $8.75 billion, about 22.5% more than the administration's FY2026 request and only a modest decline from FY2025 levels. No line-item confirmation specific to the LTER program or Hubbard Brook's own grant was found in sourcing reviewed, so this update resolves the broader agency-wide threat, not necessarily every program-level risk within it.
date_of_action: 2025-03 (reported)
what_changed: Dr. Gene Likens, the ecologist who co-discovered acid rain in the U.S. through research launched in 1963 at the Hubbard Brook Experimental Forest in New Hampshire, confirmed in March 2025 that the Trump administration had cut federal funding for his continuous rainwater-acidity monitoring program -- one of the longest unbroken datasets of its kind in the world, running since 1976. The cut comes as EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin's EPA has targeted dozens of air-quality rules for rollback, including limits on sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides, the two pollutants that cause acid rain (several of these rollbacks are tracked separately in this database's Corporate Deregulation tracker). Likens warned that defunding the monitoring itself compounds the risk of the emissions rollbacks: 'If the monitoring is disrupted or discontinued, we won't know what is changing.' Separately, and not conflated with the already-executed monitoring-program cut above, the administration's proposed FY2026 budget requested a 55% reduction to the National Science Foundation (to roughly $4 billion), reporting on which noted the cut could force the closure of up to 26 Long-Term Ecological Research sites nationwide, including Hubbard Brook itself -- a distinct, larger, and as of reporting reviewed still-proposed (not enacted) threat to the site's broader research funding beyond the specific acid-rain monitoring grant already cut. Update 2026-08-17: The proposed FY2026 NSF budget cut described above did not take effect. Congress enacted the FY2026 Commerce-Justice-Science appropriations act (P.L. 119-74, H.R. 6938) on 2026-01-23, providing NSF $8.75 billion -- roughly 22.5% more than the administration's FY2026 budget request and a decline of only about 3.4% from FY2025 levels, rejecting the proposed ~55-57% reduction that had put up to 26 LTER sites at risk. This entry's original, already-executed cut to Likens' specific rainwater-monitoring grant, reported in March 2025, is unaffected by this correction and remains in effect as originally documented.

primary_proponent.role: No single named official is identified in sourcing reviewed as personally directing this specific monitoring-grant cut
primary_proponent.note: Attributed institutionally per this tracker's standing convention for undocumented individual attribution; the related, larger FY2026 NSF budget request (55% reduction) is a Trump administration budget proposal, not yet enacted.

estimated_impact.summary: Ends continuous funding for a 49-year (at time of the cut), unbroken rainwater-acidity dataset that originally enabled the discovery of acid rain and the scientific case for the 1990 Clean Air Act amendments that curbed it -- removing the monitoring capacity needed to detect any resurgence just as EPA moves to roll back the SO2/NOx emissions rules that originally caused acid rain.
estimated_impact.caveat: This entry documents the specific, already-executed cut to Likens' rainwater-monitoring program reported in March 2025 -- that cut has not been reversed. It does not include dollar figures for that specific grant, which were not identified in sourcing reviewed. The separate, larger FY2026 NSF budget-reduction proposal this entry previously tracked as a distinct, unresolved risk was rejected by Congress via the enacted FY2026 CJS appropriations act (see status/what_changed above); that risk should no longer be described as pending. No source reviewed confirms the LTER program or Hubbard Brook's specific line item was preserved beyond the agency-wide topline, so avoid asserting the 26-site closure risk is fully and specifically resolved, only that the proposed agency-wide cut that would have driven it did not happen.

confidence_note: HIGH confidence on the monitoring-program funding cut itself and Likens' warning, independently corroborated across The Guardian, the Cary Institute (Likens' research home institution, republishing the Guardian piece), and Envirotech Online's direct interview with Likens. MODERATE confidence on precisely which funding mechanism was cut (Hubbard Brook's core support comes from NSF Long-Term Ecological Research grants, per Union Leader and NSF-history reporting, but no single source in this review names the exact grant or agency line-item cut in March 2025 with full specificity) -- attributed to NSF broadly rather than a more specific mechanism. The $8.75B enacted NSF total and the 22.5%-above-request figure are corroborated across the American Astronomical Society, Chemistry World, and CRS report R48783 (via congress.gov). No source reviewed specifically confirms Hubbard Brook's or the LTER program's own line item, so the correction is written at the agency-wide level this tracker's sourcing actually supports, per this tracker's standing discipline against conflating a topline resolution with every program-level detail beneath it. Re-verified 2026-08-30: no material change -- no reporting found confirming Likens' March 2025 monitoring-grant cut has been restored. title: Judge Rules HUD's Rewrite of $75M Homeless-Housing Funding Criteria Unlawful, Calling It a 'Slapdash Imposition of Political Whims'
institution: Department of Housing and Urban Development
status: Blocked -- a federal judge ordered the new policy scrapped
date_of_action: 2025 (new NOFO issued) through 2026-03/04 (court ruling)
what_changed: HUD issued a new Notice of Funding Opportunity for its Continuum of Care Builds program -- a separate $75 million funding stream from the broader $3.9 billion Continuum of Care Program documented separately in this tracker (hud-supportive-housing-shift-2026.json) -- that dramatically changed the criteria nonprofits and local providers must meet to receive funding to build housing for homeless families and individuals. Several nonprofits sued, alleging HUD rewrote the criteria to better align funding decisions with the administration's broader social-policy priorities rather than housing need. title: HUD's Fair Housing Office Cut by Roughly Two-Thirds Amid Whistleblower Allegations
institution: U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development, Office of Fair Housing and Equal Opportunity
status: Ongoing -- staffing cuts and enforcement-guidance rollback both stand unreversed; a 16-state AG coalition suit against the guidance (California v. HUD, N.D. Cal., filed 2026-03-16) and the Osadebe/Heenan whistleblower-retaliation suit are both pending with no ruling identified as of this recheck
date_of_action: 2025-01 through 2025-11 (staffing reductions); enforcement policy changes ongoing through 2026
what_changed: Internal documents revealed in January 2025 that HUD officials, working with the Department of Government Efficiency, planned to cut staff at the Office of Fair Housing and Equal Opportunity (FHEO), which investigates housing discrimination complaints nationwide, by 77%. Following the March 2025 confirmation of Secretary Scott Turner, probationary employees were terminated, according to a former HUD civil rights attorney, 'with no real justification.' The earliest concrete evidence of case-stalling predates the September 2025 whistleblower complaint by roughly six months: within weeks of the new administration taking office, HUD rescinded its own Department of Justice litigation referrals in two Texas civil-rights investigations it had already substantiated -- one finding a Texas state agency steered $1 billion in Hurricane Harvey disaster-mitigation funds away from Houston-area communities of color, the other finding a homeowners association in Providence Village, a mostly-white Dallas suburb, barred Section 8 voucher holders (predominantly Black tenants) starting in 2022, displacing Black families. HUD offered no public explanation for withdrawing either referral, per ProPublica's March 2025 investigation. By October 2025, Office of Management and Budget data showed 442 total HUD employees had been dismissed since the administration began, including 114 from FHEO specifically, a 45% cut by that count. A subsequent National Fair Housing Alliance analysis published in its November 2025 Fair Housing Trends Report found FHEO then operating with roughly one-third of the staff it had in January 2025, a reduction of nearly two-thirds, reflecting cuts that continued to deepen through an additional 400-plus HUD-wide layoffs issued during the October-November 2025 government shutdown. Outside experts estimated total HUD departures, including voluntary and buyout-driven exits, at as many as 2,300 employees since January 2025. In September 2025, HUD issued a memorandum withdrawing previously issued fair housing enforcement guidance. Days later, four HUD attorneys, including Paul Osadebe, filed a whistleblower complaint with Senator Elizabeth Warren alleging the department was illegally winding down and stalling active fair housing discrimination cases; co-whistleblower Palmer Heenan was fired, and Osadebe was placed on administrative leave before being formally terminated on February 9, 2026. On January 13, 2026, Osadebe and Heenan testified before the Senate Banking Committee (in a forum organized by Sen. Elizabeth Warren titled 'Fair Housing Under Fire'), describing the department blocking investigations, barring attorneys from speaking with clients, and prohibiting attorneys from citing prior civil rights case law. Following their terminations, both filed a lawsuit against HUD alleging they were unlawfully targeted and forced out for whistleblowing. Re-verified 2026-07-26: no material change -- no new developments identified in the Osadebe/Heenan litigation or FHEO staffing beyond what this entry already documents. Real-correction update 2026-08-30 (GSR recheck batch 30): this entry's prior rechecks (through 2026-08-17) documented the September 2025 HUD memorandum withdrawing fair housing enforcement guidance but missed that a coalition of 16 state attorneys general, led by California's Rob Bonta, sued HUD over that same guidance on March 16, 2026 in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California. The suit alleges the guidance violates the Administrative Procedure Act and the Constitution by threatening to decertify state and local fair housing agencies that enforce protections broader than the federal Fair Housing Act (including disparate-impact liability, gender-identity protections, and source-of-income safeguards) while separately imposing unrelated funding conditions tied to abortion, immigration, and 'gender ideology.' The coalition seeks declaratory relief, APA vacatur, and a permanent injunction; no ruling had been identified in sourcing reviewed as of this recheck. (A separate, unrelated HUD lawsuit -- over Continuum of Care homelessness-grant funding restrictions, where Bonta secured a preliminary injunction and the administration dropped its appeal in April 2026 -- concerns different funding conditions and is out of scope for this fair-housing-enforcement-staffing entry.) Update 2026-08-31: no ruling identified yet in California v. HUD, but this recheck adds the coalition's own stated dollar-impact figures for the September 2025 guidance, not previously documented here: AG Bonta's office estimates California alone stands to lose approximately $3 million in fair-housing enforcement funding if the guidance takes effect, with the total loss across all 17 states in the coalition estimated at roughly $10.7 million.

title: HUD Proposed Shifting Two-Thirds of Its $3.9B Homeless-Services Program From Permanent Supportive Housing to Short-Term Shelter, Risking Eviction for 170,000 People
institution: Department of Housing and Urban Development
status: Blocked by federal courts three times as of August 2026, but not permanently resolved -- the original Nov/Dec 2025 NOFOs were vacated in a June 29, 2026 summary judgment, and a subsequent FY2026 NOFO was blocked again on August 7, 2026 for skipping required notice-and-comment procedure; because the court declined to issue a permanent injunction, HUD retains the ability to attempt a similar shift for FY2027. Separately, a statutory auto-renewal mechanism (Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2026) has funded nearly all FY2026-expiring projects at pre-cut PSH terms while the litigation continues, substantially reducing near-term eviction exposure even though the underlying legal dispute over HUD's authority remains unresolved for FY2027 and beyond
date_of_action: 2025-11 (NOFO released) through 2026-01 (court blocks it, HUD reinstates prior NOFO) and ongoing litigation into 2026-03
what_changed: In November 2025, HUD released a Notice of Funding Opportunity for its Continuum of Care Program -- which funds shelters, permanent supportive housing, and other homelessness responses -- proposing to shift roughly two-thirds of the program's $3.9 billion budget away from permanent supportive housing and toward transitional housing and other short-term interventions. Advocacy groups estimated up to 170,000 formerly homeless people already housed through these programs, including veterans, could be evicted and forced back into homelessness if facilities lost their permanent-housing funding and had to convert to short-term models. Nonprofits and local governments sued to block the change. On December 23, 2025, a federal judge ordered HUD to revert to the original, Biden-era NOFO pending a final ruling, and HUD reinstated the prior funding notice on January 9, 2026. California Attorney General Rob Bonta separately secured a court order blocking the changes, which he said would also have pressured shelters to discriminate against transgender people and encouraged criminalization of homelessness. Despite the reinstatement, CNN's March 29, 2026 reporting described the eviction risk to formerly homeless people, including veterans, as still live, reflecting that the underlying litigation over HUD's authority to make the shift had not been finally resolved. Litigation continued through mid-2026: on June 29, 2026, the same U.S. District Court (Rhode Island) issued summary judgment vacating HUD's November and December 2025 NOFOs as arbitrary and capricious and exceeding the agency's statutory authority, finding HUD had failed to adequately consider the effects of abandoning its 'Housing First' approach. HUD then issued a new FY2026 NOFO in June 2026 -- a $4.04 billion allocation that again set aside roughly $1.3 billion for new temporary-housing and treatment programs instead of permanent supportive housing. On August 7, 2026, District Judge Mary McElroy blocked that FY2026 NOFO too, ruling HUD had again violated the Administrative Procedure Act by skipping the required public notice-and-comment process. The court again declined to issue a permanent injunction, leaving HUD free to attempt similar changes for FY2027. Update 2026-08-29: per KCRHA's tracking of the ruling's practical effect, the entire FY2026 NOFO was set aside, and the competition's original application deadline (KCRHA cites July 3, 2026; other reporting cited August 26, 2026 for a later-extended window) is no longer in force -- HUD cannot currently accept applications under it. No HUD response, appeal, or replacement NOFO had been identified as of this recheck. Update 2026-09-01 (GSR recheck batch 50): identified a statutory backstop this entry had not previously documented, running in parallel with the litigation the whole time. The Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2026 (P.L. 119-75, signed Feb. 3, 2026) directed HUD to automatically renew any Continuum of Care projects expiring in Q1 2026 at their prior (FY2024/2025 program-competition) terms, with escalating triggers if HUD had not issued awards under a new NOFO by set dates: Q2-expiring projects auto-renew if no awards by April 1, 2026, and ALL remaining (Q3/Q4-expiring) projects auto-renew if no awards by July 1, 2026. HUD complied with the Q1 trigger, announcing $349,205,436 in FY2025 renewal funding for the 622 projects that expired in Q1 2026 (confirmed directly via National Network for Youth's April 1, 2026 reporting). Because HUD's NOFO attempts were repeatedly blocked in court and no awards were ever issued under a new competition, the July 1 trigger also activated: HUD announced $2,402,872,704 in FY2025 renewal funding for the 4,241 projects expiring in Q3/Q4 2026, per the Consolidated Appropriations Act (this $2.4B/4,241-project figure came from a single WebSearch synthesis not independently re-fetched from a named outlet, so is flagged MODERATE pending direct confirmation). Critically, NACo's April 1, 2026 reporting confirms these statutorily-renewed projects are funded 'based on Fiscal Year (FY) 2024 program competition terms' and 'will not be subject to the planned reductions in PSH or protected renewal funds' -- meaning the specific eviction-risk mechanism this entry documents (projects losing permanent-supportive-housing funding because they couldn't compete under HUD's PSH-cutting NOFO) has been substantially mitigated for the projects covered by these renewals, independent of and prior to the litigation's outcome. This does not resolve the underlying dispute over HUD's authority to shift the program's structure for FY2027 and beyond, where no statutory auto-renewal protection currently exists.

title: Trump Administration Froze $16B in Committed Funding for the Hudson River Tunnel Project, Threatening Construction Shutdown
institution: U.S. Department of Transportation
status: Resolved in the states' favor -- a federal judge permanently restored the funding on June 29, 2026, ruling the freeze 'flagrantly violated federal law'; the 2nd Circuit had already declined to block a February 2026 order requiring interim resumption, and construction has continued since February 13, 2026 without further interruption
date_of_action: 2025-09-30 (DOT announces indefinite funding suspension) through 2026-02-04 (NY/NJ file suit)
what_changed: On September 30, 2025, DOT announced it would indefinitely suspend payment of all previously-committed federal funds for the Gateway Program's Hudson Tunnel Project -- a roughly $16 billion effort to build new rail tunnels under the Hudson River and rehabilitate the existing, more-than-a-century-old crossing between New Jersey and New York City -- pending a newly announced compliance review. The White House budget director stated officials believed the project's spending was based on 'unconstitutional diversity, equity, and inclusion principles,' and DOT said it was reviewing for 'unconstitutional practices.' After roughly four months of the states covering costs with limited operating funds, they warned construction would be forced to shut down entirely by February 6, 2026 without resumed federal funding, immediately costing an estimated 1,000 workers their jobs. On February 4, 2026, New York Attorney General Letitia James and New Jersey Acting Attorney General Jennifer Davenport filed suit in the Southern District of New York against the Trump administration, seeking emergency relief to stop the indefinite funding freeze. Update 2026-08-17 (correction -- this entry's original 'litigation ongoing' framing is now outdated): the 2nd U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals declined to block a lower-court order requiring DOT to resume payments, and funding resumed on an interim basis, with construction restarting February 13, 2026. On June 29, 2026, U.S. District Judge Jeannette Vargas issued a permanent ruling: the administration's September 2025 funding freeze 'flagrantly violate[d] federal law' because DOT skipped required procedures and never gave the Gateway Development Commission an opportunity to object -- a point the government itself did not dispute. The court rejected DOT's argument that the dispute belonged in the Court of Federal Claims, finding New York and New Jersey could challenge the freeze under the Administrative Procedure Act since the states were not parties to the underlying funding agreements. The Gateway Development Commission said the project -- slated for completion in 2035 -- remained on schedule before the freeze and has made 'significant progress' since funding resumed.

title: Six Months After Promising Body Cameras for All Immigration Agents, DHS Still Hasn't Deployed Them -- Agents in Subsequent Fatal Shootings Had None
institution: Department of Homeland Security / Immigration and Customs Enforcement
status: Ongoing -- reporting is split on the deployment deadline itself (NBC/Venturella said end of August 2026; the same-day AP/PBS account said end of September, with 'more than half' of field officers equipped as of early August), and no independent reporting confirms completion under either deadline as of this recheck; ICE separately disputed AP's characterization of its footage-withholding policy for serious-injury/death cases on August 8-9, 2026, without disputing the underlying policy itself
date_of_action: 2026-01 (body camera pledge made) through 2026-07 (still not fully deployed, additional fatal shootings without cameras)
what_changed: After immigration agents fatally shot two U.S. citizens (Alex Pretti, a VA hospital ICU nurse, and Renee Good) in Minneapolis in January 2026, then-DHS Secretary Kristi Noem pledged to rapidly expand body camera deployment to immigration agents nationwide. Congress allocated $20 million in FY2026 DHS funding for body camera procurement, deployment, and operations, with plans to purchase more than 5,000 body-worn cameras; as of February 2026, roughly 3,000 of approximately 13,000 ICE agents wore body cameras, with another 6,000 in the deployment pipeline. Nearly six months after the pledge, none of the officers involved in two subsequent fatal ICE shootings -- of Lorenzo Salgado Araujo and Johan Duran Guerrero -- were wearing body cameras, according to NPR reporting; a separate fatal shooting in Houston also involved ICE agents without body cameras despite the DHS funding allocation. Update 2026-08-17: on August 7-8, 2026, ICE Acting Director David J. Venturella said the agency expects to complete nationwide body-camera deployment to every field officer by the end of August 2026 -- a significant acceleration from the ~3,000-of-13,000 partial deployment this entry documents as of February 2026, following the additional fatal shootings without cameras already covered above. Independent confirmation that the rollout was actually completed by the announced deadline was not available as of this update, since the deadline itself had not yet arrived. Separately, ICE's body-camera policy has drawn scrutiny for provisions that let agency leadership withhold or indefinitely delay release of footage following serious injuries or deaths in custody; Venturella defended the restrictions as protecting investigations and privacy and consistent with other federal law enforcement agencies' policies, while reporting noted this means the expanded camera coverage will not automatically translate into public access to the footage. Update 2026-08-30 (GSR recheck batch 32): on August 8-9, 2026, ICE publicly disputed the Associated Press's framing of the footage-release policy, with Venturella issuing a statement saying the AP conflated the narrower expedited-release provision that applies specifically to serious-injury/death-in-custody cases with a claim that ICE would broadly withhold routine footage; ICE maintains the underlying policy -- expedited release when appropriate, withholding when release could compromise investigations or privacy -- is unchanged from what this entry already documents. As of this recheck, which falls on the announced end-of-August 2026 completion deadline itself, no independent reporting confirming (or disputing) that the full nationwide rollout was actually completed was found in sourcing reviewed -- consistent with this entry's existing caveat that the target had not yet been independently verified. Update 2026-09-01 (GSR recheck batch 47): a same-week (Aug 7-8, 2026) PBS/AP account, published within hours of the NBC/Venturella 'end of August' report already documented above, instead described the rollout target as 'the end of September,' with more than half of field officers already equipped and the rest to follow by then -- a discrepancy this entry documents rather than resolves, since sourcing reviewed does not establish which deadline is the agency's operative one. The PBS/AP reporting also added funding and design detail beyond what this entry previously documented: ICE spent $30.9 million in July 2026 to purchase equipment from Axon, on top of the $20 million FY2026 congressional appropriation already documented above; and the deployment plan's actual coverage standard requires only 'at least one member of every arrest team' to wear a camera, not every individual field officer, a materially narrower standard than the 'every officer' framing in HHS's own public statements. The same reporting detailed the footage-release policy more specifically than previously documented: the ICE Director may withhold or indefinitely delay release following 'specific and compelling circumstances,' on a review committee's recommendation, if release is not determined to be in the agency's 'best interests' -- a broader, more discretionary standard than this entry's prior 'expedited release when appropriate' framing suggested. As of this recheck (Sept. 1, 2026), no reporting confirming rollout completion under either the August 31 or end-of-September deadline was found.

title: Education Department Cancels $881M in Research Contracts, Then Fires Nearly All Staff at the Agency Behind the 'Nation's Report Card'
institution: Institute of Education Sciences and National Center for Education Statistics (U.S. Department of Education)
status: Complete (contracts terminated February 2025; NCES staff RIF carried out March 2025; no indication of reinstatement as of the last-verified date)
what_changed: On February 10, 2025, the Department of Government Efficiency directed the Department of Education to terminate 89 contracts held by the Institute of Education Sciences (IES), the department's independent research and statistics arm, which DOGE valued at $881 million. The same evening, IES canceled its peer review panels that evaluate the scientific merit of grant applications for its research centers. Canceled work included the National Postsecondary Student Aid Study, a congressionally mandated survey conducted every four years and described by the American Educational Research Association as the 'backbone' of two other longitudinal higher-education studies; the Beginning Postsecondary Students survey; an 11-year study of youths with disabilities that was roughly halfway complete and was meant to serve over 1,000 students in 2025-2026; and U.S. participation in international assessments comparing American student performance with other countries. On February 13, 2025, the Department separately terminated an additional $336-350 million in contracts and grants to Regional Educational Laboratories and Equity Assistance Centers. The Department stated that the National Assessment of Educational Progress, the College Scorecard, and the College Navigator were not affected by the February contract cancellations. That assurance came under direct strain a month later: as part of the Education Department's broader March 11, 2025 reduction-in-force (documented separately in education-department-dismantlement-trump2.json), ABC News reported nearly all of the roughly 130 staff at the National Center for Education Statistics (NCES) -- the IES division that has collected and analyzed U.S. education data since the 1860s and administers NAEP, the congressionally mandated 'Nation's Report Card' considered the gold standard of education testing since 1969 -- were fired. One terminated NCES employee told ABC News that producing NAEP without a full staff would be 'the equivalent of manning a 13-person sailboat with a 12-month-old,' and outlets including THE Journal and EdWeek reported researchers warning the cuts put NAEP's continued administration itself in doubt, a direct complication of the Department's earlier February statement that NAEP would be spared.

estimated_impact.caveat: The Department's stated rationale, in its own words, is that IES spent '$14 billion and countless contracts later' without evidence that student outcomes improved, and it specifically flagged $101 million in DEI-related contracts and line items such as $4.6 million 'to coordinate Zoom and in-person meetings.' Notably, this is a genuinely mixed-reception story: Mark Schneider, who led IES during Trump's first term, said in a public LinkedIn discussion that the agency needed significant modernization and called the disruption 'an opportunity' rather than a catastrophe, even while acknowledging DOGE had not articulated a modernization plan. Researcher and data organizations, including AERA, the Council of Professional Associations on Federal Statistics, and the Data Quality Campaign, countered that the specific programs cut, especially the National Postsecondary Student Aid Study and international assessment participation, are congressionally mandated, multi-year data series that lose scientific value once interrupted, since gaps cannot be retroactively filled. The Department confirmed core public-facing tools (NAEP, College Scorecard, College Navigator) were not affected by the February contract cuts specifically, indicating those cuts targeted research contracts rather than IES's full range of functions -- but the March 2025 NCES staffing cuts are a separate action that reporting says undermines that same assurance by removing the staff capacity needed to actually produce NAEP, rather than cutting a contract NAEP itself depended on.

confidence_note: Strong. Corroborated by a formal bicameral congressional oversight letter to the Department of Education, multiple independent education-press outlets (Inside Higher Ed, K-12 Dive, Higher Ed Dive, Hechinger Report, Washington Times) with some factual disagreement between sources on exact contract counts and dollar figures (which is itself documented and included above), and the Department of Education's own public statement providing its stated rationale. The March 2025 NCES staffing cuts are corroborated by ABC News/Good Morning America, THE Journal, EdWeek, and EdSource, all reporting the same ~130-staff figure and the same NAEP-continuity concern from named former employees.
