what_changed: The International Labour Organization rescinded the planned July 2026 appointment of U.S. nominee Sheng Li as Deputy Director-General after the United States failed to pay its outstanding contributions -- 257 million Swiss francs (roughly $328 million) in arrears for 2026 and prior years (2024-2025) -- to the agency. title: IMLS Dismantlement Permanently Blocked by Federal Court — A Rare Full Reversal
institution: Institute of Museum and Library Services (IMLS)
status: Reversed — federal court permanently blocked the dismantlement; agency fully restored via binding DOJ settlement
date_of_action: 2025-03-14 (executive order issued) through 2026-04-09 (binding settlement agreement finalized)
what_changed: On March 14, 2025, Trump issued Executive Order 14238 directing the elimination of IMLS -- the only federal agency dedicated to the nation's libraries and museums. The administration moved quickly: by March 31, all but 12 of the agency's roughly 70-75 employees were placed on administrative leave, with a reduction-in-force notice set for May 4; nearly all IMLS board members were dismissed; and beginning April 1, the agency's Acting Director (Keith Sonderling, who stated he would act 'in lockstep' with the administration) began terminating previously-awarded, congressionally-appropriated grants nationwide, including Grants to States, National Leadership Grants, and Laura Bush 21st Century Librarian grants. Unlike most entries in this tracker, this story does not end in unreversed loss: the American Library Association and AFSCME sued (ALA v. Sonderling), and 21 state attorneys general separately sued in Rhode Island v. Trump. On May 1, 2025, a federal judge issued a temporary restraining order blocking further staff terminations. In November 2025, the U.S. District Court for Rhode Island ruled the dismantlement actions 'arbitrary and capricious and contrary to federal law,' and IMLS reinstated all previously terminated grants that December. On April 6, 2026, the administration withdrew its appeal of that ruling, and on April 9, 2026, ALA, AFSCME, and the Department of Justice signed a binding settlement agreement ensuring IMLS remains intact and continues its congressionally mandated work going forward -- closing the litigation with the agency fully restored, not merely paused.

primary_proponent.name: Keith Sonderling
primary_proponent.role: Acting Director of IMLS (appointed to implement the executive order)
primary_proponent.note: Sonderling stated publicly he would act 'in lockstep' with the administration's directive to eliminate the agency, and personally signed the grant-termination notices sent to states. This is the same official covered in this project's Cabinet-Level Legal Exposure tracker for a related action at the Department of Labor, where a federal court similarly blocked his agency's actions -- a recurring pattern across Sonderling's various acting-director roles during this period.

estimated_impact.summary: ALA President Sam Helmick called the November 2025 court ruling 'a powerful affirmation of what libraries mean to America,' noting it restored 'shared access to books in rural and remote areas, essential virtual learning tools, children's reading programs and the countless library services available to anyone who walks into a public, school or academic library.' During the roughly 8-month period before reinstatement, real, documented harm occurred at the institutional level: the Dubuque Museum of Art in Iowa had already begun hiring and training staff against a $74,979 grant that was frozen: the Science Center of Iowa's planned internship program, backed by a $196,046 grant, was jeopardized. IMLS awarded $266 million in grants to museums and libraries in 2024, the baseline scale of funding that was disrupted before being restored.

Real institutions (documented above) experienced genuine disruption, delayed programming, and staffing uncertainty during the roughly year-long period before restoration, and the Trump administration's FY2027 budget request, released the same day as the settlement, still proposed cutting IMLS funding going forward -- meaning the underlying policy dispute over the agency's funding level remains live even though the dismantlement-without-Congress legal question has been resolved against the administration.

title: Surge in Immigration-Detention Habeas Corpus Cases Is Pulling Prosecutors Off Criminal Casework Nationwide
institution: U.S. Attorney's Offices nationwide, Department of Justice
status: Ongoing as of this entry's addition (February 2026 reporting) -- no indication in sourcing reviewed that DOJ has added prosecutorial capacity to offset the habeas caseload surge
date_of_action: 2025-2026 (surge intensifying alongside expanded immigration-detention enforcement)
what_changed: A sharp increase in immigration detentions under the administration's enforcement push has produced a corresponding wave of habeas corpus petitions -- detainees' court challenges to the legality of their detention -- that CBS News's reporting describes as overwhelming U.S. Attorney's offices nationwide. Prosecutors are being pulled away from criminal casework to respond to the volume of habeas filings, straining offices already reduced by earlier staffing cuts and departures. The strain compounds separately-documented office-specific staffing collapses this tracker records elsewhere (e.g. the Minnesota U.S. Attorney's Office exodus, prosecution/cabinet-level/bondi-doj-renee-good-widow-investigation-2026.json), applying the same underlying dynamic -- civil/immigration litigation demand outpacing available career prosecutorial staff -- at a national scale rather than a single office. Update 2026-08-17: subsequent reporting has quantified the surge far more precisely than was available when this entry was added. Habeas petitions related to immigration detention rose roughly 36-fold nationally, from about 222 filed in 2024 to approximately 8,000 filed in 2025; one federal district alone received nearly 3,900 immigration habeas petitions in just the first five months of 2026, and the federal court in Minnesota received more than 1,200 such cases in the first half of 2026, up from just 12 two years earlier. DOJ's own Executive Office for United States Attorneys has acknowledged the strain directly: it sent a request to the civil chiefs of all 93 U.S. Attorney's offices asking them to report their pending immigration-habeas caseloads and civil-AUSA staffing levels since the start of fiscal year 2025, as of a January 26, 2026 data pull -- confirming DOJ leadership is tracking the capacity strain this entry documents, even though sourcing reviewed does not show additional prosecutorial capacity has been added to offset it.

title: Treasury Watchdog Finds ICE Didn't Meet Data-Safeguarding Standards Before Signing Taxpayer Data-Sharing Deal; Judge Separately Found 47,000 Unlawful Disclosures
institution: Internal Revenue Service (IRS) / Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), under a Treasury-DHS data-sharing agreement
status: Data-sharing agreement remains in effect as of this entry's sourcing; the Treasury Inspector General's findings and the federal court's unlawful-disclosure ruling are both matters of record, with no indication in reporting reviewed that the underlying agreement has been suspended or restructured in response
date_of_action: 2025-04 (ICE-IRS memorandum of understanding signed) through 2026-06 (Treasury IG report released)
what_changed: In April 2025, ICE and the IRS signed a memorandum of understanding allowing ICE to submit names and addresses of immigrants it identified as in the U.S. illegally to the IRS for cross-verification against confidential tax records, supporting the administration's mass-deportation operation. In June 2026, the Treasury Inspector General for Tax Administration (TIGTA) released a partially-redacted report finding that ICE did not meet required data-safeguarding standards before the MOU was signed, and that inconsistent formatting in ICE's submitted data and mismatches with the IRS's own matching criteria produced errors, incomplete records, and improper disclosures of taxpayer information. Separately, a federal judge ruled in February 2026 that the IRS broke the law by disclosing confidential taxpayer information to ICE, specifically identifying 47,000 unlawful disclosures.

estimated_impact.summary: The combination of a documented pre-agreement safeguarding failure (per TIGTA) and a court's independent finding of 47,000 unlawful taxpayer-data disclosures (per the February 2026 ruling) establishes both a systemic design flaw and a concrete, quantified harm: confidential taxpayer information -- information millions of Americans, including immigrants who file taxes using ITINs, provide under a decades-old expectation of confidentiality -- was shared through a system that failed basic data-quality and legal-compliance standards.

title: IRS Lost 27% of Its Workforce and a Third of Its Auditors — Independent Watchdogs Project $600B in Lost Revenue
institution: Internal Revenue Service (IRS)
status: Ongoing (2026 filing season completed under reduced staff; FY2027 budget request proposes a further ~4,800-employee cut, concentrated almost entirely in enforcement)
date_of_action: 2025-02 (initial probationary firings) through 2026-04 (most recent GAO/TIGTA reporting)
what_changed: Beginning February 2025, the IRS workforce was cut by approximately 27%, falling from roughly 102,000 employees in January 2025 to about 74,000 by December 2025 -- a reduction of nearly 28,000 people, primarily via probationary-employee terminations (~7,300), deferred-resignation buyouts (~4,700), and further attrition. The cuts were not evenly distributed: Taxpayer Services (which processes returns, answers phones, and handles correspondence) lost about 21-22% of its staff; the agency's IT function lost 27%; and revenue agents -- the specialists who conduct complex audits of high-income individuals, partnerships, and large corporations -- lost roughly 3,600 people, about 31% of the entire auditing workforce. Within the IT-function losses, one dramatic episode stands out: on March 31, 2025, roughly 50 senior IT executives -- most at the Senior Executive Service level, largely associate chief information officers with expertise spanning cybersecurity, modernization, applications, contracts, networks, and data-center operations -- were placed on administrative leave and had their system access cut off immediately, in the middle of tax-filing season. The decision was made by Elon Musk's Department of Government Efficiency and carried out by then-acting IRS Commissioner Melanie Krause; CNN reported the sidelined officials were seen internally as possible 'blockers' to a separate, controversial push to share IRS taxpayer data with immigration enforcement authorities. The IRS's chief information officer, Rajiv Uppal, and chief technology officer, Kaschit Pandya, were not among those dismissed. Of the roughly 50, 26 eventually departed via Treasury's deferred-resignation offer, while the other 22 remained on administrative leave. The cuts extended to physical infrastructure as well as headcount: in late February 2025, the General Services Administration sent the IRS a letter proposing to terminate or not renew leases on more than 110 (some reporting says up to 120) Taxpayer Assistance Centers -- the walk-in offices where taxpayers get in-person help with identity theft, audits, and other complex issues -- right at the height of tax-filing season. After pushback from taxpayers, tax professionals, and lawmakers, the IRS agreed to keep TAC offices open through the 2025 filing season, but the closures resumed afterward: by September 2025 the IRS confirmed it would close nine specific centers across six states (Pennsylvania, Iowa, New York, Kentucky, California, and West Virginia), effective November 30, 2025. Congress separately cut the IRS enforcement budget by 8% for FY2026 (the lowest inflation-adjusted level since 1988) and cut $1.1 billion (12%) from the IRS's base budget overall, rescinding most of the remaining Inflation Reduction Act funding that had been allocated to rebuild the agency; the base budget is now about 40% below its 2010 level after inflation. The IRS responded by lowering its own phone-service target from 85% to 70% of calls answered, and an independent analysis by the Center for Taxpayer Rights found call wait times on the main line increased more than 70% between February 2025 and February 2026. A March 2026 GAO audit found the IRS's staffing reductions 'were not targeted or strategic' and that the agency still lacks an updated strategic workforce plan. Notably, IRS Commissioner Frank Bisignano simultaneously serves as the Senate-confirmed Commissioner of the Social Security Administration -- see the related SSA entry in this tracker -- splitting his attention across both agencies during this period. The IRS's FY2027 budget request, released in 2026, seeks $9.8 billion in discretionary funding, down $1.4 billion from the $11.2 billion Congress enacted for FY2026, and proposes eliminating roughly 4,800 more positions (about 17% of remaining staff) on top of the 27% already lost in 2025. Nearly all of the proposed staffing reduction falls on enforcement -- examinations and collections -- which would see an 18% budget cut, while taxpayer-service funding would see a small 3% increase. The IRS's own budget documents describe the enforcement-side cuts as yielding roughly $778 million in savings once implemented. Re-verified 2026-07-26: no material change -- the FY2027 budget request remains a proposal, not enacted; no new congressional action identified since the prior update. Re-verified 2026-08-05: despite Bisignano's 'less people and better results' framing, internal documents reported by NOTUS show the IRS has been rushing to backfill critical staffing gaps, hiring roughly 2,000 employees as of January 2026 -- a partial rehire that still leaves the agency at a net ~28% workforce reduction from its January 2025 level, and that reporting characterizes as evidence of operational strain the agency's public statements had downplayed. Added 2026-08-11 (round-4 candidate discovery, cluster c0132): the Taxpayer Advocate Service (TAS) -- the statutorily independent office within the IRS, quoted throughout this entry, that helps individual taxpayers resolve problems and reports directly to Congress -- was itself targeted for a roughly 25% staff cut, losing 430 of its approximately 1,900 employees in an initial phase of reductions reported in March 2025, on top of more than 90 TAS employees who had already left via deferred resignation or earlier layoffs. Former National Taxpayer Advocate Nina Olson (2001-2019) said the cuts 'will have devastating consequences to the taxpayers that are in need of help.' The reduction directly shrank the capacity of the same watchdog office whose independent reporting on IRS-wide staffing and filing-season risk is cited elsewhere in this entry. Added 2026-08-11 (round-4 candidate discovery, clusters c0134/c0136): internal IRS emails reveal that senior IRS lawyer Joseph Rillotta warned agency officials in February 2025 that citing 'poor performance' as the justification for the roughly 7,000 probationary terminations that month was false -- no performance assessments had been conducted -- and amounted to fraud; the warning went unheeded, and termination letters citing performance issues went out February 20, 2025. Judge Alsup, ruling on the multi-agency probationary-firings case that also covered Treasury (the IRS's parent department), found in his March 13, 2025 preliminary injunction that the stated justification was 'a lie' and ordered reinstatement; the Supreme Court stayed that reinstatement order on April 8, 2025 on standing grounds, without addressing the merits of the fraud finding, and separate litigation -- including a California case alleging one of the largest employment-fraud schemes in U.S. history -- remained pending as of the reporting reviewed. In the interim, employees who had been reinstated under the since-stayed order were left in administrative limbo: CNN reported in May 2025 that reinstated IRS staff faced lapsed health insurance, unprocessed pension paperwork, and denied workers'-compensation claims amid a decimated HR function, with some describing emergency-room bills and delayed cancer screenings during the gap. Real-correction update 2026-08-18: this entry's prior rechecks (through 2026-08-13) described the FY2027 budget request's proposed further cuts as 'a proposal, not enacted,' without noting that the House Appropriations Committee had already voted to advance it, months earlier. On April 24, 2026, the House Appropriations Committee approved the FY2027 Financial Services and General Government funding bill in a 34-28 vote, setting IRS funding at $10.2 billion -- higher than the administration's own $9.8 billion request but still roughly 8.5% below the $11.2 billion FY2026 enacted level, with close to $1.4 billion of the reduction concentrated in enforcement. An amendment offered by FSGG Subcommittee Ranking Member Steny Hoyer (D-MD) that would have restored $1.8 billion to enforcement funding failed. The bill has not yet passed the full House or been taken up by the Senate as of this update, so it remains short of enactment -- but a committee-level vote already exists, which is a materially different posture than 'a proposal' alone, and this entry's five prior re-verification passes (2026-07-20 through 2026-08-13) did not catch it despite the vote predating all but the first of those.

title: LIHEAP Heating Assistance Program Staff Eliminated, Funding Delayed for Millions
institution: Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program (LIHEAP), Administration for Children and Families, HHS
status: Funding eventually released (Nov. 28, 2025); underlying staff elimination not reversed
date_of_action: 2025-04-04 (entire program staff terminated); 2025-10-01 through 2025-11-28 (funding delayed during shutdown)
what_changed: In April 2025, the Trump administration fired the entire federal staff team responsible for administering LIHEAP -- the ~$4.1 billion program that helps roughly 6 million low-income households pay heating and cooling bills, serving all 50 states, D.C., U.S. territories, and federally recognized tribes. This is the same program Trump's budget proposed zero-funding entirely. Six months later, when the October-November 2025 government shutdown (the longest in U.S. history at 43 days) hit, LIHEAP's annual funding allocation -- normally distributed to states by early November -- was delayed with no dedicated federal staff left to expedite the process once Congress acted. States including Pennsylvania, New York, Massachusetts, Minnesota, Connecticut, and Kansas had to delay or suspend their heating-assistance seasons entirely during the onset of winter. The $3.6 billion in delayed funding was finally released to states on November 28, 2025, over two weeks after the shutdown ended (Nov. 12) and roughly a month later than the program's normal early-November distribution. Trump's FY2027 budget, released April 3, 2026 and documented in more detail elsewhere in this tracker (trump-fy2027-budget-defense-tradeoff-2026.json), again proposed eliminating LIHEAP entirely, even as utility costs continued to rise and the program retained bipartisan congressional support.

primary_proponent.name: Trump administration / HHS Administration for Children and Families
primary_proponent.role: Executed the April 2025 staff elimination; oversaw the subsequent funding delay
primary_proponent.note: HHS did not name a specific individual responsible for the staff terminations in available reporting -- flag as agency-level, not individually attributable, though HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. was specifically the recipient of a bipartisan House member letter urging release of the delayed funds. An HHS spokesperson publicly blamed the delay entirely on 'congressional Democrats' without directly answering PBS's question about whether the earlier staff firings affected the agency's ability to process the funding quickly once released.

estimated_impact.summary: Roughly 6 million households nationally depend on LIHEAP, and about 68% of LIHEAP households also receive SNAP -- meaning the same families were simultaneously hit by both the LIHEAP delay and the SNAP funding freeze during the same shutdown window, compounding hardship. An estimated 21 million U.S. households were already behind on energy payments heading into the delay, with nearly 4 million disconnections possible for the season per the Center for Law and Social Policy.

What is specifically attributable to the administration is the April 2025 decision to eliminate the program's entire dedicated staff -- which several outlets (PBS explicitly) raised as a contributing factor to how slowly funding moved even after the shutdown ended, though HHS did not directly answer that question on the record.

title: FDA Commissioner Marty Makary Resigned After Being Pressured to Approve Flavored Vapes and Restrict the Abortion Pill
institution: U.S. Food and Drug Administration
status: Resignation effective as of May 12, 2026; Deputy Commissioner for Food Kyle Diamantas serving as acting commissioner
date_of_action: 2026-05-06 (FDA approves flavored e-cigarettes under reported White House pressure) through 2026-05-12 (Makary's resignation)
what_changed: FDA Commissioner Marty Makary resigned on May 12, 2026, amid internal conflicts over two major policy disputes. On flavored vaping products: the FDA approved flavored e-cigarettes from vaping company Glas Inc. on May 6, 2026, a move the Wall Street Journal reported came only after President Trump personally pressured Makary to approve the fruit-flavored vapes, which Makary had been refusing to authorize; a source told CBS News Makary is leaving specifically over this dispute, having been forced by other administration officials to approve products he did not want to approve. Kyle Diamantas, the FDA's deputy commissioner for food, stepped into the role on an acting basis. This resignation is distinct from, but adds to, the extensive leadership churn already documented in this tracker's separate entry on FDA's CBER (vaccine/biologics) division, where Makary had previously intervened as Commissioner during 2025-2026 turmoil -- this entry covers Makary's own departure from the top FDA post over non-vaccine disputes (vaping and the abortion pill).

title: DOGE Moved to Eliminate Nearly All Staff at the Millennium Challenge Corporation, a Bush-Era Foreign Aid Agency
institution: Millennium Challenge Corporation (MCC)
status: Partially reversed -- MCC survived as an agency after congressional/outside pushback, but more than half its programs were slated for cancellation and its workforce was sharply reduced; a leaner, more geopolitically-focused agency emerged rather than the full shutdown DOGE initially ordered
date_of_action: 2025-04-23 (DOGE staff briefing) through 2025-08 (agency confirmed surviving with a reduced portfolio)
what_changed: In late April 2025, Elon Musk's Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) informed Millennium Challenge Corporation leadership that the agency's programs would be closed and its staff minimized, with employees told in an internal meeting that the workforce-reduction plan called for eliminating all employees except the agency's acting CEO -- a position MCC is statutorily required to maintain. Staff were told they could be placed on administrative leave as soon as May 5, 2025, roughly a week after DOGE first arrived at the agency. MCC, created by Congress in 2004 under President George W. Bush, provides time-limited grants to developing countries -- including Ukraine, El Salvador, and Nepal -- conditioned on governance and policy reforms, distinguishing it structurally from USAID (tracked separately in this database) even though both are independent foreign-aid agencies targeted by the same DOGE-driven downsizing campaign. Senate Foreign Relations Committee Ranking Member Jeanne Shaheen and House Foreign Affairs Committee Ranking Member Gregory Meeks both issued statements condemning the move. Following that pushback, the shutdown plan did not fully proceed: reporting from August 2025 found MCC would survive as an agency, but more than half of its existing programs were slated for cancellation, and the agency's own public statements said its 'resulting portfolio will clearly align with the Trump Administration's America First foreign policy.' MCC's inaugural Trump-era CEO, Sean Cairncross, departed after roughly four months in the role, with coverage describing his brief tenure as focused on executing the downsizing before moving to a different administration post. By FY2026, MCC's own figures show it planning to award $287.3 million in new contracts against an annual budget of $830 million -- a functioning but substantially narrowed agency compared to its pre-2025 scope.

estimated_impact.summary: DOGE's initial plan would have eliminated MCC's entire staff outside its statutorily-required CEO position, effectively erasing a 21-year-old bipartisan foreign-aid agency without congressional action. After pushback, the agency survived in sharply reduced form -- with more than half its programs canceled and its remaining portfolio explicitly reoriented around the administration's 'America First' foreign-policy priorities rather than MCC's original development-and-governance-reform mission.

title: 446 Hospitals Across 44 States Found at High Risk of Closing or Cutting Services Because of Republican Medicaid Cuts
institution: Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services / hospitals nationwide reliant on Medicaid funding
status: Ongoing -- risk assessment based on funding changes already enacted (OBBBA) and being implemented (work-requirements rule documented separately in this tracker). Updated 2026-08-17: several individually-named hospitals disputed the risk analysis's methodology as applied to them, and separately, confirmed maternity/OB service closures at specific hospitals since publication show the risk has begun materializing in at least some cases, not just as a projection. Updated 2026-08-30: Public Citizen's own report adds concrete scale figures (beds, patients, workers, and a decade-scale dollar figure) not previously in this entry, and confirms -- with its own breakdown of the full 446-hospital set, not just the smaller Harvard subset already cited -- that the risk skews urban: 267 of 446 (60%) are in urban areas.
date_of_action: 2025-07 (OBBBA Medicaid funding provisions signed into law) through 2026-04 (hospital risk analysis published)
what_changed: An earlier analysis, published November 17, 2025 by Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health's Healthcare Quality and Outcomes Lab (researchers Jose Figueroa and Thomas Tsai) in collaboration with the New York Times, examined data on more than 4,400 U.S. hospitals from the American Hospital Association, Medicare's Healthcare Cost Report Information System, AHRQ, and the Private Equity Stakeholder Project, and identified 109 hospitals -- those serving 25%+ Medicaid patients, financially distressed, and already caring for vulnerable populations -- as facing the greatest risk from OBBBA's Medicaid cuts. 85% of those 109 highest-risk hospitals are in urban areas, and are therefore ineligible for the $50 billion Rural Health Transformation Fund OBBBA created to cushion rural hospitals from the same cuts; the researchers noted these urban safety-net hospitals disproportionately serve low-income and racial-minority patient populations. A new analysis, published by Public Citizen on March 31, 2026 (identified by name via HFMA's follow-up reporting; the original entry cited it only as 'an analysis' via NBC News's coverage), found that 446 hospitals across 44 states and Washington, D.C. are at high risk of closing or cutting services as a result of Medicaid funding reductions enacted in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA), the same law whose work-requirements provisions are documented separately in this tracker (medicaid-work-requirements-cms-rule-2026.json). Public Citizen's methodology flagged hospitals with a 20%+ Medicaid payer mix and negative net margins over 2022-2024. Many of the at-risk hospitals already operate at a financial loss and rely heavily on Medicaid reimbursement to remain viable; NBC News reported the cuts put jobs, maternity care, mental health services, and general local access to treatment at risk in the affected communities, particularly in rural and underserved areas where Medicaid patients make up an outsized share of hospital revenue. Trump himself connected these funding pressures directly to military spending priorities: speaking at a private White House Easter luncheon in April 2026, NBC News reported he said the federal government could not fund Medicaid, Medicare, and child care because military spending had to come first, arguing those responsibilities should shift to the states. At least four individually-named hospitals on or near the flagged list publicly disputed the risk assessment as applied to them, per HFMA's follow-up reporting: Northwest Mississippi Regional Medical Center's CEO said the analysis's 2022-2024 data window captured a temporary financial disruption from the hospital's May 2023 reacquisition by the county, not its actual trajectory; Minden Medical Center (Louisiana) said flatly it was not at risk of closing; Welch Community Hospital (West Virginia) said the analysis ignored that it is a state-operated facility funded by legislative appropriations rather than exposed to the federal Medicaid cuts the same way; and Metropolitan Hospital Center (NYC Health + Hospitals) pointed to record patient-care revenue and staff expansion as evidence it was securely positioned rather than at risk. None of these four rebuttals were independently adjudicated in sourcing reviewed -- they are hospital self-assessments, not a third-party re-analysis -- but they are documented here for balance given the risk analysis is itself already presented as a projection rather than a confirmed count. Separately, since the risk analysis's publication, at least three hospitals have confirmed actual Medicaid-cuts-linked service closures rather than projected risk: St. Mary's Sacred Heart Hospital (Lavonia, GA) closed its labor-and-delivery unit and OB/GYN center in fall 2025; Centra Southside Community Hospital (Farmville, VA) closed labor-and-delivery and OB/GYN surgical services; and Greene County General Hospital (Linton, IN) ended obstetrics services in January 2026. A broader 2026 rural-hospital report (Center for Healthcare Quality and Payment Reform) found 139 rural hospitals have closed labor-and-delivery units since 2020 (a 13% drop nationally), with OBBBA's Medicaid cuts cited as an accelerating pressure on top of pre-existing rural obstetric-unit attrition, not the sole cause -- the report does not attribute the full 139-hospital figure to OBBBA specifically, and this entry does not either. Additional detail from Public Citizen's own report, not previously broken out in this entry: the 446 at-risk hospitals collectively operate 68,986 beds, served approximately 6.6 million patients in 2024, and employ approximately 275,458 direct patient-care workers; 267 of the 446 (60%) are in urban areas, and five states -- Connecticut (36%), California (31%), New York (31%), Massachusetts, and Washington -- each have more than a quarter of their hospitals on the at-risk list. Public Citizen frames the underlying cause as OBBBA's roughly $1 trillion reduction in federal Medicaid funding over the next decade.

primary_proponent.note: The underlying Medicaid funding cuts were enacted through the OBBBA reconciliation legislation Trump signed July 4, 2025; sourcing reviewed did not identify a single named administration official personally responsible for the hospital-level risk analysis's findings, which is an independent third-party assessment of the funding law's downstream effects.

estimated_impact.summary: Nearly 450 hospitals nationwide -- spanning 44 states and the District of Columbia -- were found to be at high financial risk from reduced Medicaid funding, threatening not just coverage for Medicaid beneficiaries but broader local access to jobs, maternity care, mental health services, and emergency treatment in the communities those hospitals serve.

title: CMS Narrows Medical Frailty Exemption Beyond Statute in Medicaid Work-Requirement Rule -- Cancer and HIV Patients Left Unexempted
institution: Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS), Department of Health and Human Services
status: In effect -- interim final rule published June 1, 2026; national enforcement deadline January 1, 2027; several states (Nebraska, Montana, Arkansas) already implementing ahead of that deadline; public comment period on the rule remains open
date_of_action: 2026-06-01 (CMS interim final rule published)
what_changed: The One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA), signed into law July 4, 2025, required Medicaid expansion-population adults aged 19-64 to complete at least 80 hours per month of qualifying work, education, job training, or volunteer service to keep coverage, with a statutory exemption for individuals who are 'medically frail.' On June 1, 2026, CMS -- under Administrator Dr. Mehmet Oz -- published an interim final rule implementing the requirement nationwide. Rather than applying the statute's medical-frailty categories as written, CMS added an additional functional-capacity requirement: individuals must affirmatively demonstrate that their condition 'significantly impairs' their ability to perform the 80 hours of required activity, a threshold not present in the underlying statute. In practice, advocates and reporting say this leaves out people with early-stage cancer who are undergoing radiation treatment but are still nominally capable of some work, and people with HIV who are stable on treatment but technically employable -- both groups are not automatically exempted under CMS's narrower reading, and must instead navigate state reporting/paperwork processes to prove exemption eligibility or ongoing compliance. The Congressional Budget Office estimated the work-requirement provisions would cause roughly 5 million people to lose Medicaid coverage, out of a program covering about 68 million low-income Americans, and that the requirements account for roughly a third of the $900 billion in Medicaid savings scored under OBBBA overall (i.e., roughly $300 billion of that total tied to work-requirement-driven disenrollment). Nebraska became the first state to implement the requirement on May 1, 2026; Montana and Arkansas followed by July 1, 2026 (Arkansas delayed enforcement to January 2027), with additional states phasing in through the January 2027 national deadline. Update 2026-08-02 (detail): Per CNN's June 6, 2026 reporting on the same rule, the medical-frailty exemption requires more than a diagnosis -- enrollees must submit documentation, such as a signed statement from a medical professional, affirmatively showing their condition 'significantly impairs' their ability to meet the 80-hour work standard. A cancer patient in active chemotherapy who remains physically able to sit at a desk part-time may not qualify for the exemption on that documentation standard alone, regardless of diagnosis.

primary_proponent.name: Dr. Mehmet Oz
primary_proponent.role: CMS Administrator
primary_proponent.note: Oz publicly framed the rule as reducing loneliness and building 'skills and independence through work,' stating: 'This rule helps Americans build skills and independence through work, education, job training, or community service, creating new opportunities for themselves and their families.' CMS's specific choice to add a functional-capacity threshold beyond the statute's medical-frailty categories -- the discretionary regulatory action this entry documents -- was made under his administration of the agency.

estimated_impact.summary: Health-policy advocates and reporting describe the rule's core mechanism as bureaucratic rather than substantive: eligible, low-income people who are already working, studying, or too sick to reliably navigate monthly reporting requirements lose coverage not because they fail to meet the underlying policy goal, but because they fail the paperwork. People undergoing active cancer treatment or living with HIV -- conditions advocates argue should self-evidently qualify as medically frail -- are not automatically exempted under CMS's narrower functional-capacity standard.

The specific accountability question this entry documents is narrower: whether CMS's discretionary choice to layer an additional functional-capacity threshold onto the statute's medical-frailty exemption -- rather than applying Congress's own listed categories -- was a reasonable implementation choice or an administrative narrowing of an exemption Congress wrote more broadly. That legal/administrative question was not resolved as of this entry's sourcing.

title: Trump's Foreign Aid Freeze Halted a U.S.-Funded Anti-Fentanyl Cargo-Screening Program at Mexico's Busiest Port
institution: U.S. foreign aid programs (State Department/USAID-administered), implemented via UNODC-WCO Container Control Programme
status: Partially reversed after congressional pushback -- UNODC received a waiver restoring the specific port-screening program, but its continuation remained subject to a 90-day policy review, and other related anti-narcotics cooperation with Mexico stayed frozen
date_of_action: 2025-01-20 (global foreign aid freeze ordered) through 2025-02-24 (Reuters reporting on the disruption and subsequent waiver)
what_changed: On his first day back in office, January 20, 2025, Trump ordered a sweeping freeze on foreign aid. Within weeks the freeze stalled U.S. funding for the Container Control Programme, a joint initiative of the UN Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC) and the World Customs Organization that trained and equipped Mexico's Navy to screen cargo for fentanyl-precursor chemicals and other contraband at the Port of Manzanillo, Mexico's busiest container port. The U.S. had provided roughly $800,000 to launch the program at Manzanillo in 2023, and a planned expansion to two additional major ports -- Lazaro Cardenas and Veracruz -- was put on hold by the funding cutoff. The freeze also paused other U.S.-funded anti-narcotics cooperation with Mexico, including training for Mexican authorities to locate and dismantle clandestine fentanyl labs and U.S. donations of drug-sniffing canines. Following complaints from U.S. lawmakers, UNODC received notification of a waiver restoring the port-screening program, though State Department officials disputed characterizations that the freeze had 'stalled' it, and the program's longer-term continuation remained subject to a 90-day policy review. The contradiction drew broader notice on March 8, 2025, when Trump imposed new tariffs on Mexico, Canada, and China explicitly citing fentanyl trafficking as justification -- The Guardian noted that experts warned tariffs do little to stop smuggling itself, while the administration was simultaneously cutting the funding for the actual interdiction infrastructure (this same Container Control Programme) capable of intercepting the precursor chemicals at the source.

title: MSPB Loses Quorum for 8 Months After Trump Fires Whistleblower Board Chair Cathy Harris
institution: Merit Systems Protection Board
status: Resolved against Harris (the Supreme Court denied her petition for certiorari on June 30, 2026 -- one day after Trump v. Slaughter -- leaving the D.C. Circuit's December 2025 ruling upholding her firing as the final word in her individual case; the Board's quorum was separately restored in October 2025 via an unrelated confirmation, so the practical quorum crisis had already ended, but the removal-power precedent from the D.C. Circuit's 2-1 ruling is now permanent since the Supreme Court declined further review)
date_of_action: 2025-02-10 (firing) through present; the Board's quorum was separately restored in October 2025 via a new member's confirmation, independent of Harris's litigation
what_changed: On February 10, 2025, President Trump fired MSPB Chair Cathy Harris via a one-sentence email without citing any cause, three years before her Senate-confirmed term was set to expire in 2028. Harris sued; a district court granted a temporary restraining order reinstating her on February 18, and on March 4, Judge Rudolph Contreras granted summary judgment finding the firing unlawful. The government appealed, and a three-judge D.C. Circuit panel stayed her reinstatement on March 28. The full en banc D.C. Circuit voted 7-4 to vacate that stay and reinstate Harris on April 7, but two days later, on April 9, Chief Justice Roberts granted the government's emergency application for a stay, again removing Harris and leaving the Board without the quorum needed to issue decisions. In December 2025, a 2-1 D.C. Circuit panel (Judges Katsas and Walker, both Trump appointees) ruled on the merits that Congress cannot restrict the president's authority to remove NLRB or MSPB members who 'wield substantial executive power,' with a dissenting judge warning the majority's reasoning implies 'no independent agencies may lawfully exist in this country.' The Board separately regained a functional quorum in October 2025 through the unrelated Senate confirmation of a new member, James Woodruff. On March 17, 2026, Harris petitioned the Supreme Court for review, arguing her case is legally distinct from the FTC's Slaughter case because MSPB is purely adjudicatory, does not set policy, and structurally resembles multimember bodies with roughly 150 years of established constitutional standing. A group of Senate Democrats filed an amicus brief in April 2026 urging the Court to hear her case. The June 29, 2026 Trump v. Slaughter ruling did not directly resolve Harris's petition but substantially weakens her argument by holding broadly that agencies exercising 'executive power' must have removable leadership. Correction 2026-07-19: the Supreme Court denied Harris's petition for certiorari on June 30, 2026, one day after deciding Trump v. Slaughter -- this entry's prior 'remains formally unresolved' status is now out of date. The denial leaves the D.C. Circuit's December 2025 2-1 panel ruling (Katsas and Walker) as the final word on Harris's individual removal; the Supreme Court's order gave no reasoning beyond the standard denial, consistent with how it typically treats cert denials, so the underlying legal question (whether purely adjudicatory bodies like MSPB warrant different treatment than the FTC) was not resolved on the merits, only left undisturbed as decided below.

Circuit panel accepted in December 2025.

estimated_impact.summary: MSPB is the sole federal venue for civil servants, including whistleblowers, to appeal illegal firings and retaliation; Harris's removal left the Board without a functioning quorum for roughly eight months in 2025, echoing a prior five-year quorum gap (2017-2022) that left the agency with a backlog of more than 3,500 unresolved cases by the time quorum was restored.

Whistleblower advocates warn the practical stakes are severe because MSPB has exclusive jurisdiction over most federal whistleblower retaliation claims, meaning a quorum loss leaves affected employees with 'no realistic recourse' in the interim. This is a genuinely contested legal question rather than a settled one: a federal district court and the full en banc D.C. title: National Archives Loses Its Archivist and Digital Access Office Amid Deep Budget Cuts
institution: National Archives and Records Administration
status: Resolved as to leadership -- the Senate confirmed Bradford P. Wilson as Archivist of the United States on August 7, 2026 (Roll Call Vote No. 225, 119th Congress, 2nd Session, an en bloc confirmation of 74 nominations together, 51-47), ending an 18-month vacancy in the confirmed position; FY2026 budget cuts and office eliminations documented below remain in effect independent of the leadership question
date_of_action: 2025-02 (Archivist Colleen Shogan fired) through 2026 (ongoing reorganization, office eliminations, and records-center closures)
what_changed: In February 2025, President Trump fired Archivist of the United States Colleen Shogan without citing cause, an unprecedented removal of the position's confirmed leader. Deputy Archivist William Bosanko briefly became acting archivist before announcing his resignation along with several other senior staff. Secretary of State Marco Rubio was then named acting archivist while continuing his separate Cabinet role, a dual appointment a U.S. senator later suggested may have violated federal law given how long Rubio held both positions simultaneously; Jim Byron subsequently served as senior adviser performing archivist functions before departing in April 2026, when GSA head Edward Forst was named acting archivist. Separately, NARA's FY2026 budget request set the agency's funding at $414.7 million, nearly $60 million less than projected FY2025 spending, eliminating 136 full-time positions agency-wide. The proposal included full elimination of NARA's 50-person Office of Innovation, which runs the agency's online records catalog, digital access initiatives, and the public 'citizen archivist' transcription project, with NARA stating those functions would be 'transferred elsewhere' rather than continued directly. In June 2025, NARA issued reduction-in-force notices affecting roughly 100 employees (about 3% of staff), which two NARA employees said effectively 'wiped out' the Office of Innovation and the division supporting field offices and presidential libraries; the John F. Kennedy Presidential Library was briefly forced to close in February 2025 after probationary employees were terminated. The FY2026 proposal also cut funding for NARA's Electronic Records Initiative by roughly 33%, even as the agency faces a growing volume of incoming digital records, with only about 3% of its roughly 12 billion textual paper pages digitized as of the most recent count. In 2026, NARA also announced it would vacate three federal records centers (Chicago, San Francisco/San Bruno, and Seattle) and sunset its free public History Hub reference forum to save an estimated $370,000 annually. On March 2, 2026, Trump nominated Bradford P. Wilson to be the permanent Archivist of the United States; as of this update, Wilson's confirmation was still pending in the Senate. In the interim, GSA Administrator Edward Forst was named acting archivist under the Federal Vacancies Reform Act in April 2026, telling GSA staff he would 'dually serve' in both roles -- meaning NARA's day-to-day acting leadership is held by an official whose primary job is running a different agency. Re-verified 2026-07-26: Wilson's nomination received a hearing on June 17, 2026, but as one of 11 nominees split across two panels rather than a dedicated AOTUS hearing, with only a few minutes of questioning devoted to him specifically -- notable given the position's usual dedicated-hearing custom, per the Society of American Archivists' own monitoring of the nomination. No confirmation vote had occurred as of this update; Forst continues serving as acting archivist. Update 2026-08-17: the Senate confirmed Bradford P. Wilson as Archivist of the United States on August 7, 2026, as part of an en bloc vote covering 74 nominations together (51-47), per the Senate's own roll call and nominations-confirmed records. This resolves the entry's central open leadership question -- NARA now has a Senate-confirmed archivist for the first time since Colleen Shogan's February 2025 firing, ending the sequence of acting/dual-hatted leaders (Bosanko, Rubio, Byron, Forst) that this entry has tracked. Independent confirmation of Wilson's swearing-in date and formal transition from acting archivist Edward Forst was not found as of this update; the confirmation vote itself is the sourced fact. The FY2026 budget cuts, Office of Innovation elimination, and records-center closures documented above are unaffected by this leadership resolution and remain the entry's standing findings.

what_changed: Separate from -- but compounding -- a proposed FY2026 budget request that would cut NCI's funding by 37.3% (about $2.69 billion, from roughly $7.22 billion to $4.53 billion), NCI had already lost hundreds of staff and had more than $180 million in active research grants cancelled as of a June 26, 2025 Guardian report, with key prevention, clinical-trial, and community-research programs being dismantled in the process. A May 2025 U.S. Senate Minority Staff report separately found the federal government had cut approximately $2.7 billion in NIH funding overall in the first three months of 2025, including a 31% year-over-year decrease in cancer-research funding through March 2025 compared with the same period in 2024 -- a distinct, already-executed reduction from the proposed FY2026 request. By September 2025, the New York Times Magazine reported NCI's public-facing website and communications functions had been 'devastatingly dismantled,' leaving patient calls for cancer information unanswered, and that labs studying specific cancers -- including pediatric brain tumors -- were being gutted, with researchers forced to suspend ongoing studies and lay off their own staff as grant funding lapsed. Analysts and cancer-research organizations warned that if the proposed 37% FY2026 cut were enacted, NCI's grant-approval rate would collapse to roughly 4% of new applications (down from historical norms several times higher), rejecting 96% of new research proposals. Update 2026-08-17: The proposed FY2026 37.3% NCI cut described above did not take effect. Congress enacted the FY2026 Labor-HHS-Education appropriations act (P.L. 119-75, H.R. 7148, Division B) on 2026-02-03, providing NCI $7.4 billion -- an increase over FY2025 funding, not the proposed $2.69 billion/37.3% cut to ~$4.53 billion. This entry's date_added (2026-08-12) came more than six months after that enactment, so the 'proposed, not yet enacted' framing had already gone stale before this entry was first written. The already-executed 2025 harms described above -- the 2025 staff losses, the $180M+ in cancelled grants, and the dismantled communications infrastructure -- are separate, already-completed actions and are unaffected by the FY2026 appropriations increase; they have not been reversed.

title: National Climate Assessment Gutted -- 400 Authors Dismissed, Reports Pulled Offline, Climate Skeptic Installed to Run the Program
institution: U.S. Global Change Research Program (USGCRP) -- National Climate Assessment
status: Ongoing and escalated -- USGCRP, now under Wielicki, published a formal proposed amendment to the already-released Fifth National Climate Assessment (NCA5) on August 25, 2026, open for public comment through September 9, 2026; the Sixth Assessment (due 2028) remains in doubt
date_of_action: 2025-04-01 (ICF International coordination contract cancelled) through 2026-07-09 (skeptic appointed to lead USGCRP)
what_changed: In early April 2025, NASA cancelled a contract with ICF International, the consulting firm hired to support the U.S. Global Change Research Program's (USGCRP) logistical coordination work across the 15 federal agencies and hundreds of volunteer authors that produce the National Climate Assessment -- a report on climate change's impacts on the United States that has been congressionally mandated every four years since the Global Change Research Act of 1990. On April 28, 2025, nearly 400 scientists and scholars who had already begun volunteer work on the Sixth National Climate Assessment (due for publication by early 2028) were informed by email that they had been 'released' while the report's scope was 'reevaluated.' By June 30, 2025, the National Climate Assessments -- including prior, already-published editions -- were no longer accessible on federal websites, with no explanation or referral to alternative sources. The move was consistent with Project 2025, the Heritage Foundation policy blueprint, whose chapter on the National Climate Assessment (co-authored with input from OMB Director Russell Vought) called for the report to be reshaped and its contributors 'better scrutinized.' The dismissal left the administration able to either skip the congressionally mandated report or pursue an alternative version. On July 9, 2026, the White House confirmed that direction: it appointed Matthew Wielicki, a former University of Alabama geochemist and prominent skeptic of mainstream climate science, to lead USGCRP -- the program responsible for compiling the assessment the administration had gutted fifteen months earlier. Update 2026-08-18: this entry's existing caveat noted that the eventual shape of any future National Climate Assessment under Wielicki's leadership was 'not yet known' as of the entry's original verification -- but work on the Sixth Assessment did not sit idle between the April 2025 author dismissals and Wielicki's July 2026 appointment as USGCRP director. Starting in December 2025, the administration invited a new group of researchers known for climate skepticism to resume work on the Sixth National Climate Assessment, months before Wielicki was named to formally lead the program. This is a distinct fact from, and should not be confused with, a separate Department of Energy effort covering similar ground: DOE Secretary Chris Wright separately convened his own five-scientist 'Climate Working Group' (John Christy, Roy Spencer, Steve Koonin, Judith Curry, and Ross McKitrick) earlier in 2025 to produce a contrarian report critiquing the existing Fifth National Climate Assessment and the EPA's endangerment finding; Wright dissolved that group himself in a September 3, 2025 letter after its report drew a rebuttal from 85+ scientists, and a federal court (Judge William Young, D. Mass., January 30, 2026) later found the Climate Working Group's secretive operation violated the Federal Advisory Committee Act. That DOE action is institutionally separate -- a different agency, a different responsible official (Wright, not the USGCRP/NASA officials and Vought documented in this entry), and a different specific action -- and is already tracked in this database's Cabinet-Level tracker (see wright-faca-violation-2026.json); it is not folded into this entry despite the thematic overlap. Update 2026-08-29: on August 25, 2026, USGCRP published a Federal Register notice announcing a proposed amendment to NCA5 -- the existing, already-published Fifth National Climate Assessment, not the still-pending Sixth -- open for public comment through 11:59 p.m. ET on September 9, 2026. The proposed amendment addresses NCA5 findings that depend materially on RCP8.5, SSP5-8.5, SRES A2, or similar high-emissions pathways, stating that those pathways should not be treated as expected, likely, baseline, business-as-usual, central, or policy-relevant planning futures, and that NCA5 findings substantially dependent on them should be labeled as resting on 'implausible high-end scenario assumptions.' This is the first concrete action under Wielicki's USGCRP leadership that reaches backward to reclassify an already-published, congressionally mandated assessment's own findings, rather than only shaping the still-pending Sixth Assessment -- resolving this entry's prior caveat that no completed or published document existed yet to assess. Update 2026-09-01 (GSR recheck batch 49, during the still-open comment period): the amendment's core technical premise -- that RCP8.5/SSP5-8.5 shouldn't be treated as a likely, business-as-usual future -- is not a fabricated or purely political claim; mainstream climate scientists (e.g. The Climate Brink, May 18, 2026) had already been retiring RCP8.5 as an implausible worst-case scenario for roughly a decade, independent of this administration, citing coal-reserve assumptions the scenario exceeds, clean-energy cost declines, and diverging real-world emissions trends. That same mainstream commentary explicitly separates the underlying science from what it calls a political misuse of the point: it criticizes President Trump's public framing of the scenario's retirement as an 'admission' that climate projections were 'WRONG,' and notes the irony that the administration's own climate-rollback policies (including the SO2/NOx and power-plant-GHG rollbacks tracked elsewhere in this database's Corporate Deregulation tracker) push future emissions trajectories closer to the high-end scenarios it is now dismissing as impossible. Criticism of the specific NCA5 amendment is not limited to mainstream defenders of the assessment, either: climate economist Roger Pielke Jr., who has himself long argued RCP8.5 is overused, wrote that while the administration is 'directionally correct' about the scenario's problems, the amendment 'cannot succeed' because NCA5's underlying problems are 'systemic and irreparable' -- i.e., a critique from someone otherwise sympathetic to the RCP8.5 objection that this specific fix is inadequate, not that it goes too far. No comment-period outcome exists yet since the window remains open through September 9, 2026.

No single official's name was confirmed publicly as the signer of the April 28, 2025 dismissal email; Rep. Zoe Lofgren (D-CA), ranking member of the House Science Committee, addressed her formal oversight letter on the dismissals to Michael Kratsios, Director of the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy, which has institutional oversight of USGCRP.

estimated_impact.summary: The National Climate Assessment is the U.S. government's flagship, legally mandated report on how climate change is affecting the country -- used by city and state planners, insurers, farmers, and courts. Dismissing its ~400 volunteer authors, cancelling the contract coordinating the 15-agency effort behind it, and removing existing editions from federal websites leaves the statutorily required Sixth Assessment (due 2028) in doubt, and installing a climate-science skeptic to lead the program that produces it signals the administration intends to replace mainstream scientific consensus in the government's own official climate reporting rather than simply pause it.

The July 2026 Wielicki appointment is corroborated by the Washington Post, SEJ, and Eos -- and, notably, also celebrated in identical factual terms by climate-skeptic outlets (Climate Depot, Watts Up With That, CFACT) covering their own side's win, which corroborates the characterization of this as a deliberate ideological redirection rather than a framing dispute between outlets. Re-verified 2026-08-29: the proposed NCA5 amendment is corroborated directly by the Federal Register notice and NOAA's own posted PDF of the proposed text, with the same facts (scope, RCP8.5/SSP5-8.5/SRES A2 language, September 9 comment deadline) independently reported by outlets favorable to the change (Competitive Enterprise Institute, Watts Up With That, Roger Pielke Jr.'s newsletter, AEI) -- the same same-fact-different-framing corroboration pattern already used for the Wielicki appointment in this entry. Both additions describe reactions during an open comment period, not a resolved outcome.

title: $362 Million in National Park Service Grants Stalled Awaiting Political Review in Burgum's Office
institution: National Park Service / Department of the Interior
status: Ongoing -- backlog reported as of early June 2026, with no reporting reviewed indicating it had been cleared
date_of_action: 2026-06 (backlog reported); consolidation of grant-approval authority into the Secretary's office occurred earlier in 2025-2026
what_changed: More than 1,400 active NPS grants worth roughly $362 million are sitting unapproved at the Department of the Interior, awaiting political review after the department consolidated grants-management sign-off into Secretary Doug Burgum's office. The stalled projects include nonprofit youth-program deployments to clear trails, work to prevent washouts during heavy rain, and wildlife surveys. Interior is managing the backlog with a significantly reduced staff, after the department shed roughly 13,000 employees (about 20% of its workforce) in 2025, including about 4,000 at NPS specifically. An Interior Department spokesperson described the added review layer as a 'common-sense stewardship measure' intended to 'streamline internal processes' and 'reduce unnecessary bureaucracy.' Update 2026-08-17: more than 70 House Democrats, led by Rep. Don Beyer, sent a formal letter to Interior demanding the department address the grant backlog, specifically citing delayed trail maintenance, wildfire prevention, and other critical projects -- widening the congressional pressure on this issue beyond the earlier individual questioning from Rep. Elfreth and Sen. Merkley already documented here. No reporting reviewed indicates the backlog has been cleared or the additional review layer removed. Update 2026-08-30: identified the specific review mechanism and precise date behind the letter referenced above -- House Natural Resources Committee Ranking Member Jared Huffman co-led the effort alongside Beyer, and the letter, dated July 22, 2026, specifies that the new process requires two political appointees to manually review every NPS grant and cooperative agreement over $50,000, which the lawmakers identify as the specific bottleneck producing the backlog. The letter requested a response, including a full list of backlogged grants, by July 28, 2026; no reporting reviewed confirms whether Interior met that deadline or what, if anything, it provided in response.

title: GSA/DOGE Listed 34 National Park Service Buildings for Lease Termination, Including Visitor Centers and Museums Housing Artifacts
institution: National Park Service (NPS); General Services Administration (GSA)
status: Ongoing in phases through 2026; at least two individual sites (Fairbanks, AK and Seattle, WA) reversed or found to have been included in error; the leasing-authority bill Congress introduced in response has since advanced out of committee
date_of_action: 2025-03-06 (list publicly reported) through 2026 (phased terminations continuing)
what_changed: On March 6, 2025, the Washington Post reported that GSA, working with DOGE, had targeted the leases of at least 34 National Park Service buildings for termination as part of the administration's broader federal real-estate cost-cutting push -- including visitor centers, law enforcement offices, park headquarters, and museum/archive space housing millions of cultural artifacts. GSA said terminating the leases could save taxpayers millions of dollars; terminations were structured to arrive in waves stretching from 2025 into 2026, with example dates including a planned September 30, 2025 termination for Seattle's Klondike Gold Rush National Historical Park visitor center and a planned end-of-May-2026 termination for a National Park Service building in Fairbanks, Alaska. Park advocates warned the closures would degrade the visitor experience, particularly during peak summer season, threaten artifact preservation, and disrupt law-enforcement and emergency operations at affected parks. At least two individual terminations were subsequently reversed or corrected: GSA restored the Fairbanks-area Alaska Public Lands Information Center lease roughly 10 days after terminating it, following pressure from Sen. Dan Sullivan; and the Klondike Gold Rush visitor center lease in Seattle was found to have been placed on the termination list in error -- the lease had actually been extended by Historic Seattle in September 2024 through 2030, with GSA apparently unaware of the extension when it added the site to the list. Members of Congress, including Sens. Amy Klobuchar and Tina Smith, formally urged GSA not to proceed with terminations affecting other specific NPS buildings; a bill, the National Park System Long-Term Lease Investment Act (S.2498/H.R.4931), was introduced in Congress during this period aimed at giving NPS more stable, long-term leasing authority, though it had not been enacted as of this entry's last verification. Update 2026-08-30 (GSR recheck batch 39): H.R. 4931 advanced out of the House Natural Resources Committee markup on July 22, 2026, alongside several other public-lands bills, moving it a step closer to a House floor vote -- no floor vote had occurred as of this update. The bill's actual mechanism, allowing NPS to extend certain existing leases held 5+ years without competitive rebidding when the Director finds it in the park unit's best interest, drew formal opposition from the National Parks Conservation Association, which argued in December 2025 testimony to the same committee that extending leases without fair-market-rent consideration risks the government failing to secure optimal uses for the 340+ structures NPS currently leases -- a concern in tension with the bill's stated purpose of encouraging private investment in maintaining park assets. No comprehensive updated tally of the original 34 sites' current status was found in sourcing reviewed.

title: National Park Service Lost 24% of Its Permanent Staff — Internal Report Contradicts Interior's Public 'False Narrative' Denial
institution: National Park Service (NPS), Department of the Interior
status: Ongoing -- the 2025 pattern repeated into the 2026 summer season: permanent staffing losses (~24%, ~4,000 people) remain unreversed, and 2026 seasonal hiring again fell short of its own target heading into peak season
date_of_action: 2025-02-14 (initial mass layoff, dubbed the 'Valentine's Day Massacre' by affected staff) through 2025-08-27 (internal operational-status report surfaces)
what_changed: On February 14, 2025, NPS laid off approximately 1,000-1,700 probationary employees just weeks before peak visitor season began across the system's 63 national parks and 370 other managed sites. Added 2026-08-11 (round-4 candidate discovery, cluster c0136): a March 13, 2025 preliminary injunction from Judge William Alsup ordered NPS and five other agencies (Agriculture, Defense, Energy, Interior, Treasury, and VA) to immediately reinstate their terminated probationary employees; NPS and other named agencies complied only nominally, notifying fired staff they were reinstated but then placing them on indefinite paid administrative leave rather than restoring them to duty -- a workaround Alsup explicitly ruled violated the injunction, since it did not restore the services the order intended to restore. The Supreme Court stayed Alsup's reinstatement order on April 8, 2025 on standing grounds, allowing the administration to resume the firings; NPS's ~24% permanent-staff loss documented later in this entry reflects that the initial February terminations were not durably reversed. By March 11, 2025, reporting confirmed the administration was separately pushing for a 30% reduction in NPS's overall payroll -- a budget-driven target distinct from, and layered on top of, the February probationary firings -- expected to further reduce park rangers, custodial staff, and conservation-program capacity. By July 2025, independent analysis of Interior Department workforce data by the National Parks Conservation Association (NPCA) found NPS had lost 24% of its permanent staff overall (about 4,000 people) since January, while only roughly 4,500 of a promised ~8,000 seasonal positions had been filled. In April 2025, Interior Secretary Doug Burgum issued Secretarial Order 3426, mandating that every park remain 'open and accessible' regardless of staffing levels -- meaning parks could not close facilities or reduce services in response to the shortages, only quietly absorb the strain. Per Order 3426's own reporting requirement, every park unit had to submit an updated operational status by July 25, 2025; an internal NPS report compiled from those submissions, first reported by the New York Times, documented widespread, specific impacts: nearly 70 parks reduced visitor center hours, 22 postponed maintenance, and 11 closed or delayed opening facilities. Specific documented examples include all 13 lifeguard positions vacant at Assateague Island National Seashore (leaving the beach unguarded), the fire management team reduced to one person at Cumberland Island National Seashore, and Indiana Dunes National Park's ranger-led tours cut from 575 to approximately 100 for the year after 4 of 6 interpretive-division supervisors took early retirement. When this internal report became public, Interior deputy press secretary Aubrie Spady called the reporting a 'false narrative,' stating 'staffing levels and operations at our National Parks this summer are on par with previous years. Full Stop' -- a direct denial of findings drawn from the agency's own internal, Order-3426-mandated data collection. For the 2026 season, NPS again fell short of its own seasonal-hiring target: roughly 4,500 of a planned 5,000+ seasonal positions were filled heading into peak summer season, with reporting citing paperwork delays, background-check backlogs, and housing shortages as contributing causes -- a smaller absolute gap than 2025's (~4,500 of ~8,000 filled), but the same shortfall pattern for a second consecutive year. The ~24% permanent-staff loss and its downstream effects (documented in this entry's 2025 examples) had not been reversed as of this update. On September 2-3, 2025, nearly 600 employees at Yosemite and Sequoia & Kings Canyon voted overwhelmingly to unionize with the National Federation of Federal Employees, a direct workforce response to the mass purges and budget cuts documented above -- workers cited the strain of being stretched thin (scientists and other specialists covering basic operational duties) as a driving factor. Update 2026-07-26: the 2026 peak season brought the staffing crisis to a head -- record crowds collided with reduced capacity at parks including Yosemite, where seasonal employees reportedly went weeks without pay, scientists and hydrologists were reassigned to cleaning restrooms and staffing entrance gates, and some campgrounds closed for lack of staff to run them. NPS also removed timed-entry reservation systems at some of the busiest parks and introduced a new $100-per-person fee for international visitors, both of which affected entrance-line flow during the July 4th weekend's record crowds. On a partial-relief note, NPS was approved to refill roughly 600 staff positions -- a real but small fraction of the several thousand permanent positions lost since January 2025, not a reversal of the underlying staffing loss this entry documents. Update (2026-08-17 recheck): on April 3, 2026, the White House released its fiscal year 2027 budget proposal, requesting $2.14 billion for NPS operations -- a $736 million, roughly 25% cut from the prior year -- which NPCA and other outlets project would eliminate approximately 2,920 additional full-time positions on top of the ~4,000 permanent positions already lost since January 2025. As with the entry's existing budget-threat context, this is a proposal, not enacted law: Congress alone controls appropriations, and as of this update the FY2027 budget remained under congressional debate, with a final vote not expected before fall 2026 at the earliest. Notably, Congress rejected a comparable roughly $1 billion FY2026 NPS cut proposal in a January 5, 2026 appropriations bill, instead approving $3.267 billion in flat funding and adding a requirement that the administration notify Congress before any future mass firings or reorganizations -- a precedent for congressional pushback, though not a guarantee the FY2027 proposal meets the same fate. Update 2026-08-30: the National Parks Conservation Association organized a nationwide 'Day of Action,' running August 22 through September 1, 2026 with roughly 30 events across 20 states and Washington, D.C., calling on President Trump and Interior Secretary Burgum to invest in NPS staffing and address the workforce shortages this entry documents. NPCA -- a 501(c)(3) that states it does not endorse, oppose, or fund political candidates -- organized the events partly in response to Interior Department claims about employee political activity. The campaign's public materials also cited related administration actions not otherwise part of this entry's own documentation: separate pricing for international visitors, placement of Trump's image on the 2026 annual pass, and removal of 'disparaging' content from federal historic sites -- noted here for context but not independently verified by this entry, since they fall outside its core staffing-crisis subject. Update 2026-09-01 (GSR recheck batch 52): the FY2027 budget fight referenced in this entry's 2026-08-17 update ('not yet enacted, still under debate') had already moved by the time of that recheck -- the House Appropriations Subcommittee on Interior, Environment and Related Agencies released its FY2027 bill on May 20, 2026, rejecting the administration's proposed $736 million/~2,920-position cut and instead holding NPS operations funding essentially flat at $2.9 billion (a 1.3%/~$3 million reduction from FY2026), following the same pattern as Congress's FY2026 rejection of a similar cut this entry already documents. The bill still needed full-House passage and Senate reconciliation as of the sourcing reviewed, so this is a subcommittee-level rejection of the administration's ask, not a final enacted FY2027 appropriation.

primary_proponent.name: Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) / Doug Burgum
primary_proponent.role: DOGE directed the initial layoffs; Interior Secretary Burgum issued the 'stay open regardless of staffing' order that followed
primary_proponent.note: Burgum's Secretarial Order 3426 is the specific policy mechanism that turned a staffing shortage into a documented service-quality crisis -- by prohibiting parks from closing or scaling back in response to short-staffing, the order effectively required remaining staff to absorb the gap rather than allowing an official acknowledgment of reduced capacity. Interior's own deputy press secretary's 'false narrative' denial is difficult to reconcile with the fact that the cited findings came from data Interior itself required parks to report under Burgum's own order.

estimated_impact.summary: NPCA President and CEO Theresa Pierno characterized the situation as predictable: 'This crisis was both predictable and preventable. Gutting staff, freezing seasonal hiring, and pushing out experienced rangers was a recipe for disaster.' Beyond visitor-experience impacts, several documented examples touch public safety and resource protection directly -- the loss of fire response capacity at Cumberland Island, halted pest/disease monitoring (including zoonotic disease surveillance for plague, rabies, and hantavirus) at Grand Canyon, and unstaffed entrance stations at Glacier National Park during normal operating hours.

Re-verified 2026-07-26: the Yosemite specifics, international-visitor fee, and 600-position refill approval are corroborated by CNN, RV Lifestyle, and Modern Campground reporting on the 2026 peak season. Re-verified 2026-08-30: the NPCA Day of Action (Aug. 22-Sept. 1, 2026, ~30 events/20 states+DC) is HIGH confidence, sourced directly to Newsweek's reporting on NPCA's own campaign materials; the additional grievances it cited (international-visitor pricing, Trump's image on the annual pass, historic-site content removal) were left unverified and out of scope for this entry's own core subject, consistent with this tracker's stay-tight-to-the-entry's-own-subject discipline. Update 2026-09-01 (GSR recheck batch 52): the May 20, 2026 House Appropriations Subcommittee action and the $2.9 billion/1.3% figures are corroborated via direct fetch of NPCA's own reporting on the subcommittee release -- HIGH confidence on the subcommittee-level action; the bill's subsequent full-House and Senate status was not independently re-checked as of this recheck.

A proposed FY2027 budget (April 2026) would cut NPS operations by $736M/~25% and ~2,920 more positions; not yet enacted, and Congress rejected a comparable FY2026 cut proposal in January 2026.
