title: Tribes Lost Over $6 Million in Non-IHS Federal Health Grants and Technical Support Staff Despite RFK Jr.'s Promise to Protect Native American Health Funding
institution: HHS agencies outside the Indian Health Service (CDC, HRSA, and others)
status: Ongoing -- a third, distinct funding threat (ACA enhanced-subsidy expiration hitting tribal marketplace-coverage programs) identified alongside the original non-IHS grant cuts and the FY2026 IHS appropriations fight; no reversal identified in sourcing reviewed for any of the three threads
date_of_action: 2025-02 through 2025-06 (cumulative grant cancellations and staffing losses reported)
what_changed: Despite HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.'s stated commitment to protect Native American health funding by shielding the Indian Health Service (IHS) itself from cuts, tribes reported losing more than $6 million in grants from other HHS agencies -- funding that paid for community health workers, vaccinations, data modernization, and other public health efforts -- according to a May 2025 letter from the National Indian Health Board to Kennedy. The administration canceled funding for programs it classified as violating Trump's ban on diversity, equity, and inclusion initiatives, including a program supporting Native American youth interested in science and medicine careers and a program helping several tribes increase access to healthy food. Tribal health officials also reported that federal staffing cuts across HHS agencies made it substantially harder to get technical support and administer federally funded health projects, in some cases because specific staffers tribes had worked with directly were fired. Tribal leaders highlighted the contradiction between the administration's stated chronic-disease-prevention priority and its funding cuts, with one official noting it was 'very confusing to say chronic disease prevention is the No. 1 priority and then to eradicate the support needed to address chronic disease prevention in Indian Country.' Update 2026-08-18 (GSR recheck batch 22): the non-IHS pattern documented above continued into 2026 -- CDC's Healthy Tribes program (culturally tailored public health initiatives) was reported terminated, and further reductions were reported at SAMHSA (Tribal Behavioral Health and Opioid Response grants, Native Connections), HRSA, the Administration for Community Living, and NIH, with the administration's FY2026 budget proposal separately seeking to eliminate roughly $128 million in Tribal set-aside mental/behavioral health funding and the Food is Medicine program. On the IHS side specifically -- which RFK Jr.'s promise covered -- Congress rejected the administration's proposed nearly-30%/$900 million FY2026 IHS cut: the enacted FY2026 appropriations package instead increased IHS funding roughly 1.1-1.3% over FY2025 (about $8.05 billion total, plus $5.31 billion in FY2027 advance appropriations), including a $41 million boost to the Special Diabetes Program for Indians (its largest in 22 years) and a $5 million increase for Urban Indian Health. This means the entry's core distinction -- IHS protected, non-IHS agencies cut -- held up and sharpened over the following year: Congress affirmatively reinforced IHS funding while the non-IHS cuts this entry documents continued and expanded. Update 2026-08-30 (GSR recheck batch 39): identified a third, mechanically distinct funding threat missed by the entry's prior two updates -- the December 31, 2025 expiration of enhanced ACA marketplace subsidies has directly strained tribal health organizations' insurance-assistance programs, which help Native Americans access care outside limited IHS facilities. Tuba City Regional Health Care Corp. (Navajo Nation, Arizona) reported its patient-coverage costs rising roughly 170% to nearly $38,000/month without the enhanced subsidies; Fort Peck Tribes (Montana) said it is now 'limiting who gets help'; and Blackfeet Nation (Montana) paused employer-sponsored coverage for 52 people in January 2026. National Indian Health Board CEO A.C. Locklear warned that reduced access to general primary care compounds existing health disparities. This is a third, distinct mechanism from the entry's existing two threads (non-IHS HHS grant/staffing cuts, and the IHS budget-appropriations fight) -- it affects tribal organizations' own insurance-navigation and coverage-assistance programs rather than direct federal grants or IHS appropriations, and predates but was not previously captured by this entry's 2026-08-18 update. Update 2026-09-01 (GSR recheck batch 52): identified a fourth, mitigating funding thread not previously in this entry -- the Rural Health Transformation Program (RHTP), a $50 billion, five-year CMS grant program created by HR1 itself (the same law whose Medicaid cuts this tracker's related entries document) and announced Dec. 29, 2025, with awards to all 50 states announced starting late January 2026, includes Tribal-specific set-asides or initiatives in at least 13 states' approved applications (AZ, CA, CO, MN, MT, NE, NM, NY, OK, OR, UT, WA, WI). Oregon's application, developed with its nine federally recognized Tribes, dedicates $21.7 million of the state's 2026 RHTP award specifically to a Tribal Initiative improving healthcare access in rural and remote Tribal communities. This is a distinct, positive-mitigation development running alongside -- not a reversal of -- the entry's existing three threads (non-IHS grant/staffing cuts, the IHS appropriations fight, and the ACA-subsidy marketplace strain); RHTP funds tribal-specific rural-health infrastructure and access initiatives, not the specific non-IHS programs (Healthy Tribes, SAMHSA behavioral-health grants, etc.) this entry documents as cut, so it does not offset those losses directly.

primary_proponent.name: Robert F. Kennedy Jr.
primary_proponent.role: Secretary of Health and Human Services
primary_proponent.note: Publicly promised to protect Native American health funding by shielding IHS from HHS-wide cuts, while cuts to non-IHS HHS agencies serving the same tribal communities proceeded; no single official was identified in reporting as directing each individual non-IHS grant cancellation.

estimated_impact.summary: Tribes lost over $6 million in HHS grants outside the Indian Health Service, plus DEI-flagged program cancellations and technical-support staffing losses, undercutting the administration's own stated promise to protect Native American health funding and directly contradicting its stated chronic-disease-prevention priority. Separately, a new $50 billion federal Rural Health Transformation Program created by the same HR1 law includes Tribal-specific funding set-asides in at least 13 states, including a $21.7 million dedicated Tribal Initiative in Oregon for 2026 -- a mitigating funding stream running alongside, not offsetting, the cuts this entry otherwise documents.

title: Trump Administration Moves to Remove Supercomputers From NCAR, Disrupting Weather and Climate Research for 1,500+ Scientists
institution: National Science Foundation / National Center for Atmospheric Research (NCAR)
status: Blocked as of June 1, 2026 -- a federal judge issued a preliminary injunction halting the transfer of the NCAR-Wyoming Supercomputing Center's stewardship from UCAR to the University of Wyoming, following UCAR's March 2026 lawsuit alleging the plan was retaliation against Colorado; a second, distinct lawsuit filed August 20, 2026 by the Environmental Defense Fund separately challenges the planned closure of NCAR's Mesa Laboratory itself under the National Historic Preservation Act; both cases remain pending with no ruling on the merits identified as of this recheck
date_of_action: 2025-12-16 (first reporting of White House plan to 'break up' NCAR) through 2026-02-13 (NSF letter confirming supercomputer removal plan)
what_changed: Reporting first surfaced in mid-December 2025 that the administration was moving to dismantle the National Science Foundation's National Center for Atmospheric Research (NCAR) in Boulder, Colorado -- a 60-plus-year cornerstone of U.S. weather and climate science -- with officials characterizing it as a source of "climate alarmism." The news broke via a post on X from OMB Director Russell Vought, with no advance warning to NCAR's own funder, NSF, or to the White House's usual channels for announcing agency actions; CNN reported the announcement landed in the middle of the American Geophysical Union's (AGU) annual meeting, where climate scientist Katherine Hayhoe wrote on Bluesky that 'NCAR is quite literally our global mothership... Dismantling NCAR is like taking a sledgehammer to the keystone holding up our scientific understanding of the planet.' AGU convened an emergency town hall of hundreds of scientists at the meeting in response, and on March 12, 2026 formally submitted comments to NSF opposing the dismantling proposal, arguing NCAR's integrated, interdisciplinary structure is what makes it irreplaceable and that the rushed timeline and limited stakeholder consultation fell short of standard governance practice. That earliest reporting specifically named NCAR's Mesa Laboratory campus as a target for shutdown, described plans to eliminate research programs internally labeled "woke," and indicated only select functions such as weather modeling would be transferred elsewhere rather than preserved intact. Following a January 2026 White House announcement of intent to 'break up' NCAR, an NSF letter released February 13, 2026 confirmed plans to remove NCAR's supercomputing facility and transfer its stewardship to the University of Wyoming, per subsequent reporting identifying the specific recipient this entry had previously left unnamed. The facility supports weather forecasting models, climate simulations, and extreme-weather prediction research used by approximately 1,500 researchers across more than 500 universities; NOAA itself relies on the facility to run some of its current forecasting models. Former NCAR director James Hurrell and other prominent colleagues in the weather and climate research community warned NSF that 'any path that leads to the fragmentation or dismantling of NSF NCAR is fundamentally not in the nation's interest,' and that the move could further set back NOAA's own weather-modeling capabilities, which the researchers noted have already lagged behind international competitors. On March 16, 2026, the University Corporation for Atmospheric Research (UCAR) -- the nonprofit consortium of 129 universities that manages NCAR -- sued the federal agencies and officials behind the breakup plan, alleging the effort was retaliation against Colorado: specifically, that the administration was using NCAR's dismantling to pressure the state over Gov. Jared Polis's refusal to grant clemency to Tina Peters, a former county clerk convicted of tampering with voting machines in pursuit of Trump's 2020 election-fraud claims, and over the state's broader resistance to ceding authority over its own elections. OMB Director Russell Vought had publicly framed the plan as 'breaking up' NCAR because it was 'one of the largest sources of climate alarmism in the country,' and a White House spokesperson told CNN that Colorado's treatment depended on having 'a governor who actually wanted to work with President Trump.' On June 1, 2026, U.S. District Judge R. Brooke Jackson issued a preliminary injunction blocking the administration from taking further steps to dismantle NCAR, a win for the researchers and UCAR that halted the removal plan pending further litigation. Update 2026-08-31: identified the specific institution NSF planned to transfer the NCAR-Wyoming Supercomputing Center's stewardship to -- the University of Wyoming, which had offered to take over operations of the Cheyenne facility -- corroborated across DataCenterDynamics, AIP.org, and Courthouse News reporting on Judge R. Brooke Jackson's June 1, 2026 preliminary injunction; the ruling found NSF had announced the transfer more than a month before its own public-comment deadline and that officials' prior statements 'strongly suggest[ed] the outcome was predetermined,' making the reorganization arbitrary and capricious under the APA. No appeal of that injunction was identified in this recheck. Separately, a second, distinct lawsuit was filed August 20, 2026 in federal court in Colorado by the Environmental Defense Fund (EDF), unaffiliated with UCAR's suit, specifically challenging the administration's plan to close NCAR's Mesa Laboratory building -- the 1967, I.M. Pei-designed campus this entry's earliest reporting had named as an initial shutdown target. EDF's complaint adds a legal theory UCAR's suit did not raise: that closing the Mesa Laboratory without the environmental and public-consultation review required under the National Historic Preservation Act is unlawful, arguing the building -- while not currently listed on the National Register of Historic Places -- is eligible for listing given its architectural significance and the scientific discoveries made there. EDF seeks to block the closure and compel the required historic-preservation review; corroborated across EDF's own press release, Inside Climate News, E&E News, Boulder Reporting Lab, and BizWest. No ruling on EDF's suit was identified as of this recheck.

primary_proponent.name: National Science Foundation (executing White House direction)
primary_proponent.role: Federal agency overseeing NCAR, executing the supercomputer removal
primary_proponent.note: UCAR's March 2026 lawsuit alleges the White House's stated rationale was in substantial part retaliatory -- pressuring Colorado over its refusal to grant clemency to Tina Peters and over the state's election-administration authority -- rather than a neutral science-policy judgment; OMB Director Russell Vought separately and publicly characterized NCAR as a source of 'climate alarmism.'

estimated_impact.summary: Removing the supercomputing facility disrupts a shared national research resource relied on by 1,500+ scientists at 500+ universities and by NOAA's own forecasting operations, at a time when U.S. weather-modeling capability already trails international competitors according to the researchers who objected.

title: NCUA Board Reduced to a Single Member After Trump Fires Both Democratic Board Members
institution: National Credit Union Administration
status: Ongoing on a fast-track briefing schedule -- the D.C. Circuit deferred ruling on Harper and Otsuka's Fed-like-protection argument pending further briefing on how the Supreme Court's June 29, 2026 Slaughter and Cook decisions apply to NCUA, then set a schedule (administration's brief due September 12, 2026; Harper/Otsuka reply due October 3; government reply due October 17; oral argument after briefing concludes) that could produce a ruling by year-end 2026; the two remain off the single-member board as of this update
date_of_action: 2025-04-15 (firings) through 2026-06-29 (Supreme Court ruling narrowed path to reinstatement)
what_changed: In April 2025, President Trump fired both Democratic members of the National Credit Union Administration's three-person board -- former Chairman Todd Harper and Tanya Otsuka -- by email, without citing cause, leaving Republican Chair Kyle Hauptman as the sole remaining board member. Harper's term was not set to expire until April 2027 and Otsuka's not until August 2029. The Federal Credit Union Act defines the NCUA board as a three-member body with staggered six-year terms, structured (according to a subsequent district court finding) to mirror the Federal Reserve's governance model and insulate credit union regulation from political turnover. With only one board member, the NCUA could continue routine supervision and enforcement but could not vote on new rulemakings or policy changes; a scheduled board meeting was canceled. Harper and Otsuka sued; in July 2025 U.S. District Judge Amir Ali ruled the firings unlawful and ordered reinstatement, finding Congress had deliberately restricted the president's removal power when it added fixed terms to the statute in 1978. The two briefly returned to a board meeting before an appeals court granted the administration an emergency stay, sidelining them again. The case was held in abeyance pending Trump v. Slaughter; when the Supreme Court ruled for the administration on June 29, 2026, credit-union trade groups and legal analysts concluded the ruling 'effectively ends' the Harper/Otsuka challenge, since the Federal Credit Union Act -- unlike the Federal Reserve Act -- contains no explicit 'for cause' removal language for the NCUA to lean on. Harper and Otsuka's attorneys have since asked the D.C. Circuit to let them argue the NCUA deserves Fed-like treatment given its similar market-regulatory structure, but as of this writing they remain off the board, which continues to operate with a single member. Update 2026-07-19: in a filing with the D.C. Circuit in mid-July 2026, Harper and Otsuka's attorneys formally argued NCUA deserves Federal Reserve-like removal protection, leaning on the district court's earlier finding that Congress deliberately modeled NCUA's governance structure on the Fed's -- the same distinction that succeeded for Cook but was rejected for MSPB's Harris. No ruling on this argument had issued as of this update; the appeal remains pending. Re-verified 2026-07-26: no ruling identified yet on Harper and Otsuka's mid-July D.C. Circuit filing arguing for Fed-like removal protection; the appeal remains pending and the board continues to operate with Chair Hauptman as its sole member. Re-verified 2026-08-17: no ruling identified on Harper and Otsuka's mid-July D.C. Circuit filing arguing for Fed-like removal protection; their reply (due August 5, 2026 per the court's prior order) was not independently located, and no further D.C. Circuit action was found as of this update. The board continues to operate with Chair Hauptman as its sole member. Update 2026-08-29 (real correction): the D.C. Circuit did not rule on the removal-protection argument directly. Instead, before the August 5 reply deadline, the court deferred consideration of Harper and Otsuka's motion and ordered the administration to explain by July 29 how the case should proceed in light of the Supreme Court's June 29, 2026 Slaughter and Cook decisions, with Harper and Otsuka permitted to respond by August 5. Following that exchange, the D.C. Circuit set a fast-track briefing schedule: the administration's brief is due September 12, 2026; Harper and Otsuka's reply is due October 3; the government's reply is due October 17; oral argument will follow "the first appropriate date following the conclusion of briefing." Legal press described the expedited schedule as one that could produce a ruling by the end of 2026. Harper and Otsuka's central remaining argument is that NCUA falls within the narrow financial-regulator exception the Supreme Court recognized in Cook for the Federal Reserve, rather than the broader removal-power holding in Slaughter. The board continues to operate with Chair Hauptman as its sole member pending this schedule.

title: NEA Terminates Over Half of Its Open Grants in a Single Weekend
institution: National Endowment for the Arts
status: Complete for terminated grants (effective May 31, 2025); the agency's proposed full elimination was not enacted as of the last-verified date, though grantmaking priorities remain altered under new leadership
date_of_action: 2025-05-02 to 2025-05-12 (termination notices); leadership confirmed December 19, 2025
what_changed: On the evening of May 2, 2025, hours after the administration released a preliminary FY2026 budget proposing to eliminate the NEA entirely, the agency emailed termination or withdrawal notices to hundreds of grantees nationwide, affecting more than half of its open awards, in amounts ranging from $10,000 to $100,000, effective May 31, 2025. A second round of termination notices followed on May 12, 2025. Affected organizations spanned all 50 states, Puerto Rico, and Washington, D.C., including theaters, orchestras, literary magazines, and community arts programs. Some grantees whose projects appeared to match the NEA's own newly stated priorities were terminated anyway; California Symphony, for example, lost funding for a commission specifically written to celebrate the 250th anniversary of American independence, one of the NEA's own listed new priorities. On May 5, 2025, ten NEA discipline directors and two members of senior leadership announced they would take deferred resignation, departing by the end of May. Mary Anne Carter, who had led the NEA during Trump's first term, was serving as senior adviser overseeing the agency at the time the terminations were issued (the previous Biden-appointed chair, Maria Rosario Jackson, had resigned on Inauguration Day); Carter was confirmed by the Senate as permanent NEA Chair on December 19, 2025. Separately, a federal judge in Rhode Island struck down a related NEA policy disfavoring grant applications the agency deemed to 'promote gender ideology' on September 19, 2025.

primary_proponent.name: Mary Anne Carter
primary_proponent.role: Senior Adviser overseeing NEA operations at the time of the terminations; later confirmed as NEA Chair (Dec. 19, 2025)
primary_proponent.note: Was in charge of the agency when the mass grant terminations were issued in May 2025, and the NEA emails were sent under her oversight before her formal confirmation as chair later that year.

estimated_impact.summary: More than half of the NEA's active grant commitments to arts organizations nationwide were terminated within a single week, with a compressed appeal window and a leadership exodus that left the agency's discipline-specific grantmaking expertise significantly thinned.

estimated_impact.caveat: The NEA's stated rationale is that funding is being redirected toward specific new priorities, including projects supporting HBCUs and Hispanic-Serving Institutions, the 250th anniversary of American independence, AI competency, disaster recovery, and military/veteran and tribal communities, rather than eliminated outright, and the agency offered a 7-day appeal window for grantees who believed their project matched the new criteria. Critics point to apparent inconsistencies in the rollout, including cases like California Symphony's, where a project matching a stated new priority was terminated anyway, and argue the 7-calendar-day appeal window (which included a weekend) was procedurally unfair given the scale and suddenness of the cuts. It is worth distinguishing this from the separate, better-documented case of the sister agency National Endowment for the Humanities, where a federal court found in a May 2026 summary judgment that a comparable mass grant termination process was unlawful; no equivalent final court ruling specific to these NEA terminations has been identified as of the last-verified date, so that outcome should not be assumed to extend to the NEA. Update (GSR recheck batch 2, 2026-09-08): separately, for FY2027 the House has proposed cutting NEA's annual appropriation by 36% (from $207 million to $135 million); the Senate had not yet acted on this proposal as of this recheck. This is a proposed, not-yet-enacted budget cut for a future fiscal year, distinct from the 2025 grant terminations documented above.

confidence_note: Strong. Corroborated by dozens of independent, named grantee statements, multiple journalism outlets (NPR, KQED, American Theatre, ArtNews, San Francisco Classical Voice), and arts-advocacy organization trackers (MASSCreative, Chorus America, Mid-America Arts Alliance) reporting consistent dates, dollar ranges, and termination language across widely dispersed organizations. Update (GSR recheck batch 2, 2026-09-08): the FY2027 36% House cut proposal independently confirmed via The Creative Coalition's own call-to-action page, fetched directly.

title: National Endowment for Democracy Funding Withheld, Partially Restored Only After Court Order
institution: National Endowment for Democracy (funded via State Department appropriation)
status: Ongoing, with a real correction to this entry's funding-status framing -- FY2026 NED funding was fully enacted at $315 million (not merely 'recommended' as this entry previously stated) when President Trump signed the National Security, Department of State, and Related Programs Appropriations Act, 2026 (H.R. 4779) on February 3, 2026; the D.C. Circuit appeal of the FY2025 withholding (docket 25-5361) remains separately pending
date_of_action: 2025-01-22 (funding access first denied) through ongoing litigation as of 2026
what_changed: Since January 22, 2025, the executive branch withheld the National Endowment for Democracy's (NED) access to congressionally appropriated funding, according to NED's federal lawsuit. NED, a nonprofit created by the 1983 National Endowment for Democracy Act, is statutorily directed to receive annual grants through the State Department; it distributes roughly 83% of its funds directly to democracy, free-press, and anti-corruption groups in more than 90 countries. NED sued in March 2025, alleging the withholding of nearly $240 million violated the Administrative Procedure Act, the NED Act, and constitutional separation-of-powers and appropriations provisions. The funding halt forced NED to furlough 75% of its staff and, per the lawsuit, created a 'devastating' cash flow crisis affecting 226 approved grants, 124 board-recommended grants, and 53 'core institute' projects. On August 11, 2025, U.S. District Judge Dabney Friedrich -- a Trump appointee -- granted a preliminary injunction, finding the administration had likely violated the NED Act by conditioning fund disbursement on alignment with 'Administration priorities,' calling that rationale 'not plausible' given repeated delays and shifting justifications. Following the ruling, DOJ released the roughly $95 million that remained withheld from NED's FY2025 appropriation. The administration appealed to the D.C. Circuit on October 9, 2025 (case ongoing as of this writing), and separately proposed eliminating NED's funding entirely in its FY2026 budget request, citing (among other claims) an allegation -- which NED's own fact sheet disputes as false -- that NED funded a Ukrainian group accused of doxing U.S. journalists. As of early 2026 court filings, the parties remained in disputes over whether and when NED's FY2026 appropriation would be obligated and disbursed. Re-verified 2026-07-26: no ruling change -- the D.C. Circuit appeal (docket 25-5361) remains held in abeyance. A concrete counter-signal to OMB's proposed elimination of NED funding: the House Appropriations Committee has recommended $315 million for NED in FY2026, well above both the administration's zero-funding request and NED's FY2025 baseline -- meaning the FY2026 funding fight, like several others in this tracker, pits congressional appropriators against the administration's budget request rather than reflecting a settled outcome. CORRECTION 2026-08-17: this entry's prior text (added 2026-07-26) described the $315 million figure as something 'the House Appropriations Committee has recommended,' framing FY2026 funding as still pending. That was already out of date at the time it was written -- the National Security, Department of State, and Related Programs Appropriations Act, 2026 (H.R. 4779), which fully funds NED at $315 million ($210,316,000 in the traditional/core-institute manner and $104,684,000 for democracy programs) and rejects the administration's request to eliminate the funding, passed Congress with bipartisan support and was signed into law by President Trump on February 3, 2026 -- roughly five months before the entry's own prior recheck. This is a correction to the entry's funding-status claim, not a new development: FY2026 funding has been enacted law, not a pending committee recommendation, since February 2026. Separately, the underlying FY2025 withholding dispute and D.C. Circuit appeal (docket 25-5361) are unaffected by this correction and remain pending as previously documented -- FY2026 enactment resolves the forward-looking funding question but not the still-open legal dispute over the earlier withholding. Update 2026-08-29: no material change -- the D.C. Circuit appeal (docket 25-5361) remains held in abeyance pending district-court proceedings, consistent with this entry's existing account. Update 2026-08-31: no material change to the appeal's abeyance status, but this recheck adds the district-court motion-to-dismiss briefing schedule not previously documented here: the government's motion to dismiss was due on or before March 16, 2026, NED's opposition on or before April 13, 2026, and the government's reply on or before April 27, 2026. More than four months after that briefing closed, no ruling on the motion to dismiss has been identified, and the Civil Rights Litigation Clearinghouse's most recently documented docket activity remains a January 29, 2026 joint-status-report deadline -- meaning the case has been fully briefed and awaiting decision on the motion to dismiss since late April 2026 with no order issued in the sourcing reviewed for this recheck.

title: National Endowment for the Humanities Grants Terminated, Staff Cut, Funds Redirected
institution: National Endowment for the Humanities (NEH)
status: Partially Reversed (grant terminations ruled unconstitutional and reinstatement process underway as of mid-2026; staff cuts and Council dissolution unaffected by the ruling)
date_of_action: 2025-04-02 (initial grant terminations) through 2025-10-01 (National Council on the Humanities firings)
what_changed: Beginning April 2025, NEH terminated more than 1,000 previously-awarded, congressionally-funded grants covering fiscal years 2021-2025, informing 56 state and jurisdiction humanities councils their funding was being 'repurposed in a new direction in furtherance of President Trump's agenda.' NEH then placed the majority of its staff on immediate administrative leave, followed by formal termination notices to 65% of its ~180 employees (about 117 people) in April 2025 -- letters described the cuts as necessary to comply with a Trump executive order directing DOGE to eliminate 'waste, bloat, and insularity.' NEH Chair Shelly C. Lowe, the first Native American to head the agency, was forced out about a month before the mass layoffs. In October 2025, during the government shutdown, all but 4 of the 26 members of the National Council on the Humanities (the body that advises NEH on funding priorities) were fired by email from the White House Office of Presidential Personnel. Separately, the 2025 tax-and-spending law directed NEH to contribute $40 million toward constructing Trump's proposed 'National Garden of American Heroes' sculpture garden -- redirecting endowment funds toward a specific administration priority rather than the competitive peer-reviewed grants the agency traditionally funds. Update: On May 7, 2026, U.S. District Judge Colleen McMahon (S.D.N.Y.) ruled in American Council of Learned Societies v. NEH -- brought by ACLS, the American Historical Association, and the Modern Language Association -- that the mass termination of more than 1,400 grants was 'unlawful, unconstitutional, ultra vires, and without legal effect,' violating the First Amendment and the Fifth Amendment's equal-protection component, and undertaken without statutory authority. NEH has since begun a reinstatement process: starting June 30, 2026, the agency began sending affected recipients a 'Reinstatement Assurances Form' asking whether they still want the award, disclosing any personnel changes since termination, confirming continued capacity to complete the project, and specifying whether a restart period or reimbursement is needed. This is not automatic restoration -- it functions closer to a new award action, requiring a fresh institutional review of personnel, budget, subrecipient status, and timeline for each grant. The ruling does not affect the separate staff terminations or the National Council on the Humanities dissolution described above.

title: NIH Let Contract-Staff Work Orders Lapse and Was Ordered to Cut $2.6 Billion (35%) in Contracts -- Hitting Nearly Half Its Workforce
institution: National Institutes of Health (NIH)
status: Ongoing as of last verification -- contract cancellations continued through 2025 with no reported reversal; a May 2025 Science/AAAS report puts the actual scale of contract-staff job loss at roughly 2,200 contractors NIH-wide since January 2025, resolving the entry's prior LOWER-confidence anecdotal estimate
date_of_action: 2025-01 (communication freeze begins, contract renewals stall) through 2025-04 (formal 35% contract-cut order and initial implementation)
what_changed: Starting when the Trump administration took office in January 2025, NIH allowed a growing number of contract-staff work orders to lapse without renewal, effectively ending those positions -- NOTUS reported this on March 20, 2025, noting contract staff make up nearly half of NIH's total workforce. The lapses stemmed in part from a since-lifted Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) communications freeze imposed at the start of the administration: contract renewals require NIH to communicate with the outside contracting agencies that formally employ and insure NIH's contract staff, and NOTUS found that communication remained effectively stalled even after the freeze was formally lifted in February. A contract employee at NIH's Vaccine Research Center told NOTUS they personally knew of roughly 10 colleagues whose contracts had recently expired and gone unrenewed -- an early, anecdotal data point NOTUS could not yet size against the full workforce. The lapses were followed by a formal directive: on April 3, 2025, Science reported the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) had ordered NIH to eliminate $2.6 billion in contracts, requiring each of NIH's 27 institutes and centers to cut contract spending by roughly 35% by April 8, 2025 -- part of a broader HHS-wide DOGE directive (reported separately by NOTUS) to cut $13.6 billion in annual contract spending across the department. NIH contracts fund staff scientists, clinical-trial support at universities, biospecimen repositories, and long-term health studies; an NIH official told Science a 35% cut would be 'devastating' given how much of the fiscal year's contract funding had already been committed. By the time of that reporting, a DOGE-linked contract-cut tracking site showed NIH had already cut more than 400 contracts totaling about $780 million, including funding for biospecimen repositories and long-term health-study support. A May 11, 2025 Science/AAAS follow-up, reporting on the Vaccine Research Center specifically, put a number on the scale NOTUS's March 2025 reporting could only estimate anecdotally: data shared with staff at one NIH institute showed the contractor purge had reached roughly 2,200 contract workers agency-wide since January 2025 -- rivaling the ~2,500 federal staff lost to two rounds of layoffs since mid-February. At the Vaccine Research Center itself, one immunology lab had lost 40% of its workers and stopped developing antibody tests for some future clinical trials.

title: NIH Strips DEI Requirements From Grant Applications, Then Terminates $783M in Active Grants on Disfavored Topics
institution: National Institutes of Health (NIH)
status: Ongoing (Supreme Court allowed the $783M in terminations to proceed Aug. 21, 2025 while the underlying guidance documents remain vacated by a lower court; NIH settled in Dec. 2025 to reconsider some frozen/denied grants, but its director said in the same period that grants already restored under court order would not be renewed; NIH continued issuing new topic-based terminations into August 2026, cancelling a further $15M combined across Emory and University of Pittsburgh Alzheimer's/discrimination research grants)
date_of_action: 2025-02 (initial grant terminations begin) through 2026-01 (settlement on reconsidering stalled grants)
what_changed: Starting in late February 2025, NIH began terminating active research grants tied to topics the administration classified as DEI, gender identity, LGBTQ+ health, or vaccine hesitancy, eventually withholding or terminating $783 million across dozens of active awards. On March 25, 2025, NIH separately notified staff it was eliminating DEI-related requirements from grant and conference-funding applications going forward: applicants would no longer need to submit 'Plans for Enhancing Diverse Perspectives,' 'Recruitment Plans to Enhance Diversity,' or 'Trainee Diversity Reports,' diversity plans would no longer be evaluated in funding decisions, and training-data tables used in review were revised to drop calculations of the percentage of underrepresented minorities. On April 21, 2025, NIH went further, publishing a notice amending the civil-rights provisions of the NIH Grants Policy Statement to require institutions receiving new, renewal, supplement, or continuation awards to certify they do not operate DEI programs 'in violation of Federal anti-discrimination laws' and are not boycotting Israel, on pain of termination and clawback of funds -- a condition industry commentary (FierceBiotech) characterized as NIH asserting authority to override how recipients interpret their own obligations under the Civil Rights Act of 1964. In June 2025, U.S. District Judge William Young (D. Mass.) ruled the terminations violated the Administrative Procedure Act, finding NIH had unlawfully targeted research on 'disfavored' topics and populations -- including training grants meant to diversify the biomedical research pipeline -- without adequately defining what 'DEI' meant or weighing the grants' value, and calling the terminations 'racial discrimination, and discrimination against America's LGBTQ community' on the record; he ordered the funding reinstated. The Trump administration asked the Supreme Court to stay that order, and on August 21, 2025, the Court allowed the $783 million in terminations to proceed while the case continued, even as Judge Young's ruling vacating NIH's underlying guidance documents themselves remained in effect below. NIH Director Jay Bhattacharya (confirmed by the Senate March 25, 2025 -- the same day as the initial application-requirement change, though sworn in April 1 and not in office for the February terminations) said on December 31, 2025 that DEI-related grants restored to plaintiffs under the court order would not be renewed once their current funding cycles ended. Days earlier, on December 29, 2025, NIH separately settled a related suit by agreeing to reconsider a batch of frozen and denied DEI-related grant applications -- reported in January 2026 (Government Executive) as the administration agreeing to drop anti-DEI evaluation criteria for that specific stalled-grant backlog, distinct from the $783 million already terminated and litigated separately. Update 2026-08-17: the termination campaign continued into August 2026 -- on August 4, 2026, Bhattacharya notified the University of Pittsburgh that a five-year, $9.6 million grant to social epidemiologist Tamara Dubowitz studying cognitive aging and Alzheimer's risk among African Americans in poor Pittsburgh neighborhoods, with $7 million already spent, would be terminated in full, part of a stated shift toward 'measurable health outcomes' and away from health-disparities framing in NIH's funding priorities. Update 2026-08-30 (GSR recheck batch 35): the August 2026 wave was broader than the single Pittsburgh/Dubowitz grant already documented -- Bhattacharya's letters also terminated a second, separate University of Pittsburgh grant (Andrea Rosso and Ann Cohen, studying racial discrimination's links to Alzheimer's diagnosis and other sociologically-driven dementia risk factors) and a National Institute of Mental Health grant to Emory University clinical neuropsychologist Negar Fani, a five-year study (awarded December 2024) examining how racial discrimination affects white-matter brain microstructure in 220 Black volunteers via wearable devices and MRI. Fani's team had been told as recently as June 5, 2026 that its second year of funding was approved, then was notified by the end of July 2026 that the grant was cancelled. NIH's termination notice for the Emory grant stated the research's discrimination measure was 'subjective and problematic' and that studying only Black participants 'seriously limits possible comparisons and controls and does not seem scientifically justified' -- an explicit NIH rationale for why race-specific health-disparities research itself fails its new 'measurable health outcomes' standard, not just a funding-priority reshuffling. Combined, Science/AAAS and The Week/Yahoo report the Emory and Pittsburgh cuts announced in this wave total $15 million. Separately, the Supreme Court's August 2025 ruling in this case -- previously described in this entry without a case name -- is identified in legal commentary (Ogletree, Crowell & Moring, The Arc) as NIH v. APHA; the ruling itself created a jurisdictional split (Justice Jackson dissenting) under which challenges to NIH's underlying guidance continue in district court while claims seeking restoration of terminated grant funding must be filed separately in the Court of Federal Claims, a more burdensome path for affected researchers. The First Circuit heard oral argument on the broader guidance challenge in January 2026 but had not ruled as of this recheck (a separate First Circuit ruling that same month, upholding the block on NIH's indirect-cost-rate cap, is a related but distinct case and should not be conflated with this still-pending DEI-guidance appeal).

Kennedy Jr.'s oversight and acting NIH leadership; Bhattacharya is the named, on-the-record official for the ongoing implementation, including his December 31, 2025 statement that court-restored grants would not be renewed.

estimated_impact.summary: The story split into two tracks that resolved differently: the $783 million in already-terminated grants was allowed to stay terminated by the Supreme Court's August 2025 stay, while a separate, smaller batch of frozen-but-not-yet-terminated applications was reopened for reconsideration under a December 2025 settlement. NIH's own director has stated publicly that restoration under the court order is not being treated as a durable outcome -- grants reinstated by Judge Young's order will not be renewed going forward, meaning the practical effect of the litigation win for affected researchers is temporary continuation, not a reversal of NIH's underlying policy direction.

title: NIH Grant Freeze Found to Violate the Impoundment Control Act (GAO)
institution: National Institutes of Health (NIH), Department of Health and Human Services
status: GAO Legal Finding Issued (nonbinding; underlying funding dispute partially reversed, full compliance unconfirmed)
date_of_action: 2025-08-05 (GAO report issued); underlying actions Feb 2025 - Dec 2025
what_changed: Following Trump executive orders in early 2025 targeting DEI and 'gender ideology' funding, NIH terminated more than 1,800 previously-awarded research grants and, separately, obligated roughly $8 billion less in new/continuing grant funding between February and June 2025 than in the same period the prior year -- a drop of more than a third. NIH also paused grant review meetings entirely from late January to early March 2025, delaying funds to hospitals and universities -- NPR reported on February 22, 2025 that this freeze alone had stalled roughly 16,000 pending grant applications worth about $1.5 billion, as the administration blocked the Federal Register notices required to schedule the review meetings. Separately, on February 24, 2025, NPR reported the administration's plan to cap NIH's reimbursement rate for research institutions' indirect costs (overhead such as facilities and administrative support) at 15%, down from a historical rate as high as 56% at some institutions -- a change research universities warned would force layoffs and halt projects even where direct grant funding remained intact, since indirect-cost reimbursement funds much of the physical and administrative infrastructure research depends on. An earlier, larger staffing figure was reported on April 28, 2025: outlets described NIH as having 1,300 staff fired by that point, with $2 billion in research grants cancelled and ongoing clinical trials for Alzheimer's, cancer, and stroke treatments halted -- a snapshot that predates and is not necessarily consistent with (may reflect a different scope or a since-revised count from) the more specifically sourced 250-employee May 6 figure below. NIH's funding contraction had a direct staffing dimension too: CBS News reported NIH issued surprise layoff notices to nearly 250 employees on May 6, 2025, including about 50 from the National Cancer Institute specifically. On June 13, 2025, more than 60 NIH employees signed a public letter, the Bethesda Declaration, condemning the administration's health policies as unethical, politically driven, and dangerous -- accusing leadership of censoring science, cutting billions from NIH's budget, halting over 1,300 grants, and endangering patients in ongoing clinical trials, an internal-dissent episode directly reflecting the funding and grant-termination pattern this entry documents. The pattern continued into the funding-mechanism itself later in the year: the New York Times reported that in December 2025, Trump ordered NIH and NSF to issue multi-year grants as upfront lump sums rather than the traditional annual-installment structure, a change that depleted available budgets faster and resulted in roughly 40% fewer new projects funded, alongside mass delays and grant cancellations reported as politically motivated by affected researchers. The Government Accountability Office (GAO), a nonpartisan congressional watchdog, concluded on August 5, 2025 that the original 2025 funding actions violated the Impoundment Control Act of 1974, which requires the executive branch to spend congressionally appropriated funds unless it follows a specific legal process to formally request a rescission -- a process NIH/HHS did not use. GAO noted HHS had taken down a public spending-tracking website, which itself hampered GAO's ability to investigate.

primary_proponent.name: Russell Vought
primary_proponent.role: Director, Office of Management and Budget

title: NIH Terminates 33+ Grants Studying Vaccine Hesitancy Amid a Growing Measles Outbreak
institution: National Institutes of Health (NIH)
status: Terminations themselves ruled unlawful by a district court over a year before this entry was written, with a mixed and still-unresolved appellate outcome -- not simply "finalized." On June 16, 2025, Judge William Young (D. Mass.) ruled NIH's grant-termination directives -- covering vaccine hesitancy, DEI, gender identity, and other disfavored topics -- "void and illegal" under the APA and ordered roughly 900 grants held by the named plaintiffs reinstated. On August 21, 2025, the Supreme Court granted a partial stay: it left intact the district court's finding that the directives themselves violated the APA, but ruled the district court likely lacked jurisdiction to order reinstatement of the grants directly (a Tucker Act/Court of Federal Claims jurisdictional question), a mixed outcome for both sides. The First Circuit heard oral argument on the preliminary injunction appeal January 6, 2026; litigation remains ongoing on two tracks (district court merits and the First Circuit appeal), with no final resolution identified in sourcing reviewed as of this update. Whether the specific 33+ vaccine-hesitancy grants this entry documents are among the ~900 plaintiff grants covered by the reinstatement order, and their current funding/operational status as of August 2026, were not confirmed in sourcing reviewed.
what_changed: NIH abruptly terminated at least 33 research grants funding studies of why people are hesitant to receive vaccines and what strategies improve vaccine uptake, with an additional 9 grants flagged for modification or further cuts, after the agency adopted a policy stating it would no longer 'prioritize research activities that focus on gaining scientific knowledge on why individuals are hesitant to be vaccinated and/or explore ways to improve vaccine interest and commitment.' Affected researchers, including one whose work had identified a genuine vaccine safety signal, were notified their studies were being cut off mid-stream, an unusual mechanism for ending federally funded research already underway. The terminations came as HHS was newly led by vaccine skeptic Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and coincided with a Texas-originated measles outbreak that had grown to over 300 cases and at least one death by the time of the cuts, drawing criticism from public health researchers that the timing undercut exactly the kind of research needed to counter vaccine-preventable disease spread. The Center for Science in the Public Interest, ACLU, and Protect Democracy Project sued NIH and HHS on April 2, 2025 over what they characterized as unlawful, politically driven grant cancellations; as of early 2026 the case was on appeal, with oral argument held January 6, 2026. Update (2026-08-17 recheck): this entry, written August 11, 2026, originally described the terminations as simply "finalized" -- but a district court had already ruled the underlying termination directives unlawful more than a year earlier. On June 16, 2025, Judge William Young (D. Mass.) ruled in American Public Health Association v. NIH that NIH's directives -- which the court found had terminated roughly $1 billion in grants across categories including vaccine hesitancy, DEI, gender identity, and race-related health research -- were "arbitrary and capricious" and void under the Administrative Procedure Act; Young further found evidence of racial discrimination in the terminations he called, in his 40 years on the bench, among the most "palpable" he had seen. The ruling ordered roughly 900 grants held by the case's named plaintiffs reinstated -- a subset of the estimated 2,300 grants NIH terminated administration-wide, not a reinstatement of every terminated grant nationwide. The First Circuit denied the government's request to stay Young's order on July 18, 2025. On August 21, 2025, the Supreme Court granted the government a partial stay: a 5-4 majority left intact the district court's APA conclusion that the directives themselves were unlawful, but ruled the district court likely lacked jurisdiction to order the grants reinstated directly, since grant-funding disputes may belong in the Court of Federal Claims under the Tucker Act rather than district court -- a mixed ruling that left the underlying policy void as illegal while complicating the remedy. The First Circuit separately heard oral argument on the case's preliminary-injunction appeal on January 6, 2026 (already reflected in this entry's original text); no decision in that specific appeal was identified in sourcing reviewed as of this update. Note: a separate First Circuit ruling on January 5, 2026 (one day earlier) in APLU v. NIH unanimously struck down NIH's 15% cap on facilities-and-administrative cost reimbursement -- a different NIH policy dispute with a different plaintiff group; it is not the same case or ruling as the vaccine-hesitancy grant-termination litigation this entry covers, and should not be conflated with it despite the near-identical dates. Separately, under a related stipulation agreement, NIH agreed to evaluate more than 5,000 stalled or previously rejected funding applications in the "ordinary course" of its scientific review process, without applying the challenged directives. Whether the specific 33+ vaccine-hesitancy grants named in this entry are among the ~900 plaintiff grants covered by Young's reinstatement order, and whether those grants are currently funded and operating as of August 2026 or have lapsed again amid the ongoing jurisdictional dispute, were not confirmed in sourcing reviewed -- this entry should be rechecked specifically for that operational-status question when clearer sourcing becomes available. Re-verified 2026-08-29: no First Circuit ruling identified on the January 6, 2026 oral argument in the preliminary-injunction appeal. The Georgetown Health Care Litigation Tracker's most recent entry for this case is a March 19, 2026 defendants' response to a notice of supplemental authority, with briefing described as ongoing; no docket activity or ruling was identified between then and this update. The operational status of the specific 33+ vaccine-hesitancy grants named in this entry remains unconfirmed in sourcing reviewed.

title: NIH Fired 11 of Its Most Senior Neuroscience Lab Heads -- Including a Breakthrough Prize Winner -- in a Reduction-in-Force Attributed to a 'Coding Error,' Kept Them Terminated for Seven Weeks While RFK Jr. Told Congress No Scientists Had Been Fired
institution: National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke (NIH/HHS)
status: Reversed -- HHS formally revoked all 30 reduction-in-force notices on May 21, 2025, before the June 2, 2025 termination date took effect
date_of_action: 2025-04-01/02 (RIF notices issued) through 2025-05-21 (formal revocation)
what_changed: On April 1-2, 2025, as part of the Trump administration's broader HHS-wide reduction in force under Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., 30 employees at the National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke (NINDS) received reduction-in-force (RIF) notices, including 11 of the institute's most senior lab heads and distinguished investigators: Richard Youle, Miguel Holmgren, Steve Jacobson, Dorian McGavern, Joseph Mindell, Katherine Roche, Zu-Hang Sheng, David R. Sibley, Kenton Swartz, Susan Wray, and Ling-Gang Wu, plus senior associate scientist Silvina Horowitz. Youle, at NIH since 1978 and winner of the $3 million 2021 Breakthrough Prize in Life Sciences for identifying a cellular mechanism behind Parkinson's disease, was among those terminated. NIH and HHS officials later attributed the firings to a 'coding error' in the RIF process that swept up senior investigators who were not supposed to be included. Despite verbal reassurances from NIH leadership, including Director Jay Bhattacharya, that the layoffs would be rescinded, the RIF notices remained formally in effect for seven weeks. On May 14, 2025, testifying before the Senate health committee, Kennedy stated, 'As far as I know, we have not fired any working scientists... our policy was to make sure none of them were lost and that that research continues' -- a claim contradicted by the NINDS scientists' still-active termination notices at the time he made it. HHS did not formally revoke the RIF notices until May 21, 2025, via email, days before the scheduled June 2 termination date. The 11 affected labs employed roughly 100 total staff, described by reporting as mainly young trainees whose research and career trajectories were disrupted during the seven-week uncertainty. After news of his firing broke, Youle received four outside job offers, three of them from institutions abroad.

title: NIOSH Loses 85-90% of Staff, Gutting Firefighter Cancer Research, the 9/11 World Trade Center Health Program, and Fatality Investigations
institution: National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health (NIOSH), Department of Health and Human Services (part of CDC)
status: Mixed as of this update -- two genuinely separate problems that this entry's original framing did not distinguish. (1) The WTC Health Program's chronic funding-formula shortfall, which this entry's sources describe as part of the same crisis, was permanently fixed by the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2026 (P.L. 119-75), signed February 3, 2026 -- funding is now secured through 2040. That fix predates this entry's own 2026-08-08 write date and was not reflected in the original entry. (2) The underlying NIOSH/WTC Health Program STAFFING crisis this entry actually documents is not resolved by that funding fix: congressional letters in 2026 describe roughly 30% of the WTC Health Program's 120 authorized positions still vacant, backlogged treatment authorizations, and disrupted ongoing treatment for ill survivors, and a bipartisan group of lawmakers was still pressing HHS Secretary Kennedy in July 2026 to reappoint Dr. John Howard as NIOSH director and WTC Health Program administrator, a position he had not yet been reappointed to as of that letter.
date_of_action: 2025-02-21 (initial WTC Health Program staffing cut reported) through 2025-06-03 (training-program funding shortfalls reported)
what_changed: On February 21, 2025, the New York Times reported layoffs and buyouts had already cut about 20% of staffing at the World Trade Center Health Program specifically, jeopardizing research grants and delaying certifications critical to treating 9/11 responders and survivors -- a cut initially reinstated after pushback from lawmakers and veterans' groups, though the program's staffing crisis recurred and deepened in the following months as described below. Beginning February 20, 2025, Trump administration cuts began hitting NIOSH more broadly, the CDC institute responsible for occupational safety and health research. Early casualties included Patrick Montague, an investigator for the National Firefighter Registry for Cancer, fired along with colleagues in his program citing probationary status. By April 3, 2025, hundreds of NIOSH staff had been fired, including key personnel from the World Trade Center Health Program -- which provides medical care to 9/11 first responders and survivors -- and the program's longtime director, Dr. John Howard, was also removed. By April 13, the Guardian reported the WTC Health Program had been plunged into disarray, with cancer treatment, PTSD care, and other services for 9/11 survivors and first responders disrupted with no public transparency about what coverage remained available. By April 22, ProPublica reported the purge had eliminated 7 of the 8 members of NIOSH's firefighter fatality investigation team, halting major studies into firefighter cancer risk alongside the WTC-program disruption. On May 12, more than 100 current and former NIOSH employees sent a joint letter to Congress warning that mass purges were putting American workers at risk, stating more than 90% of NIOSH staff had received layoff notices and that critical programs -- the 9/11 Health Program and black lung screening among them -- had already been disrupted. By May 27, the Guardian confirmed an 85% NIOSH staff purge, with only a fraction of positions reinstated after public backlash. By early June, Reuters reported the cuts -- nearly 900 staff purged in April alone -- were forcing shutdowns of occupational-safety training programs specifically serving fishermen, farmers, and loggers, among America's most dangerous occupations, with key training centers warning they would run out of funding by summer or fall 2025. Update, 2026-08-17: two later developments clarify how this crisis evolved. First, the WTC Health Program's separate, longstanding funding-formula shortfall -- which periodically threatened the program's ability to pay for care independent of the 2025 NIOSH staffing purge -- was permanently fixed via a bipartisan provision (led by Rep. Andrew Garbarino, Speaker Mike Johnson, Rep. Brett Guthrie, Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand, and Sen. Chuck Schumer) in the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2026 (P.L. 119-75), signed by President Trump February 3, 2026, securing funding through 2040. This resolves the funding-formula problem specifically; it does not restore the staff this entry documents being purged in 2025. Second, on the staffing side, HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. said in April 2026 he was 'fixing' the WTC Health Program's problems, but reporting found only four job vacancies had actually been posted against the program's need. A bipartisan, bicameral letter led by Sen. Gillibrand and Rep. Garbarino, sent July 10, 2026 ahead of the September 2026 25th anniversary of the September 11 attacks, urged Kennedy to reappoint Dr. John Howard to a new six-year term as NIOSH director and WTC Health Program administrator, while acknowledging HHS had taken 'recent steps' on staffing shortages, delayed research grants, and pending petitions for additional covered conditions -- language consistent with the vacancy rate cited above, not with the crisis being over.

what_changed: NIST, the 125-year-old nonregulatory agency that sets the country's measurement, cybersecurity, and technology standards (including the widely used Cybersecurity Framework, the AI Risk Management Framework, and post-quantum encryption standards), lost more than 700 positions between the start of the Trump administration and January 2026 through resignations, retirements, and voluntary deferments, including roughly 500 recent hires who were let go early in 2025 while still in probationary status. A lab responsible for testing and validating the federal government's encryption implementations lost 89 staff. On March 26, 2025, the administration moved to eliminate NIST's Atomic Spectroscopy Group, which maintains atomic measurement data used as a foundational reference across nuclear fusion, astrophysics, and semiconductor-manufacturing research nationwide -- a specific, named-program elimination distinct from and in addition to the broader probationary and encryption-lab losses already documented in this entry. The administration's FY2026 budget request proposed cutting NIST's $1.2 billion budget by $325 million, eliminating the Hollings Manufacturing Extension Partnership Program entirely (97 positions, $175 million, serving small and mid-size manufacturers in all 50 states and Puerto Rico) and cutting $125 million and 556 positions from NIST's core Scientific and Technical Research and Services program, citing cybersecurity/privacy, health and biological measurements, and physical-infrastructure research as target areas. House appropriators later rejected the steepest of these cuts and restored funding above the administration's request, but the agency has already absorbed the workforce losses and, as of early 2026, is still awaiting a formal Reduction-in-Force and reorganization plan. Congress's final FY2026 appropriation funded NIST's Scientific and Technical Research and Services program at $1.25 billion -- more than $542 million above the administration's request, and higher than even the $980 million House figure already cited in this entry -- and fully funded the Hollings Manufacturing Extension Partnership at $175 million, rejecting the administration's proposal to eliminate it. Despite that enacted funding, NIST issued Reduction-in-Force and possible-separation notices to every MEP employee, prompting Sen. Chris Coons and colleagues to send a formal letter demanding an explanation for what they characterized as an 'unauthorized dismantling' of a program Congress had just funded. NIST's Computer Security Division also lost its division head and roughly a dozen subordinates to retirement offers, a specific loss to the cybersecurity-standards function this entry already documents as strained. Update 2026-07-26: NIST released a Notice of Funding Opportunity for 14 Manufacturing Extension Partnership centers (Alabama, Alaska, Arkansas, California, Georgia, Louisiana, Massachusetts, Missouri, Montana, Ohio, Pennsylvania, Puerto Rico, Utah, and Vermont), with an informational webinar scheduled July 28, 2026 and applications due August 21, 2026. Trade press (Advanced Manufacturing) frames this as a real reversal after NIST's earlier funding notice for the program's next tranche of centers was delayed until December 4, 2025 -- itself more than six months behind schedule and a gap that, combined with the RIF notices, had already pushed roughly 90% of MEP centers into layoffs or hiring freezes, with some at risk of closing entirely. This doesn't resolve Sen. Coons's still-unanswered oversight letter about the RIF notices themselves, but is a concrete sign the program is continuing rather than being wound down. Update 2026-08-29: on July 3, 2026, Sens. Maria Cantwell and Gary Peters -- Ranking Members of the Senate Commerce and Homeland Security/Governmental Affairs Committees, respectively -- sent a letter to Acting Comptroller General Orice Williams Brown formally requesting a GAO investigation into whether Commerce, under Secretary Lutnick, followed the law in funding and managing the MEP program. The senators state that Commerce's own Inspector General personally confirmed to Democratic committee staff that the IG findings the Department cited as its stated justification for defunding MEP (concerning executive-compensation limits and overstated economic-impact claims) were not legal or otherwise appropriate grounds for defunding the program -- directly undercutting the administration's own stated rationale for the RIF notices this entry already documents. No GAO findings or response were identified in sourcing reviewed as of this update. Update 2026-09-01 (GSR recheck batch 48): the MEP funding-uncertainty pattern this entry already documents (the 14-center July 2026 NOFO) recurred separately and earlier at a distinct set of 13 existing state MEP centers (Arizona, Colorado, Connecticut, Indiana, Maryland, Michigan, New Hampshire, North Carolina, Oklahoma, Oregon, Tennessee, Texas, and Virginia), which were left operating without renewed federal award obligations into mid-2026; trade press reported 12 of the 13 had received their federal MEP awards by July 6, 2026, with Colorado still delayed over budget revisions. Separately, and in apparent tension with both the RIF notices and the elimination proposal this entry documents, NIST simultaneously launched a new $40 million MEP Pilot Program (Federal Register notice, May 20, 2026; public webinar June 24, 2026) committing roughly $20 million per project over two years to accelerate additive manufacturing for aerospace components and build a domestic critical-minerals supply chain, open only to existing MEP centers. No response to Sen. Coons's original RIF-notice oversight letter, and no findings from the Cantwell/Peters-requested GAO investigation, were identified in sourcing reviewed as of this update.

title: NLRB Loses Statutory Quorum for Nearly a Year After Trump Fires Board Member Wilcox
institution: National Labor Relations Board
status: Complete (Wilcox's removal is now considered constitutionally settled following Trump v. Slaughter, June 29, 2026, though the Supreme Court has not yet formally disposed of her specific case)
date_of_action: 2025-01-27 (firing) through 2026-06-29 (Supreme Court's Slaughter ruling resolves the underlying legal question); board lacked a working quorum for roughly 11 of the intervening months
what_changed: On January 27, 2025, President Trump fired NLRB Board Member Gwynne Wilcox without citing any of the statutory grounds (neglect of duty or malfeasance) required by the National Labor Relations Act, leaving the five-seat Board with only two active members, below the three-member quorum required to issue decisions. Wilcox sued on February 5, 2025. U.S. District Judge Beryl Howell ruled the firing unlawful on March 6, 2025, calling it a 'blatant violation of the law' and a 'power grab,' and ordered Wilcox reinstated, which briefly restored the Board's quorum. A three-judge D.C. Circuit panel stayed that ruling on March 28; the full en banc D.C. Circuit reversed course and reinstated Wilcox again on April 7; Chief Justice Roberts then issued an emergency stay removing her again on April 9. On May 22, 2025, the Supreme Court declined to reinstate Wilcox in a 6-3 emergency-docket order, explicitly not a ruling on the merits. The Board remained below quorum until regaining one in December 2025 through new Trump nominations. On January 28, 2026, the D.C. Circuit declined en banc review of the panel decision upholding Wilcox's termination. On June 29, 2026, the Supreme Court's decision in the related case Trump v. Slaughter overruled the 90-year-old Humphrey's Executor precedent underlying Wilcox's legal theory; legal analysts across firms now consider her removal constitutionally settled even though the Court has not yet formally disposed of her specific still-pending case. Update (GSR recheck batch 2, 2026-09-08): On August 7, 2026, the Senate confirmed James Macy as a new Republican Board member (alongside the renomination of Democratic member David Prouty), giving the NLRB a full 3-1 Republican majority for the first time since Wilcox's firing. A bare quorum had technically been restored in December 2025, but this confirmation is the first point at which the Board has held the three Republican votes needed to formally overturn Biden-era precedent, not just issue decisions.

primary_proponent.name: Donald Trump
primary_proponent.role: President
primary_proponent.note: Fired Wilcox directly via a short email citing loss of confidence in her leadership, then pursued the legal theory that his Article II authority permitted the removal all the way to the Supreme Court, a position the Court substantially validated in the related Slaughter case.

estimated_impact.summary: The National Labor Relations Board, the sole federal agency responsible for enforcing private-sector labor law and adjudicating unfair-labor-practice and union-election disputes, was left without a functioning quorum for nearly all of 2025, halting its ability to issue binding decisions during that period.

estimated_impact.caveat: The administration's position, ultimately validated in substance by the Supreme Court's Slaughter ruling, is that the President's Article II authority requires the ability to remove officials exercising executive power at will, regardless of statutory for-cause protections. Labor advocates and a 20-state coalition of attorneys general (led by California AG Bonta, in an amicus brief) argued the firing created a 'dangerous regulatory vacuum' that left workers without a functioning forum to resolve unfair-labor-practice complaints or conduct union elections for most of a year. Notably, the legal question was genuinely unsettled for over a year: a federal district court and an initial D.C. Circuit panel sided with Wilcox, before the en banc D.C. Circuit, a Supreme Court emergency stay, and ultimately the Slaughter precedent sided with the administration, reflecting real legal uncertainty rather than a one-sided dispute.

confidence_note: Very strong. Anchored in multiple federal court opinions cited directly by name (Judge Howell's summary judgment order, the D.C. Circuit's en banc and panel rulings, the Supreme Court's emergency stay and later Slaughter opinion), a California Department of Justice press release quoting the district court's language, and extensive corroborating litigation tracking from four independent labor-and-employment law firms. Update (GSR recheck batch 2, 2026-09-08): the Aug. 7, 2026 Macy confirmation and resulting 3-1 majority independently confirmed via Troutman Pepper Locke and UE Union coverage, both fetched directly.

title: NNSA Nuclear-Weapons-Complex Staffing Crisis -- From Accidental Firings to a Shutdown Furlough That Halted Weapons Work for the First Time in History
institution: National Nuclear Security Administration (NNSA), a semi-autonomous Department of Energy agency responsible for the U.S. nuclear weapons stockpile; related developments at the Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC)
status: Ongoing, with escalating severity through the year -- initial erroneous firings (Feb 2025) gave way to a documented brain-drain (Mar-May 2025), then a historic shutdown-driven near-total work stoppage (Oct 2025), followed by a policy shift that reduces regulatory oversight of new reactor construction (Dec 2025); a April 2026 Stimson Center workforce-pipeline report quantifies the structural gap underlying the crisis, finding NNSA still roughly 200 positions short of the ~2,369-person staffing benchmark a 2020 agency study identified as needed by fiscal 2026
date_of_action: 2025-02-17 (initial erroneous firings) through 2025-12-30 (Reactor Pilot Program launch)
what_changed: In February 2025, DOGE-driven federal workforce cuts mistakenly fired NNSA employees -- some working on the nuclear stockpile and on tracking nuclear threats, including in Ukraine -- and the administration then could not contact them about reinstatement because their government email accounts had already been deactivated. ABC News reported on February 21, 2025 that this confusion was not limited to NNSA: hundreds of federal employees initially terminated from agencies including NNSA, the VA, and USDA had their dismissals rescinded, but many remained unclear on their actual employment status even after the reversal, reflecting a broader pattern of chaotic, poorly-tracked terminations across the initial wave of DOGE-directed cuts. By March 2025, the New York Times reported more than 130 senior scientists, engineers, and security experts had been forced out of NNSA, jeopardizing nuclear modernization programs and safety protocols. By May 2025, USA Today reported the cuts had derailed years of hiring progress and raised new safety concerns at weapons facilities including Los Alamos, the Y-12 National Security Complex, and Pantex. The staffing erosion reached the Nuclear Regulatory Commission as well: at a September 4, 2025 Senate hearing, two of the NRC's three remaining commissioners said they feared Trump could purge them too if they resisted his push to fast-track new reactor approvals, part of a stated goal to quadruple U.S. nuclear generating capacity by 2050. The crisis peaked during the October 2025 government shutdown: NNSA warned it would furlough 80% of its workforce as shutdown funding ran out, leaving only 375 'essential' employees and placing facility contractors in 'minimum-safe' status; by October 21, more than 1,400 employees -- over 75% of staff -- had actually been furloughed, leaving fewer than 400 on duty and suspending nearly all work on the U.S. nuclear weapons program, the first time in the program's history that weapons assembly and modernization work came to a complete stop. Funding for the Office of Secure Transportation, which physically moves nuclear warheads and materials, was confirmed only through October 27 as the shutdown continued. Then, on December 30, 2025, Trump officials launched a Reactor Pilot Program fast-tracking construction of new, largely untested nuclear reactor designs, with oversight shifted from the traditionally independent Nuclear Regulatory Commission to the Department of Energy itself -- aiming to bring at least three experimental reactors online by July 4, 2026 under an aggressive political deadline and with limited public transparency. In April 2026, the Stimson Center published a report, 'Securing the Future: Building the US Nuclear Security Workforce Pipeline,' putting a structural, longer-horizon number on the staffing gap underlying the year's crisis: a 2020 NNSA study had identified a need for 2,369 personnel by fiscal 2026, but the agency's own FY2026 budget request targeted a workforce of roughly 200 positions below that benchmark. The report attributes the shortfall not just to the year's disruptive events but to durable structural competition -- weak internal career-advancement pathways compared to the private sector, and NNSA's technical talent pool increasingly drawn instead toward AI, quantum computing, and biotechnology roles.

primary_proponent.name: Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE)
primary_proponent.role: Directed the initial 2025 workforce cuts across NNSA and related agencies
primary_proponent.note: No single named individual was identified in sourcing reviewed for this entry as personally directing the NNSA-specific cuts; the erroneous-firing episode in particular was reported as a process failure (deactivated emails preventing reinstatement contact) rather than a deliberate targeting decision, though it occurred within DOGE's broader, deliberately aggressive workforce-reduction push. The later Reactor Pilot Program and its shift of oversight from NRC to DOE reflects a distinct, deliberate administration policy choice.

estimated_impact.summary: Substantial, escalating loss of specialized nuclear-weapons-complex staffing capacity, culminating in the first complete halt to U.S. nuclear weapons assembly and modernization work in the program's history, alongside a shift of new-reactor oversight away from the traditionally independent nuclear safety regulator

The Stimson Center's ~200-position shortfall figure describes a structural, years-long gap against a 2020 benchmark, not a fresh cut attributable to 2025-2026 events specifically -- it contextualizes why the year's disruptions land on an agency that was already understaffed, rather than quantifying new losses.

The convergence of independent national-security, general-news, and Senate-hearing sourcing on the same underlying staffing trajectory makes this one of the more thoroughly corroborated entries in this tracker.
