title: NOAA Climate Research Zeroed Out in FY2026 Budget Proposal, Princeton Partnership Defunded
institution: National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration
status: Partially implemented, and repeating -- the Princeton funding cut took effect and the administration proposed eliminating NOAA's climate research office again in its FY2027 budget, for the second year running; Congress rejected the same elimination in FY2026 and House appropriators' initial FY2027 markup signals they are likely to do so again
date_of_action: 2025-04-08 (Princeton funding cut announced) through the FY2026 budget cycle (proposal released July 2025; Congress had not enacted it as of the last-verified date)
what_changed: On April 8, 2025, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick announced the termination of nearly $4 million in NOAA cooperative research funding to Princeton University, effective June 30, 2025, covering three programs including the Cooperative Institute for Modeling the Earth System, which supports Princeton's partnership with NOAA's Geophysical Fluid Dynamics Laboratory (GFDL), widely regarded as producing some of the world's most advanced climate modeling. The Commerce Department's official announcement stated the program 'promotes exaggerated and implausible climate threats, contributing to a phenomenon known as climate anxiety.' In July 2025, NOAA's proposed FY2026 budget was reported to contain a literal line reading 'Total, Climate Research: $0,' along with the proposed elimination of the entire Office of Oceanic and Atmospheric Research (OAR), NOAA's research arm, and defunding of all of OAR's climate and weather cooperative institutes nationwide, including CIRES at the University of Colorado Boulder, which houses the National Snow and Ice Data Center. The overall proposal called for cutting NOAA's budget by more than 25% and its ~13,000-person workforce by roughly 17%, along with a 44% reduction in planned investment in next-generation geostationary weather satellites. Congressional spending panels rejected the FY2026 budget request as proposed, but the administration proceeded with some of the changes administratively regardless, including terminating contracts for planned satellite instruments in August 2025 as what agency officials described to staff as a 'down payment' on the broader proposed cuts. The administration's FY2027 budget request, released in 2026, again proposes eliminating the Office of Oceanic and Atmospheric Research (OAR) -- the same office Congress rejected eliminating in the FY2026 cycle -- along with more than $1 billion in additional NOAA program cuts, including defunding the network of global monitoring laboratories and 14 other climate laboratories nationwide. At an April 2026 budget hearing, NOAA officials defended the cuts while members of both parties on the relevant committee pushed back. The House Commerce-Justice-Science Appropriations subcommittee's initial FY2027 markup was reported as favorable to NOAA's weather enterprise, suggesting Congress may again decline to enact the full elimination, consistent with the FY2026 outcome. The administration's separate FY2026 budget request also proposed eliminating all $43.5 million in federal support for NOAA's Integrated Ocean Observing System, a real-time data source used by harbor pilots, weather forecasters, and military operations, according to AP reporting in May 2025. By September 2025, the Washington Post reported the cuts had moved beyond budget proposals into concrete instrument shutdowns: the administration was closing down climate-monitoring satellites, shutting off carbon-tracking instruments, and scrapping sensors used to monitor water contamination and greenhouse gases, with internal budget documents directing NOAA to focus solely on 'weather-only' tools -- consistent with Project 2025's earlier call to dismantle federal climate research capacity. One consequence of NOAA's shrinking disaster-tracking function became visible that fall: NBC News reported in October 2025 that after the administration effectively shut down NOAA's billion-dollar disaster-cost-tracking database, a group of former NOAA scientists rebuilt an equivalent tracker independently through the nonprofit Climate Central -- their reconstruction found the costliest six-month stretch of U.S. weather disasters on record, with 14 separate events each exceeding $1 billion in damage, led by the Los Angeles wildfires at more than $61 billion.

primary_proponent.name: Howard Lutnick
primary_proponent.role: Secretary of Commerce (NOAA's parent department)
primary_proponent.note: Personally announced and was quoted defending the Princeton funding termination, and oversees the Commerce Department's NOAA budget proposals implementing the broader climate-research defunding.

estimated_impact.summary: A federal agency responsible for the data and modeling underlying weather forecasting, hurricane prediction, and climate research had its dedicated climate research funding line proposed at zero and lost a 57-year research partnership with one of the world's leading climate modeling laboratories.

title: DOGE/GSA Listed the Support-Office Lease for NOAA's Mauna Loa Observatory -- Home of the Keeling Curve -- for Termination, Then Quietly Resolved It
institution: National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) Global Monitoring Laboratory -- Mauna Loa Observatory; General Services Administration (GSA)
status: Resolved -- NOAA confirmed in July 2025 the lease matter was settled before the August 31, 2025 expiration, without specifying how; the observatory continued operating and was reported in 2026 to be expanding, not closing
date_of_action: 2025-03-11 (lease publicly reported as targeted) through 2025-07 (NOAA confirms resolution)
what_changed: In March 2025, Reuters and other outlets reported that DOGE/GSA had listed the lease for an eight-person NOAA support office in Hilo, Hawaii (suite 102, Kilauea Financial Plaza) among the federal office leases slated for early termination as part of the administration's real-estate cost-cutting push. The office is the ground-support base for the Mauna Loa Observatory, established in 1956 on the mountain's northern flank, which holds the world's longest continuous record of atmospheric carbon dioxide measurements -- the Keeling Curve -- and was already operating under strain from the loss of its only road access after Mauna Loa's 2022 eruption, making the Hilo office's remote-support role especially load-bearing. The lease was set to expire August 31, 2025. As of a late-August 2025 report, no resolution had been announced and Hawaii's congressional delegation -- Sen. Mazie Hirono and Reps. Jill Tokuda and Ed Case -- introduced a formal resolution expressing concern and reaffirming support for the observatory, with Hirono calling the threatened closure 'yet another attack on science.' NOAA subsequently confirmed to reporters that the lease matter was resolved in July 2025, before the deadline, without detailing the mechanism (renewal, relocation, or reversal of the termination decision). By mid-2026, reporting described the observatory not merely surviving but being rebuilt and expanded, with measurement programs that had been curtailed since the 2022 eruption road closure increasingly restored.

primary_proponent.name: General Services Administration, with DOGE (Department of Government Efficiency)
primary_proponent.role: GSA administered the lease-termination list that included this office; DOGE's broader federal-real-estate cost-cutting push provided the policy driver
primary_proponent.note: No named individual was identified in sourcing reviewed as personally responsible for including this specific office; this is the same GSA/DOGE lease-termination sweep documented separately for the USGS Hawaiian Volcano Observatory's Hilo office, a different agency and mission housed in a different Hilo building, targeted in the same week -- see [[doge-volcano-observatory-lease-terminations-2025]].

estimated_impact.summary: One of the eight-person support offices keeping alive the world's longest-running atmospheric CO2 record was briefly listed for lease termination with no documented contingency plan, at a moment when the observatory's summit instruments were already isolated by 2022 eruption damage and dependent on this office's remote-support role -- an example of a blanket real-estate cost-cutting sweep reaching a scientifically irreplaceable, decades-long dataset without an apparent case-by-case review.

NOAA's own account of the resolution mechanism is vague ('resolved') rather than specific, and no source reviewed states whether the termination decision was formally reversed or the office was relocated on the same footprint.

confidence_note: HIGH confidence on the core facts (lease listed, deadline, congressional resolution, NOAA's July 2025 confirmation of resolution) -- corroborated across Reuters/AP wire distribution, Honolulu Civil Beat, and congressional-office sourcing (Hirono/Tokuda/Case). MODERATE confidence on the precise resolution mechanism, since NOAA's own public statement did not specify how the lease issue was settled. Distinct from, and should not be merged with, [[doge-volcano-observatory-lease-terminations-2025]] -- that entry covers the USGS Hawaiian Volcano Observatory (Ironworks Building, Kilauea volcanic-hazard monitoring) and the Alaska Volcano Observatory; this entry covers NOAA's separate Mauna Loa Observatory support office (Kilauea Financial Plaza, atmospheric CO2 monitoring). Both are in Hilo and were targeted in the same DOGE sweep the same week, which is likely why several outlets -- and an earlier version of the existing tap entry -- conflated the two facilities' reported savings figures; verified independently here against direct wire reporting for each.

title: DOGE Cuts Gutted NOAA's Space Traffic Coordination Office, Then FY2026 Budget Sought to Eliminate Its Core System Entirely
institution: NOAA Office of Space Commerce (Commerce Department)
status: Mixed and recurring -- the February 2025 staffing cuts stand and were never fully reversed. The FY2026 threat to eliminate TraCSS funding entirely was rejected by Congress in enacted law (P.L. 119-74, signed 2026-01-23, $52.5 million against an $11 million request), but the same fight restarted for FY2027: the administration's April 3, 2026 budget request again proposed just $11 million with no dedicated TraCSS funding, and the House Appropriations Committee again restored funding (to $50 million, approved May 13, 2026) with report language explicitly supporting TraCSS. The FY2027 appropriations cycle was not yet finalized as of this update. TraCSS itself remains operational and growing, with 70 pilot users representing 11,345+ satellites onboarded as of August 2026.
date_of_action: 2025-02-27 (initial firings) through 2026 budget cycle (proposed elimination of TraCSS funding)
what_changed: On February 27, 2025, DOGE-driven cuts hit NOAA's Office of Space Commerce (OSC), a roughly 25-person office, on a few hours' notice -- about a third of the office's staff, including the chief of the Traffic Coordination System for Space (TraCSS), Dmitry Poisik. TraCSS is the civilian satellite traffic coordination system OSC has been building since 2018 (under Space Policy Directive 3, signed in Trump's first term) to warn commercial and government satellite operators of potential collisions as low Earth orbit becomes increasingly crowded. The cuts also hit OSC's Commercial Remote Sensing Regulatory Affairs Division, which licenses commercial imaging satellite companies; affected licensees received an email stating 'no senior personnel remain in the office' and warning of 'significant delays' processing licensing actions. Since the initial layoffs, three staffers in leadership roles were brought back, but congressional Democrats (Reps. Valerie Foushee and Zoe Lofgren among others) continued to warn about the office's reduced capacity. In 2026, the administration's budget request went further, proposing to cut OSC's budget by 85% and eliminate 18 positions, while eliminating federal funding for TraCSS entirely -- a group of space-industry organizations wrote to House and Senate leaders warning the cuts would put both commercial and government satellite operators at risk of collision. Update, 2026-08-17: the FY2026 defunding threat this entry describes as an unenacted budget proposal was resolved -- and rejected -- in enacted law before this entry was even written. The House Appropriations Committee's FY2026 Commerce-Justice-Science bill (approved May 2026) funded the Office of Space Commerce at $50 million against the administration's $11 million request; the Senate Appropriations Committee proposed $60 million; the final enacted figure, signed into law as part of P.L. 119-74 on January 23, 2026, settled at $52.5 million -- preserving TraCSS rather than eliminating it, following sustained pressure from a coalition of 450+ space, satellite, and defense companies. As of July 2026, TraCSS had 68 pilot users representing more than 11,290 satellites in orbit onboarded to the system, though work is reportedly proceeding more slowly than the pre-budget-threat schedule that had targeted full operational capability by January 2026. This funding resolution does not address the February 2025 staffing cuts themselves, which this entry's original reporting describes as only partially reversed (three leadership-role staffers reinstated of the roughly one-third of the office cut). Update, 2026-08-30 (GSR recheck batch 29): the defunding fight recurred for FY2027. The administration's FY2027 budget request, released April 3, 2026, again proposed only $11 million for the Office of Space Commerce with no dedicated TraCSS funding -- industry sources described it to SpaceNews as 'another attempt by the White House Office of Management and Budget to cancel or severely curtail TraCSS,' the same pattern as the FY2026 request a year earlier. The House Appropriations Committee's FY2027 Commerce-Justice-Science bill, approved May 13, 2026, again restored funding, to $50 million, with report language explicitly supporting continued TraCSS work. As of this update the Senate had not yet completed action and no FY2027 appropriations bill had been enacted (the federal fiscal year begins October 1, 2026), so this remains an unresolved, recurring threat rather than a settled one. Separately, TraCSS's pilot-user base grew modestly since the prior update, from 68 to 70 pilot users representing over 11,345 satellites in orbit.

primary_proponent.name: Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE)
primary_proponent.role: Directed the February 2025 firings; the 2026 budget proposal to eliminate TraCSS funding originated from the administration's Commerce Department budget request
primary_proponent.note: DOGE's cross-agency probationary/short-notice terminations reached OSC directly; the later FY2026 budget proposal to zero out TraCSS funding is a separate, subsequent administration action extending the same disruption to the office's core mission rather than just its staffing.

estimated_impact.summary: Space-industry organizations and congressional Democrats warn the cuts leave commercial and government satellite operators without adequate collision-warning infrastructure at exactly the moment low Earth orbit is becoming most crowded -- and that eliminating TraCSS funding entirely would end the program TraCSS was built to replace (an aging, overloaded Defense Department system never designed for today's commercial satellite volume).

title: NOAA-Wide Staffing Collapses by Roughly a Quarter in Six Weeks, With Disaster Training Cancelled and Privatization Floated
institution: National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), agency-wide (distinct from this database's separate, NWS-specific weather-balloon and staffing-loss entries)
status: Implemented and escalating across the documented period
what_changed: Over a roughly three-week span in March 2025, multiple outlets documented an escalating wave of NOAA-wide staffing cuts, distinct from the NWS-specific weather-balloon suspensions and 600-person NWS staffing loss already tracked in separate entries in this database. On March 12, the Associated Press reported plans to cut another 1,000 NOAA jobs, amounting to a 10% agency-wide workforce reduction affecting weather forecasting, ocean research, and fisheries management. The same day, The Hill reported the administration had cancelled disaster-response training for NWS meteorologists specifically due to staffing shortages and travel-budget cuts, with employees blocked from booking travel and some forced to cancel trips they had already booked. On March 13, ABC News reported NOAA was preparing mass layoffs affecting over 1,000 employees, describing a cumulative 25% workforce reduction since January as the agency was forced to eliminate entire functions rather than trim personnel within existing ones. On March 15, FedScoop reported NOAA had fired 800 probationary employees, on top of roughly 500 additional departures under the agency's deferred-resignation program, with former officials warning the combined losses endangered NOAA's weather forecasting, climate monitoring, and hurricane-tracking capabilities. On March 26, ABC News reported the administration was considering privatizing the National Weather Service entirely, a proposal tracing to Project 2025's recommendation that NOAA be 'broken up and downsized' and that NWS 'fully commercialize its forecasting operations.' By April 2, The Guardian reported NOAA was 'reeling' from the cumulative effect of more than 1,000 staff cuts, with some critical roles (including hurricane trackers) hastily rehired after the initial firings, and separately reported the agency's switch to an unsecured email server had left remaining staff flooded with spam.

title: NRC Commissioner Fired Without Cause, Agency Independence and Staffing Cut Under DOGE Reorganization
institution: Nuclear Regulatory Commission
status: Ongoing (Hanson's firing remains final and unlitigated; the commission remains at its full five members under Chairman Ho Nieh; the DOGE-directed reorganization and regulatory rewrite are continuing on EO 14300's original schedule, with NRC targeting completion of its organizational restructuring by the end of September 2026 and a new rulemaking-procedure rule published August 11, 2026)
date_of_action: 2025-05-23 (executive order) and 2025-06-13 (Hanson firing)
what_changed: On June 13, 2025, President Trump fired NRC Commissioner Christopher T. Hanson, effective immediately, via a two-line email from the White House Presidential Personnel Office. It was the first removal of an NRC commissioner since the agency's creation in 1974; Hanson's term was not set to expire until 2029, and no cause was cited beyond a White House spokesperson's comment that 'all organizations are more effective when leaders are rowing in the same direction.' Hanson, originally appointed by Trump in his first term and later chaired the commission under Biden, said he was terminated 'without cause, contrary to existing law and longstanding precedent regarding removal of independent agency appointees.' The firing left the five-member commission at a 2-2 partisan split with one vacancy, and came three weeks after Trump signed Executive Order 14300, 'Ordering the Reform of the Nuclear Regulatory Commission' (May 23, 2025), which directs the NRC to reorganize and undertake reductions in force in consultation with its DOGE Team, shrink the Advisory Committee on Reactor Safeguards to the statutory minimum, and complete a 'wholesale revision' of its safety regulations and guidance documents within 18 months, with rulemaking routed through OMB Director Russell Vought's office -- a process not previously applied to this traditionally arms-length safety regulator. Career staff departures followed; NRC's No. 2 career operations official, a 32-year veteran and self-described two-time Trump voter, retired in May 2025 partly in protest of political operatives being embedded in senior leadership positions with what he called potential to 'significantly influence decision-making.' The DOGE-directed reorganization required by EO 14300 has proceeded on the order's own timeline: the NRC issued its notices of proposed rulemaking for the 'wholesale revision' of safety regulations by the February 2026 deadline, and in mid-2026 launched a major organizational restructuring -- consolidating around new-reactor, operating-reactor, and materials/waste business lines, and creating two new offices (Office of Advanced Reactors; Office of the Chief Nuclear Reactor Inspector) -- targeted for completion by September 2026, with final rules due under the EO's 18-month deadline (November 2026). No update on Hanson's own removal was found; it remains final and unlitigated as of this recheck. CORRECTION 2026-07-26: this entry's prior recheck (2026-07-20) still described the commission as sitting at a 2-2 partisan split with one vacancy from Hanson's June 2025 removal -- that vacancy was actually filled months earlier, when Doug Weaver was sworn in December 22, 2025, restoring the commission to its full five-member statutory complement. Separately, on January 8, 2026, Trump designated Commissioner Ho Nieh -- a Republican who previously ran NRC's Office of Nuclear Reactor Regulation from 2018-2021 -- as the NRC's 20th chairman, succeeding David Wright, who continues serving as a commissioner. The commission's current composition includes Republicans Nieh and Wright alongside Democratic commissioners Matthew Marzano and Bradley Crowell. Hanson's own removal remains final and unlitigated as of this update; the leadership-composition correction here is about the vacancy his firing created, not about the firing's legality. Extending the deregulatory push, the NRC voted in April 2026 to phase out its own agency-led 'force-on-force' security drills at nuclear power plants -- mock attack exercises historically run and evaluated by NRC inspectors to test each plant's defenses -- shifting to a model where plant operators run their own exercises and NRC staff only observe. Reuters reported the change came as Trump pressured the NRC to speed reactor approvals for a major nuclear-capacity expansion tied to AI, data-center, electrification, and crypto-mining electricity demand. Update 2026-08-17: the reorganization continued on schedule, with NRC reaffirming a target of implementing its new organization chart by the end of September 2026. On August 11, 2026, NRC published a Federal Register rule, 'NRC Modernization: Rulemaking Procedure, Federal Advisory Committee Act Alignment, Access, and Security,' extending the regulatory rewrite already documented in this entry into a formal rule governing how the agency itself makes rules and manages its federal advisory committee. No update on Hanson's own removal was identified in sourcing reviewed; it remains final and unlitigated.

estimated_impact.caveat: The administration's stated rationale, laid out in EO 14300 itself, is that NRC over-regulation has stifled the industry -- only two new reactors have come online since 1978 -- and that reorganization is needed to meet a stated goal of quadrupling U.S. nuclear capacity to 400 GW by 2050 to meet AI-driven electricity demand; the order also directs staffing increases in new-reactor licensing offices even as it mandates cuts elsewhere. Nuclear safety and watchdog groups (Union of Concerned Scientists, American Nuclear Society, Nuclear Innovation Alliance) and congressional Democrats have raised the independence and safety-oversight concerns described above; some pro-nuclear industry voices have also flagged the licensing deadlines and workforce cuts as potentially undermining the very buildout the order seeks to accelerate. No senior administration or NRC official has published a defense of the Hanson firing beyond the 'rowing in the same direction' comment; NRC's own public statement was limited to noting the agency can function with fewer than five commissioners.

The staffing-shortfall figure and career-departure detail (Techdirt/ProPublica) are well-sourced but describe broader trends rather than counts specific to the Hanson firing alone; framed accordingly in the summary above. title: NSF Fires 168 Staff Including Antarctic Program Managers, Disrupting U.S. Polar Research Logistics
institution: National Science Foundation
status: Escalated, not just implemented -- the February 2025 firings were followed roughly a year later by a structural reorganization (April 2026) that further reduced and reassigned Office of Polar Programs staff specifically
date_of_action: 2025-02-18 (NSF firings) through at least 2025-03-10 (reported downstream Antarctic Program disruption)
what_changed: On February 18, 2025, DOGE-driven cuts eliminated 168 NSF positions -- roughly 10% of the agency's staff -- including probationary employees and expert appointments. Several of those fired were program managers for the U.S. Antarctic Program, the office responsible for maintaining communication with the Antarctic infrastructure and logistics contractor, planning scientist deployments to the continent, and tracking budgets and funding for operations and maintenance work at the three permanent U.S. Antarctic stations (McMurdo, Palmer, and the Amundsen-Scott South Pole Station), which host research including the South Pole and BICEP telescopes, the IceCube neutrino detector, and long-running atmospheric climate monitoring. One scientist whose NSF project manager was fired told WIRED, 'Without them, everything stops.' By early March 2025, researchers reported losing clarity on reporting structures and proposal-submission processes, and warned that a shutdown of the South Pole station in particular would be 'basically nearly impossible to bring... back up' given the logistical difficulty of restarting polar operations. Around the same time, NSF also removed gender-inclusive housing-preference language from Antarctic staffer forms for McMurdo Station. Scientists and members of Congress warned the disruption risked ceding ground at the South Pole: reporting identified Germany, Canada, Spain, and China as already recruiting displaced or frustrated American Antarctic researchers, and raised concern that Russia and China could expand their own polar presence into any resulting U.S. capability gap. House Science Committee leaders Zoe Lofgren and Valerie Foushee separately criticized the broader wave of NSF firings publicly and pressed the National Science Board to intervene. Update, 2026-08-17: as part of NSF's broader elimination of all 37 of its divisions (announced to staff May 8, 2025, driven in part by a proposed 55% FY2026 budget cut), the Office of Polar Programs -- previously housed in the Geosciences Directorate -- was moved by April 16, 2026 into a newly created Office of Research Infrastructure under NSF's Office of the Director. NSF's own announcement and subsequent reporting describe further staff reassignments and reductions specifically within the Office of Polar Programs as part of this move, on top of the February 2025 program-manager firings this entry already documents, deepening rather than resolving the disruption to Antarctic program logistics and support.

title: DOGE Terminated 1,752 Active NSF Research Grants Worth $1.4 Billion, Bypassing Peer Review
institution: National Science Foundation
status: Ongoing nationwide -- NSF's peer-review process itself was subsequently restructured (effective December 15, 2025), reducing external review requirements. Partial court-ordered reversal for one plaintiff class: on May 25, 2026, the Ninth Circuit affirmed a preliminary injunction in Thakur v. Trump ordering NSF, NEH, and EPA to reinstate ~$324 million in grants terminated from University of California researchers, on First Amendment viewpoint-discrimination grounds. The separate, broader nationwide case (American Association of Physics Teachers v. NSF, 1:25-cv-01923, D.D.C.) is now in summary-judgment briefing on the merits: plaintiffs filed their motion for summary judgment July 23, 2026; the government filed a combined opposition and cross-motion for summary judgment August 20, 2026; plaintiffs' reply and cross-opposition are due September 3, 2026, and the government's final reply is due September 17, 2026, per the court's May 7/July 9, 2026 scheduling order -- meaning the roughly $1.1 billion in non-UC terminations remain in effect while the case's merits are actively being briefed, not merely awaiting a ruling on a stalled motion to dismiss.
date_of_action: 2025-04-18 (NSF announces terminations begin) through 2025-05 (bulk of terminations completed)
what_changed: Beginning April 18, 2025, NSF started terminating active research grants that had been flagged in an initial Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) review for containing language related to diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI). Between April and May 2025, DOGE terminated 1,752 active NSF grants worth a combined $1.4 billion. The terminations were administrative actions taken at the agency level against grant-abstract language, not decisions run back through the scientific peer-review process or NSF program officers' subject-matter judgment -- the normal mechanism by which NSF grants are awarded and, when necessary, reconsidered. Affected projects spanned a wide range of fields; reporting on individual terminated grants included projects in physics education, computer science mentoring programs for women ("sister circles"), and numerous other social-science and STEM-education projects that referenced diversity or inclusion in their framing, alongside grants in climate and public-health-adjacent research. NSF separately halted new grant awards for a period to conduct a second administrative review of pending awards. Later in 2025, NSF restructured its peer-review process itself, effective December 15, 2025: the minimum number of required external reviewers per grant was cut from three to two (with one of the two now permitted to be an NSF staff reviewer rather than an outside scientist), panel discussions became optional rather than mandatory, and required panel summary write-ups were shortened to three-to-five sentences. Update 2026-08-17: this entry's original write-up (2026-08-12) omitted a material court ruling that predated it by more than two months. Six University of California faculty had sued in Thakur v. Trump (N.D. Cal.), and on June 23, 2025, Judge Rita Lin issued a class-wide preliminary injunction ordering NSF, NEH, and EPA to stop DEI/environmental-justice-based grant terminations and reinstate previously-terminated grants to two certified UC plaintiff classes (those who received generic form-letter terminations, and those terminated specifically under the DEI/environmental-justice executive orders). The Ninth Circuit denied the government's stay request on August 21, 2025, then on May 25, 2026 affirmed the injunction on the merits, ordering NSF, NEH, and EPA to reinstate approximately $324 million in grants to UC researchers -- finding that selecting grants for termination based on recipients' perceived support for DEI or environmental-justice research was unconstitutional viewpoint discrimination, not a neutral application of programmatic criteria. The court routed any monetary damages claims (as opposed to reinstatement) to the U.S. Court of Federal Claims under recent Supreme Court precedent. This reinstatement is specific to the certified UC plaintiff classes -- it does not reopen or resolve the roughly 1,700 other NSF terminations nationwide, which remain subject to a separate, still-unresolved district court case. Update 2026-08-29: that separate case is American Association of Physics Teachers v. NSF (1:25-cv-01923, D.D.C.), filed June 18, 2025 by AAPT, AAC&U, WEPAN, AERA, AAUP, and the UAW, and assigned to Judge Jia Cobb. Judge Cobb denied plaintiffs' preliminary-injunction motion on September 11, 2025 -- the same Tucker Act/jurisdictional theory later used against the Vera Institute DOJ-grants case elsewhere in this tracker, finding the court lacked jurisdiction to order interim restoration of the funds and that plaintiffs had not shown irreparable harm -- meaning the roughly $1.1 billion in non-UC NSF terminations were allowed to stand while the case proceeds, not because a court found the terminations lawful on the merits. The case continued past that point: per a June 17, 2026 docket update, Judge Cobb partially denied NSF's motion to dismiss, finding plaintiffs' APA claims regarding NSF's 2025 'change in priorities' decision sufficiently pleaded to proceed. No ruling on those merits claims was identified as of this recheck. Update 2026-08-31 (real correction): this entry's prior text stopped at the June 17, 2026 partial motion-to-dismiss ruling in AAPT v. NSF and stated 'no ruling on those merits claims was identified as of this recheck.' The case has since moved well past that point: per the court's July 9, 2026 amended scheduling order, plaintiffs filed their motion for summary judgment (with supporting memorandum and multiple declarations) on July 23, 2026, plus an errata/additional declaration on July 24; the government responded on August 20, 2026 with a combined memorandum opposing plaintiffs' summary-judgment motion, a cross-motion for its own summary judgment, and a motion to strike certain plaintiff exhibits. Plaintiffs' reply and cross-opposition are due September 3, 2026, the government's reply due September 17, 2026, and a joint appendix due October 1, 2026. This is a substantive procedural advance -- from a motion-to-dismiss stage where only the sufficiency of the pleadings was at issue, to full summary-judgment briefing where the merits of NSF's 'change in priorities' termination rationale are now squarely before the court.

title: DOGE Terminated 1,752 NSF Research Grants Using a Senator's Keyword List, Then NSF Formally Weakened Its Own Peer Review Standards
institution: National Science Foundation (NSF)
status: Largely complete (terminations executed; peer-review rule changes formally in effect since Dec. 15, 2025)
date_of_action: 2025-04-14 (DOGE arrives at NSF) through 2025-12-15 (formal peer-review process change takes effect)
what_changed: On April 14, 2025, three DOGE personnel arrived at NSF headquarters and were given direct access to the agency's internal grant management systems -- an unusual level of access for political appointees into a agency's live award-processing systems, which one NSF program officer told Nature 'raises the hairs on the back of our neck.' DOGE ordered NSF's grants division to pull back all proposals that had already cleared full peer review and internal approval but were awaiting final signoff, instructing career program officers to perform undefined 'mitigation work' to bring the proposals into compliance with Trump executive orders restricting research related to diversity, equity, and inclusion or climate change. NSF ultimately terminated 1,752 active grants worth $1.4 billion. The screening process relied substantially on a list of roughly 3,400 grants compiled by Sen. Ted Cruz's office, which Cruz characterized as funding 'neo-Marxist class warfare propaganda'; independent analysis by the Grant Watch project found the terminated grants' titles and abstracts most frequently contained the words 'Black,' 'climate,' 'student,' 'justice,' 'identity,' and 'teacher' -- and that NSF's STEM Education directorate alone lost 839 grants worth $888 million, nearly half of all dollars terminated agency-wide despite being a small fraction of NSF's total budget. NSF Director Sethuraman Panchanathan resigned during this period. Separately, effective December 15, 2025, NSF formally revised its own peer review standards (PAPPG 24-1 Supplement 1): the minimum number of required external reviews per proposal dropped from three to two, one of which may now be an NSF staff member rather than an outside expert; panel discussions became optional rather than required; and panel summary write-ups were capped at three to five sentences, down from what had often run several paragraphs. NSF attributed the peer-review changes to a proposal backlog and workforce reductions, not to the DOGE-driven terminations directly. Update 2026-07-28: On April 24, 2026, all 22 members of the National Science Board (NSF's presidentially-appointed governing/oversight body) received an email notifying them, without explanation, that their positions were 'terminated, effective immediately.' On May 12, 2026, roughly 1,500 members and supporters of the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine -- including 37 Nobel Prize winners -- denounced the dismissal in an open letter calling it 'an alarming attack on the ability of the US to engage in basic and applied research.' Separately, nearly 150 NSF employees sent their own letter of dissent to Congress, warning that the administration's actions -- including steep budget cuts, mass firings, grant terminations, and withholding of billions in appropriated funds -- threaten to dismantle the agency, and calling for congressional intervention.

primary_proponent.name: DOGE personnel Luke Farritor and Zachary Terrell
primary_proponent.role: DOGE staff embedded at NSF with direct grant-system access
primary_proponent.note: Then-NSF Director Sethuraman Panchanathan wrote in an internal priorities update that efforts to broaden research participation 'should not preference some groups at the expense of others' -- the stated policy rationale for the review -- before resigning shortly afterward. Sen. Ted Cruz is the named source of the keyword-flagged grant list that substantially shaped which proposals were targeted, though NSF and the White House have not published an official list or criteria of their own, leaving outside researchers (Grant Watch) to reconstruct the pattern independently from grant titles and abstracts.

estimated_impact.summary: Congress separately and explicitly rejected a much larger cut: the FY2026 appropriations bill (signed January 23, 2026) funded NSF at $8.75 billion, refusing the White House's request to cut the agency to $3.9 billion (roughly 55%), which NSF's own internal projections said would have dropped grant funding rates to approximately 7%. The Senate Commerce Committee described the enacted funding level as preventing 'an existential threat to U.S. science funding.' This creates a notable split: Congress protected NSF's overall budget, while DOGE's targeted, keyword-driven terminations and the subsequent peer-review rule changes altered the agency's internal operations and standards in ways that did not require, and were not subject to, the same congressional appropriations fight.

title: NSF Announced Dismantling 80% of $368M Ocean Monitoring Network, Then Reversed Course After Bipartisan Congressional Revolt
institution: National Science Foundation (NSF)
status: Reversed -- NSF announced in mid-June 2026 it would terminate the dismantlement plan and reinstall already-removed Pacific Northwest instruments, following bipartisan Senate and House letters demanding the array's preservation
date_of_action: 2026-05 (dismantlement announced) through 2026-06-18 (reversal announced)
what_changed: In May 2026, NSF announced plans to remove roughly 900 deep-sea instruments from the Ocean Observatories Initiative (OOI), a $368 million network operating continuously since 2016 that monitors ocean currents, marine heat waves, carbon absorption, coastal flooding risk, fisheries conditions, and broader climate indicators across sites off Oregon, Washington, Alaska, North Carolina, and the Irminger Sea between Greenland and Iceland. NSF said it would begin removing instruments in June 2026, projecting roughly $48 million in annual operational savings, and had in fact begun removing equipment from Pacific Northwest waters before Congress intervened. On June 16, 2026, a bipartisan group of senators -- led by Democrat Jeff Merkley and Republican Lisa Murkowski, joined by Sens. Markey, Warren, Baldwin, Murray, Cantwell, Whitehouse, Van Hollen, and Wyden -- sent a letter to NSF directing it to terminate the dismantlement plan and maintain the array; House lawmakers sent a parallel letter the same day. On June 18, 2026, NSF issued an unsigned statement reversing course: it would terminate the plan to disband 80% of OOI and reinstall the equipment already removed from Pacific Northwest waters.

primary_proponent.name: National Science Foundation leadership (unsigned June 18, 2026 reversal statement; original dismantlement announcement made under NSF's Trump-appointed leadership)
primary_proponent.role: Federal agency responsible for basic-science funding and infrastructure, including OOI
primary_proponent.note: NSF's original decision to dismantle 80% of a $368 million active climate-monitoring network -- and its reversal only after direct, bipartisan congressional intervention -- is the accountability record this entry documents; no single named official's public statement defending the original dismantlement decision was identified in reporting reviewed.

estimated_impact.summary: Scientists and lawmakers characterized the initial plan as eliminating one of the only continuous, real-time ocean-climate monitoring systems along U.S. coasts at a moment of accelerating climate risk, warning it would create a lasting data gap for tracking phenomena like Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC) slowdown, marine heat waves, and coastal flooding risk. The bipartisan, cross-chamber reversal within roughly five weeks of the announcement is itself notable: an unusually fast congressional check on an agency-level dismantlement decision, in contrast to many other entries in this tracker where similar actions proceeded without reversal.

title: National Weather Service Lost ~600 Staff, Including a Vacant Position Tied to the Texas Flood Warnings
institution: National Weather Service (NWS), National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), Department of Commerce
status: Partially reversed (active rehiring underway, but experience/institutional-knowledge loss is not recoverable by rehiring alone)
date_of_action: Early-mid 2025 (initial cuts); ongoing reorganization through at least April 2026
what_changed: Early in 2025, DOGE-driven early retirement incentives and probationary-employee firings cut roughly 600 employees (about 15% of staff) from the National Weather Service nationwide, part of broader cuts to its parent agency NOAA. NOAA workers described the process to NBC News as chaotic and intentionally disorienting: employees reported being fired, then reinstated, then fired again within the same stretch of weeks, in some cases losing pay, health insurance, and unemployment-benefit eligibility during the gaps. By May 2025, 52 of the NWS's 122 weather forecast offices had staffing vacancy rates above 20%, and at least 8 offices could no longer maintain 24/7 operations, including Sacramento, Goodland (KS), and Jackson (KY). Former NWS directors wrote publicly that 'our worst nightmare is that weather forecast offices will be so understaffed that there will be needless loss of life.' Specifically at the Austin/San Antonio forecast office -- which covers the Texas Hill Country -- the warning coordination meteorologist position (responsible for working directly with emergency managers and the public on what to do when a disaster strikes) had been vacant since the person who held it for decades accepted an early-retirement offer at the end of April 2025, roughly two months before the deadly July 4, 2025 Guadalupe River flash flood that killed more than 100 people. Two days after that flood, the administration issued a memo stating no federal vacancies could be filled until October, after the extreme weather season ended. By late September 2025, with hurricane and wildfire season underway, the Washington Post reported the ~600-person, roughly 1-in-7-staff loss was leaving dozens of forecast offices short-staffed in practice -- forecasters described pulling double shifts, running informal 'buddy systems' to cover gaps, and trimming nonessential services just to keep core forecasting running. In 2026, NOAA began actively rehiring (recruiting ~150 entry-level meteorologists, filling 200+ positions since late 2025), but experienced meteorologists warn the resulting workforce skews inexperienced -- 'because there are no old-timers left,' as one Alaska-based former NWS meteorologist put it -- and 'upper air' atmospheric data collection has noticeably degraded since January 2025, a data source considered fundamental to forecast accuracy.

primary_proponent.name: DOGE (Department of Government Efficiency) / NOAA leadership
primary_proponent.role: Executed the early-2025 workforce reductions
primary_proponent.note: No single named individual was identified in available reporting as personally directing the NWS-specific cuts -- this was part of the broader, DOGE-driven federal workforce reduction effort. NOAA Administrator Neil Jacobs stated during his confirmation hearing that he would 'ensure that staffing the Weather Service offices is a top priority,' an on-the-record commitment worth checking against subsequent NWS staffing trends.

estimated_impact.summary: The Center for American Progress's analysis of the Texas floods specifically is careful to note the Austin/San Antonio office still issued timely, accurate, impacts-based forecasts despite the vacancy -- crediting 'the extraordinary dedication of the current staff' -- while also stating plainly that the vacant warning coordination meteorologist role is 'responsible for working with emergency managers and the public to ensure people know what to do when a disaster strikes,' the exact communication function that came under scrutiny after the floods. This is a case where the forecasting itself held up, but a specific staffing gap affected the human coordination layer between forecast and public action.

title: NWS Suspends or Cuts Weather Balloon Launches at Multiple Sites Following Staffing Cuts, Coinciding With Missed Tornado Warnings
institution: National Weather Service (NOAA, Department of Commerce)
status: Ongoing -- suspensions/reductions announced March 2025 remained in effect through mid-2026, with some restored launches shifted to midday rather than the original schedule
date_of_action: 2025-03-20 (initial suspension/reduction announcement) through 2026 (ongoing effect)
what_changed: On February 26, 2025, OMB Director Russell Vought and then-Acting OPM Director Charles Ezell issued a memo directing federal agencies to prepare for mass layoffs. The next day, February 27, 2025, the Office of Personnel Management fired approximately 880 NOAA employees; NOAA followed roughly two months later by approving over 1,000 additional deferred resignations or buyouts. Citing the resulting staffing shortages, the National Weather Service announced on March 20, 2025 that it would suspend or reduce twice-daily weather balloon (radiosonde) launches at 11 upper-air observation sites: full suspension at Kotzebue, Alaska; Omaha, Nebraska; and Rapid City, South Dakota; reduction to once daily at Aberdeen, South Dakota; Grand Junction, Colorado; Green Bay, Wisconsin; Gaylord, Michigan; North Platte, Nebraska; and Riverton, Wyoming; and intermittent suspension at Albany, New York, and Gray, Maine, with NWS stating twice-daily launches would resume 'when staffing permits.' At sites that kept launching, many shifted the traditional early-morning flight to midday to align with when day-shift staff are on duty, rather than the pre-dawn atmospheric-sampling window the schedule was originally designed around. The disruption continued into the 2026 severe-weather season: NPR and NBC News reported that meteorologists in Kansas and Missouri linked reduced balloon data to tornado outbreaks catching forecasters by surprise, including a specific April 13, 2026 episode in which NWS forecast almost no chance of tornadoes in East Central Kansas and a balloon was launched only after storms had already begun forming. The Boston Globe reported that March 2026 saw 202 tornadoes nationally -- more than double the 30-year average for that month -- and April 2026 saw 250 versus a 180 average, with forecasters attributing part of the shortfall in advance warning to staffing and resource gaps at NWS offices, of which 122 exist nationwide. Re-verified 2026-08-17: no confirmed restoration to twice-daily service, or further reduction, identified at any of the 11 specifically tracked sites (Kotzebue, Omaha, Rapid City, Aberdeen, Grand Junction, Green Bay, Gaylord, North Platte, Riverton, Albany, Gray) since the prior update. Separately, at least one other NWS office not on this entry's tracked list (Salt Lake City) restored its pre-cut launch schedule in August 2026 after filling vacancies -- noted here as context for the broader staffing picture but not treated as a change to this entry's own 11-site claim, since Salt Lake City was never one of the sites this entry documents.

title: HR1 ("One Big Beautiful Bill") Federal Funding Cuts Strip Essential Plan Coverage From ~450,000 New Yorkers
institution: New York State of Health Essential Plan (federal Basic Health Program, funded through HHS/CMS)
status: Ongoing -- eligibility changes took effect July 1, 2026; the August 30, 2026 gap-free-enrollment deadline has now passed with interim data (as of July 31) showing roughly 44% of the ~450,000 affected still without confirmed replacement coverage; New York State has taken some mitigating action and may seek further restoration funding in the 2027 legislative session, but has not restored coverage to all affected enrollees
date_of_action: 2026-07-01 (eligibility changes take effect, following earlier-2026 enactment of HR1)
what_changed: HR1, the reconciliation law Trump signed in 2026 and that the administration has branded the 'One Big Beautiful Bill,' cut federal funding underlying New York's Essential Plan -- a Basic Health Program that had provided low-cost coverage to low- and middle-income residents who earn too much for Medicaid but still qualify for ACA marketplace subsidy support. As of July 1, 2026, New Yorkers earning between 200% and 250% of the federal poverty level (a single-person household income of roughly $31,920 to $39,900 per year) lost eligibility for subsidized Essential Plan coverage entirely, and an estimated 450,000 New Yorkers lost coverage as a result. The law is projected to eliminate $7.5 billion in annual federal funding for the program, which had covered nearly 1.7 million low- and middle-income New Yorkers before the cuts. New York Governor Kathy Hochul's administration used a Basic Health Program waiver mechanism to access billions in a federal trust fund and partially mitigate the impact, preserving coverage for a majority of enrollees, but did not fully offset the loss for the affected income band. Additional Medicaid work-requirement provisions in the same law are expected to strip coverage from hundreds of thousands more Americans nationally beginning in 2027. Re-verified 2026-08-17: no material change to the ~450,000-affected figure or the state's mitigation approach; no further developments beyond what's already documented were identified as of this update. Update 2026-08-30: affected enrollees have until today, August 30, 2026, to enroll in a Qualified Health Plan without a coverage gap, since loss of Essential Plan coverage is treated as a qualifying life event under NY State of Health's own guidance; separately, per Spectrum News reporting, the state government will have another opportunity to seek funding to restore Essential Plan coverage during the 2027 legislative session -- meaning the current ~450,000-affected figure documents the gap as of this recheck, not necessarily a permanent settlement. Update 2026-09-01 (GSR recheck batch 52): interim enrollment data reported in late August shows replacement-coverage uptake lagging well behind the ~450,000 affected -- as of July 31, 2026, more than 183,000 of those who lost Essential Plan eligibility had re-enrolled in the (still free) Essential Plan or now qualified for Medicaid due to income changes, but fewer than 60,000 had enrolled in a Qualified Health Plan through the marketplace, leaving roughly 44% -- close to 200,000 New Yorkers -- without confirmed replacement coverage as the August 30 gap-free-enrollment deadline arrived. The state Department of Health said it is 'committed to using every resource at its disposal' to reach those still uncovered. This interim-outcome data predates but was missed by this entry's own 2026-08-30 update, which documented the deadline itself but not what enrollment looked like heading into it.

Interim data as of July 31, 2026 shows only about 56% of the affected population had secured replacement coverage (Essential Plan/Medicaid re-enrollment or a new Qualified Health Plan), leaving an estimated ~200,000 New Yorkers at risk of an actual coverage gap as the state's own August 30 deadline arrived.

status: Resolved -- Section 71113's one-year Medicaid funding cutoff expired July 4, 2026 without congressional renewal or replacement; litigation had already been voluntarily dismissed by March 17, 2026. Medicaid funding to Planned Parenthood and other affected providers has resumed. This entry now documents the completed one-year defund episode and its documented harm, not an ongoing cutoff.
date_of_action: 2025-07-04 (OBBBA signed into law) through 2026-07-04 (Section 71113's one-year Medicaid cutoff expired without congressional renewal)
what_changed: Section 71113 of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA), signed July 4, 2025, cut off Medicaid reimbursement for one year to any tax-exempt 'essential community provider' focused on family planning that both provides abortions beyond the Hyde Amendment's exceptions and received more than $800,000 in combined federal/state Medicaid expenditures in fiscal year 2023 -- a threshold designed to target Planned Parenthood and similarly-sized independent clinics, including Maine Family Planning, while leaving smaller providers unaffected. Nationally, roughly 200 Planned Parenthood health centers across 24 states were identified as being at risk of closure, more than 90% of them in states where abortion remains legal, since over half of Planned Parenthood's patients rely on Medicaid for care unrelated to abortion (contraception, cancer screenings, STI testing, and general primary/reproductive care). Planned Parenthood Federation of America and Maine Family Planning separately sued, along with 22 state attorneys general and Pennsylvania challenging the provision as unconstitutional; a federal judge (Talwani) granted Planned Parenthood a preliminary injunction blocking the cutoff nationwide. On December 30, 2025, the First Circuit Court of Appeals stayed that injunction, ruling the provision was not an unconstitutional bill of attainder because it did not itself impose 'punishment' in the legal sense -- allowing the funding cutoff to proceed in most states while other litigation continued; the separate Planned Parenthood Federation of America v. Kennedy suit was dismissed January 30, 2026. In Maine, the funding loss had already produced concrete, documented harm by that point: effective October 31, 2025, Maine Family Planning discontinued primary care services (not abortion services specifically) at three rural locations -- Houlton, Ellsworth, and Presque Isle -- affecting roughly 800-1,000 low-income patients who had relied on those clinics as their primary-care provider, not just for reproductive health. Maine Governor Janet Mills proposed $2.25 million in one-time state supplemental funding on January 27, 2026 to offset the federal loss; the state budget signed in April 2026 went further, establishing an ongoing $5 million-per-year state funding stream for reproductive health providers beginning in 2027, alongside Washington State's governor separately announcing the state would cover its own affected providers' funding gap. Corrected 2026-08-17: Section 71113 was a one-year provision by its own statutory text (July 4, 2025 - July 3, 2026), and Congress missed the deadline to extend or replace it before it expired; all remaining litigation challenging the provision had already been voluntarily dismissed by March 17, 2026, before the expiration mooted the underlying dispute. Medicaid funding to Planned Parenthood and other affected providers resumed after the cutoff lapsed on July 4, 2026. A Planned Parenthood Federation of America report published in the weeks after expiration found that during the one-year cutoff, nearly 30 Planned Parenthood health centers closed nationally (serving roughly 41,000 birth control patients, two-thirds of the closures in rural or medically underserved areas), while Medicaid visits fell by roughly 25% (over 250,000 visits) and specific service categories declined further: birth control pill dispensing down almost 25%, IUD/long-acting contraception visits down 26%, breast exam visits down 20%, and STI testing down 10%. Update 2026-09-01 (GSR recheck batch 49): a renewal push did in fact exist and has since failed to advance. The House Freedom Caucus, in a letter to Speaker Mike Johnson, demanded a 'Reconciliation 3.0' bill extend Section 71113's abortion-provider funding ban; Johnson pursued the idea through July 2026, but the White House-approved Reconciliation 3.0 package that ultimately moved forward -- built around Iran-war spending and voter-ID legislation -- did not include the Planned Parenthood defund extension, and a budget expert cited in coverage noted a 'Reconciliation 4.0' is not procedurally available this Congress since Reconciliation 3.0 exhausts the one reconciliation bill allowed per budget year. Senate Republicans were separately reported as 'cooler' to a third reconciliation bill given reluctance to reopen an abortion fight close to the midterms. This closes the loop on this entry's own prior caveat: Congress did consider renewing the cutoff, but the renewal effort failed to make it into the vehicle that passed, and no further reconciliation opportunity remains this Congress.

title: Acting DNI Bill Pulte purges Office of the Director of National Intelligence staff
institution: Office of the Director of National Intelligence (ODNI)
status: Concluded for Pulte, agency-transition ongoing -- the Senate confirmed Jay Clayton, 51-47 along party lines, on July 28, 2026, but the administration delayed his swearing-in for nearly a week, until August 3, 2026, with Pulte continuing to serve as acting DNI in the interim despite bipartisan senators' objections and a Cato Institute legal analysis arguing that under the plain language of the Federal Vacancies Reform Act, Pulte's authority to serve lapsed the moment Clayton was confirmed -- making everything Pulte did as acting DNI during that week, including announcing a 5th round of layoffs (an approximately 30% staff reduction, by his own description) hours before Clayton's swearing-in, potentially legally invalid and vulnerable to court challenge. ODNI's workforce reduction under Pulte's roughly six-week tenure is not fully reconciled across sourcing (the Washington Post's July 23 count of ~200 purged since June 1, reducing the workforce to ~1,300, predates this final round). No indication in sourcing reviewed that Clayton has reversed or reviewed the cuts.
what_changed: Before he had officially taken office, Bill Pulte showed up at ODNI headquarters a day early, catching staff -- including outgoing DNI Tulsi Gabbard, who was given only a brief heads-up -- off guard. CNN reported Pulte requested a list of every ODNI employee so he could assess whom to fire, repeatedly asked whether he would have access to a government plane, requested a security detail, asked about the status and classification level of his newly issued security clearance, and asked ODNI staff in a briefing whether he could bring the President's Daily Brief to his house. Pulte was the first person to lead ODNI since its creation after September 11, 2001 without any prior intelligence or national-security experience and without having previously held a security clearance. Beginning about a week after Tulsi Gabbard resigned as DNI, Acting Director Bill Pulte began firing and reassigning ODNI staff in successive rounds of cuts. An initial round removed 6 career and political intelligence staff and sent 45 others back to their home agencies -- just over 50 people removed from ODNI roles in total. A source told NBC News that Pulte had ordered staff to identify roughly 400 employees for termination at the National Counterterrorism Center, though other sources said the Center itself was ultimately not hit by that specific round; the National Counterintelligence and Security Center was separately reported as expected to face significant cuts. Pulte has said publicly that his goal is to reduce the size of ODNI and refocus it on national security. Separately, Pulte's authority to hold the role at all has been disputed: the DNI has no supervisor other than the president, making it a 'principal officer' under the Constitution's Appointments Clause that legal analysts (Cato Institute, Lawfare) say should require Senate confirmation even in an acting capacity, and federal law arguably required the Senate-confirmed principal deputy DNI to assume the role automatically once it became vacant rather than a new outside appointee. A Project on Government Oversight legal expert said the appointment meets the Vacancies Reform Act's technical requirements but flagged that the Act's eligibility rules are so broad (allowing the president to choose from 350+ federal officials regardless of relevant qualifications) that they may not satisfy the Constitution's stricter requirement for principal officers. Senate Intelligence Vice Chairman Mark Warner publicly objected to the appointment, and Sen. Elissa Slotkin introduced the MERIT Act on July 16, 2026 to require any acting DNI to have national security experience -- legislative responses that read as a direct rebuke of the Pulte pick. If a court ultimately found the appointment invalid, Pulte's purge decisions and other agency actions taken under his tenure could themselves be legally exposed to challenge. As of July 27, 2026, Pulte's office confirmed a 4th round of what it called 'measured layoffs' had just been completed, indicating the reductions are continuing rather than a single one-time action. Update 2026-07-27: The Washington Post separately reported ODNI has purged approximately 200 employees through firings and reassignments since June 1, 2026, reducing the office's workforce to roughly 1,300 -- just over half its size when Trump returned to office -- describing the cuts as part of a broader campaign to replace experienced civil servants with political loyalists. CORRECTION 2026-08-17: this entry's prior 'Ongoing' framing described Pulte as still leading ODNI as of its 2026-08-06 last-verified date, without reflecting that his tenure had already effectively ended days earlier -- the Senate confirmed Jay Clayton as DNI on July 28, 2026 (51-47, party-line vote), and Clayton was sworn in August 3, 2026. Pulte used what were reported as his final hours in the acting role to announce a 5th round of ODNI layoffs, which he described on social media as 'Executing a 5th and Near Final Round of TERMINATIONS, an approximately 30% Staff Reduction from Weeks Ago' -- a move Senate Democrats had previously warned him against making in an unconfirmed, temporary capacity. Pulte retained his separate, Senate-confirmed post as FHFA director throughout the ODNI stint and continues to hold it. Sourcing reviewed did not identify any decision by Clayton to reverse, pause, or review the cuts made under Pulte. Update 2026-08-30: this entry's prior framing understated how contested the transition itself became. Although the Senate confirmed Clayton on July 28, 2026, the administration held his swearing-in until August 3, 2026 -- an unusual delay, since Senate-confirmed nominees are typically sworn in the same day -- while Pulte continued serving as acting DNI for that entire intervening week. Bipartisan senators publicly called for Clayton to be sworn in immediately, and a Cato Institute legal analysis went further, arguing Pulte's service during that week was affirmatively illegal: under the Federal Vacancies Reform Act, an acting official's authority ends the moment the Senate confirms a permanent successor, so everything Pulte did as acting DNI after July 28 -- including publicly announcing the 5th layoff round hours before Clayton's swearing-in -- occurred without valid legal authority, per this analysis. Separately, the delay had a concrete legislative cost: Senate Democrats, led by Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, had conditioned consideration of FISA Section 702 surveillance-authority renewal (lapsed since mid-June 2026) on Pulte's removal from ODNI, so the week-long delay in swearing in Clayton directly prolonged the Section 702 standoff into Congress's limited remaining pre-recess floor time. No source reviewed indicates any court has yet ruled on the Vacancies Act theory, and existing Section 702 certifications continue operating under a statutory grandfather clause through March 2027 even with the underlying authority lapsed, so neither the legal-exposure question nor the surveillance-authority question is resolved by this update.

title: Office of Government Ethics goes over a year without a permanent or acting director after Trump firing
institution: U.S. Office of Government Ethics
status: Ongoing in practice -- no confirmed director has served since the February 2025 firing, but Trump nominated a permanent successor on June 24, 2026 (Michael Chamberlain), correcting this entry's earlier 'no nominee put forward' framing; the nomination remains pending in the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee as of the most recent reporting reviewed, with no confirmation hearing yet scheduled
date_of_action: 2025-02 (firing) through 2026-05 (ongoing vacancy)
what_changed: In February 2025, Trump removed David Huitema as Director of the Office of Government Ethics -- the federal agency responsible for monitoring executive-branch financial conflicts of interest and ethics violations -- despite Huitema having been confirmed by the Senate in November 2024 to a five-year term. More than a year later, as of May 2026, no permanent or acting director has been named; a series of acting directors filled the role temporarily before the position went fully vacant, with no one currently serving in an acting capacity and no nominee put forward. Senate Democrats, led by Sens. Elissa Slotkin and Adam Schiff, sent a formal letter pressing the White House on the vacancy. Critics say the leadership gap has curtailed, delayed, or put on hold some of the office's work; the agency had not published its usual annual increase in ethics-violation fines for 2026 as of this reporting. Update 2026-08-17 (correction): this entry previously stated no nominee had been put forward; that is no longer accurate. On June 24, 2026, Trump nominated Michael Chamberlain -- director of Protect the Public's Trust, a conservative-leaning watchdog group he founded in 2021 that frequently targeted Biden-administration officials with ethics complaints, and a first-Trump-administration veteran -- to serve a five-year term as OGE Director. The nomination was referred to the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee and, as of the most recent reporting reviewed, had not yet received a confirmation hearing date. Watchdog groups (Center for Western Priorities) raised concerns that Chamberlain's own organization misrepresented its IRS nonprofit status in public-records requests and that his selection reflects a partisan rather than independent approach to the office. The underlying vacancy -- no one confirmed or serving in an acting capacity -- continues while the nomination is pending. Update 2026-09-01 (GSR recheck batch 47, moderate): NOTUS reported June 29, 2026 that Protect the Public's Trust, the watchdog group Chamberlain founded and led, filed 'hundreds of actions' against Biden-administration officials during that administration's term, but that 'few' of those actions led to any substantive findings -- a more concrete characterization of the group's track record than this entry's prior general description. No confirmation hearing date has been identified as of this recheck; the nomination remains listed as received and referred to the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee (June 23, 2026 referral date, per the committee's own nominations page).

title: OMB Proposes Political-Appointee Pre-Issuance Review of Federal Grants, Ending Post-WWII Norm of Apolitical Peer Review
institution: Office of Management and Budget (OMB)
status: Proposed rule, not yet finalized -- published in the Federal Register May 29, 2026; public comment period closed July 13, 2026 after drawing roughly 90,000 comments; implementation targeted for October 2026
date_of_action: 2026-05-29 (proposed rule published)
what_changed: On May 29, 2026, OMB -- led by Director Russell Vought -- published a more than 400-page proposed rule in the Federal Register that would overhaul the federal government's Uniform Grants Guidance, the regulatory framework governing how agencies award more than $1 trillion annually in federal grants to research institutions, state and local governments, nonprofits, and small businesses. The proposal requires senior political appointees to conduct 'pre-issuance reviews' of grant awards, including assessing whether funded projects 'demonstrably advance the President's policy priorities.' It also states that 'peer review remains advisory and does not replace agency discretion' -- a direct departure from the practice, standard since the post-World War II establishment of federal science funding, of grant approval being determined primarily by apolitical technical experts assessing scientific and programmatic merit. The proposal additionally grants agencies broad new authority to terminate already-awarded grants at any time and imposes new restrictions on international research collaborations. Public comment closed July 13, 2026, drawing more than 90,000 submissions, with implementation targeted for October 2026.

primary_proponent.name: Russell Vought
primary_proponent.role: OMB Director (concurrently Acting CFPB Director, documented separately in this tracker's cfpb-dismantlement-trump2 entry)
primary_proponent.note: The proposed rule was issued under Vought's OMB, which authored and published it in the Federal Register; it directly operationalizes the political-loyalty-screening approach to federal spending Vought has pursued across multiple agencies documented elsewhere in this tracker.

estimated_impact.summary: Critics -- including Senate Democrats and higher-education and scientific organizations -- argue the rule would functionally end merit-based federal grantmaking by giving political appointees, rather than subject-matter experts, final say over which research, local-government, and nonprofit projects receive federal funding, and would allow the administration to reward political allies and defund institutions or projects perceived as opposed to it. More than $1 trillion in annual federal grant funding would become subject to a presidential-policy-alignment test under the proposal.

title: OPM/MSPB Propose Scrapping the Douglas Factors, the 44-Year-Old Framework Protecting Federal Employees From Arbitrary Discipline
institution: Office of Personnel Management (OPM) and Merit Systems Protection Board (MSPB)
status: Proposed rule -- published in the Federal Register July 7, 2026, not yet finalized as of this entry
date_of_action: 2026-07-07 (proposed rule published)
what_changed: OPM and the Merit Systems Protection Board jointly proposed eliminating the 'Douglas factors' -- a 12-part framework established by a 1981 MSPB case that agencies have used for over four decades to ensure federal employee discipline is proportionate and considers factors like offense severity, past performance, and rehabilitation potential. The proposed rule, published in the Federal Register on July 7, 2026, would replace the Douglas factors with a vaguer 'totality of the circumstances' standard, which OPM and MSPB argue is more flexible than what they characterized as agencies' 'rigid, mechanistic' application of Douglas. The same proposal includes shortening performance improvement plans to 30 days, banning settlement agreements that remove misconduct documentation from personnel files, and eliminating union officials' paid 'official time' for handling adverse-action appeals.

primary_proponent.role: Federal civil service's central HR agency, acting jointly with the Merit Systems Protection Board
primary_proponent.note: OPM and MSPB jointly authored and published the proposed rule eliminating the Douglas factors, framing the current framework as overly rigid and an obstacle to agency discipline.

estimated_impact.summary: The proposal would give federal agency managers substantially more discretion to discipline or remove career employees by replacing an established, 12-factor proportionality test with a vaguer standard -- critics warn this would let agencies remove employees for a single instance of misconduct with no prior discipline, undermining protections designed to prevent politically motivated firings across the career civil service.

title: OPM's Musk-Directed 'Five Bullet Points' Email Throws Federal Agencies Into Conflicting-Orders Chaos
institution: Office of Personnel Management (OPM), government-wide
status: Resolved as an acute two-week episode (through at least early March 2025) -- the email/compliance conflict and its associated AI-review plan were short-lived and not confirmed to have resulted in any documented firings tied specifically to non-response, but the episode illustrates a broader governance pattern (mass workforce-management-by-ultimatum, conflicting agency guidance, and opaque AI-assisted personnel decisions) documented across other entries in this database
date_of_action: 2025-02-22 through at least 2025-03-02 (a second week of the same email request, reported by Forbes)
what_changed: The Office of Personnel Management sent an email to federal employees government-wide on February 22, 2025 demanding roughly five bullet points summarizing each employee's accomplishments for the prior week, cc'ing their manager. Elon Musk warned on X that failing to respond would be treated as a resignation, and separate reporting (NBC News, the Daily Beast) indicated DOGE was building a system to feed the responses into an AI/large-language-model that would help determine whether each employee's role was 'mission-critical' -- a characterization Musk publicly denied ('No LLM needed here'). The directive immediately produced conflicting guidance across agencies: Politico reported several agency heads, including FBI Director Kash Patel, told their employees to disregard the email entirely, while other agencies ordered compliance -- at Treasury, counselor John W. York (a former Heritage Foundation analyst) emailed employees a hard Monday-midnight deadline to respond, and Bloomberg Law/Gizmodo reported the IRS specifically was directed to comply by that same deadline. CNN reported the resulting confusion left workers scrambling amid mixed messages, with employees at agencies including DOJ, the State Department, and the FAA describing themselves as distracted from their primary duties navigating the conflicting instructions; Wired reported the chaos spread across agencies from NOAA to NIH. Forbes reported the ultimatum recurred into a second week (through at least March 2, 2025), with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth directing Pentagon employees to respond to that round. HHS took a third distinct posture from Treasury/IRS's compliance order and FBI's outright dismissal: on February 24, HHS told employees responding was voluntary with no employment consequence for declining, but separately warned that any response 'may be read by malign foreign actors' and instructed staff who did respond to 'assume that what you write will be read by malign foreign actors and tailor your response accordingly,' keeping any submission at a high level of generality to protect sensitive data, PII, and applicable privileges.

primary_proponent.name: Elon Musk, former DOGE leader / Special Government Employee
primary_proponent.role: Issued the compliance ultimatum via OPM and publicly on social media
primary_proponent.note: Musk's public warning that non-response would be treated as resignation was the specific trigger for the cross-government confusion documented here; several individual agency heads (e.g. FBI Director Patel) are named as having countermanded the directive for their own agencies, while others (Treasury's John W. York, Defense Secretary Hegseth in a second week) ordered compliance.

estimated_impact.summary: Produced government-wide operational confusion and distraction across multiple agencies with unrelated, sensitive core missions (law enforcement, diplomacy, aviation safety, health research, weather forecasting) during the window the conflict was unresolved, and raised unresolved questions about whether federal personnel decisions were being partly delegated to an undisclosed AI system
estimated_impact.caveat: No reporting reviewed for this entry quantified how many federal employees ultimately complied, how many treated non-compliance as a resignation trigger, or whether any employee was actually separated from federal service specifically because of non-response to this email. Whether an LLM/AI system was actually used to evaluate responses is itself contested -- Musk denied it publicly while NBC News and the Daily Beast reported DOGE was building such a system.

confidence_note: HIGH confidence on the email, Musk's ultimatum, and the cross-agency confusion -- corroborated across Wired, Politico, CNN, NPR, Bloomberg Law, Gizmodo, 404 Media, and (for the HHS security warning specifically) Newsweek and NBC Washington. MODERATE confidence on the specific claim that an AI/LLM system was used to evaluate responses, since Musk publicly denied it even as NBC News and the Daily Beast reported otherwise -- presented here as a contested claim, not a settled fact.
