Ryan's exit and the settlement pattern coincide with a broader enforcement-strategy shift under the current SEC leadership toward traditional fraud/market-manipulation cases and away from several compliance-focused enforcement areas, including certain crypto-related actions, that were more common under the prior administration's SEC leadership.

title: White House-directed content review and exhibit alterations at the Smithsonian
institution: Smithsonian Institution (Washington, DC museums, via White House Domestic Policy Council/OMB)
status: Ongoing and escalated -- President Trump signed a second executive order, 'Restoring Trust in the Smithsonian Institution' (E.O. 14416), on July 24, 2026, directing agencies to use funding/contract leverage to compel compliance and ordering NPS-installed warning signage outside the National Museum of American History; a bipartisan Senate letter (Murkowski/Merkley, Aug. 6, 2026) is now seeking implementation details on the signage directive; second-phase museums beyond the original 8 still not announced as of this update
date_of_action: 2025-03-27 (executive order) through 2026-07 (findings report)
what_changed: President Trump's March 27, 2025 executive order 'Restoring Truth and Sanity to American History' directed Vice President JD Vance, who sits on the Smithsonian's Board of Regents, to work to 'remove improper ideology' from Smithsonian museums, and instructed OMB and the Vice President to condition future appropriations on exhibits not 'degrading shared American values' or 'dividing Americans based on race.' In August 2025, White House aide Lindsey Halligan, Domestic Policy Council Director Vince Haley, and OMB Director Russell Vought sent a letter to Smithsonian Secretary Lonnie Bunch launching a formal review of eight flagship DC museums (including the National Museum of American History, the National Museum of African American History and Culture, and the National Portrait Gallery), demanding exhibition texts, future exhibition plans, internal curatorial guidelines, staff manuals, and organizational charts, with a 120-day deadline for museums to begin 'content corrections' replacing 'divisive or ideologically driven language.' The National Museum of American History removed references to Trump's two first-term impeachments from a display in July 2025 as part of an internal content review the Smithsonian undertook under White House pressure; the references were restored about a week later after public criticism. The Smithsonian's Office of Diversity was closed. National Portrait Gallery director Kim Sajet resigned in mid-2025 after Trump publicly said he was firing her, calling her 'a highly partisan person, and a strong supporter of DEI' (the Smithsonian said only Secretary Bunch could make that personnel decision). Artist Amy Sherald canceled a planned exhibition of her work at the National Portrait Gallery in late July 2025 following a dispute over a painting depicting a transgender Statue-of-Liberty figure. In July 2026, the White House Domestic Policy Council published a report titled 'Saving America's Story' accusing the National Museum of American History of 'extreme political activism' and faulting it for not having created a dedicated exhibit on the Founding Fathers, the Declaration of Independence, or the Revolutionary War even in the 250th-anniversary year. The White House's July 2026 report -- formally titled 'Saving America's Story: How Ideological Capture at the Smithsonian Institution's National Museum of American History Erases Our Heritage,' issued July 4, 2026 by the Domestic Policy Council -- specifically accused the museum of 'anti-white,' 'illegal alien,' and transgender-related 'activism' in addition to underemphasizing the Founding era. Secretary Bunch responded publicly on July 8-9, 2026, writing that the report 'is not a fair characterization of the work and totality of the National Museum of American History' and that the institution 'remain[s] focused on what grounds us: a steadfast commitment to scholarship, nonpartisanship, independence, accuracy and integrity' -- a direct, specific, on-record rebuttal to this particular report, distinct from his earlier general September 2025 independence statement already cited in this entry. Re-verified 2026-07-26: no material change -- no announcement identified yet of which museums comprise the review's second phase. Update 2026-08-17: on July 24, 2026 -- two days before this entry's prior 'no material change' recheck, which missed this development -- President Trump signed Executive Order 14416, 'Restoring Trust in the Smithsonian Institution,' formalizing the July 2026 'Saving America's Story' findings report into a directive. The order instructs the Secretary of the Interior, the OMB Director, the GSA Administrator, and the Domestic Policy Council to 'identify and utilize any and all available authorities' to push compliance, explicitly including funding and contract conditions -- an escalation from review and public criticism to stated administrative/financial leverage. It also directs the National Park Service to install temporary signage along the public sidewalks/walkways leading to the National Museum of American History warning visitors that the museum reflects 'ideological capture' per the findings report and directing them to alternative sources for 'accurate' history, and mandates temporary outdoor counter-exhibits focused on the 56 signers of the Declaration of Independence timed to the 250th-anniversary Semiquincentennial. No announcement of which museums comprise the review's second phase was identified as of this update. Update 2026-08-30: on August 6, 2026, Sens. Lisa Murkowski (R-AK) and Jeff Merkley (D-OR) sent a bipartisan letter to Interior Secretary Doug Burgum and NPS Director Jessica Bowron questioning the E.O. 14416 signage directive's legal basis, seeking the total number, size, placement, content, and manufacturing/installation cost of the planned signs, the funding source within Interior, the number of DOI/NPS staff assigned, and where visitors would be directed for 'accurate' information and who compiles it; no response from Interior/NPS was identified as of this update. Still no announcement of which museums comprise the review's second phase.

title: 770,000+ Children Lost SNAP Benefits in the Year After Trump's Domestic Policy Law, Despite Promises Children Would Be Protected
institution: USDA / Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP)
status: Ongoing and worse than first measured -- ProPublica's original 12-state analysis (776,134 children) was superseded in scope by a 19-state CBPP analysis (1.06M+ children, 44% of all losses) reported July 23, 2026
date_of_action: 2025-07-04 (One Big Beautiful Bill Act signed) through 2026-06 (ProPublica analysis published)
what_changed: A ProPublica analysis published June 17, 2026 found at least 776,134 children stopped receiving SNAP benefits in the 12 states that report participation by age, in the year following Trump's signing of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act on July 4, 2025 -- legislation that cut roughly $186 billion from SNAP over a decade, the largest cut in the program's history, imposed new work requirements on older adults and parents of teenagers, and shifted billions in administrative and benefit costs onto states. Children made up nearly half of everyone cut from the program across the states studied. The impact was highly uneven: Arizona alone lost 205,223 children from its SNAP rolls since July 2025, a 55% decline (driven in part by the state's own error-rate-penalty response, tracked separately in this database), while Louisiana recorded the second-steepest child decline at 22%. Republicans had promised during the law's passage that children and other vulnerable groups would be shielded from its effects. A subsequent Center on Budget and Policy Priorities analysis, reported by Newsweek on July 23, 2026, extended the picture across 19 states (versus the original ProPublica analysis's 12) and found more than 1.06 million children had lost SNAP benefits since the law's enactment, with children accounting for 44% of all enrollment losses in those states -- a materially larger scope than the 776,134/12-state figure this entry was originally built around, though the two analyses use overlapping but not identical state samples. Update 2026-08-30: NPR/member-station reporting published August 3, 2026 places the child-specific figures already in this entry within the total program's collapse: national SNAP participation fell from 42 million to 37 million recipients (11%, roughly 4 million people) between July 2025 and April 2026, with over 1 million children losing benefits across the same 19 states CBPP examined. Arizona -- already this entry's steepest-decline example -- lost more than 400,000 total participants and saw enrollment fall to about half its year-earlier size, with more people visiting food banks monthly than remained enrolled in SNAP for the first time on record; Texas separately lost roughly 500,000 participants, a state not previously named in this entry's state-level breakdown.

estimated_impact.summary: Hundreds of thousands of children lost federal food assistance as a direct downstream consequence of SNAP funding cuts and administrative changes that Republicans specifically promised would not affect children, with impact concentrated heavily in a handful of states.

title: SNAP Benefits Withheld During 2025 Government Shutdown
institution: U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA), Food and Nutrition Service
status: Resolved (shutdown ended, full funding restored through Sept. 2026) but litigation exposed underlying legal violations
date_of_action: 2025-10-31 through 2025-11-13 (peak crisis); shutdown began Oct. 2025, was the longest in U.S. history
what_changed: During the government shutdown, the Trump administration initially announced SNAP benefits (food stamps for ~42 million Americans, about 1 in 8 people in the U.S.) would not be paid in November 2025 at all, breaking from the precedent of prior administrations tapping a contingency fund to keep benefits flowing during shutdowns. After lawsuits, a federal judge in Rhode Island (John McConnell) first ordered partial funding (~65% of normal benefits) from the contingency fund, then found the administration's partial-payment approach itself 'arbitrary and capricious' and ordered full funding by a set deadline. Some Democratic-led states issued full benefits before the Supreme Court intervened with a temporary stay blocking the order, creating a chaotic situation where some recipients got full benefits and others got partial or none, based on which state they lived in and how quickly that state's officials acted. USDA then ordered states to 'immediately undo' full benefit issuances already made. The dispute was ultimately mooted when Congress passed a bill ending the shutdown with SNAP funded through September 2026. Re-verified 2026-07-26: one additional litigation detail worth noting -- the administration itself moved to drop its own First Circuit appeal of the Rhode Island judge's order, rather than the appeal being denied on the merits, consistent with this entry's existing framing that the dispute was ultimately mooted by the funding CR rather than resolved by any appellate ruling. Re-verified 2026-08-17: no material change to this entry's own claims. (A separate, related case -- Rhode Island State Council of Churches v. Rollins, over work-requirement waiver terminations rather than the contingency-fund payment dispute this entry documents -- was dismissed by joint stipulation in early 2026 after the waivers in question expired on their own terms; noted here only to distinguish it from, not as new information about, this entry's tracked dispute.)

primary_proponent.name: Trump administration / USDA leadership
primary_proponent.role: Executive branch decision not to use the SNAP contingency fund
primary_proponent.note: Attorney General Pam Bondi publicly defended the administration's position, calling Judge McConnell's order 'judicial activism at its worst' and arguing a 'single district court in Rhode Island should not be able to seize center stage.' USDA official Patrick Penn signed the memo directing states to reverse full benefit payments already issued. Judge McConnell's own order found the administration's justification for partial-only payment was 'arbitrary and capricious' and suggested the delay may have been for 'political reasons.'

estimated_impact.summary: Nearly 42 million Americans -- disproportionately children, seniors, and people with disabilities -- had food assistance disrupted or fully withheld for a period during the shutdown, forcing food banks nationwide into 'unprecedented demand' per multiple contemporaneous reports, and leaving benefit amounts dependent on which state a recipient lived in rather than a uniform national standard.

The 'arbitrary and capricious' finding is Judge McConnell's, a single district court, not an appellate or Supreme Court determination.

confidence_note: Strong, multi-outlet sourcing (NPR, CNN, NBC, Time, PBS, Axios, The Hill, UPI) all confirming the same core timeline and figures. The judicial 'arbitrary and capricious' finding and named-official statements (Bondi, Penn, multiple governors) make this well-documented and attributable, though the underlying legal question was never fully resolved on the merits -- frame as 'the administration's conduct during this episode was found arbitrary and capricious by one federal judge,' not as a final, appellate-level legal determination. Re-verified 2026-07-20: no material change -- confirmed the litigation timeline already in this entry (Judge Talwani's Massachusetts ruling, Judge McConnell's Rhode Island ruling and 'arbitrary and capricious' finding, the 1st Circuit appeal, the Supreme Court's administrative stay) matches independent sourcing (NBC, CNN, FindLaw). The dispute remains formally mooted by the funding CR through September 2026, not resolved on the merits by any appellate ruling. Re-verified 2026-07-26: no material change to report; the First Circuit appeal-withdrawal detail is corroborated by Courthouse News Service. Re-verified 2026-08-17: no material change to report. Re-verified 2026-08-30 (GSR recheck batch 30): no material change to this entry's own claims. SNAP's funding runs on the same September 30, 2026 government-funding deadline as the rest of the federal budget; no new litigation or benefit-disruption development was identified, but this is a dated hook worth rechecking again once that deadline passes. Re-verified 2026-08-31 (GSR recheck batch 45, light touch): no new litigation or benefit-disruption development identified. The September 30, 2026 funding-cliff hook flagged in the prior recheck is now one month out; the House returned from recess August 31, 2026 specifically to begin reconciling its own Dec.-4 continuing resolution against the Senate's Dec.-11 CR (passed 90-6 Aug. 8, 2026) ahead of that deadline -- the same reconciliation fight already documented in this tracker's House WIC benefit-cut entry -- but no SNAP-specific funding action or court filing beyond that general appropriations context was identified as of this recheck.

title: NIH, CDC, and USAID Cut HIV and TB Research Funding to South Africa, the Largest Non-U.S. Recipient of NIH Grants
institution: National Institutes of Health, CDC, and U.S. Agency for International Development
status: Partially reversed going forward -- NIH lifted its broader 'country of concern' funding ban on South Africa on August 17, 2026, permitting new grant applications to proceed; this does not retroactively restore the ~280 grants terminated in March 2025, new awards are not expected before 2027, and a narrower Fogarty International Center training-grant exclusion remains in place
date_of_action: 2025-02-07 (executive order freezing South Africa aid) through 2025-03-21 and following weekend (mass NIH grant cancellations)
what_changed: On 2025-01-20, Trump signed an executive order pausing nearly all U.S. foreign aid pending review. On 2025-02-07, the administration issued a separate, South-Africa-specific executive order freezing aid to the country, citing what it characterized as 'egregious actions' by the South African government (a land-expropriation law and South Africa's ICJ case against Israel were the cited triggers). Beginning 2025-03-21, NIH started terminating research grants it deemed not aligned with agency priorities under the new administration, including all HIV-prevention research; more than 300 grants funding South African universities' HIV and TB research were cancelled with immediate effect over a single weekend. South Africa was, at the time, the largest recipient of NIH funding outside the United States, receiving an estimated $400 million annually in direct and indirect NIH grants -- funding researchers say supported up to 70% of the country's HIV and TB research. The cuts came alongside separate, parallel reductions to USAID and PEPFAR (the President's Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief) funding flowing to South Africa, and a suspension of CDC grant support to South African health institutions. Public health researchers and rights organizations (including Physicians for Human Rights, which later published a detailed 2026 report on the cuts' downstream effects) warned the combined cuts threatened to reverse two decades of progress against South Africa's HIV epidemic, one of the world's largest, and undermined ongoing tuberculosis research and treatment programs that depend on the same funding streams. Update 2026-08-17: this entry's original write-up (2026-08-12) framed the situation as having no reversal at all, but omitted a narrower, already-public policy change from over a year earlier. On June 30, 2025, NIH announced a workaround for the foreign-subaward funding mechanism it had ended May 1: existing subawards supporting clinical research in South Africa could continue, and about 100 ongoing prime awards to South African researchers 'may proceed,' via conversion into direct supplements to foreign collaborators. Critically, this exception applied only to human-subjects research applications submitted before May 1, 2025, not to lab or animal-study work, and per NIH's own contemporaneous reporting it was unclear even at the time whether the fix would restore awards that had been fully terminated, as opposed to merely frozen mid-process -- an NIH grants official called it 'still a huge administrative lift and unnecessary.' Separately, per South Africa's National Treasury 2026 Budget Review, the South African government committed to reprioritizing R410 million (over the medium term) from the national Department of Health to the South African Medical Research Council specifically to offset the U.S. funding withdrawal -- a domestic mitigation measure, not a reversal of the U.S. cuts themselves. Update 2026-08-30 (GSR recheck batch 43, real correction, major): a much broader reversal than the narrow June 2025 workaround, and one dated the same day as this entry's own 2026-08-17 last-verified date -- NIH Director Jay Bhattacharya signed an internal memo on August 17, 2026 formally lifting the 'country of concern' designation that had blocked essentially all new NIH funding to South Africa since the February 2025 executive order, on the stated legal basis that NIH grants are 'distinct from the objectives traditionally associated' with foreign aid or assistance and so fall outside that order's scope -- the same rationale NIH had used narrowly for the June 2025 workaround, now applied broadly. This is forward-looking, not retroactive: it permits new grant applications and 'meritorious research projects' to proceed, but does not itself restore the ~280 grants terminated in March 2025, and researchers quoted in coverage said the first new grants likely would not be awarded until 2027. The Fogarty International Center exclusion is a new, separate restriction layered on top of the broader lift: as of December 5, 2026, Fogarty will no longer process training/career-development grant applications from South Africa specifically because the country is classified upper-middle-income and a G20 member -- Salim Abdool Karim (director, Centre for the AIDS Programme of Research in South Africa) called this exclusion 'unfortunate' and a 'self-inflicted wound.' Named South African researchers reacted with relief to the broader lift: Glenda Gray (University of the Witwatersrand, lost HIV/TB grants) said 'It's a huge deal. I am almost crying'; Linda-Gail Bekker (Desmond Tutu Health Foundation) called it 'a lifeline to rebuild.' Coverage citing South African sourcing puts the combined NIH-ban-plus-PEPFAR-cuts loss to South Africa at almost $450 million (R7.4 billion), a broader figure than this entry's existing $400M/year NIH-only estimate since it also incorporates PEPFAR.

Kennedy Jr.'s direction, consistent with this tracker's other NIH grant-termination entries.

estimated_impact.summary: South Africa lost access to funding researchers estimate supported up to 70% of the country's HIV and TB research, at a moment researchers and rights groups warned could reverse roughly two decades of progress against one of the world's largest HIV epidemics.

estimated_impact.caveat: The $400M and 70% figures come from South African university/researcher sourcing reported by AllAfrica rather than an independent U.S. government accounting; this tracker treats them as researcher/institutional estimates, not officially confirmed U.S. figures, consistent with how comparable foreign-aid-cut entries in this tracker caveat non-U.S.-government dollar estimates. The June 2025 NIH workaround did not restore the ~280 terminated grants -- it only let a subset of frozen, not-yet-terminated human-subjects awards continue via a new funding mechanism, and NIH itself was unsure at the time whether it would ever cover terminated awards. Read the R410 million South African government figure as a domestic backfill measure, not evidence the U.S. cuts were reversed. The August 17, 2026 ban lift is likewise forward-looking only -- reporting explicitly frames it as enabling new grants, not restoring the ~280 already-terminated awards, and researchers quoted expect no new awards before 2027; treat 'partially reversed' in this entry's status field as reversal of the funding *ban going forward*, not reversal of the terminations themselves.

confidence_note: Multi-source corroboration across South African and international outlets (AllAfrica, ScienceOpen-hosted academic analysis, Physicians for Human Rights, and a peer-reviewed PubMed article on TB-specific impacts) all describe the same underlying timeline and mechanism. The core facts -- the February 2025 South Africa-specific executive order and the March 2025 NIH grant terminations -- are well corroborated; the specific dollar and percentage estimates rest more heavily on South African institutional sourcing than independent U.S. verification. Update 2026-08-17 (GSR recheck batch 20, real correction): the June 30, 2025 NIH policy change is corroborated by Science/AAAS (via EATG's republication) and MedicalBrief; the R410 million South African Treasury commitment is corroborated by the National Treasury's own 2026 Budget Review as reported by SAnews/AllAfrica. Both predate this entry's 2026-08-12 write date by months to over a year and were omitted from the original 'no reversal identified' status framing -- the same aged-backlog root cause the GSR recheck sweep has flagged in prior batches. The correction adds nuance, not a reversal claim: the underlying terminations remain in effect for the vast majority of the ~280 affected grants. Re-verified 2026-08-30 (GSR recheck batch 43, real correction, major): the August 17, 2026 ban lift -- dated the same day as this entry's own prior last-verified date, so missed by that recheck -- is corroborated across five independent outlets (EWN, SA People, Innovation Village, Sunday Times South Africa, and Science/AAAS), including named on-the-record reactions from South African researchers (Gray, Bekker, Abdool Karim) rather than institutional press-release framing alone. Confidence on the lift itself is HIGH; confidence that it will translate into actually-disbursed new funding is necessarily LOWER, since reporting itself notes no new grants are expected before 2027 and the memo's 'meritorious research projects' language leaves NIH discretion over which specific projects proceed.

title: Social Security Administration Lost 8,000+ Staff — Lowest Headcount Since 1967 — Then Stopped Publishing Its Own Service Metrics
institution: Social Security Administration (SSA)
status: Ongoing (staffing losses not reversed; some but not all withheld metrics later restored)
date_of_action: 2025-02-24 (earliest documented office closures under Leland Dudek) through 2026-04 (ongoing, per Center on Budget and Policy Priorities' most recent tracking); see also the March 2025 O'Malley warning and April 2025 reclassification push noted below
what_changed: Since January 2025, the Trump administration drove out more than 8,000 SSA employees -- the agency's largest one-year staffing reduction on record, leaving SSA with fewer employees than at any point since 1967, even as it now serves roughly 52 million more beneficiaries than it did then (nearly 75 million total). More than 40 states and D.C. saw staffing cuts greater than 10% between January 2025 and April 2026. This pattern was already visible within DOGE's first weeks at SSA: ProPublica reported that by February 24, 2025, DOGE operatives working inside the agency under appointee Leland Dudek had already closed at least 10 local field offices and eliminated 41 positions, drawing early alarm from beneficiaries and staff. Later that same month, the Associated Press reported that DOGE's internal, government-wide list of nearly 800 federal real estate leases targeted for cancellation named 47 SSA field offices, 26 of them with lease-termination dates in 2025 -- but SSA publicly disputed the closure framing in a March 27, 2025 agency blog post, stating that since January 1, 2025 it had not permanently closed or announced the permanent closure of any local field office, a direct conflict between DOGE's internal planning documents and the agency's own public position that later reporting in this entry does not resolve. The website-crash pattern documented below had already begun by then: the Washington Post reported on March 25, 2025 that SSA's website had crashed roughly 10 times over the preceding three weeks due to overloaded servers, that dozens of senior SSA officials -- including its entire cybersecurity leadership -- had resigned or retired amid pressure from Musk's team, and that remaining office managers were personally answering phones because so many receptionist-level staff had been pushed out. Separately, Wired reported in late March 2025 that DOGE -- led by Musk associate Steve Davis, with unvetted operatives embedded in the agency -- was pushing to rewrite SSA's roughly 60-million-line COBOL codebase (which underpins benefit processing for more than 70 million Americans) into Java and other modern languages within a few months, using generative AI to compress a migration SSA had itself previously estimated would take five to ten years; outside engineers quoted in the report warned the accelerated timeline risked exactly the kind of system errors and outages documented below, foreshadowing in specific technical terms the more general IT-overhaul warning Sens. Warren and Wyden issued in June 2025. The staffing cuts produced concrete technical and administrative failures in the following months: the Washington Post reported the SSA website repeatedly crashed starting around April 8, 2025, disrupting access for millions, with the outages tied directly to Musk-led cuts that slashed IT staff and rushed out undertested software; the next day, CBS News reported SSA mistakenly told some Supplemental Security Income recipients -- including disabled individuals and low-income seniors -- that their benefits had been terminated, with their benefit histories temporarily disappearing from their accounts before the error was corrected roughly a day later. This error pattern had already become individually documented in local and national press starting the same week: on March 21, 2025, the Seattle Times and CNN reported that 82-year-old Ned Johnson of Seattle had been erroneously added to SSA's Death Master File, clawing back his December and January benefits (a combined $5,201) and canceling his Medicare coverage and credit standing until he resolved it in person weeks later; the same week, 9News reported that 90-year-old Denver veteran Tom Kind had likewise been wrongly marked deceased, losing benefits, healthcare coverage, and bank access for more than 10 days. Newsweek later reported the specific mechanism behind cases like Johnson's: DOGE staffers conducting a self-described 'major cleanup' of SSA's death records -- adding death dates to more than 7 million Social Security numbers that previously lacked one, part of Musk's push to counter his own since-debunked claim that millions of implausibly old people remained on SSA's rolls -- mistakenly moved living people's records onto the Death Master File in the process; SSA's own response to the reporting characterized the affected records only as lacking 'a recorded date of death' rather than acknowledging erroneous death designations outright. A third individual case followed the next month: on April 12, 2025, KSAT reported SSA had incorrectly declared 40-year-old San Antonio epilepsy patient Joseph Arce deceased, halting his disability payments and terminating his Medicaid and Medicare coverage, cutting off access to his seizure medication. By May 6, 2025, CBS News reported this had become a further, more consequential error pattern agency-wide: thousands of Americans, disproportionately immigrants and other vulnerable individuals, were being wrongly declared dead or purged from SSA's systems entirely, cutting off Social Security benefits, disability payments, and in some cases banking access tied to a valid Social Security number. SSA has separately noted a baseline error rate of roughly 10,000 wrongly-recorded deaths per year (about 0.3% of the ~3 million deaths it processes) even absent any policy change, and no source found for this entry quantifies whether the 2025 rate rose above that historical baseline -- but Newsweek's and the Center for American Progress's reporting ties the DOGE cleanup effort directly to specific documented cases including Johnson's, distinguishing this from an ordinary-course error. On June 16, 2025, Wired reported Senators Elizabeth Warren and Ron Wyden formally warned that DOGE's rushed, AI-driven overhaul of SSA's IT systems was jeopardizing the agency's core function, citing the website outages and access failures already documented above as evidence of elevated risk of further benefit disruptions, data loss, or security compromise going forward. In April 2025, SSA briefly eliminated most phone-based benefit applications entirely (reversed after public backlash), while permanently requiring in-person visits or multi-factor online authentication for direct-deposit changes -- a change CBPP notes the agency's own fraud data does not support, since direct-deposit fraud is rare and rarely phone-initiated. As wait times climbed (86 minutes average by April 2025, a 25% increase over the prior year), SSA responded largely by reassigning field-office staff to phone duty rather than hiring -- pulling employees away from processing claims and creating new backlogs elsewhere. In June 2025, amid worsening press coverage, SSA stopped publicly releasing several of its own regular service-performance metrics, including call wait times and appointment-scheduling delays; some measures were later restored, but key ones (hold-time data, appointment-wait data, backlog counts) remain unreported as of CBPP's most recent tracking. During the federal government shutdown that began October 2025, NPR reported SSA field-office staff said they were unable to issue benefit verification letters -- documents beneficiaries need to access housing assistance, fuel assistance, and other aid -- even as regular benefit payments continued; staff told NPR the letters accounted for an estimated 60-70% of field-office call volume during the shutdown and said they were frustrated the service wasn't classified as essential, while an SSA spokesperson said the agency was operating under its shutdown contingency plan. By early 2026, disability-appeal backlogs had grown by 73,000+ cases in just over a year, and fewer than 850 of SSA's roughly 50,000 remaining employees had less than two years of federal service -- the agency hired fewer than 100 new employees in all of 2025, the lowest annual hiring total on record. In June 2026, Commissioner Bisignano told the House Ways and Means Committee and stated in an SSA press release (June 29, 2026) that the agency achieved its 'best all-around performance ever': the National 800 Number's average speed of answer reportedly fell from 34 minutes (2024) to 8 minutes, a 75% reduction; field-office wait times reportedly fell 30%; the initial disability-claims backlog reportedly fell from a high of ~1.3 million (2024) to 853,000, and disability hearing wait times reportedly fell to 266 days, a historic low; the agency also reported 385 million online transactions in FY2026 to date, up 37% from 2024. SSA's workforce continued to shrink over this same period -- roughly 7,000 additional employees left via separation incentives, leaving a workforce of about 50,000, still its lowest headcount in decades. As part of that continued shrinkage, in April 2025 the Washington Post reported the administration was preparing to lay off thousands more SSA workers even after the earlier ~7,000-job elimination, with offices in rural areas losing over half their staff and IT systems already crashing under the strain. Two named-official developments from this same window are worth noting on their own. First, on March 3, 2025, former SSA Commissioner Martin O'Malley (Biden-era) publicly warned SSA could suffer a full 'collapse of the entire system' and an interruption of benefit payments within 'the next 30 to 90 days' if the DOGE-driven cuts continued -- a high-profile, widely covered warning that did not literally materialize on that timeline (Social Security continued issuing payments past the 90-day mark), though the underlying staffing and service-quality trend O'Malley was warning about is independently documented throughout this entry. Second, in April 2025 Acting SSA Commissioner Leland Dudek moved to reclassify entire SSA offices -- including mission support, hearings, and communications staff -- under the newly renamed 'Schedule Policy/Career' (formerly Schedule F) excepted-service category, which strips normal civil-service removal protections; roughly 8,000 GS-15-level federal employees government-wide had already been shifted into equivalent categories by that point. This drew bipartisan pushback, and following pressure from Sen. Ron Wyden and colleagues, the administration confirmed by June 27, 2025 that no SSA frontline workers had actually been recategorized under Schedule Policy/Career -- meaning the April reclassification push, as reported, did not fully proceed as originally described, at least for frontline staff, as of that confirmation. Separately, in May 2025, incoming Commissioner Frank Bisignano told reporters AI would 'soon' handle a significant share of SSA's roughly 400,000 daily phone calls -- an early on-the-record statement of the automation strategy that appears consistent with, and may partly explain the mechanism behind, the dramatically faster call-answer times SSA and its Inspector General later reported for FY2025-2026 (see below), even as field-office staffing and hiring remained sharply reduced. Update 2026-07-26: the independent corroboration this entry's prior update said was missing has since emerged. After Sen. Elizabeth Warren raised doubts about SSA's reported phone-service improvements, Commissioner Bisignano agreed to an independent review, and SSA's own Office of Inspector General published an audit in June 2026 confirming the agency's released 800-number performance data was accurate and that service genuinely improved during FY2025: SSA served 68 million callers (a 65% increase over the prior year), with average wait times falling from a January peak of about 30 minutes to roughly 7 minutes by September. This meaningfully corroborates part of Bisignano's disputed 2026 turnaround claim -- specifically the phone-service metrics -- though it does not address or resolve this entry's separate, independently-sourced findings on workforce reduction (8,000+ lost), the disability-appeal backlog, or the 2025 decision to stop publishing certain other service metrics, which remain accurate and unaffected by this audit. Update 2026-08-18: On August 14, 2026 (SSA's 91st-anniversary press release), the agency claimed further improvement beyond the June 2026 figures already documented above -- an average phone wait time of 0.6 minutes in July 2026 (down from the 8-minute figure SSA reported in June and independently corroborated by the OIG audit already cited), a 30% reduction in field-office wait times while serving 25 million visitors, an initial disability-claims backlog of 884,000 (down from the ~1.3 million 2024 high, though nominally higher than the 853,000 SSA itself reported as of the June 29, 2026 release already cited above), and 505 million online transactions in FY2026 to date. These later-2026 figures are presented in the same self-reported, not-independently-audited category as the entry's existing caveat already treats the June 2026 claims -- a continuation of the disputed pattern, not a new resolution of it. Separately, AFGE Council 220 (the union representing SSA employees) continued pressing Congress in August 2026 for $3 billion in additional SSA funding above enacted FY2026 levels and 20,000 new hires, with Council 220 President Jessica LaPointe stating the agency is 'simply bleeding staff and have problems with recruitment and retention as a result' -- consistent with, not a change to, this entry's existing workforce-loss findings.

title: SSA Instructed Newly Reassigned, Minimally-Trained Phone Agents to Tell Suicidal Callers That 'Suicide Is Only One Option'
institution: Social Security Administration
status: In effect as of February 2026 reporting -- no reversal or policy correction confirmed in sourcing reviewed
date_of_action: 2026-02 (reporting period)
what_changed: As part of SSA's broader staffing collapse (see ssa-staffing-service-collapse-trump2.json), the agency reassigned employees from other roles to newly-created phone duty with as little as three hours of training, according to GovExec's reporting. Internal guidance reviewed by GovExec instructed these newly-reassigned, minimally-trained agents that when a caller expressed suicidal thoughts, they should tell the caller that 'suicide is only one option' rather than following established crisis-response protocols used by trained crisis counselors. Current and former SSA employees raised concerns that agents with only a few hours of training were being placed in a position to respond -- with agency-scripted language -- to callers in acute mental health crisis, a role normally requiring specialized training SSA phone agents do not have.

title: More than 100 U.S. ambassador posts left vacant, more than double the rate of Trump's first term
institution: U.S. Department of State / Foreign Service
status: Ongoing -- 98 of 196 ambassador posts vacant as of the American Foreign Service Association's own tracker, last updated August 21, 2026, an improvement from 107 of 195 in late June following the early-August Senate confirmation batch, but still roughly half of all posts
date_of_action: 2026-05 through 2026-07 (reporting period)
what_changed: More than 100 of the United States' 195 ambassador posts remained vacant nearly 18 months into Trump's second term -- 109 of 195 as of mid-May 2026 and 107 of 195 as of late June 2026 -- more than double the vacancy rate at the equivalent point in Trump's first term, when 45 posts were vacant. Vacancies include strategically significant posts: Ukraine, Russia, Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Qatar, Germany, Australia, and South Korea, among others. Of 101 ambassador nominations made during the second term, only 9 have gone to career Foreign Service diplomats, a sharp departure from traditional practice of pairing political and career appointees. In place of confirmed ambassadors, the administration has relied on political allies, megadonors, and informal special envoys to handle diplomacy in many of these countries. Update 2026-08-17: the Senate confirmed a batch of Trump's nominees in early August 2026, including 11 ambassadors and 5 more to ambassador-rank positions -- among them David Brat (Australia) and Michael Kavoukjian (Norway) -- narrowing the vacancy count somewhat. Despite that batch, the underlying pattern this entry documents persists: a Semafor report published August 6, 2026 found Middle East ambassadorships continuing to sit vacant, with the administration relying on special envoys rather than confirmed ambassadors, and broader reporting from earlier in the year found the vacancy pattern extended heavily into Africa (37 of 51 posts without ambassadors as of May 2026) following Secretary Rubio's December 2025 recall of roughly 30 career ambassadors. Update 2026-09-01 (GSR recheck batch 47): the August 7, 2026 confirmation batch (approved 51-47 along party lines, as part of a broader 74-nomination package) named additional confirmed ambassadors beyond the two this entry previously listed -- John Breslow (Cyprus), Joseph Burkhalter (Moldova), Daniel Perez (Brazil), Laurence Socha (The Gambia), John Hurley (OECD, ambassador rank), and Todd Steggerda (UN Geneva, ambassador rank), alongside Brat and Kavoukjian. The American Foreign Service Association's own tracker (afsa.org/list-ambassadorial-appointments, last updated August 21, 2026) puts the current count at 98 of 196 posts vacant -- note the total shifted from the 195 used in this entry's earlier figures to 196 in AFSA's own count, a denominator change not otherwise explained in sourcing reviewed. This is an improvement from the 107-of-195 figure as of late June, consistent with the confirmation batch, and materially better than a since-discarded WebSearch-synthesis claim of 115 vacant 'as of August 26, 2026' that could not be corroborated against AFSA's own primary tracker and is not used here. Despite the improvement, the entry's core throughline -- roughly half of all posts vacant, with a historically low career-diplomat nomination rate -- remains accurate.

title: State Department overhauls diplomat performance reviews into a forced-competition, zero-sum ratings system
institution: U.S. Department of State / Foreign Service
status: Ongoing, and diplomats' own avenue for challenging it has been weakened -- new Employee Evaluation Report (EER) system implemented for the 2026 review cycle; AFSA's January 2026 unfair-labor-practice complaint has no confirmed resolution, and an August 2026 DOJ opinion strips the Foreign Service Grievance Board of final decision-making authority, giving the Secretary of State override power over any grievance the EER system generates
date_of_action: 2026-03 (reporting of the planned overhaul) through 2026-08 (DOJ opinion curtailing the grievance board's authority)
what_changed: The State Department rolled out a new, data-driven Employee Evaluation Report (EER) system for Foreign Service officers, requiring diplomats to compete for a limited, fixed number of top ratings rather than being evaluated against an independent standard -- with supervisors themselves facing consequences if they award too many top scores. The new form was rolled out January 15, 2026 without negotiation with AFSA and more than three-quarters through the current evaluation cycle. In May 2026, the department directed some managers to go back and 'revise and recalibrate' scores on evaluations they had already submitted, lowering them, and postponed the overall evaluation deadline to May 29, 2026. The American Foreign Service Association (AFSA), the union representing Foreign Service officers, formally objected, with AFSA President John Dinkelman warning the new format 'risks making career-defining decisions less fair, less transparent, and more vulnerable to bias' and creates 'a seemingly intentional...zero-sum game' among diplomats. The overhaul follows the mass layoffs State undertook in 2025 and is reported to be positioned to push out additional diplomats. Update 2026-09-01 (GSR recheck batch 49): AFSA's own January 15, 2026 statement announcing the EER rollout also stated the union would be 'filing an unfair labor practice against this move by the department' -- a formal legal escalation beyond the 'formally objected' framing already in this entry; no outcome of that complaint was found in sourcing reviewed. Separately and more consequentially, on August 24, 2026 AFSA warned that a Department of Justice Office of Legal Counsel opinion had concluded that provisions granting the Foreign Service Grievance Board (FSGB) final decision-making authority are 'unconstitutional and should no longer be enforced.' Under the opinion, the FSGB could continue hearing cases, but its decisions would no longer be final -- the Secretary of State or another presidentially accountable official would have ultimate authority to modify or reject them, converting the board from an independent decision-maker into an advisory body. AFSA argues 'an independent review process cannot provide the same safeguards if the department whose action is being challenged ultimately has the power to overrule the decision.' This directly narrows the one formal recourse (the grievance process) through which diplomats could contest EER scores or the 'revise and recalibrate' directive.

title: State Department Told Americans to 'Depart Now' From 16 Middle East Countries, Then Told Its Own Evacuation Hotline Callers Not to Rely on Government Help
institution: Department of State
status: Ongoing as of this entry's addition -- the war's evacuation-assistance strain and the underlying staffing losses were not reported as resolved in sourcing reviewed
date_of_action: 2026 (Iran war escalation period)
what_changed: As the U.S. war with Iran escalated, the State Department issued 'DEPART NOW' alerts urging U.S. citizens to leave 16 countries across the Middle East -- including Bahrain, Egypt, Iraq, Israel, the West Bank, Gaza, Jordan, Kuwait, Lebanon, Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, Syria, the UAE, and Yemen -- citing serious safety risks. Americans who called the department's evacuation-assistance hotline were told: 'Please do not rely on the U.S. government for assisted departure or evacuation.' NOTUS reported stranded Americans described receiving little practical help as regional airports closed and commercial travel options rapidly disappeared. The Intercept reported that foreign service officers fired in earlier DOGE-driven State Department workforce cuts had previously and specifically warned the department would be unable to adequately assist Americans stranded in a Middle East crisis -- a warning this episode is reported to have borne out. NBC News separately reported thousands of Americans were left stranded in the war zone amid the department's response gap. The State Department did publicize a 24/7 emergency hotline and reported assisting over 130 Americans evacuate Israel specifically, indicating the department was not wholly inactive, but the gap between the 16-country 'depart now' directive and the hotline's own explicit disclaimer against relying on government assistance was widely reported as a substantive breakdown in crisis-response capacity. Additional reporting corroborated and extended the scale of the crisis: as many as 1 million Americans were estimated to be in the Middle East when the war escalated (following an Israeli airstrike that killed Iranian Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei), and the 'DEPART NOW' advisory for 14-16 countries did not go out until the Monday after the weekend strike -- a delay Trump attributed to the conflict having 'happened all very quickly' when asked why no evacuation plan existed in advance. CBS News reported Americans arriving back in New York described a 'zero plan for evacuation,' and travelers transiting hubs like Dubai, Doha, and Amman were told for four days not to rely on the U.S. government for assisted departure. The State Department did not open a crisis intake form offering free charter flights until March 4, 2026, with its first chartered evacuation flight arriving in the region and returning to Washington that same week. Separately, NOTUS and Truthout reported that DOGE had fired the State Department's entire team of oil and gas experts in July 2025 -- six months before the Iran war began -- as part of a roughly 1,300-person State Department RIF. The cuts eliminated staff responsible for modeling scenarios in which the Strait of Hormuz was closed, maintaining relationships with Middle East energy companies, and liaising with the International Energy Agency on coordinated strategic-reserve releases; after the cuts, the Bureau of Energy Resources retained only staff focused on critical minerals and clean energy, none with Middle East oil-and-gas crisis expertise. Geoffrey Pyatt, a former assistant secretary of state for energy resources, said of the losses once the Strait of Hormuz became effectively closed during the war: 'I'm sure Secretary Rubio wishes he had that expertise available today.' Update 2026-08-17: Sen. Elizabeth Warren publicly criticized the State Department for not tasking U.S. Transportation Command (TRANSCOM) with evacuating non-government-affiliated Americans from the region, contrasting it with the 2006 U.S.-Lebanon war evacuation, in which TRANSCOM partnered with State to evacuate roughly 15,000 Americans -- a specific, named operational-capacity criticism distinct from the staffing-cuts causal argument already documented in this entry. Separately, broader-scope reporting on the department's response put the total assistance picture in fuller context: by late February 2026, nearly 24,000 Americans had returned home from the Middle East and the department said it had directly assisted nearly 13,000 of them -- figures that sit alongside, not in conflict with, the 130+ Israel-specific evacuation figure already in this entry, which covers a narrower slice (Israel only) of the same broader effort. As of this recheck, the underlying crisis context remains active rather than resolved: the U.S.-Iran ceasefire/memorandum of understanding collapsed in July 2026 after Iran struck three commercial vessels, hostilities resumed, and a U.S. naval blockade of the Strait of Hormuz was reimposed, with no new evacuation-capacity reporting specific to this later phase identified in sourcing reviewed. Re-verified 2026-08-30: no material change -- the naval blockade remains in effect (Trump stated August 18, 2026 that no talks with Iran were underway), and no new reporting specific to State Department evacuation capacity was identified since the prior update.

title: Rubio Eliminated 132+ State Department Offices and Cut 1,300+ Positions, Including Human Rights and War-Crimes Functions
institution: U.S. Department of State
status: Largely complete (first-stage cuts executed following Supreme Court ruling clearing the way; further changes ongoing)
date_of_action: 2025-03-06 (Western Europe consulate-closure plan first reported) through 2025-09-29 (delayed Trafficking in Persons Report finally released)
what_changed: Added 2026-08-10: an earlier, distinct thread preceded the official April 22 announcement below -- in early March 2025, NYT and other outlets reported the State Department was preparing to close nearly a dozen diplomatic missions, mainly consulates in Western Europe (including Dusseldorf, Leipzig, and Hamburg in Germany; Rennes, Lyon, Strasbourg, and Bordeaux in France; Florence, Italy; and Edinburgh, Scotland), alongside a roughly 20% staff cut at those posts, with closures reportedly targeted for summer 2025. A State Department spokesperson at the time denied any closures had been 'announced.' Sourcing reviewed found no confirmation the Western Europe consulate closures were ever executed -- to the contrary, the U.S. Embassy Germany website shows new Consul Generals assumed duty at both the Leipzig (October 2025) and Hamburg (August 2025) posts, indicating those specific consulates remained open and staffed well past the original summer 2025 closure target. This earlier consulate-closure plan appears to be a distinct, apparently-unexecuted proposal, separate from the domestic office eliminations described below, which did proceed. Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced a sweeping State Department reorganization in April 2025, describing the existing structure as 'bloated bureaucracy that stifles innovation.' The plan consolidated 734 bureaus and offices down to 602, and specifically eliminated 132 domestic offices, including the entire Undersecretary of State for Civilian Security, Democracy, and Human Rights position, the Office of Global Criminal Justice (which supports international war-crimes prosecutions), the Bureau of Conflict and Stabilization Operations, and the Office of Global Women's Issues. Refugee, religious-freedom, and human-trafficking offices were downgraded and folded under a general foreign-assistance coordination office rather than retained as standalone bureaus. The reorganization drew immediate pushback: Reuters reported on July 3, 2025 that more than 130 former U.S. diplomats and officials, including Susan Rice, condemned the planned purge, and the layoffs were temporarily blocked by a federal court order before being cleared to proceed. The Supreme Court ruling that cleared the way was Trump v. AFGE, decided July 8, 2025, which stayed a lower-court injunction blocking Executive Order 14210's agency-wide reorganization/RIF plans nationwide (the Court explicitly declined to rule on the legality of any specific agency's RIF plan, including the State Department's). Following that ruling, the department executed layoffs affecting more than 1,300 employees (1,107 civil servants and 246 foreign service officers with domestic assignments); affected foreign service officers were placed on 120 days of administrative leave before formal termination, civil servants on a 60-day separation period. The department's own contemporaneous count described the total departures tied to the reorganization as 'nearly 3,000,' a figure that includes staff who took the earlier 'Fork in the Road' voluntary-departure offer in addition to the 1,353 RIF-specific terminations -- both figures are real and consistent, describing overlapping but distinct populations (involuntary RIF vs. total reorganization-linked departures), not a factual conflict. The reorganization is explicitly stated to be 'highly complementary' to the concurrent dismantling of USAID, whose remaining functions were folded into State with reduced independence. Re-verified 2026-07-26: no material change -- no new reorganization phase or ruling identified since the July 2025 layoff execution already documented. Update 2026-07-28: Federal News Network reported the ~250 foreign service officers laid off in the July 2025 wave had their terminations finalized as of May 2026, with former employees, federal unions (AFGE), and lawmakers continuing to press for reinstatement, warning the reduction has weakened agency expertise and harmed national security. The affected officers are explicitly ineligible to compete for vacant State Department positions even as the department simultaneously runs a new Foreign Service recruitment campaign -- a documented recruit-while-firing contradiction distinct from the original 2025 reorganization announcement. Added 2026-08-10: the human-trafficking office's downgrading described above proved more severe than 'folded under a general foreign-assistance coordination office' alone conveys -- reporting found the Office to Monitor and Combat Trafficking in Persons lost more than 70% of its staff, leaving fewer than three dozen employees to carry out the office's central anti-trafficking mission. The cuts' effects became concrete in 2025: for the first time in the report's history, the State Department missed the legally required June 30 deadline to deliver its annual Trafficking in Persons (TIP) Report to Congress, finally releasing the delayed 2025 report on September 29, 2025 after months of pressure. During the House Foreign Affairs Committee's September 2025 State Department Reauthorization markup, Rep. Sarah McBride passed a bipartisan amendment directing the department to report to Congress on how the reductions-in-force and reorganization affected the office's work, including the TIP Report's timeliness and accuracy, with a detailed analysis due within 180 days. Update 2026-08-13 (round 4 batch 29, cluster c0172): a December 2025 AFSA (American Foreign Service Association) survey found 98% of U.S. diplomats reported collapsed morale, with roughly a quarter of the foreign service resigning, retiring, or being forced out amid the reorganization and USAID's concurrent dismantlement; diplomats described severe staffing losses, budget cuts, and diminished capacity to conduct U.S. foreign policy, per CNN. Update 2026-08-18 (GSR recheck batch 22): this entry's existing 'finalized as of May 2026' framing skipped an intervening legal battle over those same ~250 officers. The shutdown-ending continuing resolution Congress passed in November 2025 (signed into law November 12, 2025) included Section 120, barring any federal RIF from being implemented between October 1, 2025 and January 30, 2026, and requiring rescission of any RIF action taken during that window. The State Department proceeded anyway, notifying roughly 250 foreign service and civil-service employees on December 1, 2025 of a new December 5 separation date. AFGE and AFSA sued, and U.S. District Judge Susan Illston issued a preliminary injunction on December 18, 2025 blocking the December terminations and ordering the RIF notices withdrawn -- the administration briefly appealed, an appeals court sided with the government on the narrower question of whether agencies had to fully unwind the layoffs, then the administration voluntarily withdrew its own appeal and told the plaintiffs it would rescind the State RIFs. On January 9, 2026, Illston clarified her injunction applied only to the December 2 notice, not the original July RIF notices, and that the State Department could proceed against the same ~250 officers once the statutory freeze expired January 30, 2026 -- which is what ultimately produced the 'finalized as of May 2026' outcome already documented above, not a separate, uncontested administrative process. Separately, Democratic lawmakers introduced the Foreign Service Test-Free Reentry Act in mid-2026, which would let officers separated in the RIF (Jan. 2025-Jan. 2030 window) rejoin without retaking entry exams -- an introduced bill, not enacted, and a State Department official told House lawmakers the department has no plans to reinstate the laid-off officers. Update 2026-08-31 (GSR recheck batch 45, light/moderate): the Foreign Service Test-Free Reentry Act referenced in this entry's prior update is named, with sponsors: Reps. James Walkinshaw (D-VA), Don Beyer (D-VA), Gregory Meeks (D-NY), and Dina Titus (D-NV) introduced it July 16, 2026, to authorize the Secretary of State to waive Foreign Service entry exams for officers involuntarily separated by a RIF between January 20, 2025 and January 31, 2030. It remains introduced only, referred to committee, with no hearing or markup identified as of this recheck; a separate, broader Republican-sponsored bill introduced the same period (the Foreign Service Modernization Act, H.R. 9086, Reps. Mast and Lawler, June 2, 2026) reforms Foreign Service personnel rules generally but does not address RIF reentry and is not a competing response to the same laid-off-officer question.

title: State Department Ends 17-Year Global Embassy Air-Quality Monitoring Program, Erasing Historical Data and the Only Independent Pollution Data Many Countries Had
institution: U.S. Department of State
status: Implemented -- program ended March 4, 2025, historical data subsequently removed from AirNow.gov
what_changed: The State Department ended a 17-year-old program that used air-quality sensors at more than 80 U.S. embassies and consulates worldwide to monitor pollution levels, citing 'funding constraints that have caused the Department to turn off the underlying network.' The program had provided real-time, validated air-quality data to the public via AirNow.gov and, for many countries with limited or unreliable government monitoring of their own, was the only independent source of that data. The Beijing embassy's monitor, launched in 2008, was historically credited with embarrassing Chinese officials into greater transparency and stronger air-quality policy -- reporting on the program's shutdown noted this same catalytic effect had extended to other countries over the years. Following the shutdown, roughly 17 years of accumulated historical air-quality data were removed from AirNow.gov, eliminating a public-health and research benchmark, not just halting future collection. title: March 2025 Stopgap Bill Stripped Veterans' Toxic-Exposure Fund of Its Guaranteed Advance Funding, Though FY2026 Was Ultimately Fully Funded Anyway
institution: Department of Veterans Affairs -- Cost of War Toxic Exposures Fund (TEF)
status: Resolved without an actual funding cut -- the FY2026 advance appropriation was removed as feared, but Congress separately and fully funded TEF for FY2026 through the normal appropriations process at a higher level than the original $22.8 billion figure
date_of_action: 2025-03-08 (House-passed version reported) through 2025-03-15 (H.R. 1968 signed into law)
what_changed: The 2022 PACT Act created the Cost of War Toxic Exposures Fund (TEF) to cover expanded VA healthcare and benefits for veterans sickened by burn pits, Agent Orange, and other toxic exposures, and specifically included an 'advance appropriation' mechanism -- guaranteeing TEF's funding a full year ahead of when it would be spent -- intended to insulate veterans' toxic-exposure care from being used as leverage in future annual appropriations fights. The Full-Year Continuing Appropriations and Extensions Act, 2025 (H.R. 1968), the stopgap spending bill House Republicans advanced and the Senate passed on March 14, 2025 (House 217-213, Senate 54-46; signed into law March 15, 2025), excluded the $22.8 billion FY2026 advance appropriation for TEF that the PACT Act's funding schedule called for -- though it left FY2025 TEF funding itself untouched. The Hill reported House Republicans intended the move to force TEF's future funding under the discretionary spending cap, giving Congress more leverage to cut it in ordinary annual appropriations; VA has never offered gender-affirming or other unrelated services from this fund; opposition Republicans separately criticized TEF's oversight structure, calling it effectively a 'slush fund.' Sen. Bernie Sanders and veterans' groups, including those representing burn-pit-exposed veterans, publicly condemned the removal as a betrayal after Congress had already committed to the funding via the PACT Act. Despite the removed guarantee, Congress ultimately did fund TEF for FY2026 through the ordinary appropriations process rather than the automatic advance mechanism: per VA and congressional budget documents, the FY2026 Continuing Appropriations Act provided $52.68 billion to TEF, reflecting the program's actual growing costs ($20 billion in FY2024, $30.4 billion in FY2025, and the FY2026 figure) -- more than double the originally-scheduled $22.8 billion figure that had been removed.

estimated_impact.summary: The removed guarantee created genuine, contemporaneous alarm among veterans' advocates and Democratic lawmakers that toxic-exposure healthcare funding would become a future bargaining chip -- a real structural change to how the PACT Act's funding was protected -- but the feared FY2026 funding shortfall did not materialize: Congress separately appropriated TEF funding at more than double the removed guarantee's dollar figure once actual program costs were known.

title: US Commanders Moved Troops Into Hotels and Civilian Office Spaces After Iranian Strikes Damaged Gulf Bases, Raising Law-of-War Concerns
institution: Department of Defense
status: Ongoing as of this entry's addition -- relocations reported as continuing amid active hostilities
date_of_action: 2026 (Iran war escalation period, relocations reported late March/early April 2026)
what_changed: After Iranian ballistic missile and drone strikes damaged U.S. bases including Prince Sultan Air Base in Saudi Arabia and Al Udeid Air Base in Qatar -- with at least a dozen service members killed -- U.S. commanders relocated significant numbers of troops away from those vulnerable, insufficiently defended installations into hotels and office spaces in civilian areas. title: DHS Suspended, Then Partially Reversed, TSA PreCheck and Global Entry During a Funding Lapse
institution: Transportation Security Administration / Customs and Border Protection, DHS
status: Partially reversed -- TSA PreCheck restored within about a day; Global Entry remained suspended as the shutdown continued. Noem subsequently warned PreCheck could be re-suspended as the shutdown continued. By mid-March 2026, officials warned continued TSA absenteeism (above 30% at some hubs) could force some airport shutdowns entirely if the funding standoff persisted. TSA wait times peaked at the worst levels in agency history in late March 2026 (480+ officers departed, some lines over 4.5 hours) before a funding deal was reached.
date_of_action: 2026-02-20 (suspension announced) through 2026-02-21/22 (PreCheck reversal)
what_changed: DHS Secretary Kristi Noem announced the suspension of TSA PreCheck and CBP's Global Entry expedited-traveler programs, citing the funding lapse from the ongoing partial government shutdown. Less than a day later, TSA reversed the PreCheck suspension after significant pushback from airlines and lawmakers; Global Entry, however, remained suspended as the shutdown continued. Airlines for America president Chris Sununu criticized the suspension, saying the traveling public was 'once again... used as a political football amid another government shutdown.' Sen. Mark Warner noted that in 2025 more than 18 million travelers used Global Entry, saving over 300,000 CBP officer-hours across 79 ports of entry, and that both programs had remained operational throughout the 43-day government shutdown the prior fall -- undercutting DHS's funding-lapse rationale for this specific suspension. Days later, Secretary Noem warned TSA PreCheck could again be suspended as the DHS shutdown continued, while Global Entry remained suspended throughout. The underlying staffing strain continued to escalate: by mid-March 2026, Reuters reported TSA officers were working without pay as the funding standoff continued, with absentee rates spiking above 30% at some major hubs. Officials warned some airports could be forced to shut down entirely if the standoff persisted, with smaller airports with limited checkpoints described as especially at risk. The shutdown dragged into a second month, and ABC News reported tens of thousands of TSA workers were going unpaid, with many receiving $0 paychecks while still required to report for duty; employees described taking second jobs, leaving the agency, and struggling to meet basic expenses. The prolonged standoff had an additional, explicit political dimension: the New York Times reported Trump told Republicans to halt negotiations to reopen DHS and instead use the shutdown as leverage to pass the Safeguard American Voter Eligibility (SAVE) Act, a voter-ID bill -- even as TSA workers went unpaid and airport disruptions worsened. Trump and Senate Majority Leader John Thune clashed publicly over the ultimatum. In the days before a deal was reached, the crisis peaked: the NYT reported TSA union leaders blasted Trump's deployment of ICE and other DHS agents to 14 airports to cover screening shortages, saying the officers were not trained for screening work and did little to reduce lines. CBS News reported wait times stretched up to six hours at major airports even with the ICE deployment, with nearly 12% of TSA officers calling out unpaid on a given day. Bloomberg reported TSA said wait times reached the worst levels in the agency's history after more than 480 officers left during the shutdown, with some lines exceeding 4.5 hours and major airports including Atlanta, Houston, and New York seeing checkpoint closures and lane consolidations. By March 31, 2026, CBS News reported TSA was consolidating security lanes and warned it might be forced to close smaller airports entirely if the funding standoff continued without a deal, with hundreds of agents having quit and wait times approaching 4-5 hours even at major hubs. Trump then ultimately endorsed a deal in late March 2026 to fund DHS (with the exception of key ICE provisions), allowing the SAVE Act to wait rather than continuing to hold TSA funding hostage to it. Trump's FY2027 budget, released April 3, 2026 and documented in more detail elsewhere in this tracker (trump-fy2027-budget-defense-tradeoff-2026.json), proposed cutting TSA funding and pushing smaller airports to replace federal screening officers with private security screeners -- a proposal Reuters noted came just weeks after the shutdown-driven staffing crisis and unpaid-worker escalation this entry documents.

title: Hundreds of U.S. Scientists Sought "Scientific Asylum" in Europe as France and the EU Launched Dedicated Recruitment Programs
institution: N/A -- documents a researcher-emigration trend attributed by affected scientists and European officials to the federal research-funding and policy environment, not one specific federal action
status: Ongoing and grown -- both the Aix-Marseille and EU-wide recruitment programs continued accepting applicants and expanded funding into 2026, with no reporting of the underlying U.S. funding cuts being reversed
date_of_action: 2025-03 (Aix-Marseille program launched) through 2025-07 (first wave of researchers relocated; EU 2025-27 funding pledge announced May 2025)
what_changed: In March 2025, Aix-Marseille University in France launched 'Safe Place for Science,' a dedicated program offering three-year positions and $16.3 million in combined grant funding to American researchers whose work the university said was 'threatened or hindered' by the Trump administration's research cuts. By July 2025, nearly 300 applicants -- from institutions including Stanford, Yale, NASA, NIH, George Washington University, and more than a dozen others -- had applied; the university selected an initial cohort of roughly 20 researchers, with the first several arriving in France by late June 2025 and the full initial group expected by September. Separately, on May 5, 2025, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen launched a continent-wide 'Choose Europe for Science' campaign at a Sorbonne conference in Paris, pledging EUR 500 million in new EU funding for 2025-2027 specifically to attract researchers, including a new seven-year European Research Council 'supergrant' for top scientists and a doubling of ERC relocation grants (from EUR 1 million to EUR 2 million) to cover the cost of moving to Europe and establishing a new lab. French President Emmanuel Macron announced France would separately commit EUR 100 million of its existing EUR 54 billion 'France 2030' investment plan to the same goal. The EU's 'Choose Europe for Science'/'Choose France for Science' online portal drew 30,000 visitors from 157 countries in its first month, 34% of them from the United States, with several hundred formal applications filed. Outlets covering the trend (Rolling Stone, NBC News, Mother Jones, the New York Times) tied the outflow to the cumulative effect of federal actions tracked elsewhere in this database -- NIH's 380+ canceled research grants and broader funding freeze (see nih-impoundment-gao-finding-trump2), NSF and USAID cuts, and attacks on climate-science research -- rather than any single action; European officials and departing researchers cited funding instability, canceled grants, and fears of political interference in research as their stated reasons for leaving. Both programs continued growing into 2026: Aix-Marseille's 'Safe Place for Science' selected an initial cohort of 39 researchers (in fields including health, astrophysics, the humanities, and climate science), with a second group of roughly 20 more being finalized as of mid-2026 for relocation starting that September -- bringing the total selected to roughly 60, still drawn from the ~300 July 2025 applicant pool -- backed by a EUR 15 million, three-year funding commitment. Separately, the European Commission's January 30, 2026 update reported the EU's 'Choose Europe for Science' initiative had grown to over 100 national and regional participating programs, with total committed funding expanding from the original EUR 500 million pledge to nearly EUR 900 million, including a new EUR 240 million European Research Area Chairs call under Horizon Europe for 2026-27 and a EUR 51 million Marie Sklodowska-Curie Actions 'Choose Europe for Science' call for 2027.

title: African Development Foundation Reduced to Near-Nothing Before Courts Fully Reverse Takeover
institution: U.S. African Development Foundation and Inter-American Foundation
status: Reversed (final federal court orders in 2025-2026 fully vacated the takeovers at both agencies)
date_of_action: 2025-02-19 (executive order) through 2026-03 (final court order restoring USADF)
what_changed: On February 19, 2025, President Trump issued an executive order directing USADF, the Inter-American Foundation (IAF), the U.S. Institute of Peace, and the Presidio Trust to be reduced to 'the minimum presence and function required by law.' Peter Marocco, a State Department official who also oversaw the dismantling of USAID, moved to take control of both USADF and IAF within days. At IAF, Marocco held a one-person 'board meeting' outside the agency's locked headquarters on February 28, 2025, after being unable to gain entry, and declared himself acting CEO and president in a notice entered into the Federal Register. At USADF, staff denied DOGE personnel direct access to internal systems, citing privacy and security requirements, while Marocco announced by email that he would chair the agency's board. On March 11, 2025, District Judge Richard Leon initially found that a large reduction in USADF's staff and funding could itself be legal, declining at that stage to block leadership changes, while ordering DOGE staff to explain how they would maintain the agency's minimum required functions. By early April 2025, the government acknowledged in court that IAF had been reduced to a single employee and a single active grant. On April 4, 2025, Judge Loren AliKhan ordered the indefinite reinstatement of ousted IAF president Sara Aviel and blocked Marocco from serving on IAF's board, unwinding his actions including frozen grants. On July 1, 2025, Judge Leon ruled that Trump had violated the Federal Vacancies Reform Act by installing Marocco at USADF without Senate confirmation, voiding the staff terminations and grant cancellations Marocco had directed. A final order in Rural Development Innovations Ltd. v. Marocco fully blocked the USADF dismantlement, and by March 2026, USADF staff were allowed back into their offices for the first time in months.

Court rulings distinguished between two separate legal questions along the way: Judge Leon's initial March 2025 ruling found that a large reduction in USADF's staff and funding could itself be legal, meaning the scale of cuts was not automatically unlawful, while his later July 2025 ruling found the specific mechanism used, installing Marocco without Senate confirmation, violated the Federal Vacancies Reform Act, voiding the actions taken under his leadership. This is a genuine reversal story: both USADF and IAF ultimately had their takeovers fully undone by final court orders, with USADF staff physically returning to their offices in March 2026, though Devex reporting notes the agency's reentry into the foreign-aid sector 'seems to be just beginning' after a year of program cancellations and funding freezes, and separately references newer, unrelated corruption charges connected to the agency as of that report.
